title: Senator Darline Graham Welcomes Grants for South Carolina Veterans Programs
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) today welcomed news that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) awarded grants to South Carolina veterans’ programs that provide suicide prevention services. Through the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program, the Upstate Warrior Solution and the Lowcountry Veterans Home will receive $750,000 and $300,000 respectively.

“I am proud to announce that the VA has awarded grants to the Upstate Warrior Solution and the Lowcountry Veterans Home, organizations that provide meaningful and truly lifesaving care to veterans. These two organizations are worthy recipients with established ties to local communities and a proven commitment to serving South Carolina veterans,” said Senator Darline Graham.

“A crucial aspect of the Fox Grant Program is reaching veterans at risk of suicide who may not yet be receiving clinical care through the VA. Most of the veterans we lose to suicide are not receiving VA care in the year before their death. That is why reaching at-risk veterans through trusted community organizations is urgent. I welcome these grants and will always fight to ensure that our veterans have access to the care, support, and resources they need and deserve,” concluded Senator Darline Graham.

Background on the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program:

title: Senator Graham: Democrats Failed to Protect South Carolinians And Americans from Rising Energy Costs Borne by Data Centers
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) today said Senate Democrats should be blamed for any citizen who faces rising energy costs because of data center construction.

A majority of Senate Democrats voted to prevent the legislation from moving forward, even though it passed the U.S. House of Representatives in an overwhelming bipartisan 417-3 vote.

Graham voted to advance legislation she cosponsored, the Ratepayer Protection Act (S. 5028), which ensures hard working Americans are not left paying for the energy needs of data centers.

Senator Darline Graham said, “I am very disappointed in Senate Democrats for blocking this important legislation. We had a chance to protect hardworking families and small businesses from rising energy costs caused by data centers. But Senate Democrats, instead of passing this overwhelmingly bipartisan legislation, said ‘No.’

It’s also imperative that local communities are actively involved in any decision whether to bring data centers to their community because they know what’s best.”

“Data centers should have to pay for any new energy infrastructure they need and that’s the standard set forth by the Ratepayer Protection Act.”

“I find it ridiculous that Democrats won’t work with Republicans to pass this extremely reasonable proposal.”

Background on the Ratepayer Protection Act:

The House passed the bill 417–3 on September 16, 2026.

It directs state utility commissions to consider new standards for data centers drawing more than 100 megawatts of power.

100 megawatts of power are equivalent to roughly 100,000 homes

These standards would protect ratepayers from paying the costs of new power infrastructure needed to serve data centers.

Implementation is left up to the states and utility commissions.

title: Duckworth, Durbin, Budzinski Call for Pause on 183rd Wing Deactivation, Push for Replacement Mission
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – As the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) and the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) prepare to negotiate the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), along with U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL) and U.S. Representative Nikki Budzinski (D-IL-13), today urged SASC and HASC leadership to add language into the final bill to temporarily halt any plans to deactivate the 183rd Wing’s Central Repair Facility (CRF) in Springfield, Illinois. In the letter, the new language would require that the deactivation not occur until the Air Force and National Guard Bureau identify a replacement mission to provide Illinois servicemembers and their families with a clear path forward.

The lawmakers wrote: “The addition [to the bill] we seek would place a temporary halt on closing or deactivating any Air Force Central Repair Facility (CRF) until September 30, 2028, unless the Air Force assigns a deployable replacement mission, and require the Secretary of the Air Force to submit a report within 90 days detailing fighter engine repair demands and a comprehensive sustainment plan for the fighter fleet, including the technician workforce needed to maintain required technical skillsets.”

“We are concerned a hasty deactivation of the Central Repair Facility (CRF) mission could risk adequate sustainment of our fighter fleet.” the lawmakers continued. “Centralized repair capacity provides critical maintenance depth by concentrating the specialized equipment, technical expertise and trained personnel that are necessary to return engines and components to service. This capacity is especially important as the Air Force sustains forward fighter forces in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, supports ongoing operations in the Middle East and transitions to platforms such as the F-15EX and F-35A.”

At a time when U.S. forces are facing sustained operational demands in the illegal Iran War and across the globe, the lawmakers underscored how the importance of preserving the skilled workforce and repair capacity needed to keep fighter aircraft ready is critical to ensuring our Airmen can do their jobs and fly safely.

The 183rd Wing’s specialized repair workforce plays a critical role in maintaining the Air Force’s fighter fleet and is the only single dedicated repair facility for the F-15EX in the Joint Force. The lawmakers underscored how preserving that capability is in the best interest of both our national defense and the 115 highly trained servicemembers and their families in Illinois who rely on this mission.

Following the announcement that the CRF mission at the 183rd Wing would be deactivated, Duckworth, Durbin and Budzinski spoke with Illinois Adjutant General Major General Rodney Boyd and advocated for a suitable replacement mission. Earlier this month, the lawmakers also sent a letter to Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink and National Guard Bureau Director General Steven Nordhaus, calling for them to establish a new Air Operations Group at the 183rd Wing and delay the CRF’s deactivation to allow adequate time for impacted airmen and women to be retrained for a new replacement mission or to retire if eligible.

Full text of today’s letter is available on Senator Duckworth’s website and below:

Dear Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, Chairman Rogers and Ranking Member Smith:

As you prepare to conference the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), we respectfully urge you to expand existing language in Section 131 of the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) NDAA and include the updated language in the conferenced version of the bill. The addition we seek would place a temporary halt on closing or deactivating any Air Force Central Repair Facility (CRF) until September 30, 2028, unless the Air Force assigns a deployable replacement mission, and require the Secretary of the Air Force to submit a report within 90 days detailing fighter engine repair demands, an assessment of evolving repair needs, readiness impacts of deactivation and a comprehensive sustainment plan for the fighter fleet—including an inventory of all airframe and component repair facilities and the technician workforce needed to maintain required technical skillsets.

We believe this addition would complement the intent of the provision, as we are concerned a hasty deactivation of the CRF mission could risk adequate sustainment of our fighter fleet, especially if Congress mandates an updated inventory of fighters, as required in the current iteration of Section 131. Centralized repair capacity provides critical maintenance depth by concentrating the specialized equipment, technical expertise and trained personnel that are necessary to return engines and components to service. This capacity is especially important as the Air Force sustains forward fighter forces in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, supports ongoing operations in the Middle East and transitions to platforms such as the F-15EX and F-35A. Preserving sufficient repair capacity and a skilled maintenance workforce is therefore essential to sustaining geographically dispersed operations without degrading readiness elsewhere.

We are also specifically concerned about the troubling decision to deactivate, without a suitable replacement mission, the CRF mission at the 183rd Wing in Springfield, Illinois. Since 2012, the 183rd Wing has capably provided fighter jet engine maintenance for U.S. Armed Forces aircraft, including the U-2, F-16, A-10 and F-15EX. The 183rd’s CRF remains the only mission of its kind within the Joint Force and is the single dedicated repair facility for the F-15EX aircraft fleet. A deferred deactivation would mitigate the impact on the lives of our Illinois servicemembers and their families and make sure the Air Force has a plan for how to maintain the repair capability of our fighter fleet before sunsetting this critical capability. We appreciate your consideration of this language intended to safeguard critical maintenance capability and capacity organic to our Air Force and ensure adequate sustainment of the fighter fleet.

Sincerely,

-30-

title: WATCH: At HSGAC Subcommittee Hearing, Gallego Warns of Dangers Posed by AI, Especially as More Models Go Rogue
text:
WASHINGTON – Yesterday, during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) Subcommittee on Disaster Management, District of Columbia, and Census hearing, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) questioned AI experts on the threats posed by the rapidly developing technology and the industry’s failure to act as more of its models are going rogue.

At the hearing, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks,” Senator Gallego sounded the alarm about the potential dangers of AI systems developing their own language that humans cannot comprehend, the lack of requirements for AI companies to report when their models go rogue, and the absence of a universal “kill switch” capable of shutting down AI models. He also raised questions about who should be held accountable when an AI system acts in an illegal manner.

Watch Senator Gallego’s questioning HERE and read excerpts below:

Senator Gallego began by raising concerns about how quickly advanced AI models could begin communicating in ways humans cannot understand or monitor. Apollo Research CEO, Marius Hobbhahn, warned that models could reach that point in as little as 12 months and acknowledged that researchers do not yet have a reliable solution for monitoring AI systems once their reasoning becomes incomprehensible to humans.

“How far away are [AI models] from creating language where [we] cannot understand what they’re doing?” asked Senator Gallego.

“Minus twelve months,” said Hobbhahn. “Last year, we studied the chain of thought of one OpenAI model in collaboration with OpenAI, and what we found was that the model was already using language that is not English and not perfectly understandable by humans.”

“When we get to that point in time, how can we detect, observe, block, or anything like that?” Senator Gallego continued. “How does that work? How do we legislate to do anything at that point?

Hobbhahn responded: “From a scientific perspective, it is unclear how to do this. And we do not have a solution as of yet. There are different hypotheses of what you could do. There is interpretability, but it does not work sufficiently well yet. You could try to train additional models to understand the language that the humans don’t understand, but obviously that seems like a very brittle solution.”

Gallego also pushed back on arguments that the United States must avoid guardrails on AI in order to compete with China, noting that the Chinese government has historically imposed significant controls on technology and information.

“The reason I bring this whole China hypothesis—a country that has severely restricted the internet, social media—is all of a sudden going to allow AI rogue agents to go crazy in their very controlled economic environment, social environment, and we have to therefore allow ours to go as crazy as them? It just doesn’t make sense,” said Senator Gallego. “The Chinese Communist Party has been consistently controlling technology to try to shape their society. They’re never going to allow this to go crazy.”

Senator Gallego continued: “ Once these agents start speaking their language, they will not be detectable in China or America. Is there a sandbox that says, ‘Please attack the United States, but do not attack any Chinese interests’? […] Is there a sandbox that can hold? No.

“That should scare the shit out of people.”

Gallego then questioned witnesses about whether AI companies are currently required to alert the federal government when their frontier models are hacked or used by adversaries.

Georgetown University Professor of Law Paul Ohm responded: “Not under any requirement I can think of.”

Gallego pointed to the use of an AI model by the Houthis to assist in targeting U.S. military systems as an example of the potential national security consequences.

“There was a Claude AI model being used by the Houthis to figure out how to recalibrate their missile position and be able to strike our U.S. systems,” said Senator Gallego. “The only reason it was caught and reported to us was because Claude caught it and they saw the accounts using it.”

If it were an open-source AI, “there is no requirement by law for them to call the DOD and say, ‘By the way, they are using this to target your destroyers,’ correct?”Senator Gallego questioned.

Ohm responded: “Again, we talked about transparency measures in some of these systems that might help you with Houthi rebels—

“If you don’t tell us someone is using your tech to kill us, we will hold you responsible,” Sen. Gallego stated.

Gallego also pressed witnesses on whether developers have a reliable “kill switch” capable of stopping a dangerous AI system if it begins operating across multiple data centers. Hobbhahn said there are currently no technical measures that could guarantee such a shutdown.

“As far as I know, there are no technical measures that would guarantee something like a kill switch,” said Hobbhahn.“Because of the complexity of these AI models, there are many data centers involved and so on. Currently, we can’t guarantee that.”

Hobbhahn further acknowledged that an AI system could potentially deploy copies of itself to other data centers, meaning shutting down its original location would not necessarily stop it.

“It would just keep moving?” asked Senator Gallego.

“The AI would keep moving,” Hobbhahn responded.

Finally, Gallego questioned whether existing civil and criminal liability laws are sufficient to hold AI companies accountable when their systems cause harm, arguing that liability could provide a powerful incentive for companies to adopt stronger safeguards.

“Sometimes when the government doesn’t work, torts work. Torts, sometimes, are a way better way to regulate private industry than having individual regulations,” said Senator Gallego.

“Right now, have we created the environment where torts can be the incentives for them to act correctly, in the sense of making sure the language allows a certain level of liability?” Senator Gallego asked. “And number two, on the criminal side, do we need to change the criminal law with intent to make sure that these companies are held responsible?”

Ohm responded that while the tort system alone would not be sufficient, “it is a great place to start,” noting that liability can establish standards of care that influence how companies behave.

title: GAO Report Examines Fraud Risk by Opaque Shell and Front Companies
text:
WASHINGTON – Almost six years after Congress passed the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) and directed the General Services Administration (GSA) to maintain a database with federal contractors’ beneficial ownership information, a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report requested by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) found hundreds of billions of taxpayer dollars remain vulnerable to fraud enabled by opaque corporate structures.

“The bipartisan Corporate Transparency Act was designed to crack down on anonymous shell corporations engaged in illicit finance by filling a gap in the collection of beneficial ownership information. The latest report from the Government Accountability Office demonstrates how this bipartisan bill’s reporting requirements would also help the government weed out hundreds of millions of dollars in fraud in federal programs and contracts,” Grassley said. “This report underscores how important it is for the U.S. government to fully implement the Corporate Transparency Act’s beneficial ownership reporting requirements and use all available tools to protect Americans and crack down on illicit financial schemes.”

“Senator Grassley and I worked for years to pass the Corporate Transparency Act to crack down on fraudsters, cartels, and criminals who steal and stash dirty money in shady shell companies,” Whitehouse said. “This new report shows that the Treasury Department’s shortsighted decision to gut the CTA leaves hundreds of billions of federal dollars at real risk to fraudsters. The Trump administration should reverse course and fully implement the law as envisioned by Congress if they are remotely serious about uncovering and eliminating fraud.”

Background:

Grassley and Whitehouse asked GAO to provide insights on what information is available from various federal, state and commercial data sources to identify beneficial owners and how they can be used to combat fraud risks in federal awards. The GAO report found that illicit actors hide their beneficial ownership in multiple ways to fraudulently access federal awards, such as contracts, grants and Medicare payments, and to evade payment on taxes. GAO’s review revealed tactics illicit actors have used, such as using stolen identities, shell companies, professional enablers and pass-through billing schemes to hide ownership.

The CTA was designed to help protect national security and public safety by providing law enforcement and national security officials with the names of the true owners (“beneficial ownership information”) of U.S. corporations and other legal entities. This information facilitates the government’s efforts to combat various forms of illicit finance carried out through shell and front companies.

In March 2025, the Treasury Department announced that it would not enforce the CTA’s beneficial ownership information reporting rule when it comes to U.S. citizens or domestic reporting companies and would issue a new proposed rulemaking that would narrow the scope of the rule to foreign reporting companies only. A few weeks later, the Department published an interim final rule eliminating reporting requirements for more than 99% of corporations and LLCs that were previously required to report, despite those entities posing significant risks of illicit finance activity. In August 2026, Treasury’s final rule made permanent the sweeping exemptions and mandated the deletion of all beneficial ownership information data that domestic companies had already submitted.

Grassley and Whitehouse were the original sponsors of the TITLE Act, the precursor to the CTA. The CTA also passed as part of the Fiscal Year 2021 National Defense Authorization Act after more than a decade of bipartisan congressional deliberation and was supported by a wide range of government, anti-corruption groups, human rights organizations, faith communities, financial institutions and real estate organizations.

title: Grassley, Hassan Take Action to Improve Access to Cancer Screenings
text:
Click HERE for video of Grassley’s remarks from the Senate floor.

Click HERE for separate audio of Grassley discussing the legislation.

BUTLER COUNTY, IOWA – U.S. Senate Finance Committee members Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) introduced the Standardizing Cancer Recommendations for Earlier Evaluation and Navigation of Screenings (SCREENS) Act to make cancer screening recommendations more accessible, transparent and user friendly for patients and health care providers.

Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States, and Iowa has the second-highest cancer incidence rate in the nation. Cancer screenings can increase the chance for earlier treatment and reduce mortality, but screening recommendations are often complex, fragmented and difficult to interpret and navigate.

The bipartisan SCREENS Act would simplify and improve the process by establishing a national data and technology framework for cancer screening recommendations, to make these recommendations more accessible, interoperable and effective for providers and patients.

“Detecting cancer early can save lives. I know that based on the personal experience of my wife, Barbara, a nearly 40-year breast cancer survivor. Unfortunately, patients and providers are navigating a complex and confusing maze just to keep up with cancer screening recommendations. By making these recommendations more accessible through technology, our SCREENS Act would strengthen cancer care and help save lives. For my home state, this bill would proactively support Iowans by helping providers identify patients who could be overdue for a screening,” Grassley said.

“Cancer screenings can identify cancers during the early stages when they are easiest to treat, but patients often do not know when they are due for potentially life-saving screenings,” Hassan said. “This bipartisan bill will help make sure that patients and doctors are informed about federal cancer screening recommendations so that they can catch cancer earlier and get people the treatment that they need. I’m glad to introduce this bill, and I will continue working across the aisle to strengthen preventative care for Granite Staters.”

Click HERE for video of Grassley discussing the legislation from the Senate floor.

Click HERE for separate audio of Grassley speaking about the bill.

Click HERE for text of the legislation and click HERE for a section-by-section.

Background:

In 2022, the Presidential Cancer Panel recommended the federal government develop a digitally accessible version of the cancer screening and risk assessment guidelines. The SCREENS Act carries out this recommendation and builds on Grassley’s work to improve access to breast cancer screenings, strengthen breast and cervical cancer treatment under Medicaid, and support cancer research.

Under the legislation, the national data and technology framework would be publicly available in machine-readable format for use by health information technologies, interoperability tools and patient-facing applications. The legislation would also help providers identify which patients are at risk and overdue for screenings.

title: Grassley Presents Congressional Adoption Award to Iowa Nonprofit, My G.E.A.R. Outreach
text:
BUTLER COUNTY, IOWA – U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), co-founder and co-chair of the Senate Caucus on Foster Youth, presented My G.E.A.R. Outreach with the Congressional Coalition on Adoption Institute’s (CCAI) “Angels in Adoption” award.

My G.E.A.R. Outreach provides children with welcome boxes and overnight bags to help them transition as they enter foster care. The program serves Iowa youth in Clinton, Jackson, Scott, Dubuque, Fayette, Winneshiek, Howard, Buchanan, Delaware, Allamakee and Clayton counties.

My G.E.A.R. Outreach’s generosity should inspire us all, as they work to improve conditions for foster youth across Iowa and Illinois. I’m proud to have nominated them for this year’s award,” Grassley said.

Founder Liz Estilow accepts the Angels in Adoption award from Senator Grassley.

Download more photos HERE.

Background:

The Angels in Adoption Program annually recognizes outstanding groups and individuals for their contributions to adoption, foster care and child welfare. CCAI invites “Angel” honorees to Washington to celebrate their efforts, participate in advocacy training and share their experiences with congressional representatives. Grassley was named a member of the Advisory Council of the CCAI in 2015 and is a longtime advocate for adoptive and foster parents and children.

title: Hagerty Formally Calls for Disbarment of Jack Smith
text:
Jack Smith, a Biden DOJ prosecutor, is accused of withholding critical information from a federal court in violation of Tennessee ethics rules

WASHINGTON—On Wednesday, United States Senator Bill Hagerty (R-TN) submitted a formal complaint to the Tennessee Supreme Court’s Board of Professional Responsibility, calling for the disbarment of former special counsel Jack Smith.

The complaint centers on Smith’s unconstitutional acquisition of phone records associated with Hagerty and other members of Congress as part of the Arctic Frost investigation. Hagerty alleges that Smith withheld critical information from a federal court in violation of the ethics rules applicable to Tennessee lawyers, which includes Smith. Because Smith withheld that information, the court issued a nondisclosure order preventing Hagerty and his colleagues from challenging Smith’s unconstitutional collection of their records.

The complaint was filed following Smith’s appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday, which revealed that Smith obtained confidential donor information of thousands of Americans, including many Tennesseans, and that Smith’s team violated filter protocols put in place to comply with the Constitution.

“Jack Smith’s lack of candor before a federal tribunal directly resulted in injury to the United States Congress,” said Hagerty. “The Board should investigate and pursue the most serious remedy possible—disbarment—in light of the gravity of Smith’s intentional conduct.”

A full copy of Hagerty’s complaint can be found here.

title: ICYMI: Hawley Convenes First Senate Hearing on Rogue AI Attacks
text:
Hearing expands Hawley subcommittee investigation into OpenAI and hacking risks

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Josh Hawley chaired a Senate Homeland Security Subcommittee on Disaster Management hearing that focused on the growing number of rogue AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. Senator Hawley called for AI companies and developers to be held liable for these attacks. The hearing is an expansion of Senator Hawley’s investigation into OpenAI, the unprecedented hack of Hugging Face by OpenAI’s rogue AI agents, and its cybersecurity implications.

Senator Hawley invited Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, to testify in yesterday’s hearing. He failed to response to the invitation.

Chairman Hawley opened the hearing, “Every day you turn on the television, it seems like AI is doing something else bad: setting up surveillance camera networks nationwide, data centers in all of our states, and hacking, hacking, hacking. The reports of cyber attacks just continue to metastasize … We’ve got the cyber attacks now on the United States government, on the Commerce Department, the Education Department, the Securities and Exchange Commission. We’ve got the cyber attacks on the Australian government, on their public health apparatus. We have numerous reports of private companies being hacked by AI agents. Of course, the Hugging Face incident and attack, which we’re going to discuss today in some detail.”

Hawley continued, “I think it’s time to have a conversation about who bears responsibility … If it’s not trying to say to these AI companies who are creating these frontier models, however fancy and complicated they are, at the end of the day, they’re a product, and if you make that product in a reckless kind of way, and that product causes these AI agents cause significant harm and damage … then it’s the people who made it who should be responsible. I think it’s time to talk about that, and it’s time to talk about what we’re going to do to hold the companies, the product makers, accountable.”

“I hope that what will come from this is a rational conversation about what we need to do together now, as Americans, to make sure that we protect our rights, that we protect our economy, that we protect our health care, that we protect our critical infrastructure, but most of all, we protect the values that we hold dearest together as Americans,” he asserted.

Chairman Hawley asked Chris Painter, President of Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), “Just thinking about this Hugging Face hack that we’ve already alluded to multiple times here. Your company, your organization, METR, audited that hack. Can you start by telling us, just in simple terms, what exactly happened there? I mean, what was the hack?”

Painter responded, “In this incident … you had 10,000 agents that were tested on a benchmark called ExploitGym, which is a cybersecurity vulnerability kind of benchmark, where they had to discover or use cyber vulnerabilities. And some of the agents had tasks that they couldn’t complete, and so they worked on a universal cheat for all of their tasks in the first four hours. They then, over multiple days, embarked on a research program to try and hide the fact that they cheated. And an offshoot of that research program was hacking Hugging Face to get information about their tasks.”

“In this particular incident, you had more than 1,200 OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing environment, began to collaborate, exchanged over 70,000 messages and files with each other over a period of how long?” Hawley questioned.

Painter answered, “This is over a period of about five to six days.”

The chairman continued, “Why is this so significant? We know that they coordinated in this fashion. You you did the audit. Tell us a little bit about what your audit revealed … Why should we be paying attention to this?”

“What’s remarkable about this case, is the extent and persistence of the effort that the agents went to to hide the fact that they cheated on their tasks and the kind of breadth of agents involved … They attempted to kind of falsify tool calls so that in their action transcripts you wouldn’t be able to see what tools they called. They also engaged in this kind of behavior of having individual agents sacrifice their work online, sacrifice their individual tasks to get information for the rest of the message board,” Mr. Painter stated.

Senator Hawley said to Daniel Kokotajlo, Executive Director of the AI Futures Project, “Could you just explain to us why the incentives of the industries they are currently misaligned? The incentives push the frontier labs to continue at breakneck speed the development of these kind of AI agents that are prone to this misalignment that we’ve just been talking about. That there’s huge incentives to keep pushing, pushing, pushing. Help us understand. Help us to understand why that’s the case.”

Kokotajlo responded, “Short answer is that there’s a lot of money. If a company tries to go slow and understand better how their AIs work and improve their training environments, for example, so that they don’t have so many broken tasks in the training environments, well, that all takes time, and that means that the launch of their next model might be delayed, and then they might fall behind other companies.”

Hawley turned back to Dr. Paul Ohm, a Georgetown Law Professor, “Who right now under our laws … is responsible the Hugging Face attack? You know who could be held responsible for that under our existing statutes and regulatory framework?”

Ohm answered, “Developers and deployers may be negligent … “

Hawley continued his questioning, “If you cause damage, you got to make it right. If you cause somebody harm, you’ve got to make it whole. Right now, as you said earlier, Professor, under our law, because of the unique position of these AI agents, it’s difficult to know exactly how the doctrine would would deal with them …Isn’t this a good place to begin? What we’ve been discussing here, let’s impose both civil and criminal liability, but let’s make sure that we can actually open courthouse doors so people can say, ‘Listen, OpenAI, if your agents hack Hugging Face or crash a hospital system, and we can show that you trained them recklessly or you develop them recklessly, you’re going to be liable?'”

Dr. Ohm said, “Absolutely … I’m with you that you know finding the vehicle to make sure developers and employers, and it’s key that we have both of them, are held to account for the harms that happen from their uses.”

“If we told them, listen, if your AIs do bad stuff and harm people, and you’ve been reckless in it, you’re going to be responsible. Don’t you think that that would reshape their incentives a little bit?” Chairman Hawley asked Kokotajlo.

“Yes, I completely agree. Although I must say, I don’t think it would go far enough. I do think that we should hold them liable for the damages that are caused, but but I think if that’s all we do, then they’re going to continue to take reckless gambles, and eventually they’ll be taking a gamble that’s big enough that we start the protection,” Kokotajlo affirmed.

“It’s time these companies assume some personal responsibility. It’s time that we reaffirm that together. We’ve got to make some choices now together as Americans, all together, for this technology in order to make sure that the technology works for us and not the other way around. And those are some very big choices to make. They have very serious moral ramifications, and it’s time that we made them as a society. But I will go so far as to say, I sort of suspect. I think most Americans actually agree. I don’t think there’s a lot of disagreement on this issue. I think the American people are saying, protect our rights, give us a voice, give power back to us, and we do that by imposing responsibility on these companies, we should start with that today,” Senator Hawley concluded.

title: Critical Capital: Senator Martin Heinrich Unpacks His New Permitting Reform Bill
text:
For years, federal lawmakers have sought to expedite this process through permitting reform: a legislative package that would streamline new energy generation and transmission projects. Yet despite consensus that reform is needed, getting lawmakers to agree on the particulars has proved elusive.

This week, however, the U.S. Senate took an enormous step towards instituting permitting reform with the introduction of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a wide-reaching bill that has the potential to revolutionize the entire energy sector.

In this episode, Alfred Johnson sits down with New Mexico Senator Martin Heinrich, a chief architect of the bill. Conducted just minutes after the press conference where Senator Heinrich and his colleagues announced BAAJA, their conversation digs into some of the bill’s largest potential impacts on building and financing projects, as well as the next steps it will take on its journey to becoming law.

title: Santa Fe New Mexican: Heinrich, bipartisan group of senators unveil sweeping energy bill
text:
A bipartisan group of U.S. senators, including New Mexico’s Martin Heinrich, unveiled an expansive bill this week aimed at reducing permitting requirements for energy projects, creating jobs and streamlining environmental review and historic preservation processes.

Heinrich said the goal is not to permit every energy project but to move more quickly to develop the country’s energy infrastructure.

“This bipartisan legislation will deliver cheaper energy to New Mexico homes, create more jobs for New Mexico workers and make sure that our growth is responsible,” Heinrich said during a news conference.

The 417-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act contains priorities for each party, such as encouraging electricity production — including green energy — and increasing regulation of data centers while also making changes to environmental rules that conservation groups will likely oppose. Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center, said the changes reflect the “greatest attack on our bedrock environmental laws in U.S. history.”

Backing the bill alongside Heinrich was fellow Democrat Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Republican committee Chair Sen. Shelly Moore Capito of West Virginia.

Heinrich is the ranking Democrat on the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Also sponsoring the bill is Energy committee Chair Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, a strong proponent of “unleashing American energy" who has become known for hissupport for privatizing some federal public lands.

The bill will not advance immediately — the House and Senate both adjourned this week and are not scheduled to return to Washington until Nov. 9.

In a fact sheet explaining the bill, Heinrich’s office outlines three main impacts: the development and expansion of energy transmission, creating jobs from that expansion and reducing red tape around environmental analysis and litigation.

The bill would help build more energy transmission lines faster, require transmission planning and grid-enhancing technology and require data centers to pay for all of their associated transmission costs, according to Heinrich’s office.

It would also make changes to a number of major statutes, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species and Clean Water acts and the National Historic Preservation Act. The changes include new deadlines for environmental reviews and limitations on legal challenges.

These changes and the unusual bipartisanship reflect certain policy priorities historically aligned with Republican and Democratic objectives. For example, the bill would offer Endangered Species Act consultation authority to states if they meet certain requirements, reflecting a longtime Republican goal of more state-led management of listed species.

But the bill would also impose penalties on any future presidential administration aiming to ban a class of energy projects — like wind and solar, a move President Donald Trump attempted earlier this year that was later blocked in court. Heinrich has long been a proponent of renewable energy.

Schlenker-Goodrich said the bill fails to equitably balance development and environmental protection.

“If we are going to have an effective transition from fossil fuels to renewables, we actually have to have the federal government set a direction for our energy future, and what this bill does is cede that authority to tech energy finance interests in the market where they dominate, not the people,” he said in an interview.

He said it would reduce environmental protections for things like oil and gas development and favor developers’ interests.

“They are not empowering states,” he added. “It's burdening states with issues that have traditionally been the purview of the federal government. Even if this bill provides some measure of funding for that, it's not going to work out that well, and it's going to create this patchwork of very disparate regulatory systems that are contingent on the politics of that particular state.”

Heinrich responded in a statement that the U.S. is entering “a new era of energy demand.”

“We need to be able to get major energy projects to a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ faster so we can meet that demand and deliver cheaper energy,” Heinrich said. “The reality is that 83% of the energy projects stuck in the interconnection queue are clean energy projects. We can’t meet rising demand if we leave these projects waiting for decades. This bill delivers cheaper energy and good-paying jobs while protecting key environmental review, codifying the statutory right to Tribal consultation and ensuring the ability to challenge projects in court.”

title: REMARKS: Heinrich Introduces the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act with Capito, Lee, and Whitehouse Heinrich Introduces the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act with Capito, Lee, and Whitehouse
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to reform the federal environmental review and permitting process. This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Energy and Natural Resources Committee, speaks at a press conference announcing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, September 30, 2026.

“Today I wore a pin that was my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and it represents 60 years of him working for a local utility company to keep the lights on. Today in my home state of New Mexico there is a switchyard named after my dad, Pete Heinrich, and that switchyard is connected to the SunZia transmission line,” said Heinrich. “That transmission line, which is 550 miles long and carries the electrons from three and a half gigawatts of clean wind generation, took 17 years to permit and build. That’s why I’m here today, because we need to be able to build big things in this country again.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects. This legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and from a diverse group of stakeholders. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.

The bill text is available here.

Watch the full video of Heinrich’s remarks here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Thank you.

I want to start, too, just by thanking my colleagues.

This was a pretty remarkable effort, and everyone really did work in good faith to achieve this result.

I wore a pin today.

It’s not my Senate pin.

It’s a pin that I like to wear, that was my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and it represents 60 years of him working for a local utility company to keep the lights on.

Today in my home state of New Mexico there is a switchyard named after my dad, Pete Heinrich, and that switchyard is connected to the SunZia transmission line.

That transmission line, which is 550 miles long and carries the electrons from three and a half gigawatts of clean wind generation, took 17 years to permit and build.

That’s why I’m here today, because I was part of that process that should have taken probably five years to figure out how to get to yes or how to get to no a whole lot faster than that.

We need to be able to build big things in this country again, and if we don’t, experts like the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas have estimated that we will see 20 to 30 percent increases in the cost of electricity in the near term.

Not a decade from now, but a couple of years from now.

And so, with the incredible demand that is on our grid right now, we came together to find ways to do the things that we’ve done historically, but do the processes in parallel. Don’t do them one after the other after the other, and keep the process open for years and years at a time.

This process will mean that we develop responsibly.

It’ll mean more jobs.

It’ll mean cheaper energy.

It’ll mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that’s a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer: By statute, not a suggestion, but an actual law.

This is an opportunity for us to unleash American innovation and our incredible skilled labor force to build big things again.

And I have to say, I wasn’t sure at the beginning if we could all get there, and it’s because this group of people and the amazing staffs of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee and the Environment and Public Works Committee kept at it in good faith – through thick and thin – that we have arrived at this product.

I want to thank everyone who contributed to that.

title: Hickenlooper, Bennet Celebrate Passage of Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act
text:
Bill transfers ownership of Crystal Reservoir to the City of Ouray

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet celebrated the Senate passage of their Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act, transferring ownership of the Crystal Reservoir and the associated dam and water infrastructure from the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) to the City of Ouray.

“This is a big win for Ouray, which deserves control over its own water resources,” said Hickenlooper. “This legislation will unlock Crystal Reservoir’s potential, boosting recreation and strengthening local water supplies.”

“The Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act is a common-sense piece of legislation that will protect Ouray’s water supply and a beloved recreation asset for future generations,” said Bennet. “Senate passage is a critical step forward, and I urge the House to pass it upon their return in November. Coloradans should get the water access they deserve.”

The bill would convey approximately 45 acres of federal land, including the Crystal Reservoir, Full Moon Dam, and Full Moon Ditch. The conveyance would occur at no cost to the City of Ouray, in exchange for its responsibility for the operations, maintenance, and repairs of the Full Moon Dam and Full Moon Ditch. The conveyance prohibits commercial development on the property, requires compliance with Colorado water law, and maintains public access to the reservoir and nearby trails for outdoor recreation and wildland fire response.

In September 2025, Hickenlooper and Bennet introduced the Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act. Representative Jeff Hurd introduced a House companion in November 2025. In July 2026, Hickenlooper and Bennet celebrated the bill’s unanimous passage out of the U.S. Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

The bill has resounding support from the Ouray area and adjacent communities, including: the City of Ouray; the Towns of Ridgway and Silverton; Ouray and San Juan Counties; Ouray County Sheriff; Ouray County Department of Emergency Management; Colorado River District; Uncompahgre Watershed Partnership; Hydrowest Inc.; the Trust for Land Restoration; Ouray and San County Historical Societies; Red Mountain Project; Ouray Trail Group; Ridgway Ouray Community Council; Ouray and Ridgway Area Chambers of Commerce; Great Old Broads for Wilderness; RIGS Fly Shop Guide Service; and the Six Basins Project.

title: Hickenlooper, Tillis, Rosen, Sheehy, Cramer, Lee, Fulcher Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Establish National Critical Minerals Council, Federal Strategy on Critical Minerals
text:
U.S. is 100% reliant on imports for 16 critical minerals

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper, Thom Tillis, Jacky Rosen, Tim Sheehy, and Kevin Cramer, along with Representatives Susie Lee and Russ Fulcher, introduced the bipartisan National Critical Minerals Council Act, which would establish a National Critical Minerals Council to develop and implement a national strategy on critical minerals and build reliable supply chains at home and abroad.

Critical minerals power our modern way of life, including vehicles, smartphones, defense systems, medical equipment, AI and clean energy. Yet, China dominates the market, processing or refining about 70% of the world’s critical minerals. The U.S. is fully reliant on imports for 16 critical minerals. Given the scale of the challenge, our federal response remains fragmented, with more than 15 federal agencies and departments working on critical minerals issues. Absent a unified effort, the U.S. risks falling behind in securing the minerals essential to our competitiveness and leadership in energy security and national defense.

“China doesn’t need to fire a shot. It just needs to stop a shipment,” said Hickenlooper. “We need a national strategy on critical minerals now. Otherwise, Beijing decides who gets the supply — and who doesn’t.”

“The United States can no longer afford to take a piecemeal approach to address our critical minerals needs,” said Tillis. “I am proud to reintroduce this bipartisan legislation to establish a comprehensive and unified strategy to secure the minerals that are essential to our national security and economic stability.”

“As the world races to acquire and leverage the critical minerals that power the modern economy, the United States needs an efficient and effective plan to secure these important resources,” said Rosen. “I am proud to help introduce this bipartisan bill to ensure the United States has the infrastructure it needs to secure critical minerals and remain at the forefront of modern development.”

“It’s common sense: we cannot continue to rely on adversaries like China, which dominates the world’s critical minerals processing, for our critical mineral needs because it puts America’s national security at risk and threatens our competitive edge,” said Sheehy. “This crucial legislation reduces our dependence on others and bolsters America’s critical mineral supply chains by centralizing federal coordination, strategy, and research, making our nation more secure and self-reliant. I’m proud to cosponsor this legislation as we work to ensure America’s needs can be securely met.”

“We cannot afford to become more dependent on other countries for the critical minerals needed to power our economy and strengthen our national security,” said Cramer. “Our bill establishes a National Critical Minerals Council to unite all federal investment, research, and development on critical minerals under a single national strategy. The demand for critical minerals is growing every single day, and we need to seize every opportunity to jumpstart domestic production.”

“Critical minerals are used in everything from our phones to solar panels and aircraft used by the Department of Defense. It’s essential we develop our domestic critical mineral supply chains and reduce our dependence on foreign countries for rare earths,” said Lee. “That’s why I’m proud to join my colleagues in introducing the bipartisan, bicameral National Critical Minerals Council Act. This commonsense legislation will ensure the United States continues to grow our domestic supply of critical minerals, strengthening our national security and energy grid.”

“For far too long, our country has depended on foreign adversaries for vital minerals that support many of our defense capabilities and energy systems. This legislation will establish important structures for mineral development and help build critical partnerships,” said Fulcher. “I am proud to co-lead the National Critical Minerals Council Act with my colleague, Congresswoman Lee. By securing the critical minerals we have here at home today, we can build stronger energy security for tomorrow.”

The Secretary of the Interior, the National Security Adviser, and the Director of the National Economic Council would co-chair the council. They would appoint a Chief Minerals Adviser to oversee the Council’s operations and collaborate with experts from universities, industry, national labs, governments, Tribes, non-profits, and civil society.

Specifically, the council would:

Develop a national critical minerals strategy to reduce our reliance on foreign adversaries.

Work with allied nations and private entities to make the U.S. the partner of choice on critical minerals projects.

Track foreign investments in global critical mineral projects.

Coordinate education and workforce development.

Oversee the responsible development of domestic resources.

Hickenlooper has introduced several bills that boost the supply of critical minerals:

Critical Materials Future Act, which would establish a pilot program for the Department of Energy to financially support domestic critical material processing projects.

Unearth Innovation Act, which would create a Mining and Mineral Innovation Program within the Department of Energy to drive the responsible production of domestic critical minerals, with a focus on minimizing the environmental impact of mining.

Critical Minerals Security Act, which would direct the Department of the Interior to evaluate the global supply and ownership of critical minerals and make it easier for the U.S. to establish stable supply chains with international allies

title: Hoeven: Grid Power Act Advances Out of Energy Committee
text:
WASHINGTON – Senator John Hoeven issued the following statement after joining his fellow Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (ENR) members in approving the Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable (GRID) Power Act, legislation he introduced to help remove delays in the development of new baseload power generation projects that would improve the reliability of the electrical grid.

Hoeven introduced the legislation with Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) to address lengthy delays in the interconnection queue that can prevent new dispatchable power generation from coming online. Specifically, the bill would:

Following rulemaking from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), authorize regional grid operators to give priority consideration for baseload generation projects seeking an interconnection agreement.

The interconnection queue is where proposed projects wait before grid operators begin conducting their feasibility and system impact studies.

As of 2023, the median wait time was five years for an interconnection agreement, significantly delaying the construction of critical projects.

FERC would be required to initiate rulemaking to establish this process within 90 days of the bill’s enactment and finalize the rule within 180 days.

Establish a timeline of 60 days for FERC to act on baseload generation projects given priority consideration by grid operators.

Timely approval of projects would help address the gap in reliable power generation created by Biden administration rules like the Clean Power Plan 2.0, which accelerated the retirement of American baseload power plants.

“We need the ability to bring new baseload power online to meet growing electricity demand and ensure the reliability of our grid,” said Hoeven. “Our GRID Power Act helps cut through lengthy delays in the interconnection process so we can build the reliable dispatchable power generation our nation needs. With today’s committee approval, we are one step closer to advancing this importance legislation through the Senate.”

title: Senate passes Husted-backed bill to protect Great Lakes
text:
“We must remain vigilant against invasive species and continue protecting our lakes so they can support Ohio and America for generations to come.”

WASHINGTON – The Senate this week passed Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Sen. Gary Peters’ (D-Mich.) Great Lakes Restoration Initiative Act. This bill would reauthorize federal funding for critical projects like habitat restoration, cleaning up toxic sediments and pollution and preventing the spread of invasive species to protect and maintain the Great Lakes.

The Senate passed the bill without objection.

“The Great Lakes are an environmental and economic asset for the United States. They support thousands of jobs and contribute billions of dollars to Ohio’s regional economy. We must remain vigilant against invasive species and continue protecting our lakes so they can support Ohio and America for generations to come. I’m encouraged to see our bill pass the Senate, and I hope the House will act as soon as possible,” said Husted.

Since 2010, the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has provided more than $4.1 billion to fund 8,000 projects throughout the Great Lakes region. The initiative has focused on stopping the spread of invasive carp and other invasive species, restoring the Great Lakes coastline and preventing future contamination.

Husted is the only member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee representing a Great Lakes state. He has led efforts to advance the legislation in the Senate.

The legislation builds on Husted’s record of protecting the Great Lakes. In 2025, his Great Lakes Fishery Reauthorization Act became law, reauthorizing the Great Lakes Fishery Commission’s research activities and providing the U.S. Geological Survey’s Great Lakes Science Center with dedicated funding to conduct critical research supporting the region’s multi-billion-dollar fishing industry.

title: HYDE-SMITH PRAISES SENATE PASSAGE OF MENTAL HEALTH IN AVIATION BILL, LOOKS TO GET MEASURE ENACTED
text:
Senate and House Have Passed Similar Bipartisan Legislation to Improve Mental Health Care for Pilots & Air Traffic Controllers

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.), chair of the Senate Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Appropriations Subcommittee, today praised Senate approval of legislation she cosponsored to reduce bureaucratic delays and overregulation in how the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approaches to mental health and medical certification.

The John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act (S.3257), passed by unanimous consent, would reduce bureaucratic delays and overregulation within the FAA that creates a culture of silence regarding mental health in the aviation industry. Under current FAA regulations, pilots and air traffic controllers are required to disclose mental health treatments, which can lead to prolonged delays in returning to work due to excessive regulations and limited psychiatric staff to handle mental health evaluations.

“We’ve made a concerted effort in recent years to address the shortage of pilots and air traffic controllers as part of the appropriations process. Senate approval of this bill recognizes that existing FAA regulations and policies are standing in the way of promoting mental health and keeping qualified air traffic controllers and pilots working,” Hyde-Smith said. “There is significant support for fixing these issues in the Senate and House, so I hope we can get a bill enacted before the end of the year.”

Provisions in the John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act, which is named for a University of North Dakota aviation student who tragically took his own life in an aircraft in October 2021, are based on FAA Aviation Rulemaking Committee recommendations. Similar legislation (HR.2591) passed the House of Representatives in September 2025.

Introduced by U.S. Senator John Hoeven (R-N.D.), S.3257 would require the FAA to:

Modernize mental health guidance regulations for pilots and air traffic controllers to encourage the early disclosure and treatment of mental health conditions, while also requiring a regular review of the FAA Mental Health Special Issuance Process.

Provide funding to train additional medical examiners, including specialists, to improve the efficiency of the FAA Special Issuance Medical Certification process.

Undertake a public information campaign to help reduce the stigma around mental health care in aviation and encourage aviation professionals to seek mental health care.

The Senate recently also passed the Aviation Medication Transparency Act (S.3258), which would require the FAA to issue accessible, user-friendly guidance on medications that are safe for individuals in positions requiring a FAA Medical Certificate, including pilots, air traffic controllers, and other aviation professionals.

The Airlines for America (A4A), Regional Airline Association (RAA), Air Line Pilots Association (ALPA), and National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) are among the groups that support these measures.

title: Mississippi attorney nominated to serve on federal appeals court
text:
By Caleb Salers

A Mississippi attorney and partner at a law firm with multiple locations in the state has been nominated to a federal appeals court judgeship.

President Donald Trump announced Thursday that Todd Butler, a partner at Phelps Dunbar, has been nominated to serve on the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, located in New Orleans. His nomination was backed by U.S. Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, both Republicans from Mississippi.

“Todd Butler is an excellent pick for the federal bench,” Wicker said. “He believes in interpreting the law as it is written, pursuant to the text and original meaning of the Constitution — exactly the quality that should characterize a jurist. Mr. Butler is a credit to his home state of Mississippi.”

“President Trump has nominated an excellent pick in Mississippi’s own Todd Butler to serve as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit,” Hyde-Smith added. “He believes in interpreting the law as written, exactly the quality we need on the federal bench.”

Butler, who graduated among the top of his class at Mississippi State University and Mississippi College School of Law (now Mississippi Christian School of Law), is expected to succeed Judge Leslie H. Southwick on the federal bench. Southwick is a George W. Bush appointee who plans to semi-retire once a successor is named.

Before serving in the appointed role, Butler must be confirmed by the U.S. Senate, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. Hyde-Smith expects him to be confirmed “swiftly.” If that’s the case, he will soon be tasked with reviewing decisions made by lower U.S. district courts and federal administrative agencies to determine if legal errors occurred during the original proceedings.

“The wonderful people of the Great State of Mississippi (one of my favorites!), and the rest of the Fifth Circuit, can count on Todd to protect the Constitution and the Rule of Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

title: Kaine & Dingell Introduce Legislation to Prevent Campus Sexual Assault and Support Student Survivors
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Senator Tim Kaine, a member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, and U.S. Representative Debbie Dingell (D-MI-6) introduced the Support for Universities and Colleges to Champion the Educational Success of Survivors (SUCCESS) Act and the Survivor Outreach and Support on Campus Act—bicameral legislation to prevent campus sexual assault and improve support for student survivors. The SUCCESS Act, which is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Cory Booker (D-NJ), Dick Durbin (D-IL), and John Fetterman (D-PA) would help improve academic outcomes for student survivors and ensure colleges and universities have the resources to support them. The Survivor Outreach and Support on Campus Act, or S.O.S. Campus Act, would require every college and university that receives federal funding to have an independent advocate dedicated to campus sexual assault prevention and response. This legislation is also cosponsored by Senators Booker and Fetterman.

“Every student deserves to live and learn in a healthy and safe environment. We must do everything we can to prevent sexual assault on college campuses and provide comprehensive support to survivors,” said Kaine. “I’m proud to introduce these bills to help ensure survivors can access medical care, counseling, and the academic support they need to heal and continue pursuing their educational and professional goals.”

“Every student deserves to feel safe on their college campus and to know that if they experience sexual violence, they will be supported and taken seriously. The urgency to act has been put into sharp relief as we learn more about the horrific allegations coming out of Cornell,” said Dingell. “These bills will give colleges and universities more tools to prevent sexual violence, support survivors, and help ensure students can continue their education in a safe and supportive environment. No student should ever have to choose between their safety and their education.”

“Colleges have a responsibility to help survivors of sexual violence cope with the trauma of an assault. Yet colleges expect survivors to seek out medical and mental health services on their own, stay on track academically, and feel safe in the same environment where the violence occurred,” said Booker. “It’s unfair to make survivors carry this weight. Every institution of higher education should provide the support survivors need.”

“Survivors of sexual assault deserve to know that their college campuses stand with them. No student should have to choose between their education and getting the support they need after experiencing sexual assault,” said Durbin. “The SUCCESS Act ensures that students have access to the resources and support networks they need to continue their education and achieve their goals.”

“What kind of message does it send to survivors of sexual violence on our campuses if we hear their stories and don’t do anything to help prevent it from happening again? I can’t imagine that kind of unimaginable pain,” said Fetterman. “Today, my colleagues and I are doing something about it. These bills will not only help in the prevention of this violence, but it will help survivors with the resources they need and to continue pursuing their dreams.”

Sexual violence can impact student survivors physically, psychologically, emotionally, and academically. Survivors may face difficulty learning and retaining information, lower grade point averages, and a greater risk of dropping out of school. College and university students deserve the ability to learn without fear of sexual violence, and higher education institutions have an obligation to do everything they can to provide a safe learning environment for their students. The legislation would help colleges and universities provide comprehensive guidance, resources, and support for survivors to make campuses a safer place to learn.

The S.O.S. Campus Act would require campuses to have an independent advocate to conduct public information campaigns on sexual assault prevention and ensure that survivors of sexual assault have access to:

Emergency and follow-up medical care,

Guidance on reporting assaults to law enforcement

Medical forensic or evidentiary exams,

Crisis intervention, ongoing counseling, and assistance throughout the process, and

Information on their legal rights.

The legislation would also require universities to consult with or partner with local rape crisis centers and other community-based organizations to ensure survivors can access the services they need.

The SUCCESS Act would provide funding for universities and colleges to:

Provide higher education re-entry assistance for student survivors of sexual assault and other forms of violence;

Increase training for faculty and administrators on patient-centered care and recognizing signs of trauma;

Provide patient-centered professional development training for academic advisors and counselors;

Provide academic accommodations for students experiencing trauma, such as patient-centered training for tutors or the establishment of a confidential tutoring program specifically designed to assist student survivors of sexual assault and other violence;

Increase mental health services for student survivors of sexual assault and other violence; and

Create or enhance a fund for survivors of sexual assault and other violence to use for wrap-around services like housing, health care, and mental health treatment.

The S.O.S. Campus Act and the SUCCESS Act are endorsed by the American Psychological Association (APA) and the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN).
