title: Dingell, Kaine Introduce Legislation to Combat Campus Sexual Assault and Support Survivors
text:
U.S. Representative Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) and U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA) introduced the Support for Universities and Colleges to Champion the Educational Success of Survivors (SUCCESS) Act and the Survivor Outreach and Support (SOS) Campus Act—bicameral legislation to prevent campus sexual assault and improve support for student survivors.

The SUCCESS Act would help improve academic outcomes for student survivors and ensure colleges and universities have the resources to support them. The Survivor Outreach and Support on Campus Act, or S.O.S. Campus Act, would require every college and university that receives federal funding to have an independent advocate dedicated to campus sexual assault prevention and response.

“Every student deserves to feel safe on their college campus and to know that if they experience sexual violence, they will be supported and taken seriously. The urgency to act has been put into sharp relief as we learn more about the horrific allegations coming out of Cornell,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “These bills will give colleges and universities more tools to prevent sexual violence, support survivors, and help ensure students can continue their education in a safe and supportive environment. No student should ever have to choose between their safety and their education.”

“Every student deserves to live and learn in a healthy and safe environment. We must do everything we can to prevent sexual assault on college campuses and provide comprehensive support to survivors,” said Senator Kaine.“I’m proud to introduce these bills to help ensure survivors can access medical care, counseling, and the academic support they need to heal and continue pursuing their educational and professional goals.”

Sexual violence can impact student survivors physically, psychologically, emotionally, and academically. Survivors may face difficulty learning and retaining information, lower grade point averages, and a greater risk of dropping out of school. College and university students deserve the ability to learn without fear of sexual violence, and higher education institutions have an obligation to do everything they can to provide a safe learning environment for their students. The legislation would help colleges and universities provide comprehensive guidance, resources, and support for survivors to make campuses a safer place to learn.

The S.O.S. Campus Act would require campuses to have an independent advocate to conduct public information campaigns on sexual assault prevention and ensure that survivors of sexual assault have access to:

Emergency and follow-up medical care,

Guidance on reporting assaults to law enforcement

Medical forensic or evidentiary exams,

Crisis intervention, ongoing counseling, and assistance throughout the process, and

Information on their legal rights.

The legislation would also require universities to consult with or partner with local rape crisis centers and other community-based organizations to ensure survivors can access the services they need.

The SUCCESS Act would provide funding for universities and colleges to:

Provide higher education re-entry assistance for student survivors of sexual assault and other forms of violence;

Increase training for faculty and administrators on patient-centered care and recognizing signs of trauma;

Provide patient-centered professional development training for academic advisors and counselors;

Provide academic accommodations for students experiencing trauma, such as patient-centered training for tutors or the establishment of a confidential tutoring program specifically designed to assist student survivors of sexual assault and other violence;

Increase mental health services for student survivors of sexual assault and other violence; and

Create or enhance a fund for survivors of sexual assault and other violence to use for wrap-around services like housing, health care, and mental health treatment.

title: Dingell, Bacon Introduce Resolution Recognizing World Space Week
text:
U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) and Don Bacon (R-NE-02) introduced a bipartisan resolution designating October 4, 2026, through October 10, 2026, as ‘‘World Space Week” to recognize the contributions of space science and technology to the betterment of the human condition.

“The study and pursuit of space leads to both a greater understanding of our universe and our place in it,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “From inspiring the next generation of scientists, servicemembers, and engineers to driving innovations that improve our daily lives right here on Earth, space exploration unites us in curiosity and progress. I am proud to join Congressman Bacon in this bipartisan effort to recognize World Space Week.”

“America’s pioneering spirit has always pushed us to explore farther, innovate faster and achieve what once seemed impossible,”said Congressman Bacon. “Artemis II showed the world what American excellence looks like, bringing together our scientific talent, industrial strength and operational precision to achieve a historic mission. Today’s advances in rocket and launch technology are opening new opportunities for exploration, scientific discovery and economic growth while inspiring the next generation to look to the stars. I’m pleased to join Rep. Dingell in recognizing World Space Week and celebrating the scientists, engineers and innovators who continue pushing the boundaries of what we can accomplish.”

This year, World Space Week is celebrating its 27th year. World Space Week was designated by the United Nations (UN) in 1999 and consists of space-related events held at schools, museums, planetariums, aerospace companies, and space agencies around the world. The theme for 2026, “Rocket Revolution”, highlights transformative advancements in rocket and launch technologies and celebrates how modern rocket innovations reshape access to space and enable new missions, commercial opportunities, and broader participation in the space economy.

Text of the resolution can be found HERE.

title: Connecticut House Delegation Statement on Reports President Trump is Seeking to Ease Russian Sanctions
text:
Today, Reps. John Larson (CT-01), Joe Courtney (CT-02), Rosa DeLauro (CT-03), Jim Himes (CT-04), and Jahana Hayes (CT-05) responded to reporting from the Atlantic that President Trump is entertaining a plan to ease sanctions on Russia:

“When we voted against the Senate’s sanction bill this month, we warned that stripping out the enforcement language would leave every decision about punishing Putin to a president who keeps siding with the Kremlin. It took less than two weeks and President Trump is entertaining a plan to ease sanctions on Russia.

“Just last week President Trump went to the United Nations and bragged about the ‘enormous new tariff authorities’ this bill handed him. So, the one part of the law he seems eager to enforce will needlessly raise costs on Americans by continuing his reckless trade policies, while the power he was given to cripple Putin’s war machine he is already looking to sign away.

“That is exactly why the House-passed bill, H.R. 2913, required the president to act on sanctions. Without that requirement, sanctions are dependent on President Trump’s will to impose them – and President Trump has shown us time and time again he would rather be a friend to Putin than hold him accountable.

title: Congressman Davis Helps Deliver New 100-Foot Ladder Truck to Williamston Fire Department
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman Don Davis (NC-01) celebrated the delivery of a new 100-foot aerial ladder truck to the Williamston Fire Department, made possible in part by $1 million in community project funding he secured for the Town of Williamston. Congressman Davis secured the project for federal funding to help replace the department’s aging 1999 Pierce 75-foot ladder truck after nearly 30 years of service, and voted to approve it as part of H.R. 5371, Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-37).

The $1 million investment, delivered through the USDA Rural Development Community Facilities program, helped fund the new custom-built 2026 E-ONE HR 100-foot tandem aerial ladder truck, designated Ladder 26. The Town of Williamston covered the remaining $500,000 for the apparatus. Ladder 26 expands the department’s vertical reach by 25 feet and strengthens its firefighting and emergency response capabilities.

“Behind the wheel of Williamston’s new ladder truck are firefighters who train, prepare, and put themselves in harm’s way to protect their neighbors,” said Congressman Don Davis. “I am proud to have voted and secured $1 million to help deliver this new apparatus, and grateful to the firefighters who answer the call when our community needs them most.”

Congressman Don Davis secured nearly $54 million in Fiscal Year 2026 Community Project Funding for eastern North Carolina through federal appropriations legislation he supported. The funding was included in the Senate amendment to H.R. 7148, Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026; H.R. 6938, Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026; and H.R. 5371, Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026.

title: Congressman Davis Urges IRS to Provide Emergency Diesel Relief for North Carolina Farmers
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman Don Davis (NC-01) is urging the Internal Revenue Service to grant North Carolina the longest available period of federal penalty relief for highway use of dyed diesel fuel, providing temporary relief as farmers face record diesel prices during harvest season.

Diesel prices in North Carolina have reached all-time highs. According to AAA, the average price of diesel in North Carolina reached $6.2473 per gallon on September 19, up from $3.46 a year earlier. Nationally, the average price of on-highway diesel reached a record $6.529 per gallon for the week of September 21. As of September 3, 2026, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) projects that farm-sector fuel and oil expenses will increase by $4.8 billion, or 28.8 percent. Farmers are price takers, and many are operating on thin margins.

“Eastern North Carolina is the heart of our state’s agricultural industry. Our growers are paying for the increased expense of fuel after a severe drought. In July, USDA designated over a dozen counties in our region as primary natural disaster areas because of the drought. The growers cannot afford to wait for the cost of diesel to decline. It is vital that growers have access to lower cost diesel on highways to move their crops, livestock, and equipment over long distances,” wrote Congressman Davis.

“At least 10 state governors have suspended or relaxed the penalties for using dyed diesel on highways in their respective states. I strongly urge you to use the authority provided under IRM 25.16.1.5 to grant North Carolina the longest available period of federal penalty relief for the use of dyed diesel on highways. Protecting our farmers is more critical than ever,” continued Congressman Davis.

title: Dunn, Díaz-Balart Lead Members in Calling for Changes to College Sports Bill
text:
Congressmen Neal Dunn, M.D. (R-FL-02), and Mario Díaz-Balart (R-FL-26) led over 20 members of Congress in a letter to House leadership urging changes to the Protect College Sports Act (S. 4668) before final House passage.

The members support the effort to establish national standards for college athletics but raised concerns about Section 205, which would cap Power Four conference membership at 20 schools and require a school leaving one of those conferences to spend three years as an independent before joining another. They asked House leadership to remove or substantially amend the provision.

“College athletics need clear national standards, and there is much in this bill that I support,” said Congressman Dunn. “But Congress should not decide how many schools can belong to a conference or make a university spend three years as an independent before it can join another. Universities and conferences need the flexibility to make those decisions in the best interests of their student-athletes.”

In the letter to Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, and Majority Whip Tom Emmer, the members wrote: “Conference membership should remain a matter for universities and conferences based on a range of factors including the needs of their student-athletes, geography, competition, media agreements, academic partnerships and relationships, and financial considerations.”

Joining Congressmen Dunn and Díaz-Balart in signing the letter were Representatives Sheri Biggs (R-SC-03), Gus Bilirakis (R-FL-12), Vern Buchanan (R-FL-16), Scott Franklin (R-FL-18), Carlos Gimenez (R-FL-28), Mike Haridopolos (R-FL-08), Mark Harris (R-NC-08), Laurel Lee (R-FL-15), Addison McDowell (R-NC-06), Cory Mills (R-FL-07), Tim Moore (R-NC-14), Gregory Murphy (R-NC-03), Ralph Norman (R-SC-05), Jimmy Patronis (R-FL-01), John Rutherford (R-FL-05), Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL-27), Greg Steube (R-FL-17), William Timmons (R-SC-04), and Joe Wilson (R-SC-02).

title: Finstad Hosts Open Discussion with Fairmont Area Veterans and Veterans Organizations
text:
NEW ULM, MN – Congressman Brad Finstad (MN-01) hosted an open discussion in Fairmont to hear from southern Minnesota veterans and local organizations about improving veterans care services, sharing information on available resources, and strengthening partnerships between the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), Veteran Service Organizations (VSOs), nonprofits, and local communities. Minnesota State Representative Bjorn Olson also attended the discussion.

“I am honored to represent thousands of veterans across southern Minnesota and advocate for the care they deserve through my role in Congress,” said Rep. Finstad. “We have a responsibility to ensure our veterans can access both physical and mental health services, whether that be through the VA or through the critical community partners working to fill the gaps in care, which is why resources like the Bravo Zulu House – the nation’s only all-military, post-treatment sober home – are so critically important for our southern Minnesota veterans. Yesterday’s discussion gave me the opportunity to hear from the veterans and organizations on the front lines and gain deeper insight into what we can do to provide better support.”

title: Rep. Fischbach Met with Southern Minnesota Beet Sugar Cooperative to Discuss Industry Issues
text: Willmar, MN - Congresswoman Michelle Fischbach met with Southern Minnesota Beet Sugar Cooperative leadership and growers in Renville to discuss challenges facing the sugarbeet industry. title: As EPA Relocates Regional Lab Outside Houston,  Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher Demands Public Meeting and Answers
text:
Trump administration stopped processing new samples at the Region 6 EPA lab in August with no plan to protect Gulf Coast communities before the new Oklahoma lab is ready

Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07) called on Administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Lee Zeldin to request a public meeting to explain how EPA will protect Houston and the Gulf Coast after halting essential work at its Region 6 Laboratory in Houston. The effort comes after the Trump administration ordered the Houston lab to stop processing new samples even though EPA acknowledges that its lab in Ada, Oklahoma will not be fully operational for months. EPA has presented no plan for testing air, water, and soil across five states if a hurricane or industrial accident strikes. The closure also upends the lives of the lab's scientists, many of whom may leave EPA rather than move 400 miles away. And many questions remain about the impact of moving the lab several hundred miles away will have on Houston’s public and environmental health following disasters.

“Housto is home to a large number of chemical plants and refineries, and this lab and its highly trained staff are essential to EPA’s mission of protecting human health and the environment,” Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher wrote. “In the case of extreme weather events, these scientists are among Houston’s essential first responders. Many EPA inspectors working on the Hurricane Harvey emergency response were based out of the Houston Lab. Moving the lab to a remote area exposes real infrastructure and logistics issues, which threatens Houston’s access to the critical air, water, and soil testing performed at the lab and the return of results as quickly as possible.

“Closing the Houston lab is ill-advised and I have advocated against it for years. At a minimum, EPA should present a comprehensive plan for how the lab’s functions will be carried out as this consolidation with Ada occurs,” Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher continued. “However, EPA ordered the lab to stop processing new samples on August 28, 2026, and EPA personnel communicated to my office during a meeting on September 9, 2026, that the Ada lab will not take over the Houston lab’s functions for several months… EPA has not articulated a plan for how new samples will be processed or how emergencies will be managed during this interim period. This is unacceptable and dangerous. With no plan in place, Houston and Region 6 residents cannot feel confident that the air they breathe and the water they drink will be safe if an industrial accident or natural disaster occurs.

“In light of these concerns, I request that EPA holds a public meeting in Houston by the end of 2026 to detail its plans for the continuity of the Region 6 Houston lab’s functions and receive input from impacted stakeholders and the public,” Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher concluded. “Additionally, I request answers to the following questions by October 30, 2026:

Has EPA developed a plan to ensure continuity of the Region 6 lab’s functions during the period from August 28, 2026, when the lab stopped processing new samples, to when the Ada lab is fully operational;

When will EPA communicate, in detail, its plans regarding management-directed reassignments to the Ada lab and relocating remaining staff to another Houston facility to the Houston lab’s current employees;

Once the Houston and Ada lab consolidation is complete, how will EPA ensure samples from the coast of the Gulf of Mexico are transported and processed in Ada in a timely manner;

What impact will the Houston and Ada lab consolidation have on the processing time of samples from the coast of the Gulf of Mexico? What, if any, analysis has been conducted on the potential public and environmental health impacts of delays caused by the consolidation? What was the result of this analysis; and

EPA personnel communicated to my office during a meeting on September 9, 2026, that the consolidation of the Houston and Ada labs will result in no detrimental impact on Region 6’s analytical capability. Please provide data substantiating this claim.”

The Region 6 Laboratory is a full-service analytical lab providing critical emergency response and disaster prevention services for five states. The Houston Lab is being moved from a newer facility built in 1990 to an older facility built in 1966, which is having to undergo extensive renovations to properly function. Since the EPA ordered Region 6’s lab functions to cease last month, the lab is in flux and operating in a diminished capacity, threatening Houston’s access to the critical air, water, and soil testing performed at the lab.

In 2019, Congresswoman Fletcher led an appropriations letter to the LHHS Subcommittee asking that they include language barring the EPA from using any funds to close the Region 6 EPA lab. Following this, Congresswoman Fletcher sent multiple letters to the EPA Administrator since 2019 in opposition to the lab relocation and a letter to the EPA Office of the Inspector General asking for an investigation into the closure. During EPA’s Fiscal Year 26 Budget Hearing, Congresswoman Fletcher raised this issue with Administrator Zeldin, who committed to looking into the issue.

To view the full text of the letter, click here.

title: Fong Praises BLM Announcement of California Oil and Gas Lease Sale
text:
BAKERSFIELD, CA — Today, Congressman Vince Fong (CA-20) issued the following statement praising the Bureau of Land Management's announcement of a December 2026 oil and gas lease sale covering approximately 35,000 acres across Kern, Kings, Fresno, and San Luis Obispo counties in California:

"Action to produce more American energy, lower costs, and strengthen California's energy security. The Bureau of Land Management just announced a December oil and gas lease sale covering 35,000 acres across Kern, Kings, Fresno, and San Luis Obispo counties. This is the kind of decisive federal action I've been pushing for that produces more energy right here at home, reduces our dependence on foreign oil, strengthens our energy supply, and helps lower energy costs for California families and businesses.

“While Gavin Newsom has spent years restricting California energy production, undermining refining capacity, and driving up gas and energy costs, we are working with the Trump Administration to unleash American energy, expand reliable domestic supply, and restore California's energy security. Thank you to President Trump, Secretary Burgum, and the Department of Interior for making California energy production, energy security, and affordability a priority."

title: Congressmen Goldman and Bentz Introduce the IMD CARE Act for Patients Suffering from Serious Mental Illnesses
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congressman Dan Goldman (D-NY) and Congressman Cliff Bentz (R-OR) introduced the IMD CARE Act, legislation which would expand Medicaid eligibility to include psychiatric care facility beds in excess of the current 16 bed limit for patients suffering from severe mental illness.

When the Social Security Act was enacted in 1965, it limited Medicaid funding to psychiatric facilities that had no more than 16 beds, resulting in a shortage of beds when the need for inpatient mental health care has grown.

The IMD CARE Act would amend the Social Security Act to establish a State Plan Amendment, allowing Institutions of Mental Diseases (IMDs) with more than 16 beds to receive Medicaid funding for all mental health patients.

Under current law, States that wish to receive federal Medicaid funding for IMDs with over 16 beds must submit a request for a waiver allowing them to receive Medicaid reimbursement for individuals needing psychiatric care.

These waivers are temporary, unstable, and require complex renewal negotiations.

The State Plan Amendment option included in the IMD CARE Act would provide predictable reimbursement structures, durable financing mechanisms, and greater continuity for patients and providers. States would be required to ensure a robust continuum of care including providing outpatient and community-based mental health care and wrap-around services. States would also be required to follow evidence-based clinical criteria for admitting and transitioning patients from institutional care.

The bill is endorsed by the National Association of State Mental Health Program Directors, National Association for Behavioral Health, Treatment Advocacy Center, National Shattering Silence Coalition, and Meadows Mental Health Policy Institute.

“Outdated Medicaid restrictions on long-term mental health care have left too many Americans in crisis without access to treatment,” Congressman Goldman said. “By allowing states more authority to expand their mental health services, we can reach more Americans who are stuck in a never-ending cycle of hospitals, jail, and the streets. This legislation is a critical step towards ensuring that everyone, regardless of income, can get the help they need with dignity.”

Said Congressman Bentz: “Studies show that a significant portion of the homeless and prison population suffer from severe mental illness. These people would benefit from the availability of proper treatment in our existing mental healthcare facilities. This bill would result in an increased number of beds and treatment available for mentally ill people. Without this improvement in how we deliver mental health services, those who need such treatment will continue to cost communities more in law enforcement and healthcare expenses. The circular progression of the mentally ill from the street to the hospital to the prison and back to the street must stop.”

“When someone on Medicaid is experiencing a mental health crisis, the program often won’t cover a psychiatric hospital bed. That’s because of a rule written in 1965,” said Scott Dziengelski, President and CEO of the National Association for Behavioral Healthcare. “A 60-year-old rule shouldn’t keep people from getting the care they need today. The IMD CARE Act takes an important step toward fixing that.”

Congressman Dan Goldman is committed to alleviating the mental health crisis in America. In 2025, he introduced the ‘Michelle Alyssa Go Act’ to increase the number of federal Medicaid-eligible in-patient psychiatric beds for individuals who are seeking treatment for both mental health and substance use disorders.

title: RELEASE: Gottheimer Claws Back $500,000 in Federal Dollars for the Future Lackawanna Railway & Andover Train Station Site
text:
Above: Gottheimer announces clawed-back funds for Andover Train Station.

ANDOVER, NJ – Today, Friday, October 2, 2026, at the future site of the Andover station, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) announced $500,000 in clawed-back federal dollars secured through the Transit Security Grant Program to strengthen security and safety at the planned park-and-ride station. The station is a key part of the effort to restore the Lackawanna Cut-off railway, with the goal of service from Scranton, Pennsylvania, to Hoboken, and on to New York City.

Every day, 28,000 people commute between Northeast Pennsylvania, Northern New Jersey, and New York. Sussex County has the longest average commute of any New Jersey county, at 38 minutes, and Vernon Township has been ranked as having the worst commutes in the state. Since 2011, New Jersey commute times have increased by 8.8 percent.

“There are zero options for folks in Sussex County to make their lives easier and get on a train to get to work or see a family member, and that has to change,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “I’ve clawed back $500,000 in new federal funding from Washington to Jersey, secured through the Transit Security Grant Program, to strengthen safety and security at Andover Train Station for the families and commuters who, ultimately, will count on it every day. This funding helps harden this site as the next phase of the project gets underway.”

Watch Gottheimer’s full remarks here.

The Andover site has already seen unauthorized access to the tunnel, including damage to or displacement of the measures meant to keep people out. The new resources can support security cameras, fencing, gates, and barriers, and other related security measures. This is capital security infrastructure that will stay with the station for the long haul and protect the public investment already in place.

The tunnel construction project is complete, with final details finished in June 2025, but there has been no construction activity at the site since. The project has $94 million in resources against an estimated total cost of $112.5 million. NJ TRANSIT plans to close the gap of about $19 million with state Transportation Trust Fund dollars and toll credits.

The project also promises real economic opportunity. According to Amtrak’s Corridor Vision plan, released in May 2021, expanding service beyond the Lackawanna Cut-off to Scranton could generate about $87 million in annual economic activity, plus $2.9 billion in one-time economic impact from construction along the corridor. More rail service also means fewer cars on the road, reducing emissions, highway congestion, and transportation costs and delays.

Today’s announcement builds on Gottheimer’s record of delivering for passenger rail in Northwestern New Jersey:

In 2018, Gottheimer sent a letter urging NJ TRANSIT to allow the community to upgrade the culvert, and NJ TRANSIT agreed soon after.

In 2021, he helped craft and pass the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which included $102 billion in total rail investment.

In 2022, he rallied state and local officials to push NJ TRANSIT to rebuild beyond the Cut-off. NJ TRANSIT committed $32.5 million to rehabilitate the Roseville Tunnel and the Hudson Farm and Junction Brook culverts, construct 8,000 feet of track bed, and stabilize rock slopes.

Gottheimer was joined by Andover Mayor Thomas Walsh, Andover Deputy Mayor Krista Gilchrist, NJTRANSIT Government & External Affairs Chief Paul Wyckoff, and Andover Police Chief Eric Danielson.

Below: Gottheimer announces clawed-back funds for Andover Train Station.

Read Gottheimer’s full remarks as prepared for delivery here:

It’s great to be back here in beautiful Andover, New Jersey, at the future site of the Andover Train Station, the park-and-ride station that is part of Lackawanna Railway, which, when it’s fully restored, will have service from Scranton, Pennsylvania, to Hoboken, New Jersey, and on to New York City.

I want to thank Mayor Thomas Walsh, Deputy Mayor Krista Gilchrist, and Paul Wyckoff of NJTRANSIT, and the rest of NJTRANSIT for joining us today. This is a project we’ve been working on together for many years now.

Thanks to great cooperation with our local elected officials here, when the railway is completed in 2031, Sussex County will finally have quality rail service on NJTRANSIT, helping commuters, stimulating tourism, and boosting the local economy.

Every day, 28,000 people commute between Northeast Pennsylvania, Northern New Jersey, and New York. Sussex County has the longest average commute time of all New Jersey counties, at nearly 38 minutes. Vernon Township has been ranked as having the worst commutes in the entire state. And since 2011, New Jersey commute times have increased by 8.8 percent.

Yet, there are zero options for folks in Sussex County to make their lives easier and get on a train to get to work, or to see a family member.

I’ve heard from so many residents, businesses, and local elected officials about this issue, and the urgent need for more transportation options to New York City from across Sussex.

Restoring the Lackawanna Railway is a key part of the solution, improving convenience and travel times for hundreds of thousands of travelers across the state, including right here in Andover and across Sussex County via NJTRANSIT regional rail.

Unfortunately, because of endless bureaucratic nonsense and constant stalling, this project has been trudging along for fifteen years.

Work on the Lackawanna project actually began back in 2011. But, it was paused in 2015 because NJTRANSIT could not access and upgrade the railway culvert on Hudson Farm. So, when I got to Congress, I joined with the Andover mayor and council – and went to work.

In 2018, working together, I sent a letter to NJTRANSIT urging them to allow the community, as they had asked, to upgrade a necessary railway culvert. Soon after, NJTRANSIT agreed to do it, a positive development after years of delay.

Then, in 2021, I helped write, negotiate, and pass the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which included $102 billion in total rail funding. In 2022, utilizing those dollars, I rallied state and local officials to push NJTRANSIT to rebuild beyond the Lackawanna Railway Cut-off, and NJTRANSIT committed $32.5 million to rehabilitate the Roseville Tunnel and the Hudson Farm and Junction Brook culverts, construct 8,000 feet of track bed, and stabilize rock slopes. The Tunnel, the track bed, and the culverts are already completed.

Not too different than when the B&O and then the Transcontinental Railroad were built, this project has been subject to repeated delays and uncertain timetables, with regulatory hurdles, red tape, property disputes, and inter-agency negotiations. But, many of us, including Mayor Thomas Walsh and Deputy Mayor Gilchrist, the council, and the Sussex County Community, have never given up – we’ve continued to fight – and, because of that, we’ve continued to achieve major milestones.

Today, I’m here to announce another important milestone in our work to bring the Lackawanna Railroad to Sussex County: I’ve clawed back $500,000 in new federal funding from Washington to Jersey, secured through the Transit Security Grant Program, to strengthen safety and security at Andover Train Station for the families and commuters who, ultimately, will count on it every day. This funding helps harden this site as the next phase of the project gets underway.

Let me walk you through where this project stands. NJTRANSIT is finishing the design and engineering scope for this next phase, with a target of the end of October.

The goal is to bring on a design contractor by the end of 2026, and begin design in January 2027. The design is targeted to be complete in January 2028, with construction bidding to follow, and construction on this station is targeted to be complete in August 2031, with service for passengers to follow.

Now, every one of those dates is a target. My job is to make sure NJTRANSIT hits each one of them, and I’ll be fighting to beat them, not miss them.

Right now, thanks in part to the dollars we clawed back to Jersey in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill I mentioned, the project has $94 million in funding against an estimated total cost of $112.5 million. That leaves a gap of about $19 million, which NJ TRANSIT plans to close with state Transportation Trust Fund dollars and toll credits.

The $500,000 I’m announcing today is separate. It will be utilized to prevent any delays in the timetable that could come from vandalism or damage from trespassers – including security cameras, fencing, gates, and barriers, and related protective technology.

The Andover Train Station has already seen unauthorized access to the Roosevelt Tunnel, including damage to the tunnel itself and to measures put in place to keep people out. This funding goes straight to help solve that problem. This is a critical station, and we cannot afford any setbacks, and we have to protect the investments the public has already made in the infrastructure here.

The benefits of this project are clear: Aside from all of the commuting benefits for families, so they can get to work and see their kids at night, an expanded transit network means fewer cars on the road, which will reduce vehicle emissions and pollution, highway congestion, and transportation costs and delays. This train will also result in real economic opportunity for the region.

That’s why, back in 2022, I also pressed the Federal Railroad Administration to restore Amtrak service on the Lackawanna between New York and Scranton – including a stop right here in Andover.

According to Amtrak’s own Corridor Vision Plan, expanding service from New York to Scranton, Pennsylvania, could generate about $87 million in annual economic activity, plus $2.9 billion in one-time economic impact from construction along the corridor.

I don’t know about you, but I can’t wait to see this railway running in 2031. I already have an alert set on my calendar.

When the Lackawanna Rail Line was first built back in 1911, it ran west for about 28 miles between Port Morris Junction in Port Morris, New Jersey, and Slateford Junction in Slateford, Pennsylvania. It was part of a 400-mile line between Hoboken, New Jersey, and Buffalo, New York. Imagine that. An incredible infrastructure feat for the time.

Passenger service on this corridor ended decades ago, between 1966 and 1971, and the tracks were later removed, leaving the line inactive for more than 50 years. So, part of this project has been putting in all-new tracks.

In the end, when it’s finished, I know this project will bring significant benefits to Sussex County and Northern New Jersey, to our families, to commuters, to deliver good-paying jobs for our hard-working men and women of labor, and to strengthen our communities by reducing congestion, improving commutes, boosting tourism, and helping grow our local economies. I look forward to continuing to work closely with Andover, Sussex County, NJTRANSIT, and Amtrak to bring quality, expansive rail service to North Jersey as soon as possible, without delay.

There is nothing partisan about this – it’s just about working together to solve problems for Jersey families.

If we continue to do that, to work together to restore Lackawanna and expand New Jersey’s transportation network, I know that, in the greatest country in the world, our best days will always be ahead of us.

May God bless you and God bless the United States of America.

title: ICYMI: Congressman Pat Harrigan Pens Op-Ed on Removing Barriers for Disabled Veterans
text:
Contact: Lexi Kranich (814) 380-4408

WASHINGTON, D.C.—In a new op-ed for the Washington Reporter, Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10) and Purple Heart Homes Co-Founder and CEO John Gallina expose a federal policy that allowed disabled veterans’ VA compensation to be used against them when seeking help to make their homes safe and accessible. They explain how Purple Heart Homes, headquartered in Statesville, spent eight years documenting the problem, how Congress changed the law to remove that barrier, and why fixing failures like this is essential to making sure the benefits veterans earned actually work for them.

You can read the full piece here or below.

Cutting the Red Tape Between Disabled Veterans and a Safe Home is Essential

Housing affordability just became harder for millions of Americans. With the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reaching 7 percent, buying a home is becoming more expensive, but for many disabled veterans, the challenge is even more basic: whether the home they already have can safely meet their needs.

As veterans ourselves, we regularly hear from men and women living in homes that no longer accommodate their physical needs. For someone aging with a service-connected injury, remaining independent can depend on something as basic as a ramp, widened doorway or accessible shower.

By 2021, about half of disabled veteran renters were spending more than 30 percent of their income on rent, while nearly three in ten spent more than half. Yet for some veterans, the housing market was not the only thing working against them. Federal policy was too.

Many state and local home-repair programs rely on HUD’s Community Development Block Grant program, or CDBG. Until this year, VA service-connected disability compensation could be counted when calculating income for eligibility.

The result made little sense. A veteran could receive compensation because he was disabled serving this country, then have that same compensation used to disqualify him from assistance modifying his home around that disability.

We see problems like this from two different vantage points.

Purple Heart Homes sees them veteran by veteran, working inside homes where a poorly written rule can determine whether someone gets the ramp, bathroom or other modification needed to remain independent. The congressional side sees the same failures written into federal programs, where one rule can quietly affect thousands of veterans across the country.

That is why veterans policy has been a major focus of the work coming out of North Carolina’s 10th District. That work has included introducing legislation to strengthen oversight of the VA’s overseas health care program, introducing the COMPASS Act to protect military families during PCS moves, co-leading legislation to improve housing and financial counseling for servicemembers and transitioning veterans, and helping advance the Fort Bragg land transfer needed for North Carolina to build a new State Veterans Home.

The issues are different, but the approach is the same: find where government is failing the people who served, understand exactly why it is failing, and fix the policy behind it.

That approach mattered here because Purple Heart Homes had spent eight years documenting the problem.

Using VA data covering more than 1 million veterans with service-connected disability ratings of 50 percent or higher, Purple Heart Homes identified 35,516 veterans whose disability compensation alone exceeded 80 percent of their state’s median income, even if they earned nothing else. More than three-quarters have a 100 percent service-connected disability rating.

Some of the veterans living with the most serious service-connected disabilities could therefore be denied assistance precisely because of the benefits they earned for those disabilities.

And North Carolina’s 10th District had a unique view of both sides of that problem. Purple Heart Homes, founded and headquartered in Statesville, had the experience and data showing what veterans were encountering at home. Congress had the ability to address the federal rule behind it.

The Disabled Veterans Housing Support Act, sponsored by Rep. Monica De La Cruz of Texas, received bipartisan support and was signed into law on Jan. 20. It now requires states, local governments and tribes to exclude VA service-connected disability compensation when determining eligibility under CDBG. It also directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to examine whether the same problem exists elsewhere across HUD.

Now the law has to work where it matters.

Housing agencies and nonprofit providers need to update their eligibility policies, and veterans previously told their disability compensation put them above an income limit should know the rules have changed. If the GAO finds the same mistake elsewhere, Congress should fix it there too.

For those of us who served, this gets to a larger point about veterans policy. Creating a benefit is not enough if another part of government makes it harder for a veteran to use it.

Disability compensation reflects a cost a veteran continues to carry because he or she served this country. It should never become another obstacle to receiving help.

Purple Heart Homes can see where policy fails when it reaches a veteran’s front door. Congress can trace that failure back to federal law and remove it. Bringing those two perspectives together is how a bureaucratic problem becomes a practical solution.

For disabled veterans, that solution can be as simple, and as important, as being able to remain safely in the place they call home.

Rep. Pat Harrigan represents North Carolina’s 10th District and serves on the House Armed Services Committee. A West Point graduate and former Green Beret, he served in Afghanistan and was awarded two Bronze Stars. John Gallina is Co-Founder and CEO of Purple Heart Homes, a nonprofit organization based in Statesville, North Carolina, providing safe, barrier-free housing solutions for qualified veterans.

title: Comisionado Residente amplía la discusión del futuro de Medicaid al sector hospitalario
text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — El Comisionado Residente de Puerto Rico, Pablo José Hernández, amplió al sector hospitalario la discusión sobre el futuro de Medicaid en Puerto Rico durante su participación en la Convención de la Asociación de Hospitales, donde abordó los cambios que enfrenta el programa a partir de 2027 y la necesidad de que Puerto Rico llegue preparado a la próxima etapa de discusión en el Congreso.

El Comisionado Residente destacó que las decisiones que se tomen en Washington tendrán consecuencias directas sobre la estabilidad del sistema de salud, incluyendo la capacidad de los hospitales para sostener sus operaciones, retener profesionales de la salud y garantizar acceso a servicios de calidad para los pacientes.

“Nuestra prioridad es atender lo básico, y la salud es parte de eso. Trabajamos más allá de líneas partidistas para extender los fondos del Plan Vital.El 23 de septiembre reunimos en el Congreso a expertos, personal congresional y representantes del sector de la salud para discutir los retos que tenemos por delante, y el 25 de septiembre nos reunimos con la gobernadora y el grupo multisectorial en La Fortaleza para revisar los datos y afinar la propuesta que llevaremos a Washington. El 2027 está cada vez más cerca y queremos llegar a esa discusión preparados, con una agenda clara y con una propuesta sustentada en datos. En asuntos como este, la salud de los puertorriqueños no tiene colores políticos”, expresó el comisionado residente.

Durante su participación, el Comisionado Residente explicó que Puerto Rico enfrenta una estructura de Medicaid distinta a la de los estados, particularmente por el tope anual al financiamiento federal. Bajo la ley vigente, el porcentaje de participación federal también está programado para reducirse de 76% a 55% a partir del 1 de octubre de 2027, mientras que la asignación federal bajo la Sección 1108 enfrenta una reducción significativa al culminar las asignaciones temporeras.

Estos cambios coinciden en el tiempo y crean lo que se ha denominado el precipicio de Medicaid de 2027, un escenario que requiere atención y planificación antes de que comiencen a materializarse sus efectos.

Como parte de la discusión, el comisionado residente presentó la necesidad de evaluar una estructura de financiamiento más estable para el programa, incluyendo una propuesta para el próximo Congreso que eliminaría el tope de la Sección 1108 y permitiría que el financiamiento federal continúe respondiendo a los gastos elegibles de Medicaid, como ocurre en los estados, sujeto al límite estatutario aplicable al porciento de participación federal.

La conversación con el sector hospitalario también incluyó otros asuntos que inciden sobre la estabilidad del sistema de salud, entre ellos Medicare Advantage, la retención de profesionales, los hospitales y centros de salud 330, la salud mental, la prevención, la investigación, la salud materna y los servicios comunitarios.

El Comisionado Residente repasó además las gestiones que ha realizado durante los últimos meses para fortalecer la coordinación entre el gobierno de Puerto Rico, el sector de salud y los interlocutores en Washington. Entre estas se encuentran sus reuniones con funcionarios federales y congresistas, su testimonio ante el Comité de Energía y Comercio de la Cámara de Representantes, la coordinación de esfuerzos bipartidistas sobre Medicare Advantage y las reuniones recientes con la gobernadora y representantes del sector de salud para revisar datos y recomendaciones de política pública.

De cara al próximo Congreso, el comisionado residente señaló la importancia de que Puerto Rico llegue a Washington con información sólida sobre costos, utilización de servicios, necesidades de los pacientes y las condiciones que enfrentan los proveedores de salud.

La participación ante la Asociación de Hospitales forma parte de los esfuerzos de el Comisionado Residente para mantener la discusión sobre Medicaid y Medicare Advantage conectada con los hospitales, profesionales y demás sectores que sostienen diariamente el sistema de salud de Puerto Rico.

title: Hoyer Statement on September Jobs Report
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement on the September jobs report:

“The September jobs report, which shows that just 29,000 jobs were added to the economy last month and that unemployment ticked up to 4.2%, reflects the uncertainty Americans feel toward the job market and the economy as this Administration’s economic policies do little to address the tough challenges they face every day. For many, the American Dream is feeling farther out of reach as mortgage rates and inflation rise and real wages fall. Across the country, a lack of affordable housing is driving young people out of other communities, and prices for gas, diesel, and groceries continue to climb. However, President Trump still characterizes the affordability crisis as ‘fake,’ and Republicans in Congress have only made it worse.

“The verdict is clear: this Administration does not put working Americans first. Republicans in Congress are failing to deliver on affordability, instead fixated on President Trump’s war of choice with Iran, which has forced Americans to spend $100 billion more on fuel. If returned to the Majority, Democrats are ready to address the affordability crisis and will fight to ensure that our government of the people and by the people always works for the people.”

title: Hudson Hosts FCC Chairman Carr in Moore County to Highlight American Drone Dominance, Next Generation 911
text:
ABERDEEN, N.C. – Today, U.S. Representative Richard Hudson (NC-09), Chairman of the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Telecommunications, hosted Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr in Moore County for visits highlighting American drone manufacturing and modern emergency communications.

Hudson and Carr toured Dracoe’s manufacturing facility in Aberdeen before visiting the Moore County 911 Center, where they met with local first responders and saw Next Generation 911 technology in action.

“From building American-made drones right here near Fort Bragg to giving our first responders the latest technology when somebody calls 911, Moore County is doing some incredible work,” said Rep. Hudson. “I was proud to bring Chairman Carr here to what we like to call the Silicon Valley of American Drone Dominance to see firsthand what the FCC can do to facilitate the development of an American drone industry.”

“It was great to join Chairman Hudson in Moore County today, to visit with some of North Carolina’s dedicated defense manufacturers and 911 dispatchers. Thanks to Chairman Hudson’s strong leadership in Congress, the cutting edge of U.S. drone technology is being unleashed right in the heart of central North Carolina, which means more jobs and opportunity for so many hardworking Tar Heels,” said Chairman Carr.

At Dracoe, Hudson and Carr toured the veteran-owned company’s manufacturing operation and met with employees to discuss the growing domestic drone industry and the FCC’s role in emerging drone technology.

Hudson and Carr then visited the Moore County 911 Center, where they met with Sheriff Ronnie Fields, public safety officials, dispatchers, and county leaders to see how Moore County is using Next Generation 911 technology.

Background

Dracoe designs and manufactures small drones and components used for defense and counter-drone training. The U.S. Army evaluated a Dracoe target-management capability during a counter-drone exercise earlier this year.

The visit also comes as the FCC takes steps affecting the domestic drone market. In December, the Commission added foreign-produced drones and critical components to its Covered List, generally preventing new covered models from receiving the equipment authorization required for import and sale in the United States. Previously authorized drones are not affected.

NG911 replaces aging 911 infrastructure with modern, internet-based technology capable of supporting better location information, text and multimedia, stronger cybersecurity, and improved communication between emergency call centers and first responders.

Hudson is leading the bipartisan Next Generation 9-1-1 Act with Rep. Troy Carter (LA-02). The legislation would establish a federal grant program to help states, tribes, and local 911 centers upgrade outdated systems and support deployment, maintenance, cybersecurity, training, and public education.

The visits also come as the FCC considers a broader review of the nation’s 911 framework and how federal policy should evolve as emergency communications technology advances.

Moore County has operated on North Carolina’s Next Generation 911 network since 2021 and also offers Text-to-911 for people who cannot safely make a voice call.

title: Hudson Remembers Former First Lady Dottie Martin
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Representative Richard Hudson (NC-09) shared the following statement honoring the life and legacy of former North Carolina First Lady Dottie Martin, wife of his friend and mentor, Governor Jim Martin:

“Renee and I were saddened to learn of the passing of the extraordinary Dottie Martin, former First Lady of North Carolina. We are praying for my friend and mentor, Governor Jim Martin and the entire Martin family.

"Dottie Martin lived a life of significance with a style and grace that was unmatched. She transformed the role of First Lady as a champion for protecting children and combating child abuse, to fighting substance abuse, to her work on her beloved wildflower program.

"Dottie Martin was ahead of her time, and I fondly think of her often as I travel the highways of North Carolina and see the beautiful wildflowers planted across our state. Dottie Martin will be missed, but her life and legacy will never be forgotten,” said Rep. Hudson.

title: Brownley, Larsen, Veasey Introduce Legislation to Combat Discriminatory Voter ID Laws
text:
Washington, DC – Today, Congresswoman Julia Brownley (CA-26) joined Congressman Rick Larsen (WA-02) and Congressman Mark Veasey (TX-33) in introducing the America Votes Act, legislation to protect U.S. citizens who face disenfranchisement because of restrictive voter identification (ID) laws.

Despite claims that restrictive voter ID laws are necessary to prevent voter impersonation, there is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in the United States. Some state legislatures across the country continue to use excessively restrictive voter ID laws to target and deny certain Americans the right to vote. Restrictive voter ID laws disproportionately impact Black and transgender Americans, perpetuating the systematic disenfranchisement of certain groups in the United States.

In 2026, a total of 36 states require voters to show identification to cast a ballot, and 24 of those states require voters to present identification with a photograph. These identification requirements are in addition to those under federal law to register to vote.

The America Votes Act would establish new federal protections for registered voters to affirm their identity by submitting a sworn, written statement, even if they do not have a government-issued ID. Voters who sign a sworn, written statement can vote using a standard, non-provisional ­­ballot. The legislation is modeled on a successful Washington state law that allows voters to affirm their identity by submitting a similar written statement along with their mail-in ballot.

The full text of the America Votes Act can be found here.

In addition to Brownley, the America Votes Act is cosponsored by Representatives Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-AL), Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Hank Johnson (GA-04), Nanette Barragán (CA-44), Betty McCollum (MN-04), and André Carson (IL-07).

title: Kaptur Applauds Drug-Free Communities Award to Support Williams County

The award will support the health department’s Educating Communities on Healthy Opportunities (ECHO) Coalition, which works to prevent substance abuse in youth and adults throughout Williams County.

title: Kennedy Condemns Trump Administration’s  $17 Million Expansion of ICE Detention Facility in Batavia
text:
At Kennedy’s Demand, DHS Finally Discloses Details of Batavia ICE Facility Expansion - New $17 Million Structure Will House Women Detainees

In a Response to Kennedy’s Letter Written in His Oversight Capacity, DHS's Own Numbers Show More Than 70% of Batavia Detainees Have No Criminal Record, Contradicting Administration's "Worst of the Worst" Claims

BUFFALO, N.Y. – Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26), a member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, today condemned the Trump administration's plan to build a new detention facility at the Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia at a cost to taxpayers of nearly $17 million funded by Trump and Congressional Republicans' Big Ugly Bill. He also exposed the administration's own admission that the vast majority of the people it is detaining in Western New York have no criminal record.

In a response to Kennedy's July 8 oversight letter, which arrived on September 29, 76 days past his July 15 deadline, the Department of Homeland Security disclosed that 72 percent of detainees at Batavia have no criminal record. Rather than defend the expansion as a public safety measure, DHS wrote that known criminal history "is not a prerequisite for immigration enforcement action." Secretary Markwayne Mullin instead pointed to the 2024 election, writing that the department intends to deliver "mass deportations."

"This administration told the American people it was going after the worst of the worst. Now they've admitted in writing that it isn't true. More than 70 percent of the people held in Batavia have no criminal record, and DHS says that doesn't matter," said Congressman Kennedy. "It took them more than two months to answer, and they still can't keep their story straight about what they're building. Meanwhile, the calls coming into my office tell the real story. Every single day we’re getting calls about people who are picked up by ICE while dropping their kids off at school or going to work. People that are here lawfully are feeling threatened and afraid. This administration must be held accountable.”

"Western New Yorkers are working hard to put food on the table, keep up with their utility bills, fill their gas tanks, and afford their medical bills. Our government should be focused on making life more affordable," Kennedy continued. "Instead, the Trump administration is spending nearly $17 million to enact its cruel and inhumane agenda.”

DHS's response contradicts itself. ICE's contract approval describes a "soft sided temporary detention facility," while DHS's answers refer to a "hard-sided" structure.”

The department also revealed that ICE plans to hold women at the new facility and that men could be held there as well "if the needs of the service dictate."

Kennedy's letter requested all records related to the decision to build the facility, including cost estimates and communications with contractors. DHS provided a single approval memo, with pricing details and the planned number of beds redacted. It said staffing levels for the facility are "still being discussed."

In July, Kennedy warned that the Trump administration has a pattern of rapidly building soft-sided tents and makeshift detention facilities without ensuring detainee health and safety, and demanded that DHS halt construction at Batavia. He will continue to press DHS for answers and to oppose the expansion of ICE detention in Western New York.

Read Congressman Kennedy’s oversight letter here.

title: Kiggans, EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi Celebrate $92 Million in Grant Awards for Conservation Efforts in the Chesapeake Bay
text:
SMITHFIELD, VA — Today, Congresswoman Jen Kiggans (VA-02) was joined by Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi and the James River Association at Windsor Castle Park for a Chesapeake Bay funding announcement and a tour of the park’s living shoreline. The EPA, along with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF), announced a total conservation impact of $92 million for the Chesapeake Bay watershed.

Following the announcement, Congresswoman Kiggans and Deputy Administrator Fotouhi visited Windsor Castle Park’s living shorelines, protected coastal edges designed to prevent erosion near a public trail by using native plants and sand instead of concrete seawalls. The project was completed in 2021 in collaboration with the James River Association.

Congresswoman Kiggans said, “The Chesapeake Bay is one of the most beautiful natural treasures our Commonwealth has to offer, and one that should be preserved for future generations to enjoy. I’m grateful to the EPA and the NFWF for investing in the conservation and preservation of the Chesapeake Bay watershed. This funding will support commonsense, on-the-ground projects that protect our waterways, strengthen our coastal communities, and preserve the natural resources that are so important to Virginia’s economy and way of life.”

“I’d like to thank the James River Association for its promotion of responsible environmental stewardship, as well as Deputy Administrator Fotouhi for coming to Virginia’s Second District to celebrate this important day. I look forward to continuing to work with the Deputy Administrator and the EPA on commonsense preservation efforts to protect Virginia’s native species and its communities,” Kiggans concluded.

The grant awards announced today by EPA and NFWF totaled more than $39 million. However, the 83 new awards will leverage an additional $53 million in non-federal matching contributions to generate a total conservation impact of $92 million.

“Through these grants, EPA is working collaboratively with our local partners to deliver practical restoration solutions that improve water quality, restore habitat, and support the vital Chesapeake Bay watershed. These improvements will have a significant impact of the more than 1,800 local communities that depend on the watershed to support their economies,” said EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi. “This type of funding has a proven track record of delivering tangible environmental results and is a shining example of taxpayer dollars being put to accomplishing EPA’s core mission.”

The 83 grants were awarded through the Chesapeake Bay Innovative Nutrient and Sediment Reduction Grants and Small Watershed Grants programs, which are administered by the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.

As the representative of a coastal district, Congresswoman Kiggans serves on the House Committee on Natural Resources and remains committed to supporting legislation that protects our Chesapeake Bay, preserves Virginia’s wildlife and waterways, and strengthens the coastal communities that call them home.
