title: At CMU Summit, Rep. Summer Lee Calls for Stronger Community Protections as AI Data Centers Expand Across Pennsylvania
text:
VIDEO (Dropbox)

PITTSBURGH, PA – OCTOBER 2, 2026 — Today, Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) joined community organizers, researchers, environmental advocates, labor leaders, and policymakers at Carnegie Mellon University's Community-Centered AI Infrastructure Summit to call for stronger protections for Pennsylvania communities facing the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers.

The statewide summit, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University in partnership with Data & Society, the Center for Coalfield Justice, and the Pennsylvania Climate Equity Table, brought together residents and experts to examine the growing demands AI infrastructure places on Pennsylvania's electricity grid, water resources, workforce, and environment. Participants also explored policy solutions and community organizing strategies to inform a Community Action Plan for AI Infrastructure.

Drawing on her experience growing up in the Mon Valley, Rep. Lee warned against repeating the mistakes of Pennsylvania's industrial past, when corporations generated enormous wealth while working-class communities were left to bear the costs of pollution, disinvestment, and broken promises.

“Here in the Pittsburgh area, we have communities that have been similarly sacrificed. I grew up in one of them,” said Rep. Lee. “ We know what it looks like when these choices are made for us, but not with us. I believe that we have to establish regulatory frameworks before we suffer its consequences. Leading on AI doesn't mean building more data centers at any cost or racing toward superintelligence without considering the consequences. It means making sure that AI actually improves life for all of us, not just the CEOs or oligarchs.”

During the summit, Rep. Lee highlighted her cosponsorship of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, which would temporarily pause new data center construction and the expansion of existing facilities until Congress establishes comprehensive federal safeguards addressing AI's economic, environmental, and safety impacts. She emphasized that the pause must give lawmakers time to establish meaningful protections for communities already facing the consequences of unchecked development.

Rep. Lee called for stronger federal, state, and local regulations to address rising electricity and water costs, establish labor standards, increase community transparency, and account for the cumulative environmental and health impacts of industrial development. Drawing on her visit to Memphis, Tennessee, where residents are organizing against the environmental and noise pollution associated with xAI's data center operations, Rep. Lee warned against repeating the mistakes of Pennsylvania's industrial past and allowing corporations to make decisions that affect communities without their input.

Rep. Lee also connected the expansion of AI infrastructure to broader concerns about civil rights, workers' livelihoods, environmental harms, and corporate influence in Washington. She warned that unchecked AI could reinforce existing discrimination in healthcare, employment, and policing, while the communities bearing the environmental and economic costs of its expansion are left without meaningful protections. She also highlighted her Abolish Super PACs Act, arguing that unlimited corporate spending in elections undermines Congress's ability to establish regulations that prioritize the public over corporate profits.

Footage of Rep. Lee’s remarks can be found here.

Rep. Lee has championed legislation to protect communities, workers, and civil rights as artificial intelligence expands. She is a cosponsor of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, which would temporarily pause new data center construction and expansion until Congress establishes comprehensive federal safeguards addressing AI's economic, environmental, and safety impacts. Alongside Senator Ed Markey, Rep. Lee introduced the Eliminating BIAS Act, which would establish dedicated civil rights offices in federal agencies that use or oversee AI to combat algorithmic discrimination. She also co-leads theAI Civil Rights Act, which would strengthen protections against AI-driven discrimination in housing, healthcare, employment, and other essential services.

title: Reps. Lee, Deluzio, Khanna Press UPMC to Bargain in Good Faith With Nearly 900 Magee Healthcare Workers
text:
Letter Text (PDF)

PITTSBURGH, PA – October 2, 2026 — Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) alongside Rep. Chris Deluzio (PA-17) and Rep. Ro Khanna (CA-17), called on The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC) to bargain in good faith with nearly 900 nurses, nurse practitioners, and midwives at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital who have spent approximately eight months negotiating their first union contract.

In a letter to UPMC President and CEO Leslie Davis, the lawmakers raised concerns they have heard from workers and organizers about staffing levels, excessive workloads, and conditions that healthcare professionals say can make it harder to provide patients with the level of care they deserve.

The lawmakers specifically pointed to reports that nurses are routinely responsible for more patients than nationally recognized clinical standards recommend, including instances in which one labor and delivery nurse may be responsible for two or three patients even though professional staffing standards call for dedicated nursing care for a patient in active labor.

“For approximately eight months, nearly 900 health care professionals at UPMC Magee have been negotiating for a contract that reflects the critical role they play in caring for patients and families throughout western Pennsylvania,” the lawmakers wrote. “These workers have raised serious concerns about inadequate staffing, excessive workloads, and conditions that prevent them from consistently providing the level of care their patients deserve. UPMC has a responsibility to listen to these frontline professionals and work constructively to resolve their concerns without unnecessary delays.”

Contract negotiations between UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital, University of Pittsburgh Physicians, and SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania began in January. UPMC reported that the parties held their 38th bargaining session on September 22 and have reached tentative agreements on several issues as negotiations continue.

These staffing concerns come as Allegheny County continues to face seriousracial disparities in maternal health. In 2023, the rate of preventable hospitalizations among Black women was 3.3 times higher than among White women in Allegheny County. The disparities are especially stark in Pittsburgh, where previous reports found that Black women were more likely to die during pregnancy than their peers in 97% of comparable U.S. cities.

Rep. Lee has made confronting the Black maternal health crisis a focus of her work in Congress, including pressing HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. during Black Maternal Health Week over threats to maternal health research and community-based programs, joining congressional efforts to expand access to midwifery care, and strongly supporting the Black Maternal Health Momnibus Act to invest in community-based care, strengthen and diversify the perinatal workforce, improve maternal health data collection, and expand maternal mental health support.

In their letter, Reps. Lee, Deluzio, and Khanna emphasized that safe staffing and workplace protections are critical to patient safety, retaining experienced healthcare workers, reducing exhaustion and burnout, and ensuring hospitals can respond effectively to emergencies.

“UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital is a vital institution that generations of western Pennsylvanians have relied upon for obstetric, neonatal, reproductive, and specialized health care,” the lawmakers wrote. “We will continue to monitor UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital actions closely and strongly encourage UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital, in accordance with the law, to bargain a fair contract in good faith with these workers.”

Workers at Magee have publicly advocated for staffing standards based on recommendations from national professional organizations. Those proposals include dedicated nursing care for patients who are laboring or being induced, as well as staffing standards for neonatal intensive care, postpartum care, emergency care, oncology, and other hospital units.

The full letter can be read HERE and letter text is below:

September 22, 2026

Dear Ms. Davis:

We write to urge the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC) to bargain in good faith, as required by federal law, with the nurses, nurse practitioners, and midwives at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital. As you know, workers have a right to organize and advocate for improvements in their wages and working conditions, as well as engage in protected concerted activity under Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA).

We have received troubling reports from our constituents and organizers that nurses are routinely assigned more patients than nationally recognized clinical standards recommend. Nurses have described situations in which a single labor and delivery nurse may be responsible for two or three patients, even though established standards call for a patient in active labor to receive dedicated nursing care.

For approximately eight months, nearly 900 health care professionals at UPMC Magee have been negotiating for a contract that reflects the critical role they play in caring for patients and families throughout western Pennsylvania. These workers have raised serious concerns about inadequate staffing, excessive workloads, and conditions that prevent them from consistently providing the level of care their patients deserve. UPMC has a responsibility to listen to these frontline professionals and work constructively to resolve their concerns without unnecessary delays.

Safe staffing and other workplace protections are fundamental to patient safety, retaining experienced nurses, protecting workers from exhaustion and burnout, and ensuring that hospitals remain prepared to respond to emergencies.

UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital is a vital institution that generations of western Pennsylvanians have relied upon for obstetric, neonatal, reproductive, and specialized health care. We will continue to monitor UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital actions closely and strongly encourage UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital, in accordance with the law, to bargain a fair contract in good faith with these workers.

Thank you for your attention to these issues.

Sincerely,

Summer Lee

Member of Congress

Chris Deluzio

Member of Congress

Ro Khanna

Member of Congress

title: Reps. Tlaib, Pressley, Senator Markey Announce Legislation to Stop Big Banks from Bankrolling the Climate Crisis
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) and Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), and Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, today announced the reintroduction of the Fossil Free Finance Act. The legislation would require banks to adopt emission transition plans to reduce financial sector emissions and deforestation risks.

Under this legislation, large bank holding companies would be required to implement plans to reduce financial sector emissions 50 percent by 2035 and reach zero financial sector emissions by 2050. Additionally, it would require banks to discontinue financing for new or expanded fossil fuel projects within 60 days of enactment, immediately discontinue thermal coal financing and facilitation, and eliminate facilitation of deforestation risk commodities. Despite climate-driven wildfires, floods, and other disasters continuing to devastate regions across the country, banks continue to invest in contributing fossil fuel projects. Plans created from this legislation will help the financial sector align with science-based projections for emissions.

“Our financial institutions and banks are funding the pollution of our air and water that make us sicker. They choose to invest billions of dollars in dirty fossil fuel projects,” said Rep. Tlaib. “Instead of acting to protect us, the Federal Reserve allowed these banks to finance the destruction of our planet and our health. I’m taking action with Senator Markey and Congresswoman Pressley to require the Federal Reserve to finally do something and address the dangers of our climate crisis.”

“Our economy and global financial systems have a codependent relationship with the fossil fuel industry. We cannot wait for big banks to address the very climate crisis they are financing if we are serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation. It’s like giving an arsonist a hose for one hand while they hold a gas can in the other,” said Senator Markey. “The Fossil Free Finance Act would require our financial institutions, including banks, to protect Americans’ savings, investments, and our economy by addressing the threats posed by climate change. We need to put the planet over profit and get fossil fuels out of our finances.”

“We should be using every tool available to protect our planet, our people, and our economy, and one way we can do that is by stopping giant banks from financing fossil fuel projects,” said Rep. Pressley. “Our Fossil Free Finance Act would help confront the climate crisis by stopping financial institutions, including our nation’s largest banks, from providing trillions in fossil fuel financing and deepening the health inequities and harms that already plague our communities. I’m grateful to Senator Markey and Congresswoman Tlaib for their ongoing partnership on this bill to take urgent action to help prevent a massive, climate-induced economic collapse.”

“Major US banks’ ongoing finance for fossil fuel expansion is driving worsening climate change and putting the entire financial system and public at risk,” said Alex Martin, Climate Finance Policy Director at Americans for Financial Reform. “The Fossil Free Finance Act would recognize the role that fossil fuel finance plays in driving climate-related financial risk, and require banks to develop climate action plans that address those risks, creating a critical safeguard for the public and the financial system.”

“While financial policymakers around the world actively work to decarbonize their economies, U.S. policymakers have fallen behind, leaving our financial system exposed to the impacts of climate change,” said David Arkush, Director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program. “Financial institutions continue to finance, invest, and underwrite unnecessary projects—creating systemic risks that can reverberate across the economy. Rather than continuing to create risks for the financial system, large and systemically important financial institutions should be required to reduce their financed and facilitated emissions in line with science-driven targets. Neither Congress nor the Federal Reserve should wait for a financial crisis to address climate-related financial risk.”

The Fossil Free Finance Act of 2026 would address climate-related threats to financial stability and help align the financial sector with science-based emissions targets by redefining financial sector emissions, mandating bank holding companies with at least $50 billion in assets to align with science-based emissions targets, and requiring the Federal Reserve to report to Congress on financial sector emissions, commitments by covered institutions, progress toward emissions targets, regulatory gaps, data challenges, and equitable transition needs.

The Fossil Free Finance Act of 2026 is cosponsored by Senators Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

The legislation is endorsed by Public Citizen and Americans for Financial Reform.

Senator Markey, and Reps. Tlaib, Pressley, and former Rep. Mondaire Jones (NY-17) first introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act during the 117th Congress in September 2021. Senator Markey first reintroduced the legislation with Senator Merkley in March 2023.

title: Underwood Introduces Bipartisan Legislation to Train More Nurses
text:
WASHINGTON—Representatives Lauren Underwood, Jen Kiggans (VA-02), and Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), introduced the Educating Future Nurses Act to expand clinical education and training opportunities for future Advanced Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs). As costs explode and our health care system confronts the historic crisis caused by Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill, fixing gaps in nursing education is critical to keeping health care affordable and accessible.

Underwood’s legislation would create permanent federal funding for hospitals to partner with schools of nursing and community-based care settings to address clinical training costs for graduate nursing students.

“In every corner of our country, nurses are doing critical work to support the health and well-being of our communities. We’re providing excellent clinical care, conducting important research, and carrying out the public health initiatives that keep our families safe and healthy,” said Rep. Underwood. “But our profession is under unprecedented attack, particularly for nurses who are looking to further their education. America needs more nurses, not fewer. Our legislation will strengthen graduate-level nursing education and make sure these dedicated professionals get more support for this vitally important training.”

“As a geriatric nurse practitioner and Congressional Nursing Caucus co-chair, I know that a strong nursing workforce starts with ensuring our future nurses have the training and resources they need to effectively care for their patients. Unfortunately, there are too many aspiring advanced practice nurses who face barriers from accessing the education required to complete their training. I’m proud to join my caucus co-chair, Congresswoman Underwood, to introduce the Educating Future Nurses Act to strengthen partnerships between our hospitals, nursing schools, and communities and expand clinical training opportunities for the next generation of nurses.” Said Rep. Kiggans.

"Health care costs are rising and more people are reliant on hospitals and emergency care,” said Rep. Bonamici."Our country is in desperate need of more nurses, including advanced practice nurses, but there are too many barriers to graduate education. As Co-Chair of the Congressional Nursing Caucus, I stand firmly behind the Educating Future Nurses Act and the opportunities it would create for nurses to advance in their careers and bolster the health care workforce."

“The Educating Future Nurses Act is an important step toward addressing our nation’s ongoing nursing shortage and ensuring that all Americans have access to high-quality healthcare,” said Dr. Julie Sanford, Chair of the Board of Directors of the American Association and Colleges of Nursing. “Enabling partnerships between hospitals and nursing schools is an innovative approach to expanding the nursing workforce."

“We applaud Congresswoman Underwood and our congressional champions for their continued support of nursing education,” said Dr. Deborah Trautman, President and Chief Executive Officer of the American Association of Colleges of Nursing. “By building on the success of the Graduate Nurse Education demonstration program, the Educating Future Nurses Act will have a profound impact on sustaining the nation’s Advanced Practice Registered Nursing workforce and access to care for all patients in need.”

The cost of clinical training has limited the number of APRN students that hospitals can accept. Funding from the Educating Future Nurses Act would help these hospitals accept APRN students, enabling them to train and work in geographically diverse areas, especially rural and underserved communities.

The legislation builds on a similar program created under the Affordable Care Act (ACA). The ACA’s Graduate Nurse Education Demonstration Program provided federal funding to hospitals to pay for the clinical training costs of APRNs.

The Educating Future Nurses Act has been endorsed by 30+ leading nursing organizations in Illinois and across the country, including the American Association of Colleges of Nursing and the American Association of Nurse Anesthesiology.

title: Rep. Vasquez Secures $96 Million to Build New Alamo Navajo Health Center
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) secured $96 million in federal funding from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to build a new, technologically advanced health center at the Alamo Navajo Chapter. The health center will serve over 2,600 Tribal residents living in the communities of Alamo, Magdalena, and Socorro.

“This $96 million investment is a major step toward ensuring the Alamo Navajo community has access to the quality health care it deserves,” said Vasquez. “For too long, Tribal communities have been denied access to reliable healthcare – being forced to drive incredibly long distances and go to great lengths just to see a doctor. This project will bring care closer to home, and I’m proud to deliver this funding and will continue working to ensure the federal government is serving New Mexico’s Tribal communities.”

The $96 million award will support the construction of a new 70,000 gross square feet (GSF) health center and will be a modern, state-of-the-art, advanced facility to provide health care services specifically designed to meet the needs of the Alamo Navajo Chapter.

This funding comes from the Interior Appropriations bill, which passed with strong bipartisan support. Congressman Vasquez also secured key funding and resources for New Mexico in the bill, including $1,092,000 for the Ramah Navajo Drinking Water Improvement project and over $3 million in projects to improve public safety and infrastructure in Southern New Mexico.

Vasquez has consistently worked to support New Mexico’s Tribal communities:

Led the Tribal HUD-VASH Act to provide housing assistance and support services for Native American veterans.

Voted to extend the Special Diabetes Program for Indians to help address health disparities in Tribal communities.

Championed the bipartisan Indian Programs Advance Appropriations Act to fulfill the US government's trust and treaty responsibilities and provide full and consistent funding for IHS and BIE programs.

Led the Parity for Tribal Law Enforcement Act to enhance public safety within Tribal communities.

title: Vindman, Virginia Democrats Release Statement on 8th Anniversary of Jamal Khashoggi’s Murder
text:
The Lawmakers Also Renewed Their Call for Trump to Release the Transcript of His 2019 Call with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Following Khashoggi’s Murder

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Representatives Eugene Vindman (Va.-07), James Walkinshaw (Va.-11), Bobby Scott (Va.-03), Don Beyer (Va.-08), Jennifer McClellan (Va.-04), and Suhas Subramanyam (Va.-10) released the following statement on the eighth anniversary of the murder of Jamal Khashoggi.

“Eight years ago today, Virginia resident and journalist Jamal Khashoggi was brutally murdered inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. His murder was an unconscionable attack on a journalist and a Virginia resident, and his family and the American people deserve the full truth about what happened and what followed.

“That includes transparency about President Trump’s 2019 call with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Congressman Vindman reviewed the transcript of that call while serving as a lawyer on the National Security Council, and we believe the American people deserve to see it for themselves.

“As members of Virginia’s congressional delegation, we will continue pressing for the transparency and accountability that this case demands. If President Trump will not release the transcript now, we will force him to do it in the next Congress when Democrats are in charge.

“Eight years is far too long to wait for answers. President Trump should declassify and release the transcript and give the Khashoggi family and the American people the truth they deserve.”

BACKGROUND

Jamal Khashoggi, a Washington Post journalist and U.S. resident, was murdered inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in October 2018 — an assassination that drew global condemnation and raised serious questions about Saudi Arabia’s leadership and the Trump administration’s response.

In November 2025, Vindman demanded that the White House release the transcript of a “shocking” 2019 call that took place between President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman following Khashoggi’s murder. Vindman reviewed this call while serving as a staff lawyer on Trump’s National Security Council.

That same month, he led 37 lawmakers in sending a letter to President Trump calling for the immediate release of the transcript. He also hosted a press conference alongside Hanan Elatr Khashoggi — Khashoggi’s wife — and U.S. Representatives Jamie Raskin (Md.-08) and Suhas Subramanyam (Va.-11) to urge President Trump to release the transcript of the call.

In October 2025, Congressman Walkinshaw and Senators Kaine and Warner introduced a bicameral resolution commemorating the seventh anniversary of Khashoggi’s murder and calling for accountability. The resolution also called for the Government of Saudi Arabia to release wrongfully detained individuals, respect the rights of Saudi citizens, and ensure the protection of the freedoms of assembly, association, and the press.

Khashoggi was a resident of Virginia’s 11th District, which was formerly represented by the late Congressman Gerry Connolly and is now represented by Walkinshaw.

###

title: Walkinshaw Introduces Bill to Fix Personnel Record Errors Delaying Federal Workers’ Retirement and Benefits
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11), a member of the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, today introduced the Federal Employee Records Relief Act, legislation to help former federal employees obtain missing personnel records, fix administrative errors and navigate their earned benefits. Missing or inaccurate records can delay retirement processing, complicate health coverage and interfere with future employment.

“Federal employees have suffered enough under the Trump administration’s mass firings and attacks on our civil service. They should not have to chase down missing paperwork to document their service and access the benefits they earned,” said Congressman Walkinshaw. “My bill would require the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and federal agencies to help former employees get their records, fix errors and get clear answers about their benefits. These public servants deserve better.”

The bill would require OPM, working with former employing agencies, to provide personnel records, correct administrative errors and offer written benefits information and coordination assistance, including information about health coverage continuation options.

Federal employees who separated for any reason on or after January 20, 2025, including retirees, would have four years after enactment to submit requests.

“Too often, federal employees leave government service only to find themselves trapped in bureaucratic limbo, waiting months for agencies and OPM to correct records or process paperwork they need to collect benefits, secure loans, or move on to their next job. This commonsense legislation creates a clear, centralized, and time-limited process to fix those problems so former federal employees are not forced to keep paying the price for administrative failures that are beyond their control,” said the National Federation of Federal Employees.

“Mass firings and pressure campaigns to force out federal employees have thrown thousands of dedicated civil servants into chaos. Now many are left hanging, trapped by botched personnel records and processing delays that stand between them and their next job, their retirement, and the benefits they earned. The Federal Employee Records Relief Act will give these workers a clear path to correct their records and move forward with their lives. NTEU applauds Rep. Walkinshaw for his work on this bill and for standing up for federal employees and their families,” said Doreen Greenwald, National President, National Treasury Employees Union.

Original cosponsors include Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D.C.), Don Beyer (VA-08), Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05), Stephen F. Lynch (MA-08), Glenn Ivey (MD-04) and Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10).

title: Sen. Banks Joins 126 Lawmakers Urging an Investigation into Planned Parenthood
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Yesterday, Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) joined Senator James Lankford (R-Okla.), Representative Chris Smith (R-N.J.) and 124 congressional colleagues in calling on the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) to investigate Planned Parenthood Federation of America and its affiliates for potential waste, fraud, abuse, and misuse of taxpayer dollars.

The lawmakers cited the Small Business Administration’s ongoing investigation into whether Planned Parenthood affiliates improperly received $88 million in Paycheck Protection Program loans during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as reports alleging violations of federal criminal laws and mandatory state child-abuse reporting requirements.

Read the Fox News Exclusive here.

Read the full letter here or below.

Dear Inspector General Bell,

We write to request that the Office of Inspector General (OIG) review and, if appropriate, initiate an investigation into the activities of Planned Parenthood Federation of America, Inc. and the organization’s affiliates, which receive federal funding connected to programs administered by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

Concerns have long been raised regarding the organization’s compliance with applicable federal laws, regulations, and program requirements governing the receipt and use of federal funds. In particular, these concerns relate to whether Planned Parenthood Federation of America, Inc., and the organization’s affiliates have adhered to applicable requirements governing program integrity, financial accountability, and the proper use of funds provided through HHS-administered programs.

Just this year, the Small Business Administration opened an investigation into whether Planned Parenthood affiliates illegally received $88 million in loans during the COVID-19 pandemic. This is in addition to numerous other reports of fraud, making false statements, violating federal criminal laws, and knowingly failing to disclose violations of criminal law. For example, state laws require medical professionals to report suspected child abuse or neglect and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services require facilities and practitioners to comply with mandatory state reporting laws, but there are reports that Planned Parenthood fails to comply.

Given the significant taxpayer resources that flow through federal health and human services programs, it is critical that recipient organizations operate with transparency, integrity, and full compliance with federal standards. Accordingly, we respectfully request that the OIG:

Review the federal funding streams received by Planned Parenthood Federation of America, Inc., and the organization’s affiliates through HHS programs, grants, contracts, or subawards.

Assess whether Planned Parenthood Federation of America, Inc., and the organization’s affiliates have complied with applicable statutory, regulatory, and grant conditions associated with those funds.

Determine whether any evidence exists of fraud, waste, abuse, misrepresentation, or other violations affecting federal health programs.

Evaluate whether enforcement actions, including administrative remedies, suspension, exclusion from federal health care programs, or referral to the appropriate authorities, may be warranted if misconduct is identified.

We also ask that the OIG coordinate with relevant oversight bodies within the Department, including the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, and also with the Office of Management and Budget to ensure a comprehensive review of the organization’s activities.

Thank you for your continued commitment to protecting the integrity of federal health programs and safeguarding taxpayer dollars.

title: Bennet, Ansari, Padilla, Hickenlooper, Schiff, Luján Introduce Legislation to Protect Public Lands and Taxpayers from Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells
text:
Denver — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet and U.S. Representative Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) led U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) to introduce the Stop Orphaned Wells Act, legislation that would prevent oil and gas companies from abandoning oil wells on public lands, a practice that shifts well cleanup costs from oil and gas companies to the American taxpayer.

“For too long, taxpayers have footed the bill to clean up abandoned wells after companies walk away from their responsibilities,” said Bennet. “As the Trump administration moves to weaken the safeguards that hold companies accountable, Congress must protect taxpayers and the public lands that power Colorado’s outdoor economy, while making sure oil and gas companies pay the cost of cleanup, rather than Colorado’s future generations.”

“Trump asked oil and gas executives to bankroll his campaign with a $1 billion contribution in exchange for a big payback. Meanwhile, Americans are left footing the bill for the damage they leave behind,” said Ansari. “Orphaned wells threaten our water, wildlife, and air. I’m proud to lead the effort alongside Senator Bennet to make the oil and gas industry clean up its own mess. Our bill would ensure oil and gas companies pay to clean up the wells they abandon.”

“Across California, there are over 5,000 orphaned oil wells that pose a threat to the health and safety of our communities and the environment,” said Padilla. “When wells are left abandoned, drinking water is polluted, greenhouse gases are emitted, and the climate crisis is accelerated. This bill will help ensure orphaned oil and gas wells are plugged so Californians and communities across the country are protected from toxic emissions and contaminated air and water.”

“Abandoned wells put Colorado communities in danger,” said Hickenlooper. “As Governor, we capped as many of these wells as we could, and that work continues here in the Senate, where we’re protecting taxpayers from getting stuck with the bill. Capping wells creates jobs and lowers pollution. It’s a win-win.”

“Oil companies can’t just walk away from abandoned oil and gas wells and leave taxpayers to bear the cleanup costs,” said Schiff. “I’m joining Senator Bennet and other colleagues to make sure that Big Oil is responsible for cleaning up their messes. Americans should not have to deal with the consequences of an oil company’s negligence.”

“In New Mexico and across the country, abandoned wells pose serious environmental harm and threaten the health of our communities,” said Luján. “We must ensure that oil and gas companies are held accountable and that taxpayers are not on the hook for the cost of cleanup. I’ve long fought to address abandoned wells, including championing the REGROW Act that was passed into law, and continue to work to ensure we identify and plug the thousands of abandoned wells nationwide. That’s why I’m cosponsoring this legislation to prevent companies from abandoning their wells and help reduce the number of abandoned wells in New Mexico and across the country.”

“When an oil and gas company goes bankrupt, New Mexicans shouldn’t be the ones left to pick up the tab for cleanup costs,” said Heinrich. “Right now, the Trump administration is making it easier for these companies to walk away without enough money set aside to clean up their wells. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act ensures that companies set aside money to meet their cleanup responsibilities, so taxpayers aren’t left paying the bill.”

Until 2024 when the Biden administration added agency rules, oil and gas fiscal assurance requirements were minimal, leading companies to abandon wells instead of remediating the land after drilling. The Trump administration is now rolling back these essential protections for public lands and American taxpayers. Nationwide, there are currently over 140,000 documented orphaned wells, including more than 15,000 on federal lands, and hundreds of thousands more that may be orphaned. Additionally, the number of documented orphaned wells in the United States has more than doubled since 2020. These sites are not only a significant liability for taxpayers and a growing threat to water resources, air quality, wildlife habitat, and private lands, but also jeopardize public health, ecosystems, grazing lands, outdoor recreation sites, and cultural resources that are at high risk from contamination.

In Colorado alone, there are nearly 1,400 orphaned wells, with almost a third of these wells on federal or Tribal lands. Estimates from Colorado’s Energy & Carbon Management Commission predict that it could cost over $36 million to clean up all of the existing orphaned wells on federal and Tribal lands in Colorado. Moreover, there are currently 245 idled federal wells in Colorado that have the potential to eventually become orphaned, which could cost taxpayers approximately $23 million to remediate. Due to new leasing policies enacted by Congress in 2025, executive orders to increase federal oil and gas drilling, and the financial assurance rollback, industry is likely to drill as many as 3.8 million wells on national public lands in the coming years, and to then pass as much as $753 billion in potential financial liabilities back onto local communities and taxpayers.

The Stop Orphaned Wells Act builds on Bennet’s Oil and Gas Bonding Reform and Orphaned Well Remediation Act and recent state-level reforms in Colorado, New Mexico, Texas, and Utah to fix this broken system and close long-standing industry loopholes around orphaned wells. This legislation would ensure operators, not taxpayers, pay for cleanups and aligns directly with the interests of Western voters, nearly 9 in 10 of whom believe oil and gas companies should cover reclamation costs once drilling ends.

“In La Plata County, orphaned wells are a nuisance for property owners and a danger for people and animals alike. This bill builds on Colorado’s innovative work to ensure that federal regulation protects our communities, livestock, and wildlife – and prevents this public health issue from happening in the first place,” said Marsha Porter-Norton, La Plata County Commissioner.

“The Board of County Commissioners strongly supports Senator Bennet’s Stop Orphaned Wells Act. When a well is abandoned, local communities must shoulder the risks to their health, environment, and taxpayer dollars. This legislation provides the accountability needed to ensure oil and gas companies, not our community, pay to restore the lands they use,” said Jody Shadduck-McNally, Larimer County Commissioner and Chair of the Board of County Commissioners.

“Adams County is glad to see Senator Bennet leading the charge on this significant bipartisan issue, as it is of critical importance to our communities. Our county has the second highest number of orphaned wells in the state; taking action to preserve the health and safety of both our residents and our environment is a top priority for our Board. We look forward to working with the Senator in honing this legislation to be as helpful and effective as possible,” said Commissioner Julie Duran Mullica, Chair of the Adams County Board of Commissioners.

“Like countless places across the country, San Miguel County has been forced to clean up after reckless operators. Orphaned wells are not only an unfair burden on our taxpayers but also a dangerous polluter of our beloved natural resources and public lands. Senator Bennet’s bill takes long-overdue actions to strengthen regulations and hold irresponsible companies accountable,” said Galena Gleason, San Miguel County Commissioner.

“The Stop Orphaned Wells Act is urgently needed in Western Colorado, where orphaned, non-producing wells irresponsibly emit harmful methane gas and harm our health, air and water quality, and critical wildlife habitat. This Act will finally make producers responsible for properly closing, remediating, and reclaiming lands after they stop producing oil and gas,” said Lynn Padgett, Ouray County Commissioner.

“The practice of stripping the land of its resources and allowing bad actors to walk away from drill sites must stop. Our hardworking families should not pay for one dollar to restore the land due to irresponsible bad actors in the industry,” said Lynn Baca, Commissioner of Adams County.

“As a grass roots organization that has been working on improving Oil and Gas regulations for 40 years, we support the proposed legislation that will hold the extraction industry to the same standards as other businesses – clean up your own mess. Our community has been on the front line of oil and gas extraction for decades, many of us with wells in our backyards and ranches. We have experienced first-hand the impacts to our health and water sources when the industry is not held to reasonable bonding or basic plugging and remediation standards. Senator Bennet’s proposed legislation will help protect communities and make long-overdue reforms to stop the orphan well crisis from growing,” said Ryan Huggins, Executive Director, San Juan Citizens Alliance.

“Communities shouldn’t have to clean up a mess left by oil and gas companies on public lands. Senator Bennet’s bill would not only work to clean up the nation’s toxic orphan well crisis but also ensure that oil and gas companies, not taxpayers, are responsible for future clean-ups. Thank you, Senator Bennet, for prioritizing cleaner, safer public lands that communities across the nation, as well as future generations, will enjoy and inherit,” said Jim Ramey, Colorado State Director at The Wilderness Society.

“There are hundreds of orphaned wells across western Colorado, left by a legacy of oil and gas extraction and boom and bust economic cycles. The taxpayers of Colorado should not be left with the clean up costs for industry that made a quick profit off of public resources. Like any responsible business, the oil and gas industry should be held responsible for the cost of doing business on our public lands. We thank Sen. Bennet for his continued leadership on this issue and ensuring the responsible management of public lands and taxpayer dollars,” said Barbara Vasques, Board member of Western Colorado Alliance

“Wilderness Workshop commends Senator Bennet for introducing legislation that targets the staggering number of abandoned wells impacting Colorado’s public lands and communities. These common-sense measures will make sure that those who profit from oil and gas extraction can no longer walk away from the responsibility to clean up and reclaim their production sites. By shutting down inactive wells, blocking non-compliant lease transfers, and forcing operators to provide honest financial assurances upfront, this bill finally closes loopholes that have been abused for decades. These measures will protect Colorado’s public lands, secure vital funding, and safeguard our water and wildlife,” said Will Roush, Executive Director, Wilderness Workshop.

“Taxpayers should not be forced to pick up the tab when oil and gas companies walk away from their cleanup responsibilities. We appreciate Senator Bennet’s leadership on legislation to hold operators financially accountable for cleaning up the wells they leave behind. By closing loopholes and updating bonding requirements, the Stop Orphaned Wells Act would take commonsense steps to protect American taxpayers,” said Autumn Hanna, vice president of Taxpayers for Common Sense.

“With more than 20 documented orphaned wells in Routt and Moffat Counties and nearly 1,000 across Colorado, these wells pose clear threats to public safety, wildlife, livestock, groundwater, and air quality. Restoring orphaned wells and modernizing federal oil and gas leasing requirements are critical to protecting our communities. The persistent lack of funding to properly plug and reclaim these wells has created unacceptable risks to public health, the environment, and local economies. Senator Bennet’s legislation would bring much-needed accountability and transparency to federal oil and gas development on public lands. Taxpayers should not be left to clean up an operator’s mess, nor should local governments be excluded from decisions affecting the public lands their communities rely on for economic opportunity and recreation,” said Michelle Stewart, Western Resilience Center’s Executive Director.

“All public lands users have a responsibility to leave the land better than they found it, including oil and gas developers. Sufficient bonding is an insurance policy for the public to know that regardless of the financial status of an operator, our public lands and resources will be reclaimed after oil and gas procurement, even if the well is orphaned. We thank Senator Bennet for his leadership introducing the Stop Orphan Wells Act and working to help modernize the financial assurance system for oil and gas development on public lands,” said Kaden McArthur, Trout Unlimited’s Congressional Affairs Director.

“For too long the oil and gas industry has abandoned low-producing or inactive wells to leak methane and health-harming chemicals into our air and water. As these companies leave the wells orphaned, they also shirk their responsibilities, leaving the cost and consequences of dealing with the leaking wells to the taxpayers. We are grateful for the leadership of Senator Bennet to ensure that the polluters profiting on fossil fuel extraction are cleaning up their mess,” said Mahyar Sorour, Sierra Club Beyond Fossil Fuels Policy Director.

“Coloradans deserve economic policies that serve the public. Yet for too long, the federal oil and gas leasing program has prioritized industry interests, allowing a trillion-dollar industry to profit from publicly owned resources while passing cleanup costs on to taxpayers. Senator Bennet’s bill addresses this growing problem by updating bonding requirements to reflect the full cost of reclaiming wells and protecting Coloradans from having to pay to clean up after oil and gas companies. It’s a common-sense step toward managing our public lands in a fiscally responsible way,” said Chris Stiffler, Senior Economist of Colorado Fiscal Institute.

“Oil and gas operators – not taxpayers – should pay to clean up the messes they leave behind after maximizing profits. This legislation would help end the practice of forcing Americans to foot the bill for abandoned wells that threaten public health and safety. We will continue to work with Sen. Bennet to raise the bar for corporate accountability,” said Laura Esquivel, Senior Legislative Representative, Earthjustice Action.

“Companies that drill on public lands have a legal duty to clean up after themselves when they’re done. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act would strengthen bonding and cleanup requirements and prevent companies from using the sale of aging wells to avoid their cleanup obligations. Taxpayers shouldn’t be left paying for someone else’s mess, and our public lands and waters shouldn’t be left bearing the damage,” said Josh Axelrod, Senior Program Advocate at NRDC.

Healthy public lands support thriving populations of wildlife, clean water, and clean air. These lands are the inheritance of all Americans. Irresponsible developers leave behind equipment that pollutes the air and water. Delayed cleanup impacts the health of animals, humans, and the land. Senator Bennet’s bill is an important step to restore our lands and ensure their benefits for future generations,” said Alison Gallensky, Conservation Geographer, Rocky Mountain Wild.

“Our public lands are an irreplaceable asset; a resource that demands careful, responsible management. Yet for too long, we’ve allowed bad actors in the oil and gas industry to drill on these lands and walk away, leaving behind thousands of orphaned wells that threaten our air and water. This outdated system lets companies off the hook for their pollution and cleanup costs while the public bears the risk. Senator Bennet is working to fix this crisis by making common-sense updates to the requirements for operating on our public lands, ensuring these places stay safe for people and wildlife. It’s time we finally bring this system into the 21st century by passing Senator Bennet’s bills,” said Russell Kuhlman, Executive Director of Nevada Wildlife Federation.

“Across the West, public lands are central to our way of life. They provide vital wildlife habitat and the places where we hunt, fish, and spend time outdoors. But these treasured landscapes are being put at risk by policies riddled with loopholes and handouts that allow irresponsible oil and gas companies to abandon their wells and offload cleanup costs onto taxpayers. Oil and gas production has its place — but we have a responsibility to do it right. Senator Bennet’s bill will begin to fix this broken system by holding companies accountable and ensuring our public lands can serve multiple uses for generations to come,” said Jesse Deubel, Executive Director, New Mexico Wildlife Federation.

“Communities across the West are utilizing access to healthy public lands to attract both visitors and business investment. Yet sadly abandoned oil and gas wells that have not been properly plugged or remediated are a growing threat to other public land uses. Senator Bennet’s bill will update regulations to update bonding rates— ensuring that funds are in place to properly clean up wells at the end of their productive lives. Without Senator Bennet’s bill the cost of clean up is passed on to taxpayers. This bill will help regions who depend on oil and gas get the most from their public lands and help create resilient economies for future generations,” said Ashley Korenblat, Managing Director, Public Land Solutions.

“Montana has a deep and complex history of extractive industries privatizing profits and sociahe losses. They get rich while Montanans are stuck to clean up and pay for the messes. Enough is enough. If oil and gas developers are going to benefit from our shared, public resources – especially the public lands that hunters and anglers rely on – then they need to cover the full costs of doing business here. It’s as simple as that, and we thank Senator Bennet for bringing forward a common-sense and fair solution,” said Frank Szollosi, Executive Director of Montana Wildlife Federation.

Bennet has consistently worked to deliver funding to clean up abandoned orphaned wells to keep communities safe and to strengthen bonding requirements to hold companies accountable for future cleanup. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act builds on Bennet’s previous legislation introduced in July, 2021, the Oil and Gas Bonding Reform and Orphaned Well Remediation Act, which would restore the public’s vital role in shaping oil and gas leasing decisions on public lands. In August 2026, Bennet and U.S. Representative Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) led their Democratic colleagues to oppose the recent rescission of two key Bureau of Land Management oil and gas rules on leasing and waste prevention. In November 2025, Bennet joined Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Hickenlooper, and Luján to urge U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and Bureau of Land Management Acting Director Bill Groffy to maintain the federal oil and gas bonding requirements in the 2024 Onshore Oil and Gas Leasing Rule to hold developers accountable for the costs of site cleanup on federal lands. In July 2023, Bennet issued a statement after the U.S. Department of Interior released a proposed rule that includes oil and gas bonding reform for wells drilled on public lands. In July 2023 and December 2022, Bennet sent letters to the Biden administration urging them to finish the work envisioned in his bill by reforming our antiquated oil and gas bonding system. In August 2022, Bennet and Hickenlooper welcomed $25 million in grant funds from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law to create jobs cleaning up orphaned oil and gas wells across Colorado.

This legislation is supported by 20 organizations, including Earthjustice Action, Colorado Fiscal Institute, Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship, Conservation Colorado, Montana Wildlife Federation, National Parks Conservation Association, Natural Resources Defense Council, Nevada Wildlife Federation, New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Public Land Solutions, Rocky Mountain Wild, San Juan Citizen’s Alliance, Sierra Club, Taxpayers for Common Sense, Trout Unlimited, Western Colorado Alliance, Western Organization of Resource Councils, Western Resilience Center, Wild Montana, Wilderness Workshop, and The Wilderness Society. In addition, this legislation was endorsed by U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

title: Blumenthal & Himes Urge Federal Agency to Investigate Incidents at Oxford Compressor Station
text:
[Hartford, CT] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal and U.S. Representative Jim Himes (CT-04) today wrote to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) urging a thorough investigation of the cause of two equipment failures at the Oxford Compression Station.

In July, two equipment failures at the station resulted in the largest release of natural gas in Connecticut in over a decade. Residents were awakened by sounds resembling a jet engine and were given no explanation or information about the malfunction at the compressor station.

“While it is now clear that the sound was caused by the rapid release of natural gas moving from high to low pressure, residents initially received no explanation. They were never formally notified that these noises were due to the malfunction at the compressor station,” Blumenthal and Himes wrote.

According to incident data from PHMSA, the compressor station released more than 35 million cubic feet of natural gas in less than an hour—an amount equal to what 450 Connecticut homes use in an entire year, and among the top 10 percent of nationwide releases reported in the last decade.

In their letter, Blumenthal and Himes ask PHMSA to conduct a fully transparent review of the malfunctions and take action to prevent similar incidents in the future.

“Given the breakdowns at the station and their impact on the community, we urge PHMSA to thoroughly investigate the causes of these malfunctions and implement measures to prevent future incidents. We also urge PHMSA to provide full transparency in its review of this situation and keep local residents abreast of the findings,” the lawmakers wrote.

A full copy of Blumenthal and Himes’ letter is copied below and available here.

October 2, 2026

The Honorable Paul J. Roberti

Administrator

Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration

Department of Transportation

1200 New Jersey Avenue SE

Washington, D.C. 20590

Dear Administrator Roberti,

I write with concern regarding a recent incident at the Oxford Compressor Station in Oxford, Connecticut. On July 12, 2026, two equipment failures at the station resulted in the largest release of natural gas in Connecticut in over a decade, startling and awakening local residents with loud, frightening noises.[1] I urge the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) to conduct a fully transparent review of the station malfunction and to take meaningful steps to prevent a similar incident in the future.

Shortly after midnight on July 12, Oxford residents reported hearing sounds resembling a jet engine near their homes.[2] According to reports, the noise lasted for approximately 45 minutes.[3] While it is now clear that the sound was caused by the rapid release of natural gas moving from high to low pressure, residents initially received no explanation. They were never formally notified that these noises were due to the malfunction at the compressor station.[4]

Moreover, residents were not told about the volume of natural gas released into their environment or whether specific health protocols were needed. According to incident data from PHMSA, the compressor station released more than 35 million cubic feet of natural gas in less than an hour—an amount equal to what 450 Connecticut homes use in an entire year, and among the top 10 percent of nationwide releases reported in the last decade.[5]

In addition to concerns about notification and transparency, I am troubled by the fact that the plant experienced two separate equipment failures. Both equipment failures involved the station’s emergency shutdown system, which is intended to respond to abnormalities and leaks.[6] According to reports, the first failure was due to a malfunction of the newly installed emergency pull switch and the second failure was a valve not closing completely.[7] These two malfunctions compounded the issue at the plant, leading to the release of gas and loud sounds. PHMSA is responsible for ensuring the safety of natural gas pipelines and related infrastructure, and these malfunctions warrant scrutiny.

Given the breakdowns at the station and their impact on the community, I urge PHMSA to thoroughly investigate the causes of these malfunctions and implement measures to prevent future incidents. I also urge PHMSA to provide full transparency in its review of this situation and keep local residents abreast of the findings.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

title: Senator Blumenthal: Week in Review 9/25/2026-10/2/2026
text:
Slamming Lutnick-Linked Crypto Firm Propping Up Iran’s Shadow Banking System

[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (PSI), released a new report detailing how Tether and its dollar-pegged stablecoin (USDT) have become a significant financial lifeline within Iran’s shadow banking network.

As part of its ongoing inquiry into the role of cryptocurrencies in illicit finance, PSI Democratic investigators conducted a forensic analysis of blockchain transaction data from 846 unique cryptocurrency wallets that have been sanctioned or targeted for seizure due to their association with Iran and its regional proxies. This analysis shows that Tether has, in effect, provided Iran access to a high-liquidity international payment system that the United States has assiduously sought to deny it.

“My new PSI report exposes how Tether and its flagship token have become central to Iran’s shadow banking system, allowing the Iranian government to fund its regional proxies, commit human rights abuses, and pursue hostile drone and missile programs as they defy our sanctions regime,” Blumenthal said. “The Trump Administration’s glaring lack of oversight of cryptocurrency issuers has undermined our own national security interests. That is why I am calling on the Department of Treasury and Justice to immediately investigate Tether and hold it accountable for these potential sanctions violations.”

A summary of PSI’s key findings is below:

Tether has become a primary illicit international payment system for Iran, allowing it to circumvent international sanctions on its banks: Of the 846 wallets sanctioned for their association with Iran and its terrorist proxies, 84% have transacted exclusively, or nearly exclusively, in USDT. These activities include efforts by the Iranian government to move funds into, and out of, Iran and to prop up the country’s currency in the face of U.S. sanctions, including through the Central Bank of Iran.

Tether serves as a central payment mechanism that interlinks Iran and its terrorist proxy organizations, undermining U.S. security interests in the region: Iran’s cryptocurrency-based shadow banking network has reached significant volumes of funds and implicate different Iranian interests. In addition to supporting terrorist organizations, there is evidence that this shadow banking network is used for the procurement and sales of drones and other military equipment.

Tether’s failure to freeze illicit wallets and prevent abuse created the permissive environment under which Iranian shadowing banking could flourish: Prior to 2024, Tether did not comprehensively and consistently freeze wallets designated by counter-terrorism agencies and continues to fail to proactively block clearly illicit wallets. This absence of deterrence invited abuse: terrorist organizations such as Hamas shifted from transacting in Bitcoin and a mix of cryptocurrencies, to promoting USDT.

In letters sent to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Attorney General Todd Blanche, Blumenthal referred PSI’s findings to the Departments and called for thorough investigations into Tether’s anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance practices.

In a letter to Bessent, Blumenthal raised concerns about the Trump Administration’s lax oversight of cryptocurrency firms despite longstanding research and reporting on Tether’s broader role in illicit finance, “Yet, since President Trump’s return to the White House, investigations and enforcement actions into the cryptocurrency industry have been dropped, settled on meager terms, or even reversed. I fear this lenient self-dealing includes Tether, despite its role in propping up a country that the United States is currently at war with.”

Blumenthal continued, “While Tether has become a powerful tool for foreign adversaries, terrorists, and illicit actors that are a danger to our national security, it has numerous close ties to the highest levels of the Trump Administration. Most prominently, Cantor Fitzgerald—which until recently was run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and is now controlled by his children—owns 5% of Tether and holds a substantial portion of the company’s more than $100 billion of assets in the United States.”

“The prospect of such a financial weapon being used against American interests is deeply troubling. I therefore request that Treasury review the Subcommittee’s report, which is enclosed with this letter, and conduct a thorough investigation of Tether’s anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance practices. If your investigation finds Tether has violated the Bank Secrecy Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or any other relevant provision of federal law, I encourage you to take the strongest appropriate action,” Blumenthal concluded.

The full text of PSI’s report is available here. Copies of Blumenthal’s letters to Bessent and Blanche are available here and here.

Blumenthal further slammed Tether for propping up Iran’s shadow banking system on Twitter/X.

“Tether seemingly has no shame—profiting from insidious use of its stablecoin for money laundering by Iran, drug traffickers & other illicit enterprises. Time to crackdown. DOJ & Trump officials can no longer look away from the overt, outrageous lawbreaking documented in my PSI report. Our national security is at stake,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal joined CNBC’s Squawk Box to highlight his PSI report and to call for action to crack down on Tether’s shady dealings.

“Tether is a preferred payment system for terrorist organizations—operating as a superhighway for the Iranian government to evade sanctions, carry out hostile drone & missile campaigns, & commit human rights abuses. I joined Squawk Box CNBC to discuss my new report,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

The full interview can be found here.

Condemning Trump’s Incitement of Violent January 6 Attack that Rightfully Led to Jack Smith’s Lawful Investigation

During a hearing with former Special Counsel Jack Smith, Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, underscored the seriousness of the events that predicated Smith’s investigations into President Donald Trump, including the violent attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021. During his exchange with Smith, Blumenthal also ran through the lawful investigative steps that Smith and his team took in order to pursue the case, including seeking an indictment from a grand jury composed of everyday Americans.

“I want to remind folks why we're here today. And I think a picture is worth a thousand words. We're here today because Donald Trump incited a mob to attack us—the Capitol, Members of Congress, to stop the counting of votes. He objected to the result of an election, and he tried to stop the peaceful transition of power by inciting rioters to attack the Capitol, including everybody here today,” Blumenthal said.

“And we came to this very room on that day seeking safety, finding refuge. We were kept here for hours, and then we were given the choice to secretly go home, to leave here, as armed guards sought to protect us in this room, and I remember sitting over in that corner, trying to recharge my phone, so I could call my wife to tell her I was OK. That's what Donald Trump did on that day.”

Blumenthal’s exchange with Mr. Smith is available here.

Blumenthal further highlighted Jack Smith’s testimony describing the lawful investigative steps Smith and his team took on Twitter/X.

“Trump incited violence on Jan 6 to prevent the transition of power—rightfully leading to Jack Smith's prosecution. Trump's blatant attack on democracy shows we must be vigilant against his assaults,” wrote Blumenthal with an accompanying video on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal joined CNN’s Jake Tapper to further discuss Smith’s testimony.

“Jack Smith's testimony yesterday highlighted the facts that led him to indict Trump—the President incited riots on Jan 6 & exploited that mob action in an effort to prevent the transition of power. I joined The Lead CNN to discuss,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

The full interview can be found here.

Demanding Answers from Trump Administration on AI Oversight

Blumenthal, PSI Ranking Member, and U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, demanded answers from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent about the Administration’s delayed, secretive, and voluntary process to test and monitor advanced artificial intelligence models. In a letter sent to Bessent, the Senators raised concerns that the Administration’s hands-off approach to A.I. oversight leaves the public, our financial system, and our national security vulnerable to the grave dangers of increasingly sophisticated, out-of-control A.I. models.

Pointing to recent revelations about the scale of the Hugging Face breach by rogue OpenAI agents and OpenAI’s subsequent steps to limit an independent into the breach, the Senators wrote, “This rapid acceleration in the severity—indeed potential illegality—of A.I. safety failures demands rigorous, independent oversight, testing, and investigations from the federal government… Voluntary measures and self-policing clearly are not working: despite these sensational reports, Anthropic and OpenAI have both acknowledged that they have no plan to solve the grave dangers of increasingly sophisticated A.I. models.”

The Senators continued, “Rather than confront the compounding risks of out-of-control and unregulated A.I., the White House has sought to shield major A.I. companies from public scrutiny, leaving Americans in the dark. In June 2026, the President signed an executive order requiring the creation of a classified ‘benchmarking’ process and ‘AI cybersecurity clearinghouse’ to test the capabilities of frontier A.I. models, a program in part led by the Department of the Treasury. However, despite reporting that some members of the Administration sought to make participation and disclosures mandatory, instead—reportedly after interventions from Mark Zuckerberg and his allies—the program was made expressly voluntary.”

The Senators continued, “Finally, although the executive order prioritizes law enforcement action against anyone using A.I. to illegally access or damage other computers, no federal investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, or Meta has been announced. The Treasury Department has not publicly disclosed any information about the incidents or what action it has taken to ensure remediation of A.I. security vulnerabilities. From all appearances, the benchmarking process and oversight regime outlined by the White House appears to be non-existent or asleep-at-the-wheel exactly when it’s needed most.”

“The American public cannot afford to wait for catastrophic failure before the White House wakes up, nor can it continue to alone trust the A.I. companies to monitor and control their increasingly sophisticated and dangerous models,” the Senators concluded.

The full text of the letter is available here.

Blumenthal also slammed President Trump’s “morally blinding” AI agreement he signed with tech leaders.

“Trump’s “morally binding” safety pledge with AI CEOs is a bad deal—a distraction from a President who thinks it’s all a hoax. OpenAI, Meta & Anthropic must be held legally accountable for their rogue, dangerous AI agents, including through my AI Risk Evaluation Act,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

On the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee

At a Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee hearing to consider pending nominations, Ranking Member Blumenthal underscored the five nominees’ jarring lack of qualifications for the roles they have been nominated for at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

“I'm just going to be very blunt. I'm gravely concerned that none of these nominees have any experience with veterans' benefits law, whatsoever, not as judges, not as lawyers, not as advocates for veterans,” Blumenthal said in his opening.

Blumenthal raised scrutiny over the nominees to be judges at the Court of Appeals for Veterans’ Claims (CAVC). He first highlighted a watchdog report on nominee Robert Fleck, which revealed Fleck engaged in nepotism and lied about sharing sensitive information when he worked at VA’s Office of General Counsel: “Mr. Fleck, you were found by VA’s Office of Inspector General to have engaged in nepotism when - as a manager in the Office of General Counsel – you advocated for the employment of your wife in that same office. You will have to explain to the Committee why the report done by the Office of Inspector General is not disqualifying, and I appreciate the Chairman's staff subsequently sharing the documents and information with us, which should prompt all of us to have very strong concerns, and I intend to make further inquiries about this issue. We have a constitutional duty of oversight.”

Ahead of the hearing, VA intentionally redacted and withheld documentation requested by Democratic Committee staff related to the investigation into Mr. Fleck, while providing the Committee Republicans with additional, unredacted documents.

Blumenthal called into question another CAVC nominee, Daniel Rendleman, and his qualifications for the role in light of his radical anti-abortion views: “Mr. Rendleman, if confirmed, you would have the power to decide whether a veteran’s claim for reproductive health care coverage or reimbursement is denied. The radical anti-abortion views you espouse call into question your ability to make impartial judgments on abortion-related claims.”
