title: Hickenlooper, Bennet, Schrier Demand Answers on Childhood Vaccines EO, Measles Deaths, & Delayed Vaccine Access
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper, Michael Bennet and U.S. Representative Kim Schrier, along with 28 colleagues, raised concerns about efforts to reject established vaccine science in a letter to Dr. Erica Schwartz, the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The letter demands answers about the CDC’s actions related to President Trump’s childhood vaccination schedule executive order, reporting of measles associated deaths, and delays in the distribution of childhood immunizations for underinsured populations.

“[…] As the United States is experiencing the largest measles outbreak in 35 years, President Trump issued an Executive Order (EO) aimed at dismantling core immunization guidelines, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) to lay the groundwork for fundamentally restructuring the routine childhood immunization schedule. At the same time, reports indicate the CDC, under your leadership, excluded verified state-reported measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania from the public mortality count. All of this is happening while the CDC delayed access to fall respiratory virus vaccines through the Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. We are deeply concerned by this administration’s persistent efforts to reject settled science. As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health,” wrote the lawmakers.

The United States is facing a decline in childhood immunization rates. Recently, the CDC reported that 280,000 kindergartners did not complete their measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine series. This is a result of the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to lower the number of recommended immunizations, break up safe and effective combination shots, and promote legal action against states unaligned with such efforts.

Additionally, the CDC has a long-standing agency precedent and prides itself on “objective data collection and reporting.” In early September, reports revealed that four measles-associated deaths verified and reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Although the CDC tracked all 4 measles-associated deaths internally, only 2 were included in the CDC’s public outbreak tracker. This omission not only violates agency standards, but raises serious concerns about whether the CDC can resist political pressure over established scientific facts.

“The health of American children and families depends on a CDC Director who is willing to follow the science, even when it may be politically inconvenient. We look forward to your response and to seeing whether the CDC under your leadership honors the commitments you made at your confirmation hearing,” concluded the lawmakers.

Hickenlooper has actively opposed the Trump administration’s anti-science agenda, leading legislation to protect public health standards. In December 2025, Hickenlooper, along with his Senate colleagues, introduced the Family Vaccine Protection Act to protect Americans’ access to vaccines and to safeguard proven science from the Trump administration’s efforts to undermine vaccines. Hickenlooper has called out RFK Jr.’s efforts to weaken Americans’ access to safe vaccines and further launched an investigation into RFK Jr.’s efforts to replace Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) experts. Hickenlooper has raised alarm about the mass firings at HHS, and demanded answers on how the firing of IVF researchers at the CDC will impact families seeking fertility treatment.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below:

Dr. Schwartz:

At your confirmation hearing, you said that your “sacred responsibility” as Director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) would be to provide “clear, honest, and evidence-based” public health guidance and to “never betray the science.” In the short time since your confirmation as CDC Director, the health and safety of our children have been subjected to further chaos and confusion. As the United States is experiencing the largest measles outbreak in 35 years, President Trump issued an Executive Order (EO) aimed at dismantling core immunization guidelines, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) to lay the groundwork for fundamentally restructuring the routine childhood immunization schedule. At the same time, reports indicate the CDC, under your leadership, excluded verified state-reported measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania from the public mortality count. All of this is happening while the CDC delayed access to fall respiratory virus vaccines through the Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. We are deeply concerned by this administration’s persistent efforts to reject settled science. As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health.

The CDC recently reported that the number of children up-to-date on their immunizations has continued to decline, including 280,000 kindergartners who did not complete the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) series. Instead of spending time and dedicating resources to promote the need for childhood immunizations, President Trump called for breaking up combination shots like the MMR vaccine into single-disease shots that are not available in the United States, cutting the number of diseases every child is recommended to be protected against from 18 to 11, and directing the Attorney General to advance legal challenges to state laws. Following this EO, HHS issued an RFI on the childhood immunization schedule, aimed at bypassing the CDC and the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which have developed recommendations for over 60 years. These efforts are only a part of the systematic attacks spearheaded by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. CDC’s scientists, not political appointees, should be at the center of any decision about the childhood immunization schedule.

During this same timeframe, CDC’s public actions under your leadership raise serious concerns regarding your willingness to counter these unscientific measures – including reports that four measles-associated deaths verified and reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health were excluded from the CDC’s public national mortality count for weeks, even as internal CDC systems continue to track these fatalities. This is a clear break from long-standing agency precedent, including last year’s standard reporting of measles deaths in Texas and directly contradicts the commitment to “objective data collection and reporting” that has been CDC’s foundation. If the agency under your leadership is altering verified state data to fit political preferences, the pledge you made at your confirmation hearing has already been broken.

We request responses to the following questions in writing by October 16, 2026.

CDC Role on the Executive Order on Childhood Vaccines

Did anyone from the White House or HHS consult you about the Executive Order either before or after it was issued?

If so, who reached out, what was discussed, and when did these communication(s) occur?

If not, have you raised, or do you plan to raise, any concerns with President Trump, Secretary Kennedy, or any other administration official(s)?

How is the CDC planning to implement the provisions outlined in the EO? What steps have been taken already and what are planned? Please provide a detailed summary of these plans.

What role, if any, did CDC career scientists have in developing the EO’s recommendations?

The EO directs the Secretary, acting through the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, to present plans to the President within 90 days on single-disease vaccine options, the timing and sequencing of childhood vaccines, and safety monitoring. What role does the CDC have in developing those plans, and which CDC officials are participating?

The EO recommends reducing the number of routine immunizations from 18 to 11. Do you support that specific recommendation? What scientific evidence supports removing the other diseases from the immunizations recommended for all children, and has the CDC estimated the additional illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths that could result?

Do you agree that spacing out immunizations across additional visits lengthens the window of vulnerability for infants and young children? If not, please provide the evidence on which CDC relies.

The EO recommends separating combination shots like MMR into single-disease shots. No single-disease MMR vaccine is currently available in the United States. Other countries that have tried this – like Japan in the 1990s – saw increased outbreaks, ultimately resulting in them reverting to a combination shot. Do you support this specific provision even though it is not currently available in the U.S., would require more shots and doctor visits, and lacks scientific backing? Why is the federal government recommending an option to families that does not exist, causing additional confusion?

What scientific evidence supports separating combination vaccines like MMR into single-disease doses? Please provide CDC analyses of peer-reviewed studies, epidemiological analyses, or international precedent that demonstrates this change would actually improve health outcomes. If no such evidence exists, will you decline to implement this provision?

The public comment period for the HHS RFI closed on September 20, 2026. Did CDC scientists review or contribute to the RFI before it was published? What role will CDC scientists have in reviewing the comments and in any resulting changes to the categories of federal vaccine recommendations?

Data Collection and Reporting

Has the CDC instituted a new policy for reviewing, altering, or withholding state-reported health data before public posting?

If so, what scientific evidence supports this change and what deliberations occurred?

If there is no such policy, on what basis were Pennsylvania’s measles deaths excluded from the public tracker, and who at CDC authorized that exclusion?

As of today, the CDC has only included two of the measles-associated deaths reported by the State of Pennsylvania. What specific technical, scientific, or epidemiological basis justified excluding Pennsylvania’s state-reported measles deaths from the CDC’s public tracker while still including them on internal trackers?

Did any White House or HHS officials contact you or your staff regarding the public reporting of Pennsylvania’s measles deaths? Please provide all communication between CDC leadership and any White House or HHS official regarding the reporting of state-verified measles deaths since your confirmation.

Vaccines for Children Program

Why did the CDC delay opening orders for COVID vaccines through the Vaccines for Children Program (VFC)? Please provide the timeline of when decisions were made concerning the VFC program.

What made the CDC decide to open ordering for COVID vaccines through the VFC program on September 24, 2026 and not earlier?

Have you personally been asked by Secretary Kennedy, the White House, or any other HHS or Trump administration official to delay or condition VFC activation for the COVID vaccine? If so, please describe the request and identify who made it. If such a request was made in writing, please provide it.

Who at CDC, HHS, or the White House made the decision to delay VFC activation for the COVID vaccine, and on what basis? Please produce all internal communications, memoranda, and legal or scientific analyses supporting that decision.

What guidance has CDC provided to state health departments, pediatricians, and VFC providers about the status of COVID vaccines under VFC? How soon can VFC vaccines be expected to be in the possession of clinicians and accessible for children?

The health of American children and families depends on a CDC Director who is willing to follow the science, even when it may be politically inconvenient. We look forward to your response and to seeing whether the CDC under your leadership honors the commitments you made at your confirmation hearing.

###

title: Hickenlooper, Colleagues Urge U.S. Department of Agriculture and U.S. Forest Service to Protect National Forests
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper, Martin Heinrich, Jeff Merkley, Alex Padilla, Jacky Rosen, Ben Ray Luján, Catherine Cortez Masto, Chris Van Hollen, Ruben Gallego, and Dick Durbin urged U.S. Department of Agriculture Under Secretary Michael Boren and U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz to maintain consistent environmental protections and local input mechanisms in any attempted revision of the 2005 Travel Management Rule.

“For years, the current rule has successfully balanced the use of motorized vehicles with other uses on public lands—ensuring that motorized use in our forests is managed responsibly, centering forest-level decision-making with state and local input, and protecting the environment,” the senators wrote. “Many of the proposed changes in the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s recently published Notice of Intent (NOI) would significantly alter the overarching framework that protects our lands and waters and supports our nation’s wildlife, clean water, and outdoor recreation economy.”

The letter identifies six core principles that the administration should maintain in any revisions to the 2005 Travel Management Rule:

Provide Meaningful Guidance that Helps Avoid Environmental Impacts;

Center State, Tribal, and Local Input;

Consider Impacts to All Types of Recreation and Uses;

Ensure Adequate Resources for Maintaining all Open Trails and Roads;

Continue to Provide Clear Information; and

Maintain Flexibility that Incorporates Public Input

“We urge the Forest Service to approach these revisions with those principles in mind and to work closely with Congress, Tribal Nations, State and local governments, and the broad range of stakeholders that depend on our national forests. We stand ready to work with you to ensure that any final rule gives land managers the tools to keep our forests accessible, safe, and healthy for generations to come,” the senators concluded.

Hickenlooper has been a consistent advocate for the preservation and expansion of public land protections. The senator introduced the Sarvis Creek Wilderness Completion Act to expand the Sarvis Creek Wilderness Area in the Routt National Forest by 6,817 acres. Hickenlooper is also a cosponsor of the CORE act which would protect approximately 420,000 acres of public land in Colorado, establish new wilderness areas, and safeguard existing outdoor recreation opportunities.

Full text is available HERE and below:

Dear Under Secretary Boren and Chief Schultz:

We write to highlight key issues and principles regarding the Administration’s proposed revision of the 2005 Travel Management Rule. For years, the current rule has successfully balanced the use of motorized vehicles with other uses on public lands—ensuring that motorized use in our forests is managed responsibly, centering forest-level decision-making with state and local input, and protecting the environment. Many of the proposed changes in the U.S. Department of

Agriculture’s recently published Notice of Intent (NOI) would significantly alter the overarching framework that protects our lands and waters and supports our nation’s wildlife, clean water, and outdoor recreation economy.

Our national forests serve a wide range of users, including hunters, anglers, hikers, horseback riders, motorized recreationists, livestock operators, outfitters, and local communities. Based on more than twenty years of experience with the Travel Management Rule in place, we know that these uses can coexist when travel management decisions are made thoughtfully and with meaningful input from the people who know these landscapes best. The 2005 Travel Management Rule was developed to allow motorized use within our national forests as a form of recreation while avoiding conflicts among users, damage to wildlife habitat or water resources, disturbance to cultural resources, and the need for new maintenance. Two decades later, these priorities are more critical than ever.

For these reasons, we urge you to ensure that any revisions to the 2005 Travel Management Rule maintain the following core principles:

Provide Meaningful Guidance that Helps Avoid Environmental Impacts: For over 20 years, the Travel Management Rule has provided a framework that helps protect fish and wildlife habitat, riparian areas, water quality, and cultural resources. The Administration’s proposal to presume that routes are open, unless required to be closed, could lead to networks of user-created trails—with significant implications for wildlife, water, and vegetation. We urge the administration to examine the types of environmental impacts that the 2005 Rule responded to, and ensure that any final rule minimizes negative impacts to habitat and ecosystems across the National Forest System.

Center State, Tribal, and Local Input: Travel management decisions should continue to be informed by robust public engagement and local input. Communities, Tribal Nations, recreationists, permittees, and other stakeholders should have a meaningful say in how they access and use their public lands. The 2005 Travel Management Rule ensures that Forest Service designations of trails and routes happen close-to-the-ground with robust local input. This core tenet should be maintained. Coordination with state and Tribal wildlife managers is particularly essential to benefit species and to support hunting access.

Consider Impacts to All Types of Recreation and Uses: Durable, well-informed travel management decisions are critical to sustaining America’s $1.3 trillion outdoor recreation economy. The existing Travel Management Rule has helped reduce conflicts between public land uses such as camping, hiking, hunting, and grazing. Many visitors to our National Forests wish to recreate in a quiet, non-motorized environment; a Travel Management Rule that helps avoid conflicts between uses will ultimately benefit our outdoor recreation economy.

Ensure Adequate Resources for Maintaining all Open Trails and Roads: The Forest Service should consider the long-term cost of properly maintaining, staffing, and administering its transportation system before adding new routes or expanding motorized use. Expanding the system without the resources necessary to maintain it would risk increasing the already significant road and trail maintenance backlog.

Continue to Provide Clear Information: The agency should continue to clearly identify where motorized travel is permitted. Clear designations, accurate Motor Vehicle Use Maps, user education, adequate signage, and reasonable enforcement are essential for visitors, land managers, and our natural resources. We support using technology to improve public access to information, including continued modernization and digitization of Motor Vehicle Use Maps.

Maintain Flexibility that Incorporates Public Input: Individual routes may warrant

reconsideration where local conditions justify it. The current rule allows for

modifications to the road and trail system through a public process and requires annual updates to the Motor Vehicle Use Maps. We believe this public input is essential to maintain.

We urge the Forest Service to approach these revisions with those principles in mind and to work closely with Congress, Tribal Nations, State and local governments, and the broad range of stakeholders that depend on our national forests. We stand ready to work with you to ensure that any final rule gives land managers the tools to keep our forests accessible, safe, and healthy for generations to come.

title: ICYMI: Hickenlooper Meets with Coloradans, Talks Food & Energy Affordability
text:
WASHINGTON – Yesterday, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper called out Trump administration policies that are increasing costs across the Denver Metro area. title: Husted, Capito visit Centrus to discuss Ohio’s future in nuclear energy
text:
“This plant is creating good-paying Ohio jobs close to home for people in Piketon, strengthening our domestic nuclear fuel supply and helping position Ohio at the center of America’s nuclear future.”

WATCH HERE.

PIKETON, Ohio – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today joined U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Chairman Shelley Moore Capito in Piketon to tour Centrus and discuss Ohio’s future in nuclear energy.

“I’m glad to host Senator Capito here in Ohio to see firsthand the work being done at Centrus to rebuild America’s nuclear fuel supply. Centrus is the only U.S.-owned company currently enriching uranium with American technology right here in Piketon. This plant is creating good-paying Ohio jobs close to home for people in Piketon, strengthening our domestic nuclear fuel supply and helping position Ohio at the center of America’s nuclear future. I’ll keep working to expand this operation, grow our workforce and make sure Ohio is leading the way in American energy production,” said Husted.

“It was a pleasure to join Senator Husted here at Centrus Energy’s American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio to see how federal investments in nuclear energy are transforming Ohio’s energy landscape. Through his work on the Environment and Public Works Committee, Senator Husted has been a strong advocate for nuclear energy as we’ve worked hard to reduce regulatory burdens and permitting inefficiencies so that we can deploy clean, reliable nuclear energy in Ohio and across the country,” said Capito.

In late 2023, Centrus began uranium enrichment operations at the American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio—the first U.S.-owned, U.S.-technology enrichment plant to start production since 1954. Under contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), Centrus is pioneering production of High-Assay, Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) in Piketon.

HALEU is an advanced nuclear fuel that can power many next-generation nuclear reactors. Establishing a domestic supply of HALEU will help reduce America’s reliance on foreign sources of nuclear fuel and strengthen the U.S. nuclear energy supply chain.

In January 2026, Husted announced that the DOE will invest $2.7 billion to strengthen domestic enrichment services over the next ten years. This funding includes $900 million for Centrus Energy’s American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio.

This announcement came after Husted sent two letters to the DOE in support of funding for the plant. In April and September 2025, he joined colleagues in writing to DOE Secretary Chris Wright, advocating for the American Centrifuge Plant and domestically produced uranium enrichment.

title: Board of Aldermen considers infrastructure strain, repairs following LSU weekend
text:
Robyn Tannehill highlighted the future plans for the city of Oxford to improve infrastructure at Tuesday’s Board of Aldermen meeting.

By Aly Bradshaw

The City of Oxford Board of Aldermen discussed issues with the city’s utility infrastructure, ongoing and future infrastructure repairs and tourism updates at its Oct. 6 meeting.

Infrastructure strain

City of Oxford Mayor Robyn Tannehill said the weekend of the Sept. 19 LSU vs. Ole Miss game was a success for Oxford, which welcomed crowds over 10 times its taxpaying population.

“We had more than 211,000 visitors to Oxford, which means there were over 311,000 people in Oxford on Saturday at the football game,” Tannehill said. “The total economic impact is estimated around $109 million.”

However, Oxford infrastructure was strained with all those visitors.

“We have a town of 28,000 taxpayers that have to be able to flush a toilet (when) an LSU game (brings) 311,000 people,” Tannehill said. “We’ve got to have help upgrading that infrastructure.”

Tannehill and Oxford Utilities released statements on Sept. 2 asking Oxford residents to reduce water consumption, specifically outdoor irrigation, as drought conditions persisted.

“To stabilize our system, we are requesting that customers cut back on their watering times by 50%, effective immediately,” Tannehill said in a statement on Facebook. “While we are currently working on multiple infrastructure projects … to add system capacity, these projects do take time.”

Tannehill and Aldermen Kesha Howell Atkinson and Mary Martha Crowe traveled to Washington D.C two weeks ago to meet with Mississippi Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith. They discussed challenges related to Oxford’s growth and infrastructure needs with the senators, according to Tannehill.

Repairs in progress

The Board of Aldermen also extended the local state of emergency from Winter Storm Fern to address outstanding projects on damaged infrastructure and landscaping across Oxford. This procedural move allows for faster contracting and greater flexibility for city staff to promptly address the remaining repairs.

The board also discussed an emergency declaration for wastewater treatment repairs.

“There’s two large valves that control flow into those tanks. One of them is hopelessly clogged, and one is hopelessly stuck open,” John Crawley, the city engineer, said. “We need to actually dig down and fix those.”

Crawley said the estimated price for the repairs would be $111,066.

The board approved a request from Delta Utilities to work overnight to repair the high pressure gas main that runs up Gertrude Ford Boulevard.

“Rather than creating a nightmare with traffic predictions during the day, they have asked to do that work overnight and do one-lane closures (during) overnight hours as needed from the hours of 7 p.m to 7 a.m.,” Crawley said. “Football game weekends or big weekends, they will stop after Wednesday night, or you can work on Thursdays or Fridays or Saturdays.”

Visit Oxford FY27 Action Plan

Kinney Ferris, executive director of Visit Oxford, outlined the fiscal year 2027 action plan for Visit Oxford, the city’s tourism and destination marketing organization.

To continue catering to the Oxford tourism experience, Ferris said the organization plans to install an interactive digital stand in the Visit Oxford center where visitors can personalize itineraries and find directions that can be sent directly to their phones.

“We are working on a digital interactive kiosk, so think of a welcome center website that you can play with,” Ferris said. “It’s going to be right when you walk in the door, and you can make itineraries there and it’ll give you directions — walking or driving — straight to your mobile device.”

Ferris also said that Oxford has done very well this year in terms of media exposure.

“We have had a record-breaking year with media coverage this past year, so we are going to continue those efforts,” Ferris said. “We are expecting more travel writers and influencers than ever, so we will keep that up.”

Visit Oxford aims to include all parts of Oxford life for tourists.

“We have quarterly meetings with all of our hotel sales managers, as well as our event venues,” ” Ferris said. “Our goal is really to create a more balanced visitation mix. We want to increase those groups, meetings and sports travel, while we continue to strengthen travel.”

Visit Oxford provides meeting partnership grants that organizations can apply to alleviate some of the costs that come with hosting events. Applicants can receive up to $3,000 for promotion, performance fees, meals and lodging.

“Last year, we gave out $104,350, which the ROI (return on investment) was a visitor spend of $10.3 million to our local businesses and hotels,” Ferris said.

title: ‘Cancer doesn’t care who you are’: Mississippian pushes federal lawmakers to prioritize research funding
text:
By Caleb Salers

A Mississippian who lost her mother to cancer at a young age is hopeful that federal lawmakers will dedicate funding to research and prevention programs.

Casey Rinewalt, a Mississippian who volunteers for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), joined more than 750 cancer patients, survivors, and those who have lost loved ones in Washington, D.C., in September. The group convened in the nation’s capital as part of ACS CAN’s annual Leadership Summit and Lobby Day.

While in Washington, Rinewalt spent time with Mississippi’s congressional delegation and staffers to push for further funding for cancer research. Rinewalt, at 12 years old, lost her mother to adrenal carcinoma. Since then, she’s been on a mission to help find a cure for cancer, so that others will not have to endure what she went through at such a young age.

“My mom is my ‘why,'” Rinewalt said. “That was my driving force to want to participate in this and help push for policies and continue to vie for the highest possible funding for research.”

Mississippi’s congressional delegation is made up of U.S. Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith, along with Reps. Trent Kelly, Bennie Thompson, Michael Guest, and Mike Ezell. Thompson is the lone Democrat of the bunch, as the rest are Republicans.

While spending time with each member of Congress and their staffers, Rinewalt said she gathered that the elected officials are serious about cancer research and doing all they can to ensure that Mississippians are taken care of. She also learned that cancer hits home for all of the state’s federal lawmakers, as each has encountered it rearing its ugly head in their lives, whether it be personally or through a loved one.

“It was fantastic to get to see and lay eyes on everybody and have everybody in the room,” Rinewalt said. “Knowing that we have their understanding of this is a no-brainer — we need to be able to do what we can to support our patients and people in Mississippi, is crucial.

“Cancer has touched every one of our legislators’ lives. They have their own stories to share. They have a deep tie and connection to it. It’s a thing we need to do. It’s something that we should do for the greater good, so that way we should take care of everybody. It was rewarding to see everybody on the same page.”

Congress could look a little different after the November midterms. Republicans hold majorities in both the House and Senate, but politicos expect that to change soon. Democrats are projected to reclaim the House and have momentum in Senate races, as well.

Rinewalt, however, is not concerned about a potential domino effect a changing of the guard could have on cancer research funding. Rather, she believes lawmakers are more than willing to cross the aisle to help patients, as cancer is indiscriminate in who it impacts. She further asserted that ACS CAN will continue its lobbying efforts regardless of which political party is in power.

“Cancer doesn’t care who you are or what side you sit on. It depends on what we can do to help support patients,” Rinewalt said. “We are here to help make sure that those voices are heard. That way, we can continue to help fight the good fight and help make sure that, regardless of whether the change of the guard happens, the mission is still seen and we’re still doing everything we can to take care of our fellow Mississippians.”

title: What the Protect College Sports Act means and what’s next
text:
The Protect College Sports Act passed through the Senate two weeks ago, but it has many obstacles ahead before becoming law.

By Russ Eddins

The Protect College Sports Act (PCSA), which would bring sweeping changes to college sports, passed through the U.S. Senate two weeks ago. The bill must still go through the U.S. House of Representatives, where it will likely be amended. The most notable features of the bill are a one-time transfer rule, a cap for teams per conference and a new revenue share limit.

U.S. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) introduced the bill on May 27.

The PCSA passed 77 to 22 in the Senate, with both Mississippi Sens. Roger Wicker and Cindy Hyde-Smith voting to approve the bill.

“College sports are at a breaking point. Fans can see their favorite teams being hollowed out by transfer chaos, fake NIL bidding wars, eligibility lawsuits and a system that allows the richest programs to keep pulling away,” Cruz said in a statement. “The Protect College Sports Act is a bipartisan plan to restore order.”

Student-athletes can still profit from their name, image and likeness, Cruz said. The senator emphasized, however, that college sports still needs real rules, competitive balance, rivalries and a true connection to education.

“This bill protects athletes and fans and keeps college sports from becoming a two-conference minor league,” Cruz said.

With the PCSA through the Senate, it will now go to the House. The SCORE Act, the PCSA’s predecessor, could not get enough votes in the House, so it will be interesting to see how the House handles the latest bill that will shake up college sports.

Most notably, the bill would more than double the revenue share cap. Currently, college athletic departments can share $20.5 million with student athletes. With the bill, they can spend an additional $22.5 million for retaining players, plus $5 million specifically for women’s and Olympic sports.

Ole Miss Vice Chancellor for Intercollegiate Athletics Keith Carter highlighted the need for legislation in an event at the Charles Overby Center for Southern Journalism and Politics on Sept. 17.

“If we get to another football portal window and the (player) market increases another 50, 60, 70%, like we’ve been seeing every year,” Carter said, “basically, you’re going to be looking at $80 to $90 million, so can (Ole Miss) hang there for a while? Maybe. Can Texas hang there for a while? Maybe a little longer than us.”

The longer college sports go without further regulation, the more money schools will spend on players. Ole Miss, and many other programs, may not be able to keep up if the checks get too big.

The bill caps agent endorsement contract fees at 5%. Agent fees now are around 20-25%. Athlete-agent law will be updated to cover NIL. Athletic associations will have to maintain a public registry of agents, allowing associations to decertify or fine agents who break rules.

The Senate attempted to vote on the PCSA in early August. Senate Majority Leader John Thune filed a cloture motion, which would end debate regarding the bill; however, the Senate went into August recess without taking action. The bill had numerous roadblocks that slowed its path to the floor, including objections from Sens. Tommy Tuberville and John Kennedy and the Congressional Black Caucus.

Florida Sens. Ashley Moody and Rick Sott voted against advancing the bill because it limits schools from changing conferences, which Miami and FSU may seek to do in the future. Both schools currently reside in the ACC and may look to move to a stronger conference.

As currently written, the PCSA caps Power Four conferences at 20 teams. The SEC is currently at 16, the Big 10 at 18, the Big 12 at 16 and the ACC at 16. Additionally, a team would have to spend three seasons as an independent program before it could join another conference.

The provision capping power conferences to 20 teams and making it harder to switch conferences prevented the bill from reaching the floor for a time. The House will almost certainly amend that portion of the bill. Reps. Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) and Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), along with 20 members of Congress, have already sent a letter to the House urging changes to the bill.

If the House amends the bill then passes it, the bill must still go back through the Senate before it can be sent to the president.

While the PCSA getting through the Senate is good news for many administrators, others are preparing for additional ways to regulate college sports.

“There’s probably plans A, B and C right now. Plan A is probably the congressional bill that today moves through another step in the process of being passed as legislation,” Yahoo Sports college football writer Ross Dellenger said at the Overby Center event on Sept. 17. “(The bill) would put up guardrails, limitations, restrictions around athlete movement, athlete pay and some agent registry stuff. Plan B is a conference-only governance structure where leagues make their own rules and enforce them as opposed to the NCAA.”

The NCAA has constantly been sued for years over antitrust violations. According to Dellenger, if conferences can make their own rules and enforce them on a smaller scale, the conferences believe they could avoid some of the issues with legal challenges.

Plan C has proved effective for many years, though it would bring a variety of new things to the sport, like employment status.

title: Kelly, Gallego Push to Protect Head Start Services for Arizona Families
text:
Arizona Senators urge the Department of Health and Human Services to not dilute quality, requirements for the Head Start Program

Today, Arizona Senators Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego called on the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to protect the quality of Head Start services that more than 16,000 Arizona children and their families rely on.

In a letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Assistant Secretary Alex J. Adams, Kelly and Gallego raised concerns about a proposed rule, “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,” that would remove federal requirements for classroom sizes, instruction, and health screenings. The senators urged HHS to preserve standards that help ensure Arizona children receive quality early education and care.

“Head Start offers a place to learn, build relationships, and receive care during years that are important to a child’s development,” the senators wrote. “These programs are an important part of Arizona communities and give families in need the support they may struggle to find or afford.”

In Arizona, Head Start and Early Head Start serve 16,172 children across 332 program sites, providing early education, meals, and health services at no cost to families. These programs also help parents maintain employment and continue their education, with 76 percent of Head Start parents working, attending school, or participating in job training.

Head Start and Early Head Start is especially important to communities where families have few child care options — including rural Arizona. There the programs provide about 17 percent of child care and serve 1,943 children eligible for services under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, 1,291 children experiencing homelessness, and 459 children in foster care statewide.

The senators also included letters from Arizona elected officials and organizations to highlight their concerns and show the importance of the Head Start program, including the Office of the Governor of Arizona and the Arizona Head Start Association, among others.

“We urge the Department to carefully review the enclosed letters and work with Arizona organizations to address their concerns before moving forward with changes to the program. Head Start is essential to thousands of Arizona families, and any changes must protect the quality of the education and services they receive,” the senators concluded.

Kelly also joined today 38 Senate colleagues to highlight the national impact of the proposed rule’s changes on children, educators, and families.

title: Lankford in Washington Examiner: “The world of Oct. 8: Where antisemitism didn’t just return — it became trendy”
text:
OKLAHOMA CITY, OK — US Senator James Lankford (R-OK), co-chair of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, today marked the third anniversary of the October 7th terrorist attacks in a new Washington Examiner column analyzing the rise of antisemitism since the attacks and the need to confront it wherever it appears. You can read it below or find it HERE.

The world of Oct. 8: Where antisemitism didn’t just return — it became trendy

By: James Lankford

Wednesday marks the three-year anniversary of one of the most brutal terrorist attacks in history: the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. Hamas terrorists flooded into Israel and murdered over 1,200 innocent Jewish men, women, and children, including 46 Americans. In addition to the death toll, Hamas captured and tormented 254 hostages, among them 12 Americans.

On Oct. 7, the world united against the horrors of antisemitism. Across the globe, people posted messages such as “Pray for Israel” and “We stand with Israel.” However, by the next morning, antisemitic propaganda was already flooding social media and college campuses around the country. People took to the streets to celebrate the “liberation” of Israel. A speaker at a rally in Philadelphia proclaimed, “I think that we should all give an applause right now to Hamas for a job well done,” and a rally in New York City chanted, “Globalize the intifada” and “smash the settler Zionist state.”

Within a few weeks of the Oct. 7 slaughter, it inexplicably became trendy on the political Left and the supposed “New Right” to say dumb and violent things about Jews and Israel. The rhetoric exceeded well beyond simple disagreement with the political or military decisions of the Israeli government. Without question, the U.S. Constitution protects the right of people in America to say epically dumb things. The Constitution also protects my right to call their rhetoric what it is — racist, ignorant, and antisemitic.

Hatred isn’t new for the Jewish people. For thousands of years, they have suffered racism, slavery, and genocide. From Egyptian slavery to Haman, Roman Occupation, the pogroms, and the Holocaust, irrational hatred toward Jewish people has persisted over millennia. But, in a more educated American society, you would hope that the lessons of the past would be applied and the scourge of antisemitism would finally end. That may be so someday, but today the social media algorithm teaches people to join in the centuries-old bias. We still have hope delayed.

Earlier this year, I visited Auschwitz-Birkenau, where Jews were unloaded from trains and sent to their death. I walked through the muddy streets that day and saw the evidence of the atrocities at the death wall and the crematoria. Hitler and his Nazi apparatus spread their vile antisemitic propaganda, then murdered 6 million Jews and absurdly declared that their brutality was justified because the Jews were “the problem.”

We are now living in the world of Oct. 8, where antisemitism is growing, and antisemitic incidents involving harassment, assault, and vandalism are more frequent now than they were before Oct. 7, 2023. Recent data from the FBI’s 2025 Hate Crimes Report shows that more than 62% of religiously-motivated hate crimes in 2025 targeted Jewish Americans — more than any other religious group. 2025 was the third-highest year of anti-Jewish hate crimes on record.

How we talk about antisemitism matters for the next generation. A recent study found that a single classroom lesson for middle and high school students on antisemitism reduces their willingness to agree with antisemitic tropes. Fact-based education matters in a free society. If you want to dive deeper into the past and help your classroom or family explore the consequences of antisemitism, the United States Holocaust Museum has excellent free online videos, visuals, and teaching materials. The deceit online needs a good dose of truth.

As a Christian and the co-chairman of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, it is my mission to work for justice for all people. I collaborate with my colleagues, law enforcement, the White House, federal agencies, state and local governments, educators, advocates, and clergy against irrational Jewish hatred. In the Oct. 8 world, we each have the responsibility to call out antisemitism wherever we see it, to defend human dignity, and to speak out for the inherent right of religious liberty for all people.

title: Luján, Bennet, Ansari, Padilla, Hickenlooper, Schiff Introduce Legislation to Protect Public Lands and Taxpayers from Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells
text:
Santa Fe, N.M. – U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) joined U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, U.S. Representative Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), and U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) to introduce the Stop Orphaned Wells Act, legislation that would prevent oil and gas companies from abandoning oil wells on public lands, a practice that shifts well cleanup costs from oil and gas companies to the American taxpayer.

“In New Mexico and across the country, abandoned wells pose serious environmental harm and threaten the health of our communities,” said Senator Luján. “We must ensure that oil and gas companies are held accountable and that taxpayers are not on the hook for the cost of cleanup. I’ve long fought to address abandoned wells, including championing the REGROW Act that was passed into law, and continue to work to ensure we identify and plug the thousands of abandoned wells nationwide. That’s why I’m cosponsoring this legislation to prevent companies from abandoning their wells and help reduce the number of abandoned wells in New Mexico and across the country.”

“For too long, taxpayers have footed the bill to clean up abandoned wells after companies walk away from their responsibilities,” said Senator Bennet. “As the Trump administration moves to weaken the safeguards that hold companies accountable, Congress must protect taxpayers and the public lands that power Colorado’s outdoor economy, while making sure oil and gas companies pay the cost of cleanup, rather than Colorado’s future generations.”

“Trump asked oil and gas executives to bankroll his campaign with a $1 billion contribution in exchange for a big payback. Meanwhile, Americans are left footing the bill for the damage they leave behind,” said Representative Ansari. “Orphaned wells threaten our water, wildlife, and air. I’m proud to lead the effort alongside Senator Bennet to make the oil and gas industry clean up its own mess. Our bill would ensure oil and gas companies pay to clean up the wells they abandon.”

Until 2024 when the Biden administration added agency rules, oil and gas fiscal assurance requirements were minimal, leading companies to abandon wells instead of remediating the land after drilling. The Trump administration is now rolling back these essential protections for public lands and American taxpayers. Nationwide, there are currently over 140,000 documented orphaned wells, including more than 15,000 on federal lands, and hundreds of thousands more that may be orphaned. Additionally, the number of documented orphaned wells in the United States has more than doubled since 2020. These sites are not only a significant liability for taxpayers and a growing threat to water resources, air quality, wildlife habitat, and private lands, but also jeopardize public health, ecosystems, grazing lands, outdoor recreation sites, and cultural resources that are at high risk from contamination. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act would ensure operators, not taxpayers, pay for cleanups and aligns directly with the interests of Western voters, nearly 9 in 10 of whom believe oil and gas companies should cover reclamation costs once drilling ends.

“Across California, there are over 5,000 orphaned oil wells that pose a threat to the health and safety of our communities and the environment,” said Senator Padilla. “When wells are left abandoned, drinking water is polluted, greenhouse gases are emitted, and the climate crisis is accelerated. This bill will help ensure orphaned oil and gas wells are plugged so Californians and communities across the country are protected from toxic emissions and contaminated air and water.”

“Abandoned wells put Colorado communities in danger,” said Senator Hickenlooper. “As Governor, we capped as many of these wells as we could, and that work continues here in the Senate, where we’re protecting taxpayers from getting stuck with the bill. Capping wells creates jobs and lowers pollution. It’s a win-win.”

“Oil companies can’t just walk away from abandoned oil and gas wells and leave taxpayers to bear the cleanup costs,” said Senator Schiff. “I’m joining Senator Bennet and other colleagues to make sure that Big Oil is responsible for cleaning up their messes. Americans should not have to deal with the consequences of an oil company’s negligence.”

“When an oil and gas company goes bankrupt, New Mexicans shouldn’t be the ones left to pick up the tab for cleanup costs,” said Senator Heinrich. “Right now, the Trump administration is making it easier for these companies to walk away without enough money set aside to clean up their wells. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act ensures that companies set aside money to meet their cleanup responsibilities, so taxpayers aren’t left paying the bill.”

Senator Luján has long fought to identify and remediate abandoned gas and oil wells. Senators Luján’s REGROW Act was adopted in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and put skilled energy workers back to work to plug abandoned wells. Additionally, Senator Luján has introduced the bipartisan Abandoned Well Remediation Research and Development Act (AWRRDA) to identify and remediate abandoned gas and oil wells, which can leak methane, contaminate groundwater, and create community safety risks.

This legislation is supported by 20 organizations, including Earthjustice Action, Colorado Fiscal Institute, Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship, Conservation Colorado, Montana Wildlife Federation, National Parks Conservation Association, Natural Resources Defense Council, Nevada Wildlife Federation, New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Public Land Solutions, Rocky Mountain Wild, San Juan Citizen’s Alliance, Sierra Club, Taxpayers for Common Sense, Trout Unlimited, Western Colorado Alliance, Western Organization of Resource Councils, Western Resilience Center, Wild Montana, Wilderness Workshop, and The Wilderness Society. In addition, this legislation was endorsed by U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

The text of the bill is available HERE. A summary of the bill is available HERE.

title: McConnell Statement on Third Anniversary of October 7th Attacks

“The invasion of peaceful homes to slaughter infants, rape women, and bludgeon elders was not the desperate act of noble freedom fighters.

title: Wyden, Merkley, Bonamici, Salinas, Hoyle, Dexter Announce $4.3 Million to Support Public Safety Across Oregon
text:
Programs in Gresham, Beaverton, Salem and Cottage Grove to benefit

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, along with U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici, Andrea Salinas, Val Hoyle, and Maxine Dexter, today announced more than $4.3 million in federal awards to support public safety programs across Oregon.

“It is absolutely essential to ensure communities across Oregon are safe, and young people are able to get the support they need in times of crisis,” Wyden said. “These federal grants will help support local police agencies, youth support programs and resources for foster youth. I’ll keep fighting to secure the federal resources Oregon communities need to thrive and stay secure.”

“Every Oregon community needs the resources to keep young people safe, support children who have experienced abuse and neglect, and build stronger relationships between families and those who serve them,” said Merkley, who helped secure funding for these community-initiated projects as a senior member of the Senate Appropriations Committee. “These federal investments will expand mentorship and opportunities for young people, ensure children have access to critical advocacy and medical services, and strengthen public safety infrastructure in several communities across the state. I’ll keep fighting to bring these federal resources home to Oregon and support the local organizations working every day to make our communities safer.”

“Beaverton’s Behavioral Health Court is doing important work to help people with mental health challenges who encounter the justice system and put them on a path to recovery,” said Bonamici. “I’m grateful this grant will support this initiative, improve lives, and make our communities safer.”

“Investments in emergency response capabilities strengthen our communities,” said Hoyle. “This funding for the Cottage Grove Police Department will replace aging equipment and bolster our emergency preparedness, prioritizing public safety and making it easier for officers to do their jobs.”

“Every child deserves to be safe, cared for, and heard. I’m thrilled to have helped secure over $2 million to protect children across Oregon. Because of this funding, children who have experienced abuse or neglect will not have to navigate some of the hardest moments of their lives alone. They will have an advocate in their corner and a safe place to turn to when they need emotional or medical support. I’m proud to see these federal dollars coming home to support the people doing this vital work in our communities,” Salinas said.

“Our young people deserve to grow up safe, supported and hopeful about their future,” said Dexter, M.D. “I fought hard to bring this $1 million investment to Gresham because children deserve opportunities to succeed. This funding will connect them with mentors, workforce readiness and programs that prevent and reduce involvement in violent crime and strengthen public safety efforts for youth and families in East Multnomah County. Investing in our children makes Oregon stronger.”

The $4.3 million in federal awards from the Department of Justice’s Byrne Discretionary Community Project Grants program will be distributed as follows:

$1.05 million to the City of Gresham to expand the East Multnomah Outreach Prevention Intervention initiative to prevent and combat juvenile delinquency, reduce youth involvement in violent crime, and strengthen coordinated public safety efforts for youth and families in East Multnomah County.

$1 million to Liberty House in Salem to increase medical clinic services to children who are victims of abuse or neglect in Marion and Polk Counties.

$1.03 million to the Oregon CASA Network in Salem to support its work to provide foster children the advocacy and support of an assigned Court Appointed Special Advocate.

$500,000 to the City of Beaverton to support the Behavioral Health Court program that targets defendants with criminal cases in the Beaverton Municipal Court who are the top utilizers of legal, jail or emergency room services living in the Beaverton area.

$800,000 to the City of Cottage Grove to support modernizing the Cottage Grove Police Department fleet and communications infrastructure to facilitate a department-wide transition to community-oriented policing practices.

“This funding will support Court Appointed Special Advocate programs across the state in recruiting and retaining volunteers who provide advocacy, encouragement, and a sense of stability to children impacted by abuse and neglect,” said Stephanie Brown, State Director, Oregon CASA Network. “Our advocates are in every corner of the state, getting to know the unique needs of each child they serve, and advocating for them in court, in school, and in the community. We appreciate the efforts of our elected officials to make this valuable investment in Oregon’s future which will help many of the state’s most vulnerable reach their full potential.

“Recovery takes time, care and support,” said Beaverton Mayor Lacey Beaty. “Our Behavioral Health Court team understands that and helps participants get treatment and rebuild their lives. I’m proud of the work Judge Britton and her team do every day, and grateful to Senator Wyden and Congresswoman Salinas for supporting it. This investment will make a real difference for our neighbors and the safety of our community.”

title: VIDEO: Senator Moody Welcomes More than 60 Florida Veterans to Washington, D.C. for Honor Flight
text:

Florida is home to more than 1.4 million veterans, one of the largest populations in the nation.

When Senator Moody served as Florida’s Attorney General, she oversaw the Florida Military and Veterans Assistance Program to assist service members and their families who have been affected by scams.

Recently cosponsored the Veterans Bill of Rights Act. The Veterans Bill of Rights Act would require the U.S. Secretary of Veterans Affairs to ensure veterans are clearly informed of their existing rights regarding VA-administered health care, benefits, and services.

Cosponsored the Major Richard Star Act, which seeks to fix unjust disability policies for retired combat veterans;

Supported the Veterans Education and Technical Skills (VETS) Opportunity Act, which would expand educational benefits for veterans;

Supported the Restore VA Accountability Act of 2025, which would help ensure that only the most dedicated individuals can serve veterans;

Held a town hall with VA Secretary Collins in Tampa to discuss issues facing veterans;

Recognized 200 years of U.S. Navy presence in Pensacola and discussed the critical importance of the Navy and Coast Guard’s presence in the Florida Panhandle; and more.

Senator Moody recently joined the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Senator Moody is proud to be part of a military family.

title: Murphy Denied Access to Military Facility by Hegseth in Unprecedented Move, Meets with Saudi Crown Prince
text:
RIYADH, SAUDI ARABIA – As Saudi Arabia is under heightened security risk amid the Iran War, U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) issued the following statements after departing Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on a Congressional Delegation (CODEL) trip to the Middle East, where he also visited Doha, Qatar.

In an unprecedented move, the U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) under Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership denied Murphy access to the Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, despite decades of precedent for DOD supporting CODELs to American military bases under active threat to uphold Congress’s oversight duties. Prior to his CODEL, Murphy requested access to the base via a letter and direct appeal to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) leadership to no avail. While DOD denied him access to U.S. military facilities, the U.S. Department of State supported Murphy’s trip to the region.

“This is one of our biggest and most important facilities in the Gulf region. I’ve been to the Middle East at least a dozen times as a Member of Congress, and I’ve never been denied access to military facilities. This is part of a coordinated, deliberate campaign by the Department of Defense to hide the consequences and the true costs of the Iran war,” said Murphy of the denial.

Murphy also met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Saudi Arabia.

“I’ve been a vocal critic of Saudi Arabia and the Crown Prince. But, I think it’s important to be here to disagree and be honest and candid about those disagreements. It’s important to recognize there are things we need to work on together: ending the war in Iran and a pathway to Palestinian statehood. We had an honest, provocative conversation, particularly about the Gulf countries’ decisions to invest in the Trump family. It’s important for the Crown Prince to hear not just from the Trump Administration, but from people who want a different path,” said Murphy of the meeting.

Additionally, Murphy met with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud; toured the damage done to the U.S. embassy in Riyadh; engaged with economic and cultural leaders; and talked with University of New Haven students at the first American university campus in Saudi Arabia, among other things.

In Qatar, Murphy met with His Highness the Emir of the State of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. Additionally, Murphy met with Ali Al Thawadi, Qatari Minister for Strategic Affairs and a key diplomat who coordinates U.S.-Iran shuttle diplomacy; Qatari royal and Qatar Foundation Vice Chair Sheikha Hind Al Thani in Education City to discuss the presence of American universities in Qatar; and Qatar Energy CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, among others.

Sen. Murphy is the first Democratic Senator to visit the Gulf since the start of the Iran War.

title: Government Watchdog: Trump Illegally Blocked Health Research Funding
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Patty Murray, Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, issued the following statement on a Government Accountability Office (GAO) decision issued today, which concludes that President Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. illegally impounded fiscal year 2025 funding for health research conducted by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) in violation of the Impoundment Control Act (ICA):

“This decision confirms what we’ve long known: President Trump lit health research funding on fire last year, and it’s clear as day he’s just done the same again this year. In fact, President Trump announced to the world just a few days ago that he was illegally cutting nearly $30 million more, and HHS has failed to detail to the Committee exactly how it has spent down AHRQ funding for fiscal year 2026.

“This is research that has saved tens of thousands of lives and saved billions of dollars in health care costs—but President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are intent on breaking the law to cut it off, and Republicans in Congress have all but let them do it. It’s past time Congress imposes real consequences on this administration for killing lifesaving health research—I’ll keep fighting to do just that.”

In its decision today, GAO concluded:

“Congress appropriated lump-sum amounts to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) to carry out various research initiatives for fiscal year 2025. .… We conclude that HHS withheld funds when it declined to obligate or expend more than $78 million of its FY 2025 appropriation before the close of the fiscal year. We further conclude that this withholding constituted an impoundment under the ICA rather than a programmatic delay. Because HHS did not submit a special message proposing to rescind AHRQ funds, HHS’s actions violated the ICA.”

GAO’s decision examines how the Trump administration illegally impounded fiscal year 2025 funding provided to AHRQ for health research after the Trump administration sabotaged the agency, pushing out 80% of all staff and cancelling grants en masse. It’s clear, however, that this administration has once again illegally withheld and misspent AHRQ funding provided by Congress for fiscal year 2026, as well. Senator Murray and Senator Tammy Baldwin, Ranking Member of the Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education Subcommittee, raised alarm bells about the fate of fiscal year 2026 AHRQ funds several weeks ago. Then, just days after HHS Deputy Secretary Nominee Chris Klomp vowed to senators that virtually all of the agency’s funding would be spent—while failing to provide details to back up that assertion—President Trump moved to permanently impound nearly $30 million in AHRQ funding in his “pocket rescission.” Republicans have repeatedly blocked Democrats’ efforts to prevent presidents from attempting to use “pocket rescissions.”

title: Murray on Trump and Duffy’s Plans to Tie Transit Funding to Birth Rates
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Patty Murray, Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, released the following statement after the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) proposed new guidance for the Capital Investment Grants (CIG) program that would increase funding for projects based on their region’s average birth and marriage rates compared to the nationwide averages. The CIG program funds infrastructure investments to expand public transit—including for bus transit and light rail and commuter rail improvements. Under the new proposal, the FTA would steer more grant funding to parts of the country where only more men and women choose to get married and more babies are born—providing an up to 10% boost.

“Tying funding for transit projects to marriage rates and how many babies a woman has is the sort of bizarre and dystopian idea you’d expect in a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the U.S. government—yet here we are. President Trump wants to weaponize federal grants to wage his backward culture wars and punish Democrats, and it’s past time Republicans join us to stand against this historically corrupt administration’s efforts to rob our communities of resources they are owed—because it’s already clear as day they are holding up projects in blue states while moving ahead with projects elsewhere.”

The new proposal would apply to 40 projects across the country already in the CIG program, forcing transit agencies and local and state governments that have already spent years planning and designing projects to follow a whole slew of new rating and cost-share requirements. This could force entities to re-design projects and re-do environmental reviews, which will increase costs and delay construction, and in the worst case potentially makes projects ineligible for CIG funding. The new requirements could reduce CIG funding for important transit projects below the 40% floor set by Congress in the annual funding bills, which has been in place since fiscal year 2020.

These significant changes to the CIG program are another attempt by the Trump administration to penalize blue states and slow down and delay transit projects. Recently, the Trump administration advanced a CIG project in a red state while it continues to hold back two projects in blue states that have been ready for much longer.

Studies conducted last year when the Department of Transportation issued an order updating its governing principles to include a general preference to communities with higher marriage and birth rates showed that such prioritization would disproportionally hurt low-income, non-white residents.
