title: Maryland Delegation Members Push for Funding for Mental Health at U.S. Cyber Command at Fort Meade
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Representative Sarah Elfreth were joined by Senator Angela Alsobrooks and Representatives Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Glenn Ivey, April McClain Delaney, and Johnny Olszewski (all D-Md.) in requesting $11 million for U.S. Cyber Command as Congress works to complete the Fiscal Year 2027 Department of Defense appropriations. In the letter to Appropriations Committee leadership, the lawmakers stressed the importance of the health and wellbeing of the service members and civilian employees of U.S. Cyber Command, as well as the importance of their work to our national security. The $11 million program increase would fund U.S. Cyber Command’s high-performance team training, an operation aimed at improving care for service members, including helping commanders establish sustainable training, recovery, care, and resilience practices.

The lawmakers begin, “We respectfully urge you to retain the $11 million program increase for U.S. Cyber Command high-performance team training under Budget Activity 12D, Cyberspace Operations, as Congress completes the Fiscal Year 2027 Department of Defense Appropriations Act. Headquartered at Fort George G. Meade, U.S. Cyber Command is central to Maryland’s national security community and relies on service members, civilian employees, and families throughout our state to conduct some of the Nation’s most demanding and persistent military operations missions.”

“As the Congressional Delegation of Maryland, we are troubled by recent public reporting describing several deaths by suicide among personnel in cyber operations and the Fort Meade community over a short period. These deaths have a severe impact on the family, friends, and wider community. The concentration of these tragedies within a small, highly specialized workforce demands sustained attention and an institutional response proportionate to the operational strain these personnel bear,” they continue.

On the need for funding for High Performance Team Training at Cyber Command, the lawmakers note, “The requested $11 million would help U.S. Cyber Command close this gap by funding the FY26 NDAA provision. Embedded support would improve access to care for service members inside secure facilities, give providers a better understanding of the mission and its operational tempo, identify concerns earlier, and help commanders establish sustainable training, recovery, and resilience practices. Models used in other high-demand military communities, including special operations and remotely piloted aircraft units, and dedicated intelligence commands demonstrate the value of treating psychological health and human performance as readiness requirements. Cyber Command noted that without this funding, burnout and force degradation will increase.”

“Preserving this funding would demonstrate Congress’s commitment to the health and readiness of the cyber workforce at Fort Meade, Maryland, and across the Nation. It would also help ensure that the Department establishes an enduring system of prevention, care, and operational resilience rather than relying solely on short-term interventions following a tragedy. One loss of life is one too many. We must do everything we can to make sure our servicemembers and everyone at the Fort has the full mental health support and resources they need, so that a tragedy like this does not occur again. We appreciate your continued leadership and support of Maryland’s servicemembers, federal employees, and families,” the lawmakers conclude.

The full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Chairman Cole, Ranking Member DeLauro, Chair Collins, and Vice Chair Murray:

We respectfully urge you to retain the $11 million program increase for U.S. Cyber Command high-performance team training under Budget Activity 12D, Cyberspace Operations, as Congress completes the Fiscal Year 2027 Department of Defense Appropriations Act. Headquartered at Fort George G. Meade, U.S. Cyber Command is central to Maryland’s national security community and relies on service members, civilian employees, and families throughout our state to conduct some of the Nation’s most demanding and persistent missions.

As the Congressional Delegation of Maryland, we are troubled by recent public reporting describing several deaths by suicide among personnel in cyber operations and the Fort Meade community over a short period. These deaths have a severe impact on the family, friends, and wider community. The concentration of these tragedies within a small, highly specialized workforce demands sustained attention and an institutional response proportionate to the operational strain these personnel bear.

Cyber personnel operate in a uniquely stressful environment. Many are effectively “deployed in place” for two- or three-year assignments, conducting real-world operations against capable adversaries without the clear start and end points, protected recovery periods, or unit-level reconstitution cycles associated with conventional deployments. Because much of their work is classified, they may be unable to discuss the sources of their stress with family members or medical professionals who lack the clearances or access to secure facilities necessary for a complete conversation. These conditions can isolate personnel, delay appropriate care, and ultimately weaken readiness, retention, and operational effectiveness.

These challenges are particularly relevant at Fort Meade, where U.S. Cyber Command, the National Security Agency, military cyber components, and other national security organizations operate within a highly secure and interconnected environment. Although Maryland has a significant network of military, federal, and civilian health resources, traditional centralized-care models do not always give cyber personnel timely access to appropriately cleared professionals in the facilities where they work.

Congress and the Department have already recognized this gap. Congress previously directed a review of the psychological and occupational demands placed on cyber operators, and the Department subsequently acknowledged that existing resources did not fully meet the needs of the U.S. Cyber Command. The Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) also expanded mental health services intended to address the U.S. Cyber Command’s unique requirements by integrating behavioral health professionals with security clearances within cyber units. Nevertheless, dedicated support teams and embedded care have not been implemented consistently across the force.

The requested $11 million would help U.S. Cyber Command close this gap by funding the FY26 NDAA provision. Embedded support would improve access to care for service members inside secure facilities, give providers a better understanding of the mission and its operational tempo, identify concerns earlier, and help commanders establish sustainable training, recovery, and resilience practices. Models used in other high-demand military communities, including special operations and remotely piloted aircraft units, and dedicated intelligence commands demonstrate the value of treating psychological health and human performance as readiness requirements. Cyber Command noted that without this funding, burnout and force degradation will increase.

This represents a modest investment compared with U.S. Cyber Command’s broader annual budget and the strategic value of its highly trained workforce. Recruiting, clearing, and developing cyber operators takes years. Losing experienced personnel harms Maryland families, disrupts operational teams, increases replacement and training costs, and reduces the Nation’s ability to defend critical systems and conduct cyber missions.

Accordingly, we respectfully request that the final Fiscal Year 2027 Department of Defense Appropriations Act retain the following program increase:

12D CYBERSPACE OPERATIONS

High Performance Team Training ........................................ $11,000,000

Preserving this funding would demonstrate Congress’s commitment to the health and readiness of the cyber workforce at Fort Meade, Maryland, and across the Nation. It would also help ensure that the Department establishes an enduring system of prevention, care, and operational resilience rather than relying solely on short-term interventions following a tragedy. One loss of life is one too many. We must do everything we can to make sure our servicemembers and everyone at the Fort has the full mental health support and resources they need, so that a tragedy like this does not occur again.

We appreciate your continued leadership and support of Maryland’s servicemembers, federal employees, and families.

title: Warnock Leads Bicameral Coalition in Opposing Trump Administration’s Proposed Head Start Overhaul
text:
Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock and 38 Congressional colleagues are calling on the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to rescind its proposed overhaul of the Head Start program

The administration’s proposal jeopardizes access to quality early learning and child care services for more than 700,000 children across the country

Head Start provides comprehensive early learning and family support services across the country, particularly in rural and low-income communities

Senator Warnock is a proud Head Start alumni and founding member of the Head Start to Congress Caucus

Senators Reverend Warnock, colleagues: “Let us be very clear: what you are proposing seriously weakens the high-quality, comprehensive research-backed services required by law, undermines access to critical services, restricts access for children and families, and creates uncertainty for Head Start programs across the nation”

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) led a bicameral group of lawmakers in opposing the Trump Administration’s proposed overhaul of Head Start, a federal program dedicated to improving academic and health outcomes for children by providing comprehensive early learning and family support services across the country, particularly in rural and low-income communities.

“Let us be very clear: what you are proposing seriously weakens the high-quality, comprehensive research-backed services required by law, undermines access to critical services, restricts access for children and families, and creates uncertainty for Head Start programs across the nation,” wrote Senator Warnock and his colleagues. “This proposed rule is a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year.”

In August, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced changes to the Head Start Program Performance Standards that effectively eliminate the central mechanism for evaluating and ensuring the quality of early childhood education services provided through Head Start. The administration’s proposal jeopardizes access to quality early learning and child care services for more than 700,000 children across the country.

As a proud Head Start alum and founding member of the Head Start to Congress Caucus, Senator Warnock has long championed the program and its mission. Earlier this year, he joined a bicameral coalition in opposing a similar HHS proposal that would eliminate salary increases and improvements to employment benefits for full-time Head Start staff. In 2025, Senator Warnock introduced the bipartisan Head Start Education and Development Workforce Advancement and Yield (HEADWAY) Act to address early childhood workforce shortages by allowing Early Head Start classroom teachers to continue teaching while earning their Child Development Associate (CDA) credential.

Alongside Senator Warnock, the letter is led by Senators Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), and cosigned by Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Chris Coons (D-DE), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Richard Durbin (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Angus King (I-ME), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ed Markey (D-MA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Patty Murray (D-WA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Gary Peters (D-MI), Jack Reed (D-RI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Tina Smith (D-MN), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Mark Warner (D-VA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-CT), Ron Wyden (D-OR), and 152 Members of Congress.

A copy of the letter can be found HERE and text is below:

“Dear Secretary Kennedy,

“We write to express our strong opposition to the proposed rule, ‘Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,’ which seeks to illegally dismantle Head Start by removing over 90 percent of standards that ensure children receive high-quality early education and comprehensive services. This proposal is a blatant effort to gut core aspects of this longstanding, anti-poverty program and is in direct conflict with the Head Start Act.

“Let us be very clear: what you are proposing seriously weakens the high-quality, comprehensive research-backed services required by law, undermines access to critical services, restricts access for children and families, and creates uncertainty for Head Start programs across the nation. Under your proposal, 80% of children in Head Start will face worse staff-to-child ratios. Nearly 1 in 10 children currently served in Head Start could become ineligible for services overnight. Key Head Start health, dental, mental health, and developmental services will be reduced nationwide. And the duration of the Head Start school day could be cut in half in many communities, leaving working families stranded and without child care. That is unacceptable.

“Since 1965, Head Start has served more than 40 million young children with age-appropriate education, health care, dental care, and healthy meals. The program has also provided working-class parents with connections to job training, adult education, nutrition services, housing assistance, and other support services that strengthen families. Research shows that children who attend Head Start are more likely to be ready for kindergarten, graduate from high school, attend college, and are less likely to have adverse health outcomes than non-participants. Every year, roughly 1,600 Head Start grantees serve over 700,000 young children and their families through a unique, multi-generational and holistic approach. The scope and quality of these programs have changed the lives of millions.

“Despite Head Start’s essential role, you have led the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to repeatedly undermine and disrupt Head Start services. Since the very start of this Administration, Head Start programs have had their funding illegally withheld and delayed, lost federal staff who were essential to their community-driven successes, and faced new requirements that create constant confusion. Last year, a leaked version of the fiscal year 2026 budget proposal indicated the Administration’s plan to eliminate the Head Start program. You made a commitment to Congress to ‘preserve’ Head Start, yet this proposed rule is the latest attempt by the Administration to deteriorate and ultimately eliminate the program by gutting the core standards and services that have long-defined and ensured its success.

“This proposal strikes nearly all of the Head Start Program Performance Standards (‘Performance Standards’) in defiance of statutory requirements and is antithetical to the mission of Head Start, which is to provide quality early learning and comprehensive services for children and families with the highest needs. Head Start’s unique federal-to-local model relies on the Performance Standards to provide clarity to grantees, while considering evolving research, science, and community needs.

“Under section 641A(a)(2)(C)(ii) of the Head Start Act, HHS cannot modify the Performance Standards in a way that will ‘result in the elimination of or any reduction in quality, scope, or types of health, educational, parental involvement, nutritional, social, or other services required to be provided under such standards as in effect on the date of enactment of the Improving Head Start for School Readiness Act of 2007.’ Yet, this proposed rule does exactly that: it illegally eliminates and reduces the core components of Head Start as they currently exist.

1. Undermine quality early childhood education and services

“We oppose your proposed elimination of federal standards for staff-to-child ratios, class sizes, safety practices; proposed removal of limits on suspensions and expulsions; and proposed removal of Head Start staff professional development, training, and wellness breaks. This overhaul of the Performance Standards will diminish the quality of services and jeopardize the safety and well-being of children.

Staff-to-Child Ratios and Group Sizes

“Removing staff-to-child ratios and group size limits in 45 C.F.R. §1302.21(b) and deferring instead to state policies will diminish program quality and threaten children’s safety. State and local policies for child care ratios and group sizes vary widely, which is why the Performance Standards include research-informed, national baselines for high-quality settings that support child development, health, and safety. For example, in Idaho, state law and regulations allow a single educator to care for up to six infants, while in 35 other states, the required ratio is 1:4 and is aligned with the current Performance Standards. According to the Children’s Equity Project, your proposal to replace these federal regulations with state child care standards is estimated to worsen staff-to-child ratios for 80 percent of children enrolled in Early Head Start or Head Start Preschool. HHS’s own analysis of the rule expects a 16 to 32 percent increase in the average number of children per Head Start educator. These changes will make it harder for staff to provide adequate supervision of children, result in poorer quality interactions with children, increase staff burnout, hinder accommodations for children with disabilities, and diminish the delivery of complex early learning science.

Child Safety

“We also oppose the proposed changes to essential safety standards that protect young children and give families peace of mind that their children will be well cared for in Head Start. Many of these changes are unconscionable, such as removing the prohibition on leaving children unsupervised and reducing protections against the maltreatment or endangerment of children, including restraint and seclusion practices. Disparities in discipline—including the use of restraint and seclusion—begin as early as preschool, with particularly concerning disparities involving children of color with disabilities. The elimination of these provisions would mean that young children could be subject to a higher risk of corporal punishment, abuse, neglect, shaming, and humiliation, or being left alone while enrolled in Head Start.

Suspensions and Expulsions

“The proposal to remove federal disciplinary standards in 45 C.F.R. §1302.17 that prohibit or severely limit the uses of suspensions, expulsions, or unenrollment of children will push children out of programs and disrupt their social and emotional development. According to a 2016 study, as many as 250 preschoolers are suspended or expelled every day. Research has found that boys of color, children with disabilities, and children who are English language learners are disproportionately more likely to experience suspensions or other disciplinary practices in preschool. Further, these disciplinary practices have negative consequences on children and families’ mental health and children’s development, education, and health.

Standards for Teaching and Learning, Staff Qualifications, Trainings, and Wellness

“The proposed rule eliminates standards for best practices for teaching and learning (currently regulated in 45 C.F.R. §1302.30-1302.36), erodes staff qualifications, limits access to training and professional development, and reduces wellness services (required under 45 C.F.R. §1302.90-93), which will worsen conditions for the Head Start workforce and their capacity to provide children with high-quality early learning. The proposed rule removes clear guidelines on individualizing instruction that integrates early learning standards into curriculum and teacher training. The proposed rule effectively prohibits postsecondary education credentials—which runs counter to section 648A of the law that outlines Head Start staff qualifications. At a time when 59 percent of the Head Start programs report challenging classroom conditions as among the top reasons for staff vacancies, the proposed rule also seek to remove coaching, some teacher training, developmental screenings for children, wellness breaks, and mental health information for Head Start staff. This elimination of professional and supportive services will worsen environments for the Head Start workforce, who are already underpaid and turning over at a rate that limits the capacity to serve more eligible children and families. Even worse, this comes at a time when HHS is in the process of finalizing another rule, ‘Restoring Flexibility to Support Head Start Program Access,’ that rolls back provisions that would have increased wages and required benefits for Head Start staff. Together, these changes will exacerbate staff stress and burnout and compound recruitment and retention challenges, making it harder to serve more children and disrupting the continuity of care.

2. Deteriorates critical comprehensive services for children and families

“Under section 636 of the Head Start Act, one of the stated purposes of Head Start is to provide ‘health, educational, nutritional, social, and other services’ to low-income children and their families across the country. The proposal guts regulatory provisions (45 C.F.R. §§ 1302.40-46) that are critical to promoting healthy child development and school readiness, and ensuring families receive comprehensive services and are equipped to build nurturing and responsive relationships with their children. Research has proven that developmental and mental health screenings, nutrition counseling, oral health programs, and parent education and support services enhance children’s outcomes and prevent long-term health issues, and Head Start has a long history of successfully providing these services for families. For example, during the 2025 program year, Head Start grantees across the country provided nearly 373,000 families (52 percent) with education on preventative medical and oral health, over 102,000 families (14 percent) with mental health services, and over 347,000 families (48 percent) with nutrition education. We oppose the proposal to roll back decades of progress and remove provisions that are central to the quality, frequency, and coordination of comprehensive services that are important for children’s development and learning and family economic stability and well-being.

Health Services for Children

“The proposed elimination of 45 C.F.R. §1302.42 will result in fewer available physical, dental, and mental health services for children. Under the proposed rule, Head Start programs would no longer have to ensure children receive developmental, vision, and hearing screenings; check for a source of health insurance; and check the status of age-appropriate medical, mental health, and dental care. Current standards not only require these services but also establish timelines for doing so to ensure children receive medical and dental care without delay and requirements to refer children to follow up services and track progress to ensure children receive intervention or treatment for any identified issues. Further, the proposed rule strikes standards for family collaboration and education about their child’s healthy development (45 C.F.R.§1302.41 and §1302.46) and the frequency and coordination of mental health services (45 C.F.R.§1302.45)

“The law requires HHS to have standards for health services (section 641A(a)(1)) and for Head Start grantees to have goals and measurable objectives for health services (section 642(f)). Notably, section 657C of the Head Start Act defines the term “health” to include services or care provided to enrolled children, their parents, or their siblings for both physical and mental health. However, the plan to eliminate almost all health, dental, and mental health standards, in addition to health and developmental screenings, service timelines, and ongoing care obligations will serve to deteriorate preventative and continuous health services for young children.

“Early screenings and services are fundamental to the mission of Head Start which recognizes children’s learning, health, and development are inextricably linked, and your proposed changes will have long-term consequences for children. Head Start plays a critical role in ensuring that children with disabilities and their families are connected with providers of early intervention services for infants and toddlers with disabilities under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Without these screenings, children who are at-risk for, or are suspected of having, a disability could be diagnosed later and miss the opportunity to receive early intervention services, increasing their risk of falling behind in elementary school and force their families to pay out-of-pocket for screenings and services traditionally offered by Head Start.

“Additionally, we object to the removal of 45 C.F.R. §1302.42(e), which explicitly requires Early Head Start programs to use funds to provide diapers and formula during the program day, as well as the provision that allows Head Start programs to use program funds to pay for professional medical and oral health services if no other funding source is available. These guidance and authorities are crucial to ensuring every Head Start child receives early, preventative, and ongoing care – regardless of their family’s ability to pay for and access these services on their own.

Services for Expecting Families

“We also oppose the proposal to eliminate most of the dedicated services for more than 10,000 expecting Head Start families. Currently 45 C.F.R. §1302.80-82 of the rule requires grantees to check enrolled pregnant women’s prenatal care or insurance within 30 days, facilitate access to comprehensive services, and provide prenatal services to reduce barriers to healthy maternal and birthing outcomes. Prenatal and postpartum referrals and education are critical to the healthy development of infants, maternal health, and fostering nurturing and responsive caregiving environments.

“The culmination of striking these research-based regulations will undermine Head Start’s current, proactive scope and the comprehensiveness of health, nutrition, and early intervention screenings and services for hundreds of thousands of Head Start children and families.

3. Restrict access for children and working families

“The proposed rule makes it harder for children and families to qualify for and be served by Head Start in a manner that meets their needs. We strongly object to the plans to shorten Head Start’s hours of operation, remove enrollment requirements for children with disabilities, require English-only instruction, and remove self-attestation and excessive housing costs considerations for eligibility, particularly for families experiencing homelessness.

Program Duration

“The proposal to shorten the Head Start day is taking the program in exactly the wrong direction and is out of step with research on early childhood education. The proposed rule reverts Head Start centers program operations to the statutory minimum of 3 hours a day. To be clear, the current duration minimums that you seek to eliminate were designed to align Head Start with state pre-kindergarten successes in making gains in language, literacy, math, and social skills. The proposal also “acknowledges that families may need to secure alternative child care arrangements or may miss work time” in response to this new rule. Head Start is often the only licensed child care option in rural communities, and an estimated 4.2 million children lack access to a formal child care slot in their local community. In many states, depending on the age of the child and child care setting, the cost of child care exceeds annual, average in-state cost of college tuition, rent payments, or even mortgage payments. It is simply unrealistic and shameful to diminish Head Start services at a time when high-quality child care is unaffordable for working families and hard to find. We urge you to abandon this provision.

Income Eligibility Barriers

“We oppose the prohibition on self-attestation in the proposed §1301.02(c)(4). This prohibition will exclude families with extremely low incomes, those who are self-employed, or those experiencing homelessness from Head Start programs. These are individuals who do not have the same access to tax documents, pay stubs, and proof of income from employers as individuals with more financial stability. HHS’s own analysis of the rule estimates that this change alone will make 8 percent of Head Start children, about 54,000 children, ineligible. It is abhorrent to remove some of the children and families with the greatest needs from Head Start.

“Current Performance Standards in §1301.12(i)(1)(ii) allow Head Start programs to adjust for excessive housing expenses when verifying income eligibility. As wages increase to respond to rising costs of living, many families earning low wages have seen their incomes rise above Head Start’s federal poverty level eligibility threshold but still struggle to make ends meet and afford the high costs of necessities like housing, food, utilities, and child care. Striking this consideration will make it harder for families who face high costs of living and would benefit from Head Start’s services to qualify for the program.

Children Experiencing Homelessness

“We are greatly concerned about the undue burden for children and families experiencing homelessness to be served by Head Start programs under your proposal. Section 640(m) of the Head Start Act requires the HHS Secretary to issue rules to ‘remove barriers to the enrollment and participation of homeless children in Head Start programs’, including ensuring children experiencing homelessness are identified and prioritized for enrollment, allowing their families to provide required documents within a reasonable time frame, offering continuity of services when housing is unstable, and coordinating with McKinney-Vento liaisons in local school districts. These legally required policies and procedures and the self-attestation pathway are critical for Head Start to carry out eligibility verification for children experiencing homelessness, allow enrollment of these children before records arrive, and hold slots for them if families relocate during the program year. In the 2024-2025 program year, Head Start served more than 60,000 children experiencing homelessness – the highest number on record. We urge you to follow the law to ensure Head Start identifies, enrolls, and coordinates services for children and families experiencing homelessness.

Children with Disabilities

“Under the proposed rule, requirements pertaining to services for children with disabilities are eliminated, exposing children and their families to increased discrimination and greater barriers to necessary supports and services. While the underlying statutory requirements remain in place, the proposal no longer mandates that children receive services while they await an IDEA evaluation, and it removes the explicit directive that programs cannot reject a child based on disability-status. We oppose the proposed rule’s removal of standards that require Head Start programs to provide early intervention or special education services consistent with IDEA, support parent participation in this process, and prohibit denying enrollment or services based on disability status. While federal disability civil rights laws remain in effect, removing the detailed Performance Standards removes the mechanism that makes those legal rights operational day to day. Without clear federal requirements, whether a child with a disability receives an assessment, an accommodation, or coordinated services would depend far more on what an individual local program happens to know about disability, what resources it has, and how effectively a family can navigate complex systems on its own. That is likely to produce significant disparities across states and communities — the opposite of the consistency Head Start’s standards were designed to guarantee. If finalized, this proposal threatens to unravel decades of progress toward inclusion for more than 100,000 children with disabilities currently served by Head Start.

Dual Language Learners

“The proposed extreme provision to impose English-only instruction in Head Start is a drastic shift from current learning and teaching science and practices to create educational access to all children. In 2024, nearly 30 percent of Head Start children’s primary, home language was not English, and nearly 10 percent of children whose families primarily speak English were acquiring or learning another language. Head Start supports dual language learner children in the acquisition of the English language and provides educational services and parent engagement in home languages. For example, programs are directed statutorily to use funds on literacy training ‘in a developmentally, culturally, and linguistically appropriate manner and support children’s development in their native language’ and include ‘specific methods to best address the needs of children who are limited English proficient’ in section 648(d)(2) of the Head Start Act. While section 641A(a)(1)(B)(x) of the law requires the Secretary to issue standards to ensure ‘progress toward acquisition of the English language’, your proposal to require English-only instruction may conflict with the statutory requirement that ‘progress [be] made through the use of culturally and linguistically appropriate instructional services.’ We ask that you withdraw this provision and maintain inclusive instruction for Head Start children, particularly dual language learners. Research is clear that your provision will slow English acquisition and can be harmful to child development and academic achievement.

4. Intentional ambiguity and misleading promises

“We are concerned that removing nearly all the Performance Standards will create a great deal of ambiguity for Head Start grantees to implement the law with fidelity. The removal of regulatory details and reduction in administrative spending places greater burdens and uncertainties for community-driven programs in fulfilling their statutory obligations. For over six decades, Head Start has been a successful federal-to-local program, but this proposal to defer to state administration will undermine the consistency and quality of the program.

Monitoring

“The intentional lack of clarity for administering a complex, high-quality early childhood education and comprehensive services leaves every Head Start program susceptible to being out of compliance and possibly losing their grants. Section 641A(c) of the Head Start Act requires the Secretary to monitor programs, and HHS holds the authority to issue deficiencies when the monitoring process identifies a systematic or substantial failure to meet program requirements. The proposed rule strikes some details under §1304.11 related to the conditions that result in a grant being designated for competition and adds a vague provision for HHS to determine and re-compete a grant if the grantee is ‘determined not to be delivering classroom quality’. The proposal puts all Head Start grantees in a vulnerable position to face arbitrary monitoring processes without adequate guidance.

Administrative Capacity

“The proposal in §1301.14 to reduce maximum administrative spending from 15 percent to 5 percent for Head Start grantees expressly contradicts section 644(b) of the Head Start Act, which allows a cap of 15 percent with the option of a waiver. Funds set aside for administrative spending allow grantees to develop and operate Head Start programs, including fiscal management, human resources, information technology, data systems, and facilities management. To continue these required functions under a 5 percent limit is untenable and many programs will be forced to have staff share functions or eliminate functions or reduce operations. Some grantees have suggested they will have to relinquish their grants altogether because they will be unable to maintain operations. HHS’s own analysis of this rule estimates that only 3.7 percent of Head Start grantees operate at or below this 5 percent threshold. To put it simply, this reduction will pose greater challenges for Head Start programs to deliver high-quality services or to expand services to serve more children, particularly for smaller and rural programs that already face limited administrative capacity.

Conclusion

“This proposed rule is a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year. Under your proposal, Head Start children could be subject to corporal punishment; left unsupervised; have larger class sizes; have less qualified teachers; and no longer receive preventative and continuous health services, including oral health and mental health services. Families might have to find alternative child care options and struggle to meet eligibility requirements, particularly for those with little to no incomes, those experiencing homelessness, and those already facing high costs of living. The Head Start workforce will lose professional development, training, and be expected to teach and supervise more children without any additional pay or support.

“We strongly urge you to withdraw the proposed rule, obey the law, and protect the legacy of Head Start.

Sincerely,”

###

title: Welch Leads Bicameral Colleagues in Urging Trump Admin to Reverse Course on Closure of Vermont’s White River National Fish Hatchery
text:
BETHEL, VT — U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Member of the Senate Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation, Forestry, Natural Resources, and Biotechnology, today led Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), U.S. Senators Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), and U.S. Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL) in urging the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Services (USFWS) to reconsider its decision to place Vermont’s White River National Fish Hatchery on inactive status.

In their letter to USFWS Director Brian Nesvik, the lawmakers warn that placing the White River National Fish Hatchery on inactive status would inhibit valuable scientific research, and risk reversing a decade of progress toward fishery restoration, including salmon. The lawmakers request that USFWS fully evaluate all facilities in the region to analyze how this action would impact Lake Champlain and long-standing service priorities before finalizing any determination about the White River facility.

“Since the 1980s, the White River National Fish Hatchery has contributed to the restoration of native fish species in Lake Champlain, the Connecticut River, and the Great Lakes,” write the lawmakers. “Lake Champlain once supported thriving populations of landlocked Atlantic salmon and lake trout, each of which disappeared by 1900 amid stress from nearby settlement runoff and dam construction. In 1972, Vermont and New York began working to restore the fisheries. USFWS opened the White River hatchery in 1984 to provide federal support for these efforts, which has only grown more critical since the introduction of aquatic invasive species like sea lamprey.”

The lawmakers emphasize how successful fishery restoration efforts will bolster the outdoor recreation economy in Vermont and New York: “ In 2016, USFWS discovered the first wild-hatched Atlantic salmon fry in the Winooski River—the first in 150 years. The following year, researchers documented a second sighting of fry in Vermont and the first sighting in New York’s Boquet River. In 2023, USFWS recorded the highest number of Atlantic salmon encountered at the Chase Mill hydroelectric dam on the Winooski River in 30 years. Meanwhile, sea lamprey control—led by the Great Lakes Fishery Commission in partnership with USFWS, the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources, and the New York Department of Environmental Conservation—significantly reduced lamprey wounding of Atlantic salmon, from 79% at the height of the infestation to just 6% in 2022.”

“Bipartisan majorities in Congress have consistently recognized the value of the National Fish Hatchery System. In FY26, Congress appropriated $79 million for system operations and an additional $24.5 million for maintenance and equipment, a nearly $3.5 million increase in funding compared to FY25,” the lawmakers continue. “We respectfully request that you stay the decision to put the facility on inactive status and brief our staff on your plans for the hatchery not later than October 30, 2026.”

Read and download the lawmakers’ full letter to USFWS Nesvik.

title: Whitehouse, Kelly Press EPA, AI Companies on Rollback of Public Input Rules for Data Center Air Permits
text:
Washington, DC – U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, and Mark Kelly (D-AZ) sent two letters last week opposing the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposal to eliminate the 30-day mandatory public notice period that allows communities to provide input on proposed facilities, like data centers, that may affect the air they breathe.

The first letter urges EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to withdraw the proposed rule and disclose any documents showing that the agency communicated with data center owners ahead of the proposal.

“We agree that permitting should be efficient, predictable, and capable of supporting theinfrastructure our country needs. But faster permitting should not come at the expense of transparency or communities’ ability to shape the decisions that affect them,” wrote the senators to Administrator Zeldin.

The second letter calls on nine major data center companies – Anthropic, AWS, Fermi, Google, Joule, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and xAI – to commit to maintaining current public participation standards regardless of the rule’s outcome. The senators asked the companies to explain their own policies governing community engagement before constructing data centers and disclose any documents showing that the companies communicated with EPA, the White House, or other federal agencies ahead of the proposal.

“Data center companies like yours…have a responsibility not to use weaker requirements to limit…communities’ ability to meaningfully shape decisions that affect them,” wrote the senators to the data center companies.“America can build the infrastructure needed to compete and innovate while keeping communities informed and involved in the decisions that affect them.”

The senators requested both parties provide relevant documents and answers to their questions by October 23, 2026.

In addition to Whitehouse and Kelly, the letter to the EPA was co-signed by Senators Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Edward Markey (D-MA), and Adam Schiff (D-CA).

In addition to Whitehouse and Kelly, the letter to the data companies was co-signed by Senators Ron Wyden (D-OR), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), and Adam Schiff (D-CA).

Read the full letter to the EPA here.

title: Whitehouse Reintroduces Legislation to Tackle Housing Affordability Crisis
text:
Affordable Housing Construction Act would expand the supply of housing financed by the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit

Washington, DC – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) has reintroduced the Affordable Housing Construction Act, legislation to address the housing affordability crisis that’s squeezing Rhode Island families. Whitehouse’s bill would more than triple the size of the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and deliver additional funding for sustainable, accessible, and energy-efficient housing developments. The bill would also loosen financing requirements and extend the required length of time that the housing must remain affordable from 30 years to 50 years.

“Rhode Island families are paying the price for decades of sluggish housing supply investment, too often getting priced out of the neighborhoods where they want to live. My legislation would help bring down skyrocketing rents by increasing the supply of affordable rental homes in the state,” said Whitehouse.

The shortage of affordable housing costs the American economy an estimated $2 trillion each year. The United States is facing a shortage of an estimated 7.2 million rental homes, and development has been unable to keep up with rising demand. High housing costs reduce disposable income and economic mobility, stifling economic opportunities for those who can no longer afford housing in their communities. In Rhode Island, no municipality is affordable for the typical renter or homebuyer, and a third of households are severely cost burdened, paying more than 30 percent of their income towards housing costs.

Whitehouse’s Affordable Housing Construction Act would decrease the cost of rent for lower-income Americans by significantly expanding the nation’s supply of housing financed under the LIHTC program. LIHTC is the nation’s most important federal program for affordable housing construction. The credit has financed the construction of 3.9 million housing units since its creation in 1986 and produces an average of 115,000 affordable rental units annually. However, the credit is oversubscribed, with too many eligible projects competing for too few funds.

The updated legislation would also eliminate the “qualified contract” process for housing developments financed with LIHTC, reforming a loophole that once allowed LIHTC owners to discontinue affordability restrictions prematurely.

The Affordable Housing Construction Act specifically would:

Make the 2018 temporary 12.5 percent boost to LIHTC permanent;

Triple both the LIHTC state allocation and the small state minimum beginning in 2027;

Set aside one-third of each state allocation for boosts to projects that meet special requirements, such as paying a prevailing wage, using renewable energy sources, proximity to public transportation, providing accessible units, or allocating at least 20 percent of the units for extremely low-income renters;

Repeal the “qualified contract” loophole that allows developers to prematurely pull units out of the required affordability period;

Lower the private activity bond threshold for the rehabilitation credit from 50 percent to 15 percent; and

Extend the required affordability period for LIHTC buildings from 30 to 50 years.

The Affordable Housing Construction Act would result in at least an additional $68 million annually for affordable housing development in Rhode Island—creating hundreds of additional affordable units in the state each year, according to an analysis by RI Housing.

Senator Jack Reed (D-RI) cosponsors the legislation. The legislation is endorsed by the Rhode Island Executive Office of Housing, Housing Works RI, RIHousing, Housing Network of Rhode Island, and the Rhode Island Coalition to End Homelessness.

“In RI, since 2020, construction material costs have risen 40 percent; between 2018 and 2024, home prices rose 65 percent and rents 60 percent, while wages in our state rose only 29 percent. Thanks to federal recovery act funding and other state resources, RI has made some progress with housing permits reaching its highest level in decades – 3,778 issued in 2025 and more than 2,100 certificates of occupancy issued. To maintain our progress, much more work is needed in RI and across the country to address housing affordability. Senator Whitehouse’s Affordable Housing Construction Act provides critical funding/financing tools needed to implement the 21stCentury ROAD to Housing Act. HWRI thanks Senator Whitehouse and our congressional delegation for their strong support of housing funding and financing and urges Congress to continue their bi-partisan efforts to ensure that every one in every state has a healthy and affordable place to call home,” said Brenda Clement, Executive Director of Housing Works RI at Roger Williams University.

“Rhode Island cannot solve homelessness without significantly increasing the supply of homes that people with the lowest incomes can actually afford. The Affordable Housing Construction Act would bring critical new resources to Rhode Island while strengthening the long-term affordability of those homes. The availability of deeply affordable housing is often the difference between having a place to call home and remaining in crisis. We are proud to support Senator Whitehouse’s continued leadership and this important investment in Rhode Island’s housing future,” said Colby O’Brien, Executive Director of the Rhode Island Coalition to End Homelessness.

“Rhode Island is working to create more homes and expand access to housing that Rhode Islanders can afford, but we cannot meet the scale of this need alone,” said Rhode Island Secretary of Housing Deborah Goddard. “Senator Whitehouse’s Affordable Housing Construction Act would strengthen the federal tools that make affordable housing possible, helping communities build and preserve more homes while creating greater long-term stability for Rhode Islanders. We are grateful to Senator Whitehouse for continuing to champion policies that recognize the importance of sustained investment in affordable housing, and we are proud to support this legislation.”

“Rhode Island needs more affordable homes, but we also need to make sure those homes help create healthy, accessible, sustainable communities for the long term. This year’s version of the Affordable Housing Construction Act recognizes that building affordable housing is about more than increasing the number of units, it’s about making strategic investments in homes that are accessible, energy efficient, and connected to jobs, services, and transportation. By directing additional resources towards complimentary priorities like transit-oriented development, accessibility, and energy sustainability and improvements, this legislation can help communities build affordable housing that works for Rhode Islanders today and for generations to come. We’re grateful to see these priorities reflected in the federal conversation around expanding the resources available for affordable housing,” said Melina Lodge, Executive Director of the Housing Network of Rhode Island.

“Low-Income Housing Tax Credits are one of our most powerful tools to encourage the development of much-needed affordable housing,” said Carol Ventura, CEO & Executive Director of RIHousing. “We wholly support Senator Whitehouse’s Affordable Housing Construction Act, which would expand the scope of LIHTC, offering further incentives to developers while extending the affordability period for renters. As we continue to face a difficult housing market, it is critical that we bolster our existing programs and seek out innovative ways to support housing development.”

Whitehouse is focused on ensuring more Rhode Islanders have access to affordable housing and a stable foothold in the middle class. In 2025, Whitehouse introduced the First-Time Homebuyer Tax Credit Act, bicameral legislation which would support homeownership among lower- and middle-income Americans by establishing a refundable tax credit worth up to 10 percent of a home’s purchase price – up to a maximum of $15,000 – for first-time homebuyers.

title: Wyden Leads Colleagues in Call for IRS to Drop Unnecessary and Harmful Immigration Status Question on Tax Form
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ron Wyden said today he is leading his Democratic colleagues in calling on the IRS to reverse a proposed rule that would, for the first time, add citizenship and work authorization questions to 2026 tax forms, in an effort to intimidate immigrants into not filing tax returns, and raising privacy concerns over the handling of private taxpayer data.

In a letter to IRS CEO Frank Bisignano, Wyden and the other senators described how adding a new immigration question serves no clear tax purpose and could result in a loss of $300 billion in tax receipts. Wyden has been a leading voice in the Senate sounding the alarm on the Trump administration’s data sharing agreement between Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the IRS, which exposed the private data of thousands of taxpayers. The letter also pushes for the release of the updated tax gap estimate, which has been delayed almost a year.

“We write to urge you to drop the newly proposed citizenship and work authorization checkbox from the final version of the 2026 Form 1040. Adding this question for the first time in history appears to serve no legitimate tax administration purpose and risks increasing the tax gap by hundreds of billions of dollars,” the senators wrote Bisignano.

“Turning the 1040 into an immigration tracker actively sabotages voluntary tax compliance and undermines the IRS’s core tax collection responsibilities. Public trust is already at a low point after the IRS illegally handed over the private data of more than 42,000 taxpayers to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Putting this question on the front page of the Form 1040 will only discourage people from filing altogether,” the senators continued .

In addition to Wyden, the letter was also led by U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M. The letter was signed by U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., Alex Padilla, p-Calif., Peter Welch, D-Vt., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., Jacky Rosen, D-Nev., Patty Murray, D-Wash., Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.

title: Wyden, Merkley, Bonamici, Salinas, Hoyle, Dexter Announce $4.3 Million to Support Public Safety Across Oregon
text:
Programs in Gresham, Beaverton, Salem and Cottage Grove to benefit

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, along with U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici, Andrea Salinas, Val Hoyle, and Maxine Dexter, today announced more than $4.3 million in federal awards to support public safety programs across Oregon.

“It is absolutely essential to ensure communities across Oregon are safe, and young people are able to get the support they need in times of crisis,” Wyden said. “These federal grants will help support local police agencies, youth support programs and resources for foster youth. I’ll keep fighting to secure the federal resources Oregon communities need to thrive and stay secure.”

“Every Oregon community needs the resources to keep young people safe, support children who have experienced abuse and neglect, and build stronger relationships between families and those who serve them,” said Merkley, who helped secure funding for these community-initiated projects as a senior member of the Senate Appropriations Committee. “These federal investments will expand mentorship and opportunities for young people, ensure children have access to critical advocacy and medical services, and strengthen public safety infrastructure in several communities across the state. I’ll keep fighting to bring these federal resources home to Oregon and support the local organizations working every day to make our communities safer.”

“Beaverton’s Behavioral Health Court is doing important work to help people with mental health challenges who encounter the justice system and put them on a path to recovery,” said Bonamici. “I’m grateful this grant will support this initiative, improve lives, and make our communities safer.”

“Investments in emergency response capabilities strengthen our communities,” said Hoyle. “This funding for the Cottage Grove Police Department will replace aging equipment and bolster our emergency preparedness, prioritizing public safety and making it easier for officers to do their jobs.”

“Every child deserves to be safe, cared for, and heard. I’m thrilled to have helped secure over $2 million to protect children across Oregon. Because of this funding, children who have experienced abuse or neglect will not have to navigate some of the hardest moments of their lives alone. They will have an advocate in their corner and a safe place to turn to when they need emotional or medical support. I’m proud to see these federal dollars coming home to support the people doing this vital work in our communities,” Salinas said.

“Our young people deserve to grow up safe, supported and hopeful about their future,” said Dexter, M.D. “I fought hard to bring this $1 million investment to Gresham because children deserve opportunities to succeed. This funding will connect them with mentors, workforce readiness and programs that prevent and reduce involvement in violent crime and strengthen public safety efforts for youth and families in East Multnomah County. Investing in our children makes Oregon stronger.”

The $4.3 million in federal awards from the Department of Justice’s Byrne Discretionary Community Project Grants program will be distributed as follows:

$1.05 million to the City of Gresham to expand the East Multnomah Outreach Prevention Intervention initiative to prevent and combat juvenile delinquency, reduce youth involvement in violent crime, and strengthen coordinated public safety efforts for youth and families in East Multnomah County.

$1 million to Liberty House in Salem to increase medical clinic services to children who are victims of abuse or neglect in Marion and Polk Counties.

$1.03 million to the Oregon CASA Network in Salem to support its work to provide foster children the advocacy and support of an assigned Court Appointed Special Advocate.

$500,000 to the City of Beaverton to support the Behavioral Health Court program that targets defendants with criminal cases in the Beaverton Municipal Court who are the top utilizers of legal, jail or emergency room services living in the Beaverton area.

We appreciate the efforts of our elected officials to make this valuable investment in Oregon’s future which will help many of the state’s most vulnerable reach their full potential.

title: Wyden Opposes Trump Administration Scheme to Redirect Money Away from Public Schools
text:
New Treasury provision continues Trump’s pattern of ignoring clear congressional mandates and benefiting the wealthy and well-connected

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said today that he and U.S. Rep Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) are battling back against proposed regulations recently issued by the Trump administration in the IRS code that further Republican schemes to undermine public school systems by directing taxpayer money toward private and religious schools.

In a letter to Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, Wyden and Neal called out the administration for its blatant attempt to circumvent the clear rules established by Congress and funneling even more taxpayer funds away from public education and using that money to subsidize the private school education of children from wealthy families.

Treasury’s baseless interpretation of federal statute would allow married couples filing jointly to potentially claim double the credit that is authorized under the law, wrote Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Neal, ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee,

“This interpretation is wildly inconsistent with the longstanding treatment of other provisions that use identical or near-identical language,” Wyden and Neal wrote.

“This throws doubt upon Treasury’s interpretation of many provisions of the Code, creates a great deal of uncertainty in the administration of our tax laws, and could balloon the deficit,” the lawmakers noted, adding that it could increase the cost of the credit by an additional $150 billion over the next decade.

Wyden and Neal closed their letter by demanding the administration provide written answers and explanations to how the new interpretation of the law will affect taxpayers, how it came to be and was coordinated internally, which other tax provisions taxpayers might take a return position that is different from previously listed guidance based on new interpretations, and other pressing matters.

title: Rep. Aguilar Highlights Importance of Food Assistance Programs for Cal State San Bernardino Students as Grocery Prices Rise
text:
Faced with rising grocery costs, more CSUSB students are turning to the on-campus food pantry or enrolling in food assistance benefits

SAN BERNARDINO, CA – Today, Rep. Pete Aguilar (CA-33) held a press conference highlighting the impact of rising food prices on students and the importance of food assistance programs. This fall semester, 2,200 students at California State University, San Bernardino (CSUSB) have used the on-campus food pantry and student applications for CalFresh, California’s version of SNAP, have more than doubled since last year.

Across the country, people are struggling to afford the skyrocketing prices of gas, groceries, housing and electricity because of Trump’s and Republicans’ policies. Last year, Republicans’ Big Ugly Bill kicked more than 5 million Americans, including more than 340,000 Californians, off their food assistance benefits in order to give a tax break to billionaires. For CSUSB students, rising costs mean cutting back spending or relying more on food assistance programs and campus food pantries to avoid going hungry. You can watch the full video of the press conference here and find photos from the event above and here.

“Students are already juggling classes, homework, housing and even jobs and childcare, so finding enough to eat shouldn’t be another concern,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar. “That’s why CalFresh and the Obershaw DEN food pantry are so important. When you don’t have to worry about your next meal, you can focus in class and have energy for everything else college offers. Even after Trump and Republicans cut millions of Americans’ food assistance, I’m grateful that CSUSB students have somewhere to turn to so they don’t go hungry. But in the wealthiest nation on earth, this shouldn’t be the case. I’ll keep fighting to bring down costs and protect CalFresh so Inland Empire students get the meals they need to do well in school and graduate.”

title: Reps. Tlaib and Green lead letter demanding release of DACA recipient in ICE custody
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) and Al Green (TX-09) joined by 21 Members of Congress demanded the release of Ya’akub Ira Vijandre, who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement a year ago as of yesterday. In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE Acting Director David Venturella, the Members pressed for answers regarding Ya’akub’s unconstitutional arrest and prolonged detention after a federal judge allowed his habeas challenge to proceed.

Ya’akub, a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient, has lived in the U.S. since he was 14 years old. He spent a decade working for American Airlines as a senior safety specialist and was recognized for supporting grieving families after a helicopter crashed into a plane in Washington, D.C. Despite having no criminal record and not being charged with any crime, he was targeted and arrested at gun point for speaking out against Israel’s genocide in Gaza and for “liking” a social media post with Quranic verses–both of which are protected by the First Amendment.

“The administration’s stated basis for [Ya’akub’s] detention has been inconsistent and appears to rely substantially on his speech and social media activity,” the Members wrote. “DHS has sought to justify his detention by citing his social media commentary regarding the prosecutions of the Holy Land Foundation Five, his criticism of the treatment of Guantanamo detainees, his advocacy for Palestine, and his engagement with religious Islamic content, including ‘liking’ Instagram posts containing Quranic verses. We are deeply concerned that constitutionally protected political and religious expression is being used as a basis for his continued detention or deportation.”

The letter renews concerns and questions from a letter Rep. Green sent in June. Rep. Tlaib also spoke on the House floor urging for Ya’akub’s release in August.

“We are also concerned by reports, previously flagged in Congressman Green’s June letter, that the FBI approached Mr. Vijandre in November 2023 seeking his cooperation as a confidential informant and that he declined,” the Members continued in their letter. “His DACA status, renewed as recently as May 2024 through May 2026, was subsequently revoked. The proximity and sequence of these events—an FBI approach he declined, followed by a DACA termination and detention grounded largely in the government’s characterization of his religious and political speech—continue to raise serious questions about possible retaliation that Congress has not yet received satisfactory answers to.”

The letter, led by Reps. Tlaib and Green, was signed by 21 other Members of Congress: Greg Casar (TX–35), Judy Chu (CA-28), Maxwell Frost (FL-10), Jesús "Chuy" García (IL-04), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Henry C. “Hank” Johnson, Jr. (GA-04), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Summer Lee (PA-12), Analilia Mejia (NJ-11), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), Ilhan Omar (MN-05), Mark Pocan (WI-02), Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), Emily Randall (WA-06), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12).

The letter was also endorsed by 38 organizations: American Friends Service Committee, Americans for Justice in Palestine Action, Arab American Caucus of the California Democratic Party, Arlington for Palestine, Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta, CAIR Action, Center for Constitutional Rights, Codepink, Community Alliance for Peace and Justice, Demand Progress, Havertown-Community Action Network, IMEU Policy Project, Indiana Center for Middle East Peace, Institute for Policy Studies New Internationalism Project, Maine Coalition for Palestine, Majdal: Arab Community Center of San Diego, MARUF CT, Massachusetts Peace Action, Methodist Federation for Social Action, Muslim Advocates, National Political Prisoner Coalition, NE Oakland Indivisible, NH Peace Action, Palestine Legal, Peace Action Montgomery, Peace Justice Sustainability NOW!, Philly Neighborhood Networks, Pittsburgh Palestine Solidarity Committee, Project TAHA, Restore The Fourth - Action, ReThinking Foreign Policy, River Valley for Palestine, The Justice Coalition, United Methodists for Kairos Response, US Campaign for Palestinian Rights Action, Virginia for Palestine, Whistleblower & Source Protection Program at ExposeFacts, Worcester Multifaith for Palestine.

title: Barragán, Leger Fernández, Colleagues Introduce Latina Equal Pay Day Resolution, Call for Closing Wage Gap
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

October 8, 2026

Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov

WASHINGTON — Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) and Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, introduced a resolution recognizing October 8, 2026 as Latina Equal Pay Day and calling attention to the wage gap that shortchanges Latinas and their families. In 2025, Latinas with reported earnings were paid just 53 cents for every dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men.

“Latina Equal Pay Day is a reminder that equal work deserves equal pay,” said Rep. Barragán. “It is unacceptable that Latinas continue to face a significant wage gap compared to White, non-Hispanic men, despite decades of progress towards workplace equality. This disparity affects not only women, but American families, communities, and our economy. We must continue working to ensure every woman —regardless of her race or ethnicity— is valued fairly and paid equally for her work. Ha llegado el momento de que las latinas reciban igualdad de salarios!”

“Latinas work hard, care for our families, and keep our communities running. Yet our paychecks still do not reflect the value of our work,” said Congresswoman Leger Fernández. “When Latinas are underpaid, our families have less money for groceries, rent and child care—all things that have already been made more expensive by the Trump administration. But our contributions are not valued, and our value is not paid. Today, we recommit to closing the gender and racial wage gap. Ya basta. Latinas deserve equal pay TODAY. ”

More than six decades after the passage of the Equal Pay Act of 1963, the wage gap persists across sectors and education levels. Latinas working full time, year round were paid just 60 cents for every dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men. The gap widens to 53 cents when including workers with part-time and part-year earnings.

The resolution recognizes how the wage gap hurts women, families, and the economy and reaffirms Congress’ support for equal pay and closing the gender wage gap. It also highlights barriers that contribute to the disparity, including a lack of affordable child care and paid family and medical leave, as well as workplace harassment.

“Latinas are paid just 53 cents for every dollar paid to white, non-Hispanic men,” said Mónica Ramírez, Founder and President of Justice for Migrant Women. “We know first hand the consequences of this gap for ourselves and our families. We also recognize the work that is being done every day to change things for the better. That is why we are marking Latina Equal Pay Day this year with three words: Power. Pay. Progress. We are reflecting on the power that Latinas hold, the pay inequities that still exist, the progress that we have made in spite of this pay gap and the work that remains to ensure that Latinas are paid fully and fairly for our work.”

“Latinas face one of the largest wage gaps in the nation, earning just 53 cents for every dollar paid to their white non-Hispanic male counterparts. That should be an urgent call to action, not a statistic we simply acknowledge,” said Jessica Ramey Stender, Policy Director & Deputy Legal Director at Equal Rights Advocates. “At a time when the federal government is rolling back basic workplace protections and attacking the rights and economic security of Latinas and other women, we cannot afford to stand by as the wage gap widens. Nearly half of Latina mothers are breadwinners, meaning the wage gap doesn’t just shortchange Latina workers; it keeps many families in poverty with consequences across generations. We know what it takes to close the wage gap: stronger protections against pay discrimination, access to well-paying jobs, and policies that support working parents. We thank Rep. Leger Fernández and the Democratic Women’s Caucus for championing the rights of women and urge all lawmakers to take decisive action to close the wage gap.”

“53 cents and 11 years after the first Latina Equal Pay Day, Latinas remain among the lowest-paid workers in the country. For more than a decade, LCLAA has stood shoulder to shoulder with trabajadoras, fighting wage theft, harassment, retaliation, and pay inequity, while championing solutions like good union jobs that deliver real, tangible economic security,” said Karla Pineda, Executive Director of the Labor Council for Latin American Advancement (LCLAA). “As meaningful contributors in our homes, communities, and workplaces across every industry, we refuse to be overlooked, undervalued, and silenced. LCLAA has, is, and will continue to commit its efforts to help ensure that all workers– including working women in our comunidad– receive nothing short of what they deserve: dignity, equity, and the real opportunity to thrive rather than merely survive.”

Cosponsors include Representatives Ansari, Bonamici, Carbajal, Castor, Chu, Cisneros, Correa, Crockett, DeLauro, Espaillat, Jesús “Chuy” García, Sylvia R. Garcia, Gomez, Mejia, Menendez, Holmes Norton, Ramirez, Randall, Ruiz, Salinas, Tlaib, Vargas, Velázquez, and Wilson.

The resolution is endorsed by numerous organizations including the A Better Balance, AFL-CIO, American Association of University Women (AAUW), California National Organization for Women (CA NOW), Clearinghouse on Women’s Issues, Equal Rights Advocates, Equal Pay Today, Family Values @ Work, Feminist Majority Foundation, FL National Organization for Women, Institute for Women’s Policy Research, Justice for Migrant Women, Labor Council for Latin American Advancement (LCLAA), Legal Momentum, Minnesota Indian Women’s Resource Center, MomsRising, Montana Chapter of the National Organization for Women for Women, National Black Worker Center, National Council of Jewish Women, National Immigration Law Center, National Network to End Domestic Violence, National Organization for Women, National Partnership for Women & Families, National Women’s Law Center Action Fund, One Fair Wage, Oxfam America, Public Justice Center, Reproductive Freedom for All, Ujima, The National Center on Violence Against Women in the Black Community, Women Employed, WorkLife Law
