title: Boozman, Alsobrooks, Armstrong, Blunt Rochester Introduce the Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act
text:
U.S. Senators John Boozman (R-AR), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Alan Armstrong (R-OK) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) have introduced the bipartisan Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act to streamline federal permitting for habitat restoration projects that produce net ecological benefits.

The legislation would establish a new permitting pathway under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act for projects that restore, enhance or rehabilitate degraded aquatic habitats. This streamlined process could help farmers and conservation partners move conservation projects forward more efficiently, including restoring wetlands on marginal farmland, reconnecting floodplains, stabilizing eroding streambanks and installing berms and water-control structures.

“Arkansas is The Natural State in part because we take great pride and care in the stewardship of the land, water and other resources. Restoring degraded habitats is an important part of conserving and strengthening them, so it should not be as hard or harder for projects that deliver a net ecological benefit to move forward. This bipartisan legislation streamlines the permitting process while maintaining strong environmental protections, giving farmers, landowners and conservationists greater certainty as they work to improve critical habitats,” said Boozman.

“I am proud to introduce the Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act alongside Senators Boozman, Blunt Rochester, and Armstrong. Our legislation will make habitat restoration more efficient, cut red tape, and create a predictable path for restoration projects. We know how important this is in Maryland as we continue to work to protect the Chesapeake Bay and support numerous wetlands restoration projects throughout the state that help to drive a booming outdoor economy,” said Alsobrooks.

"Modernizing our permitting system does not mean degrading the environment. In fact, we achieve far better ecological outcomes when private capital is directed into direct, on-the-ground conservation and habitat restoration rather than being wasted on endless litigation and administrative review loops. By streamlining Clean Water Act reviews for ecological restoration projects, we can unlock private investment for local communities and live up to the core standard I learned early in my career: we should always leave the land better than we found it. I’m proud to join Senators Boozman, Alsobrooks, and Blunt Rochester in advancing this bipartisan effort to cut red tape and make it easier to build projects that genuinely improve our environment,” said Armstrong.

“As the lowest-lying state, Delawareans know the importance of restoring our shorelines and mitigating flooding from natural hazards. However, current permitting guidelines can make it difficult to jumpstart projects that restore our natural ecosystems. I’m proud to support the bipartisan Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act to streamline projects that will strengthen our natural infrastructure, make our communities more resilient, and help preserve our environment for generations to come,” said Blunt Rochester.

This bill is supported by Ducks Unlimited (DU), the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation (CSF), Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership(TRCP), National Audubon Society and Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (AGFC).

“Restoration projects make our public and working lands healthier, and the permitting process should help expedite that work, not slow it down. The Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act would provide a more predictable path for conservation projects while maintaining a clear focus on measurable gains for habitat and wildlife. Ducks Unlimited appreciates the bipartisan leadership behind this legislation and its recognition that we can strengthen wetland functions and services while making on-the-ground restoration more achievable,” said DU CEO Adam Putnam.

“Healthy habitat is the foundation of healthy fish and wildlife populations and the sporting opportunities they support. The Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act seeks to provide a more predictable and efficient pathway for restoration projects while maintaining existing environmental safeguards. We appreciate Congressional Sportsmen’s Caucus members Senators Boozman and Armstrong, and Senators Alsobrooks and Blunt Rochester for working together on ways to help important habitat restoration projects move from planning to implementation,” said CSF Senior Vice President and COO Taylor Schmitz.

“Every month a restoration project waits on a permit is a month hunters and anglers could lose habitat and opportunity. Habitat restoration practitioners can spend years navigating a permitting process built to scrutinize development rather than approve restoration. The Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act recognizes that restoration deserves its own path through that process. We thank Senators Boozman, Alsobrooks, Armstrong, and Blunt Rochester for introducing this bill and helping beneficial projects get on the ground faster,” said TRCP Vice President of Government Affairs Zach Bodhane.

“Our coasts, wetlands, and watersheds are critical resources for people, local communities and billions of birds, but they are at increasing risk from changing environmental conditions, making habitat restoration more vital than ever. This bill will strengthen those efforts by expanding important permitting tools so restoration can move forward at the scale and pace needed to make habitats and communities more resilient,” said National Audubon Society Vice President of Government Affairs Felice Stadler.

“As Director of the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, I strongly support the Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act of 2026 because it directly enhances our ability to execute critical conservation work. The Commission conducts numerous habitat restoration projects, and streamlining this permitting process will reduce the administrative hurdles that so often delay environmental progress. Ultimately, this legislation empowers us to manage our woods and waters more efficiently, ensuring healthier ecosystems for the environment and better outdoor experiences for Arkansas’s hunters and anglers,” said AGFC Director Doug Schoenrock.

The Ecological Restoration Project Permitting Act would:

Establish a new nationwide Ecological Restoration Project (ERP) Permit under Sec. 404(e) of the CWA for projects that restore, enhance, or rehabilitate degraded habitats and result in a net ecological gain.

Direct the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to consult with federal environmental and conservation agencies to reduce duplicative reviews and preserve all existing environmental requirements.

Create a consistent permitting process with enforceable review timelines. For non-federal projects, USACE must determine application completeness within 30 days and verify the project within 45 days, with automatic permit verification if USACE misses the statutory deadline. Federal projects would submit a shorter summary report on the presumption of eligibility and may begin permitted work 30 days after the summary report’s submission.

Establish a 10-year permit term for the ERP and authorizes renewals and extensions without overburdensome frameworks. USACE currently issues nationwide permits on a five-year cycle, which can result in lengthy renewals and extensions.

Maintains strong environmental protections that nothing in the bill waives, limits or modifies requirements of the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

title: Cantwell Joins Bicameral Coalition in Opposing Trump Administration’s Attempt to Undermine Head Start
text:
Cantwell Joins Bicameral Coalition in Opposing Trump Administration’s Attempt to Undermine Head Start

More than 14,000 children in WA rely on Head Start for Pre-K education and other family support services; Administration proposal could undermine quality, worsen student-to-teacher ratios, and reduce access for children and their families

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and senior member of the Finance Committee, joined a bicameral group of lawmakers in opposing the Trump Administration’s proposed overhaul of Head Start, a federal program providing early learning and family support services in rural and low-income communities.

In August 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced changes to the Head Start Program Performance Standards that effectively eliminate the central mechanism for evaluating and ensuring the quality of early childhood education services provided through Head Start. The administration’s proposal jeopardizes access to quality early learning and childcare services for more than 14,000 children in WA and over 700,000 children across the country.

“Let us be very clear: what you are proposing seriously weakens the high-quality, comprehensive research-backed services required by law, undermines access to critical services, restricts access for children and families, and creates uncertainty for Head Start programs across the nation,” Sen. Cantwell and her colleagues wrote. “This proposed rule is a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year.”

Sen. Cantwell previously spoke out against the Administration’s proposal, saying, “Head Start provides high-quality early learning opportunities for more than 14,000 Washington children. I oppose the Trump administration’s efforts to make it harder for eligible families to access this vital program.”

The changes come after the Trump Administration abruptly closed 5 region Head Start Offices, including Head Start’s Region 10 office in Seattle, which had supported over 70 providers in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Alaska. In addition, the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) terminated 40% to 50% of federal employees in the Office of Head Start (OHS) and the Office of Child Care (OCC). According to a survey of over 157 Head Start grantees nationwide, led by the Washington State Association of Head Start and ECEAP (WSA) and Together for Head Start, these decisions resulted in over 75% of programs reporting direct operational harm to children and families. In President Donald Trump’s FY 2026 Budget request, the Administration went even further and asked Congress to eliminate Head Start; instead, Congress increased funding for Head Start in FY 2026.

Sen. Cantwell has long been a vocal advocate for Head Start programs. In April 2026, she questioned HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – who oversees Head Start – about funding delays which jeopardized a Head Start program in Walla Walla. Sen. Cantwell demanded answers, saying, “They may have to shut down their whole Head Start program. So, are you going to put out requests for proposals for funding for Head Start?”

In May 2025, she joined the entire Senate Democratic caucus in sending an open letter to the American public warning that President Trump’s so-called “Big, Beautiful Bill,” would cut funding for safety net programs like Head Start to fund tax cuts for billionaires. In March 2024, Sen. Cantwell announced federal funding to improve Head Start facilities for the Spokane Tribe of Indians.

The letter, signed by 191 Members of Congress, is led by Senators Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), and Raphael Warnock (D-GA). In addition to Sen. Cantwell, it is cosigned by Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Chris Coons (D-DE), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Richard Durbin (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Angus King (I-ME), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ed Markey (D-MA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Patty Murray (D-WA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Gary Peters (D-MI), Jack Reed (D-RI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Tina Smith (D-MN), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Mark Warner (D-VA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-CT), Ron Wyden (D-OR), and 152 Members of the House of Representatives.

A copy of the letter can be found HERE and text is below:

Dear Secretary Kennedy,

We write to express our strong opposition to the proposed rule, ‘Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs,’ which seeks to illegally dismantle Head Start by removing over 90 percent of standards that ensure children receive high-quality early education and comprehensive services. This proposal is a blatant effort to gut core aspects of this longstanding, anti-poverty program and is in direct conflict with the Head Start Act.

Let us be very clear: what you are proposing seriously weakens the high-quality, comprehensive research-backed services required by law, undermines access to critical services, restricts access for children and families, and creates uncertainty for Head Start programs across the nation. Under your proposal, 80% of children in Head Start will face worse staff-to-child ratios. Nearly 1 in 10 children currently served in Head Start could become ineligible for services overnight. Key Head Start health, dental, mental health, and developmental services will be reduced nationwide. And the duration of the Head Start school day could be cut in half in many communities, leaving working families stranded and without child care. That is unacceptable.

Since 1965, Head Start has served more than 40 million young children with age-appropriate education, health care, dental care, and healthy meals. The program has also provided working-class parents with connections to job training, adult education, nutrition services, housing assistance, and other support services that strengthen families. Research shows that children who attend Head Start are more likely to be ready for kindergarten, graduate from high school, attend college, and are less likely to have adverse health outcomes than non-participants. Every year, roughly 1,600 Head Start grantees serve over 700,000 young children and their families through a unique, multi-generational and holistic approach. The scope and quality of these programs have changed the lives of millions.

Despite Head Start’s essential role, you have led the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to repeatedly undermine and disrupt Head Start services. Since the very start of this Administration, Head Start programs have had their funding illegally withheld and delayed, lost federal staff who were essential to their community-driven successes, and faced new requirements that create constant confusion. Last year, a leaked version of the fiscal year 2026 budget proposal indicated the Administration’s plan to eliminate the Head Start program. You made a commitment to Congress to ‘preserve’ Head Start, yet this proposed rule is the latest attempt by the Administration to deteriorate and ultimately eliminate the program by gutting the core standards and services that have long-defined and ensured its success.

This proposal strikes nearly all of the Head Start Program Performance Standards (‘Performance Standards’) in defiance of statutory requirements and is antithetical to the mission of Head Start, which is to provide quality early learning and comprehensive services for children and families with the highest needs. Head Start’s unique federal-to-local model relies on the Performance Standards to provide clarity to grantees, while considering evolving research, science, and community needs.

Under section 641A(a)(2)(C)(ii) of the Head Start Act, HHS cannot modify the Performance Standards in a way that will ‘result in the elimination of or any reduction in quality, scope, or types of health, educational, parental involvement, nutritional, social, or other services required to be provided under such standards as in effect on the date of enactment of the Improving Head Start for School Readiness Act of 2007.’ Yet, this proposed rule does exactly that: it illegally eliminates and reduces the core components of Head Start as they currently exist.

1. Undermine quality early childhood education and services

We oppose your proposed elimination of federal standards for staff-to-child ratios, class sizes, safety practices; proposed removal of limits on suspensions and expulsions; and proposed removal of Head Start staff professional development, training, and wellness breaks. This overhaul of the Performance Standards will diminish the quality of services and jeopardize the safety and well-being of children.

Staff-to-Child Ratios and Group Sizes

Removing staff-to-child ratios and group size limits in 45 C.F.R. §1302.21(b) and deferring instead to state policies will diminish program quality and threaten children’s safety. State and local policies for child care ratios and group sizes vary widely, which is why the Performance Standards include research-informed, national baselines for high-quality settings that support child development, health, and safety. For example, in Idaho, state law and regulations allow a single educator to care for up to six infants, while in 35 other states, the required ratio is 1:4 and is aligned with the current Performance Standards. According to the Children’s Equity Project, your proposal to replace these federal regulations with state child care standards is estimated to worsen staff-to-child ratios for 80 percent of children enrolled in Early Head Start or Head Start Preschool. HHS’s own analysis of the rule expects a 16 to 32 percent increase in the average number of children per Head Start educator. These changes will make it harder for staff to provide adequate supervision of children, result in poorer quality interactions with children, increase staff burnout, hinder accommodations for children with disabilities, and diminish the delivery of complex early learning science.

Child Safety

We also oppose the proposed changes to essential safety standards that protect young children and give families peace of mind that their children will be well cared for in Head Start. Many of these changes are unconscionable, such as removing the prohibition on leaving children unsupervised and reducing protections against the maltreatment or endangerment of children, including restraint and seclusion practices. Disparities in discipline—including the use of restraint and seclusion—begin as early as preschool, with particularly concerning disparities involving children of color with disabilities. The elimination of these provisions would mean that young children could be subject to a higher risk of corporal punishment, abuse, neglect, shaming, and humiliation, or being left alone while enrolled in Head Start.

Suspensions and Expulsions

The proposal to remove federal disciplinary standards in 45 C.F.R. §1302.17 that prohibit or severely limit the uses of suspensions, expulsions, or unenrollment of children will push children out of programs and disrupt their social and emotional development. According to a 2016 study, as many as 250 preschoolers are suspended or expelled every day. Research has found that boys of color, children with disabilities, and children who are English language learners are disproportionately more likely to experience suspensions or other disciplinary practices in preschool. Further, these disciplinary practices have negative consequences on children and families’ mental health and children’s development, education, and health.

Standards for Teaching and Learning, Staff Qualifications, Trainings, and Wellness

The proposed rule eliminates standards for best practices for teaching and learning (currently regulated in 45 C.F.R. §1302.30-1302.36), erodes staff qualifications, limits access to training and professional development, and reduces wellness services (required under 45 C.F.R. §1302.90-93), which will worsen conditions for the Head Start workforce and their capacity to provide children with high-quality early learning. The proposed rule removes clear guidelines on individualizing instruction that integrates early learning standards into curriculum and teacher training. The proposed rule effectively prohibits postsecondary education credentials—which runs counter to section 648A of the law that outlines Head Start staff qualifications. At a time when 59 percent of the Head Start programs report challenging classroom conditions as among the top reasons for staff vacancies, the proposed rule also seek to remove coaching, some teacher training, developmental screenings for children, wellness breaks, and mental health information for Head Start staff. This elimination of professional and supportive services will worsen environments for the Head Start workforce, who are already underpaid and turning over at a rate that limits the capacity to serve more eligible children and families. Even worse, this comes at a time when HHS is in the process of finalizing another rule, ‘Restoring Flexibility to Support Head Start Program Access,’ that rolls back provisions that would have increased wages and required benefits for Head Start staff. Together, these changes will exacerbate staff stress and burnout and compound recruitment and retention challenges, making it harder to serve more children and disrupting the continuity of care.

2. Deteriorates critical comprehensive services for children and families

Under section 636 of the Head Start Act, one of the stated purposes of Head Start is to provide ‘health, educational, nutritional, social, and other services’ to low-income children and their families across the country. The proposal guts regulatory provisions (45 C.F.R. §§ 1302.40-46) that are critical to promoting healthy child development and school readiness, and ensuring families receive comprehensive services and are equipped to build nurturing and responsive relationships with their children. Research has proven that developmental and mental health screenings, nutrition counseling, oral health programs, and parent education and support services enhance children’s outcomes and prevent long-term health issues, and Head Start has a long history of successfully providing these services for families. For example, during the 2025 program year, Head Start grantees across the country provided nearly 373,000 families (52 percent) with education on preventative medical and oral health, over 102,000 families (14 percent) with mental health services, and over 347,000 families (48 percent) with nutrition education. We oppose the proposal to roll back decades of progress and remove provisions that are central to the quality, frequency, and coordination of comprehensive services that are important for children’s development and learning and family economic stability and well-being.

Health Services for Children

The proposed elimination of 45 C.F.R. §1302.42 will result in fewer available physical, dental, and mental health services for children. Under the proposed rule, Head Start programs would no longer have to ensure children receive developmental, vision, and hearing screenings; check for a source of health insurance; and check the status of age-appropriate medical, mental health, and dental care. Current standards not only require these services but also establish timelines for doing so to ensure children receive medical and dental care without delay and requirements to refer children to follow up services and track progress to ensure children receive intervention or treatment for any identified issues. Further, the proposed rule strikes standards for family collaboration and education about their child’s healthy development (45 C.F.R.§1302.41 and §1302.46) and the frequency and coordination of mental health services (45 C.F.R.§1302.45)

The law requires HHS to have standards for health services (section 641A(a)(1)) and for Head Start grantees to have goals and measurable objectives for health services (section 642(f)). Notably, section 657C of the Head Start Act defines the term “health” to include services or care provided to enrolled children, their parents, or their siblings for both physical and mental health. However, the plan to eliminate almost all health, dental, and mental health standards, in addition to health and developmental screenings, service timelines, and ongoing care obligations will serve to deteriorate preventative and continuous health services for young children.

Early screenings and services are fundamental to the mission of Head Start which recognizes children’s learning, health, and development are inextricably linked, and your proposed changes will have long-term consequences for children. Head Start plays a critical role in ensuring that children with disabilities and their families are connected with providers of early intervention services for infants and toddlers with disabilities under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). Without these screenings, children who are at-risk for, or are suspected of having, a disability could be diagnosed later and miss the opportunity to receive early intervention services, increasing their risk of falling behind in elementary school and force their families to pay out-of-pocket for screenings and services traditionally offered by Head Start.

Additionally, we object to the removal of 45 C.F.R. §1302.42(e), which explicitly requires Early Head Start programs to use funds to provide diapers and formula during the program day, as well as the provision that allows Head Start programs to use program funds to pay for professional medical and oral health services if no other funding source is available. These guidance and authorities are crucial to ensuring every Head Start child receives early, preventative, and ongoing care – regardless of their family’s ability to pay for and access these services on their own.

Services for Expecting Families

We also oppose the proposal to eliminate most of the dedicated services for more than 10,000 expecting Head Start families. Currently 45 C.F.R. §1302.80-82 of the rule requires grantees to check enrolled pregnant women’s prenatal care or insurance within 30 days, facilitate access to comprehensive services, and provide prenatal services to reduce barriers to healthy maternal and birthing outcomes. Prenatal and postpartum referrals and education are critical to the healthy development of infants, maternal health, and fostering nurturing and responsive caregiving environments.

The culmination of striking these research-based regulations will undermine Head Start’s current, proactive scope and the comprehensiveness of health, nutrition, and early intervention screenings and services for hundreds of thousands of Head Start children and families.

3. Restrict access for children and working families

The proposed rule makes it harder for children and families to qualify for and be served by Head Start in a manner that meets their needs. We strongly object to the plans to shorten Head Start’s hours of operation, remove enrollment requirements for children with disabilities, require English-only instruction, and remove self-attestation and excessive housing costs considerations for eligibility, particularly for families experiencing homelessness.

Program Duration

The proposal to shorten the Head Start day is taking the program in exactly the wrong direction and is out of step with research on early childhood education. The proposed rule reverts Head Start centers program operations to the statutory minimum of 3 hours a day. To be clear, the current duration minimums that you seek to eliminate were designed to align Head Start with state pre-kindergarten successes in making gains in language, literacy, math, and social skills. The proposal also “acknowledges that families may need to secure alternative child care arrangements or may miss work time” in response to this new rule. Head Start is often the only licensed child care option in rural communities, and an estimated 4.2 million children lack access to a formal child care slot in their local community. In many states, depending on the age of the child and child care setting, the cost of child care exceeds annual, average in-state cost of college tuition, rent payments, or even mortgage payments. It is simply unrealistic and shameful to diminish Head Start services at a time when high-quality child care is unaffordable for working families and hard to find. We urge you to abandon this provision.

Income Eligibility Barriers

We oppose the prohibition on self-attestation in the proposed §1301.02(c)(4). This prohibition will exclude families with extremely low incomes, those who are self-employed, or those experiencing homelessness from Head Start programs. These are individuals who do not have the same access to tax documents, pay stubs, and proof of income from employers as individuals with more financial stability. HHS’s own analysis of the rule estimates that this change alone will make 8 percent of Head Start children, about 54,000 children, ineligible. It is abhorrent to remove some of the children and families with the greatest needs from Head Start.

Current Performance Standards in §1301.12(i)(1)(ii) allow Head Start programs to adjust for excessive housing expenses when verifying income eligibility. As wages increase to respond to rising costs of living, many families earning low wages have seen their incomes rise above Head Start’s federal poverty level eligibility threshold but still struggle to make ends meet and afford the high costs of necessities like housing, food, utilities, and child care. Striking this consideration will make it harder for families who face high costs of living and would benefit from Head Start’s services to qualify for the program.

Children Experiencing Homelessness

We are greatly concerned about the undue burden for children and families experiencing homelessness to be served by Head Start programs under your proposal. Section 640(m) of the Head Start Act requires the HHS Secretary to issue rules to ‘remove barriers to the enrollment and participation of homeless children in Head Start programs’, including ensuring children experiencing homelessness are identified and prioritized for enrollment, allowing their families to provide required documents within a reasonable time frame, offering continuity of services when housing is unstable, and coordinating with McKinney-Vento liaisons in local school districts. These legally required policies and procedures and the self-attestation pathway are critical for Head Start to carry out eligibility verification for children experiencing homelessness, allow enrollment of these children before records arrive, and hold slots for them if families relocate during the program year. In the 2024-2025 program year, Head Start served more than 60,000 children experiencing homelessness – the highest number on record. We urge you to follow the law to ensure Head Start identifies, enrolls, and coordinates services for children and families experiencing homelessness.

Children with Disabilities

Under the proposed rule, requirements pertaining to services for children with disabilities are eliminated, exposing children and their families to increased discrimination and greater barriers to necessary supports and services. While the underlying statutory requirements remain in place, the proposal no longer mandates that children receive services while they await an IDEA evaluation, and it removes the explicit directive that programs cannot reject a child based on disability-status. We oppose the proposed rule’s removal of standards that require Head Start programs to provide early intervention or special education services consistent with IDEA, support parent participation in this process, and prohibit denying enrollment or services based on disability status. While federal disability civil rights laws remain in effect, removing the detailed Performance Standards removes the mechanism that makes those legal rights operational day to day. Without clear federal requirements, whether a child with a disability receives an assessment, an accommodation, or coordinated services would depend far more on what an individual local program happens to know about disability, what resources it has, and how effectively a family can navigate complex systems on its own. That is likely to produce significant disparities across states and communities — the opposite of the consistency Head Start’s standards were designed to guarantee. If finalized, this proposal threatens to unravel decades of progress toward inclusion for more than 100,000 children with disabilities currently served by Head Start.

Dual Language Learners

The proposed extreme provision to impose English-only instruction in Head Start is a drastic shift from current learning and teaching science and practices to create educational access to all children. In 2024, nearly 30 percent of Head Start children’s primary, home language was not English, and nearly 10 percent of children whose families primarily speak English were acquiring or learning another language. Head Start supports dual language learner children in the acquisition of the English language and provides educational services and parent engagement in home languages. For example, programs are directed statutorily to use funds on literacy training ‘in a developmentally, culturally, and linguistically appropriate manner and support children’s development in their native language’ and include ‘specific methods to best address the needs of children who are limited English proficient’ in section 648(d)(2) of the Head Start Act. While section 641A(a)(1)(B)(x) of the law requires the Secretary to issue standards to ensure ‘progress toward acquisition of the English language’, your proposal to require English-only instruction may conflict with the statutory requirement that ‘progress [be] made through the use of culturally and linguistically appropriate instructional services.’ We ask that you withdraw this provision and maintain inclusive instruction for Head Start children, particularly dual language learners. Research is clear that your provision will slow English acquisition and can be harmful to child development and academic achievement.

4. Intentional ambiguity and misleading promises

We are concerned that removing nearly all the Performance Standards will create a great deal of ambiguity for Head Start grantees to implement the law with fidelity. The removal of regulatory details and reduction in administrative spending places greater burdens and uncertainties for community-driven programs in fulfilling their statutory obligations. For over six decades, Head Start has been a successful federal-to-local program, but this proposal to defer to state administration will undermine the consistency and quality of the program.

Monitoring

The intentional lack of clarity for administering a complex, high-quality early childhood education and comprehensive services leaves every Head Start program susceptible to being out of compliance and possibly losing their grants. Section 641A(c) of the Head Start Act requires the Secretary to monitor programs, and HHS holds the authority to issue deficiencies when the monitoring process identifies a systematic or substantial failure to meet program requirements. The proposed rule strikes some details under §1304.11 related to the conditions that result in a grant being designated for competition and adds a vague provision for HHS to determine and re-compete a grant if the grantee is ‘determined not to be delivering classroom quality’. The proposal puts all Head Start grantees in a vulnerable position to face arbitrary monitoring processes without adequate guidance.

Administrative Capacity

The proposal in §1301.14 to reduce maximum administrative spending from 15 percent to 5 percent for Head Start grantees expressly contradicts section 644(b) of the Head Start Act, which allows a cap of 15 percent with the option of a waiver. Funds set aside for administrative spending allow grantees to develop and operate Head Start programs, including fiscal management, human resources, information technology, data systems, and facilities management. To continue these required functions under a 5 percent limit is untenable and many programs will be forced to have staff share functions or eliminate functions or reduce operations. Some grantees have suggested they will have to relinquish their grants altogether because they will be unable to maintain operations. HHS’s own analysis of this rule estimates that only 3.7 percent of Head Start grantees operate at or below this 5 percent threshold. To put it simply, this reduction will pose greater challenges for Head Start programs to deliver high-quality services or to expand services to serve more children, particularly for smaller and rural programs that already face limited administrative capacity.

Conclusion

This proposed rule is a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year. Under your proposal, Head Start children could be subject to corporal punishment; left unsupervised; have larger class sizes; have less qualified teachers; and no longer receive preventative and continuous health services, including oral health and mental health services. Families might have to find alternative child care options and struggle to meet eligibility requirements, particularly for those with little to no incomes, those experiencing homelessness, and those already facing high costs of living. The Head Start workforce will lose professional development, training, and be expected to teach and supervise more children without any additional pay or support.

We strongly urge you to withdraw the proposed rule, obey the law, and protect the legacy of Head Start.

Sincerely,

title: PHOTOS: Capito Celebrates Announcement of Marshall University’s Partnership with BETA
text:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), visited Marshall University’s Bill Noe Flight School to celebrate the announcement of Marshall University Division of Aviation’s partnership with BETA Technologies. Senator Capito has been a consistent supporter of Marshall’s flight school and has made several visits over the years.

BETA Technologies is a leading aerospace and defense company in the U.S., manufacturing electric aircraft systems and charging infrastructure. Marshall University’s partnership with BETA will focus on electric aircraft workforce development and training, cargo transport, intelligence gathering, medical transport, and helping prepare students for a diverse career in aviation.

“It is great to be here today in Charleston to celebrate the announcement of Marshall University’s partnership with BETA Technologies,” Senator Capito said. “Marshall University Division of Aviation sets the standard for aviation education, and I have been proud to support them in their mission to foster high-quality aviation and talent right here in West Virginia. This collaboration will have an immense impact on the future of aviation, and I look forward to seeing the many benefits it will bring to our state.”

This is a milestone moment for Marshall University Aviation as we look toward the future of aviation," Brad D. Smith, President of Marshall University, said. "Our aviation program is not solely about teaching students to fly; it is about preparing them to lead in one of the world's most dynamic and essential industries. This groundbreaking announcement is a testament to what can happen when Marshall brings the right people together and turns bold ideas into action. Kudos to everyone who made today's announcement with BETA Technologies possible."

"Investing in this complete technology ecosystem establishes Marshall University as an early adopter and regional leader in advanced air mobility education," Bill Noe, Chief Aviation Officer at Marshall University Aviation, said. "By embedding electric propulsion, thermal management and modern flight controls directly into our flight and maintenance programs, we are ensuring our graduates are ready to lead the aerospace industry into the future while driving economic opportunity across Appalachia."

On Wednesday, Senator Capito announced a $2,502,000 Congressionally Directed Spending award to Marshall University’s Aviation Program that will aim to increase capacity at Marshall University Aviation with additional training tools and equipment. Learn more here.

title: $2.8 Million from Rural Health Fund Senator Collins Authored Will Keep Penobscot Community Health Care Open
text:
BANGOR, ME – U.S. Senator Susan Collins, Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, welcomed the announcement that $2.8 million in federal funding drawn from the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), which she authored, will ensure Penobscot Community Health Care (PCHC) avoids an imminent bankruptcy filing. PCHC is Maine's largest federally qualified health center and serves approximately 50,000 patients.

“This is welcome news for the thousands of Mainers who rely on PCHC for access to essential health care services. PCHC's financial challenges demonstrate exactly why this historic federal investment is so critical. With rural hospitals and health centers across Maine facing serious financial challenges, and emergency departments, maternity wards, and other hospital units facing the threat of closure, protecting access to medical care in rural communities has never been more important,” said Senator Collins. “That is why I fought to establish this $50 billion program to help ensure that Mainers and Americans in rural communities across the country can continue receiving the care they need close to home. While significant challenges remain, I am pleased to see these federal resources being put to use to help PCHC continue serving Maine families and prevent further losses of essential health care services in communities across our state.”

The funding comes from the $50 billion RHTP, the largest single federal investment in rural health care in more than two decades, which Senator Collins proposed during negotiations over the 2025 budget reconciliation legislation. In December 2025, Senator Collins announced that Maine would receive $190 million in first-year funding through the program.

Earlier this year, when Maine's funding was at risk of being rescinded and reallocated to other states because the state had missed implementation milestones and provided inadequate information, Senator Collins intervened directly with the Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. She urged agency officials to work with Maine to bring the state into compliance with program requirements, which then occurred.

Senator Collins has also worked through her role on the Senate Appropriations Committee to secure nearly $300 million in Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS) for health care infrastructure, including $207 million for 89 hospital and rural health care projects across Maine since 2021. These investments have supported the expansion of emergency departments, community health centers, hospital modernization, and other critical medical services. Examples include nearly $13.4 million to expand Millinocket Regional Hospital's emergency department, more than $10.8 million for emergency and oncology care services at Stephens Memorial Hospital in Norway, and $6.8 million to upgrade St. Joseph Hospital's emergency department in Bangor. Senator Collins also previously secured more than $1.3 million in CDS to help PCHC expand access to dental care in Midcoast Maine.

title: As Mainers Face Rising Home Heating Oil Costs, Senator Collins Announces Release of More Than $38 Million in Federal Home Heating Aid for Maine Households
text:
BANGOR, ME – U.S. Senator Susan Collins, Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, announced today that the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) Office of Community Services will release Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) funding to help low-income Maine households and seniors with limited incomes afford their energy bills. This will mark one of the earliest releases in the program’s history as home heating oil prices rise in Maine as families prepare for winter.

Specifically, $36,675,395 in LIHEAP funding will be released for the State of Maine and $1,408,729 for Maine tribes. Included in the funding for Maine tribes is $457,771 for the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe, $316,098 for the Indian Township Passamaquoddy Tribe, $303,530 for the Penobscot Nation, $165,665 for the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, and $165,665 for the Mi’kmaq Nation.

This announcement follows Senator Collins’ conversations this week with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and OMB Director Russell Vought about the importance of the quick release of LIHEAP funding.

“With home heating oil costs soaring, many Maine families and seniors on limited incomes are facing the prospect of extraordinarily high heating bills this winter. That is why I urged the Administration to expedite the release of this critical assistance, and why I fought so hard to protect and increase funding for LIHEAP. I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” said Senator Collins.

Last month, Senators Collins, Jack Reed (D-RI), and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) along with a bipartisan group of 28 other Senators, including Angus King, urged HHS to release LIHEAP funding swiftly and at the highest level possible.

As Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Senator Collins secured a $20 million increase in funding for LIHEAP in the Fiscal Year 2026 Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act. The legislation also included a provision requiring 90% of LIHEAP funds to be distributed no later than November 1st. The legislation was signed into law in February, providing more than $4 billion in funding for LIHEAP nationwide.

Eligibility for LIHEAP is based on income, household size, and the availability of resources. LIHEAP applications are now open for income-eligible households. Senior citizens and those receiving Social Security Disability or Supplemental Security Income benefits are encouraged to apply as early as possible.

Maine residents can click here to learn more about eligibility and how to apply for assistance.

title: Cortez Masto, Rounds Push for Fed Discount Window Updates to Prevent Bank Collapses, Protect America’s Financial System
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) introduced the Bringing the Discount Window Into the 21st Century Act, which would direct the Federal Reserve to report to Congress on ways they can modernize the discount window and concerns they have identified with the current system. The discount window is the main way the Federal Reserve helps banks manage their liquidity needs.

“As we continue to be the financial hub for the world, America’s financial institutions need to ensure they have enough money on hand to meet their needs,” said Senator Cortez Masto. “In order to maintain an innovative and robust financial system, it’s critical that the infrastructure supporting them, like the discount window, is brought into the 21st Century.”

“The discount window serves as stable source of short-term funds for local banks. This helps stabilize short-term cash in a reliable and accepted format,” said Senator Rounds. “Our legislation would strengthen and modernize this tool, helping the discount window work better for institutions when they need it most.”

Read the bill here.

Senator Cortez Masto has pushed bipartisan legislation to increase the Federal Deposit Insurance cap on deposit insurance, allow credit unions more flexibility when lending for non-primary residence loans, and reform the Federal Home Loan Banks to ensure they continue to invest in housing and community development. Cortez Masto is also leading bipartisan legislation to ensure that big bank executives are not allowed to collect massive paychecks and bonuses, disregard prudent risk management, and walk away scot-free if the bank goes under.

text:

title: Duckworth Demands Independent Legal Representation for Unaccompanied Immigrant Children Being Targeted in Trump’s Mass Deportation Machine
text:
[CHICAGO, IL] – After President Trump announced plans to handpick the lawyers who would represent the children his Administration is seeking to deport, U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) today joined the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC), advocates and families to demand that the Trump Administration reverse this heinous decision and restore the federal legal aid the President cut, which helped provide thousands of immigrant kids with independent legal representation. At the press conference, Duckworth underscored how this is just the latest cruel attempt to erode due process and strip unaccompanied immigrant children of their rights as the Trump Administration schedules hundreds of asylum interviews with little to no notice. Photos from today’s press conference can be found on the Senator’s website and the full video recording can be found on the Senator’s YouTube page.

“Robbing children of their right to due process is a new low our nation cannot stand for,” said Duckworth. “None of this is happening by accident. After detaining kids by the thousands, shutting off aid to independent legal representation and rapidly scheduling asylum interviews with no notice, Donald Trump is now vindictively seeking to handpick the government lawyers that are supposed to defend these children against his own deportation machine. This is wrong on so many levels and a clear conflict of interest. The Trump Administration must immediately reverse this decision and restore the federal legal aid these kids depend on for a fair shot in court. Children who come to our country seeking safety deserve protection, not a fast-track to deportation.”

“The danger and barriers to due process immigrant children face right now are unprecedented. First, they kept kids in detention for months on end, even when their parents were ready to care for them. Next, the Trump administration came for children’s lawyers, whose funding they terminated in August. And now, they are rushing them through court hearings and asylum interviews at an absurd pace. This is resulting in hundreds of Illinois children and teenagers being pushed into the mass deportation pipeline, right before our eyes. We are grateful to Senator Duckworth for standing with these children, and we will continue to fight for their safety and human rights,” said Cecilia Mendoza, Associate Director of Government Relations at the National Immigrant Justice Center.

In July, the Trump Administration allowed a yearslong, $200 million-a-year federal contract with the Acacia Center for Justice to lapse, cutting off independent legal services for more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children nationwide through more than 100 subcontractors, including NIJC. Without federally-funded independent legal services, hundreds of unaccompanied children in Illinois facing deportation may now be forced to navigate court proceedings and asylum interviews without an attorney, making it harder to understand and exercise their legal rights.

Over the past five years, approximately 11,347 unaccompanied children have made Illinois their home. These children attend Illinois schools, have parents or caregivers in our communities and may have pending immigration cases. Last year, NIJC represented about 500 unaccompanied children in the Chicago area through the federal contract the Trump Administration cut because attorneys refused to hand over confidential client information. In the aftermath, many of these children have been forced to navigate the immigration system alone, often in a language they do not speak.

Duckworth has fiercely pushed back against the Trump Administration’s mass deportation campaign and its aggressive immigration enforcement tactics in Illinois. Alongside Senator Dick Durbin (D-IL), she conducted oversight at the Broadview ICE processing center, demanded greater transparency and accountability from federal immigration agents as well as called for ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to comply with federal body camera requirements. Duckworth also referred potential constitutional violations by federal officials and agents during Operation Midway Blitz to the Department of Justice for investigation, citing reports of warrantless arrests and excessive force against Illinois residents, including U.S. citizens. title: Duckworth, Sorensen Demand the Trump Administration Reinstate the Collective Bargaining Agreement of 30,000 Bureau of Prison Employees
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and U.S. Representative Eric Sorensen (D-IL-17) issued the following statement, calling out the Trump Administration and the U.S. Bureau of Prisons (BOP) for failing to reinstate the collective bargaining agreement with the National Council of Prison Locals, Council 33 (CPL-33), despite a federal judge’s order requiring them to do so, stalling efforts to restore worker protections and ensure prison safety. On September 29, 2026, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction ordering the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) to reinstate its national collective bargaining agreement with the union, including related amendments, supplemental agreements and memoranda of understanding, but union officials say BOP is failing to comply with the court’s order.

“Our unions help protect the workers and law enforcement officers who keep our communities safe, ensuring they have a voice on the job. These 30,000 Bureau of Prisons employees deserve fair wages, safe working conditions and the right to collectively bargain for both. A federal judge has made clear that this agreement must be reinstated, and the Trump Administration cannot simply ignore a court order because it doesn’t like the outcome. This Administration must follow the law and honor its obligations to these workers.”

On March 27, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order excluding the Department of Justice from federal collective bargaining requirements, prompting BOP to terminate its collective bargaining agreement with CPL-33 on September 25, 2025—four years before it was set to expire. The union sued on November 13, 2025, and last month, a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction, finding it likely that BOP’s decision to terminate the agreement early was unlawful.

title: Durbin Asks DOJ IG To Investigate FBI’s Decision To Modify Hiring Standards
text:
Durbin: The FBI’s recent decision to remove sex solicitation, bestiality, and theft from an employer from the list of automatic hiring disqualifications threatens to undermine the work of the FBI and poses a grave risk to the Bureau’s integrity

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today sent a letter to Don Berthiaume, U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Inspector General (IG), requesting that he investigate the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI) decision to modify the hiring standards that govern the FBI’s workforce by removing theft from an employer, sex solicitation, and bestiality from its list of automatic hiring disqualifications. In June, the FBI reportedly made these revisions to their hiring policy; however, some of these changes may have been quietly implemented as early as February 2025.

“These changes threaten to undermine the work of the FBI and pose a grave risk to the Bureau’s integrity,” Durbin wrote.

In his letter, Durbin noted that Republican and Democratic Senators questioned FBI Director Kash Patel about this policy change and its application during his appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee on September 15, 2026, but Patel’s responses did little to clarify the purpose or effects of these changes.

Durbin wrote, “Director Patel stated that these changes were made to allow victims of these acts to apply to the FBI if they had been forced to commit one of those acts against their will. However, this explanation appears to contradict the actual effect of the changes, which removed the restrictions outright without differentiating between victim and perpetrator. Changes of this magnitude with no discernible justification must be scrutinized.”

Durbin then went on to ask that the DOJ IG’s office investigate the circumstances around the development and implementation of these policy changes with seven specific requests.

Before Patel’s oversight hearing last month, Durbin led all Senate Judiciary Committee Democrats in a letter to Patel demanding answers about the FBI’s decision to gut hiring standards. The Committee has yet to receive a response to this request.

Full text of today’s letter is available here and below:

October 9, 2026

Dear Inspector General Berthiaume:

I write to request that you investigate the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI) decision to modify the hiring standards that govern the FBI’s workforce by removing theft from an employer, sex solicitation, and bestiality from its list of automatic hiring disqualifications.

In June 2026, the FBI reportedly issued an internal directive removing these restrictions, and some of these changes may have been implemented as early as February 2025. These changes threaten to undermine the work of the FBI and pose a grave risk to the Bureau’s integrity—in the case of solicitation of prostitution for example, controlling Department of Justice policy describes it as “threaten[ing] the core mission of the Department, not simply because it invites extortion, blackmail, and leaks of sensitive or classified information, but also because it undermines the Department’s efforts to eradicate the scourge of human trafficking.”

Republican and Democratic Senators questioned Director Kash Patel about this policy change and its application during his appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee on September 15, 2026, but Director Patel’s responses did little to clarify the purpose or effects of these changes. Director Patel stated that these changes were made to allow victims of these acts to apply to the FBI if they had been forced to commit one of those acts against their will. However, this explanation appears to contradict the actual effect of the changes, which removed the restrictions outright without differentiating between victim and perpetrator.

Changes of this magnitude with no discernible justification must be scrutinized. I ask that your office investigate the circumstances around the development and implementation of these policy changes, including:

The number of applicants hired, extended conditional offers, or placed under case-by-case review since June 16, 2026, whose files would previously have been automatically disqualified for theft from an employer or engagement in prostitution or bestiality, broken out by category of conduct;

The number of applicants hired, extended conditional offers, or placed under case-by-case review since February 28, 2025, whose files would previously have been automatically disqualified for theft from an employer or engagement in prostitution or bestiality, broken out by category of conduct;

Any analysis the Bureau conducted, before or after February 28, 2025, of the effect these changes could have on courtroom credibility, counterintelligence exposure, or blackmail vulnerability among personnel hired under them;

Why the FBI made these changes, what process was followed to make the changes, and who was involved in this process;

All guidance issued to background investigators, polygraph examiners, and adjudicators instructing them on how to apply the revised standards;

Whether these policies were changed in order to employ a specific applicant or applicants who otherwise would have been barred from serving in the FBI; and

Whether these changes equally to the victims of this conduct or those who were coerced to participate in this conduct, and those who willingly participated in soliciting sex or committing an act of bestiality.

Please contact my office for any additional information you may need to investigate this matter. Thank you for your attention to this request.

Sincerely,

-30-

title: Durbin Releases Insights From Congressional Oversight Visit Of Immigration Detention At Guantánamo Bay
text:
WASHINGTON – In August 2026, congressional staff conducted an oversight visit to Naval Station Guantánamo Bay, where the Trump Administration has transported immigrants despite the facility’s failure to meet some basic immigration detention standards including lack of access to counsel, failure to post required information in areas where detention operations were being conducted, and confusion amongst the agency representatives during the visit about which federal agencies’ detention standards should be followed at the facilities.

The staff noted that the Trump Administration staffs the facilities whether any immigrants are being detained at Guantánamo Bay or not, including during extended periods of time when there are none present. Detaining immigrant detainees at Guantánamo Bay comes at an exorbitant cost to taxpayers, with a total of approximately 852 immigrants being held at the facility since January 2025 at the cost of more than $100 million.

U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, issued the following statement: “Transferring immigrants to Guantánamo Bay is simply unlawful, and worse yet, inhumane. The Trump Administration has refused to provide any legal justification for housing immigrants at Guantánamo Bay while wasting millions in taxpayer dollars on facilities that cannot even meet federal standards for detention centers. The Trump Administration’s immigration policy is cruel, immoral, and an abuse of taxpayer funding.”

Congressional staff noted the following:

At the time of the congressional staff’s oversight visit, no immigrants were in detention at Guantánamo Bay; however, 445 government personnel and contractors were stationed at the base for this mission. Maintaining staff at Guantánamo Bay without immigrant detainees comes at significant cost to taxpayers and severely undermines military readiness.

Parts of the detention facilities did not appear to meet U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention standards. For example, at the time of the visit, Camp VI—a facility that was built and used for law-of-war detainees, not for immigration enforcement—was not equipped to provide secure, confidential access to counsel for detained immigrants, even by phone. At Guantánamo Bay, unlike at other ICE detention facilities, attorneys are not permitted to visit their detained clients in person.

ICE contractors and Department of Defense (DoD) officials provided congressional staff with contradictory or unclear answers as to how the facilities meet immigration detention standards and what standards applied, including conditions of confinement, medical care, and access to counsel. Longstanding law dictates that ICE maintain custody and control of immigrants, but DoD appeared to be primarily running Camp VI, where immigrants have been detained.

Information provided by government personnel and contractors at Guantánamo Bay often conflicted with public reporting on immigration detention at the base. For example, government personnel and contractors represented that immigrant detainees have secure access to counsel and can freely communicate with their families, but staff did not observe facilities for secure access, and legal aid organizations are currently suing the government for access to counsel for immigrant detainees at Guantánamo Bay.

Full text of the staff’s insights is available here.

A recently issued Government Accountability Office (GAO) report—requested by Senators Durbin, Gary Peters (D-MI), and Jack Reed (D-RI)—examined the Trump Administration’s flawed immigration detention expansion, including ill-conceived plans to convert warehouses to detention facilities and waste and performance issues at facilities such as Alligator Alcatraz and Guantánamo Bay. GAO found that despite unprecedented funding, ICE has wasted and will continue to waste millions of taxpayer dollars on immigration detention expansion efforts due to a failure to appropriately plan for facilities that would meet immigration detention standards.

Durbin has spoken out against the Trump Administration’s unlawful transfer of immigrants to Guantánamo Bay, and he has led other Senators in demanding answers for the legal justification for using the base as an immigration detention center.

Durbin has been a vocal advocate for shuttering the detention center at Guantánamo Bay. After holding the Senate’s first hearing on the need to close Guantánamo in 2013, Durbin held another hearing in 2021 where he reiterated his frequent calls to close the detention facility. Durbin emphasized that keeping the detention center open undermines America’s moral standing and credibility around the world and wastes taxpayer dollars.

title: Gallego, Colleagues File Amicus Brief in Lawsuit Against Trump Administration for Attacking Fair Housing Program
text:
Lawsuit declares that HUD’s attempt to significantly transform the FHIP program violates the law and Congressional intent

WASHINGTON – This week, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined Senators Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and 18 of their Democratic colleagues in submitting an amicus brief supporting a federal judge’s ruling that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) unlawfully restricted funding to groups that investigate and enforce laws against housing discrimination.

The amicus filed argues that HUD’s unprecedented attempt to direct $46 million away from the Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP) — while diverting an additional $10 million to government agencies with separate appropriations — has no lawful justification and would harm the nation’s fair housing enforcement infrastructure. The senators submitted the brief to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in the case of Massachusetts Fair Housing Center; National Fair Housing Alliance v. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

“Congress intended FHIP to foster a nationwide network of private organizations, like Plaintiffs, that can aid the federal government in uncovering and eliminating housing discrimination. Since Congress piloted FHIP in 1988 and codified it in 1992, FHIP has consistently sustained private fair housing organizations through three grant streams: the Private Enforcement Initiative (‘PEI’) to support investigative and enforcement activities; the Education and Outreach Initiative (‘EOI’); and the Fair Housing Organization Initiative (‘FHOI’) to build organizational capacity. With this funding, private organizations handle most housing discrimination complaints and enforcement nationwide,” the senators said.

“HUD’s July 2, 2026, Notices of Funding Opportunity (‘NOFOs’) endanger fair housing organizations and their vital work. The NOFOs deviate from FHIP’s authorizing statute, decades of FHIP practice, and Congress’s intent. For the first time since FHIP’s codification in 1992, the FY2025 NOFOs provide no new awards for PEI or EOI—the lifeblood of fair housing organizations—nor do they fulfill existing multi-year PEI awards,” the senators continued. “These unprecedented actions have no lawful justification and would seriously harm the nation’s fair housing enforcement infrastructure. The district court rightly vacated HUD’s unlawful notices and directed funding to flow under the prior framework. HUD’s request to stay that well-founded order should be denied.”

“The Doles Memo’s stated aims are misleading and contrary to FHIP’s purposes as well. […] Worse, the Doles Memo treats fair housing organizations like maligned welfare recipients—charging them with ‘perpetual dependence’ on federal funding. FHIP’s goal always has been to sustain these organizations as a vital organ of the fair housing enforcement system, particularly in areas underserved without federal resources. HUD’s NOFOs, if unaddressed, would set fair housing enforcement back decades. Defendants’ Motion for Stay should be denied,” the senators concluded.

In addition to Senators Gallego, Van Hollen, and Booker, the amicus brief was submitted by Senators Patty Murray (D-WA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Mark Warner (D-VA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Richard Blumenthal (D-CN), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Edward Markey (D-MA), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tina Smith (D-MN), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), and Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD).
