title: Blumenthal & Takano Demand Answers from Collins on Skyrocketing Costs of Oracle's VA Electronic Health Record Contract
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ranking Member of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, and U.S. Representative Mark Takano (D-CA), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, wrote Secretary of Veterans Affairs (VA) Doug Collins demanding answers about the ballooning cost of the VA’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program. Oracle’s contract for the VA EHRM program was recently modified, increasing the no-bid contract cost ceiling from $10 billion to more than $27 billion.

“The Committees on Veterans’ Affairs in the House and Senate have worked closely with VA since the original contract was signed,” Blumenthal and Takano wrote. “VA’s decline in transparency, particularly regarding recent contract modifications, is extremely troubling.”

On September 2, House Committee Democrats forced a vote to subpoena Oracle Executive Chairman Larry Ellison and CEO Mike Sicilia for testimony at a congressional oversight hearing. Chairman Mike Bost (R-IL) pushed Ranking Member Takano and Democrats to withdraw the motion, but the committee ultimately approved it 19-0.

Soon after, Blumenthal and Senate Committee Democratic members wrote Ellison and Sicilia demanding documents and an explanation for the cost increase. They backed the House subpoenas and asked Chairman Jerry Moran (R-KS) to hold a full-committee oversight hearing on the cost overruns, repeated delays, and patient safety concerns.

The full text of the letter is copied below.

Dear Secretary Collins:

We write to express serious concerns regarding the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) lack of transparency and cooperation in managing the Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program. Under the Trump administration, VA chose to rapidly accelerate the deployment of the Oracle Health product, despite no proven record of success and no assessment as to whether VA’s workforce and infrastructure could withstand such efforts.

On August 11, 2026, VA quietly issued a modification to Oracle Health’s contract to deliver VA’s EHRM to all VA facilities. In this modification, VA extended the period of performance to the year 2031 and increased the contract ceiling by an amount that the Department chose to redact, though news reports indicate that this figure is over $17.5 billion dollars.2 Further, VA’s citation of “unanticipated complexities” as the rationale for nearly tripling the original contract remains unexplained.

In light of the contract modification, and in preparation for the September 2, 2026, House Veterans’ Affairs Committee hearing on EHRM, Committee staff requested a number of documents on August 27, 2026. To date, those documents have not been received. We insist that VA immediately comply with that request, and in addition provide the following information:

The complete and un-redacted contract modification document 36C10B18D5000 Modification P00008 and all associated documents;

Documentation sufficient to explain the need for the increase, including detailed descriptions of the “unanticipated complexities”, and any related cost analysis or determination, including, but not limited to, the price negotiation memorandum;

All communications, including emails, text messages, and memoranda, between VA and Oracle related to the contract increase;

VA’s most recent Life Cycle Cost Estimate broken down by contract costs, infrastructure costs, and VA program costs; and,

All documents related to the market research conducted by VA supporting its claim that no other software vendor could meet the Government’s requirements.

Additionally, VA must provide written responses to the following:

Who approved the ceiling increase and under whose direction?

Who ordered the redaction of related documents and why?

How did VA arrive at the new estimated contract ceiling? What assumptions informed this number? How will those assumptions effect the VA Medical Centers that have yet to go-live?

What assurances does VA have that Oracle is not using veterans’ data to benefit its commercial products? If Oracle IS doing so, how is VA ensuring veterans’ privacy is protected and that VA receives appropriate compensation?

Will VA commit to obtaining an independent total life-cycle cost estimate for EHRM? If so, by what date will that estimate be completed and provided to Congress? If not, why?

Given that Oracle committed to absorbing the additional costs for the EHRM program contract, please provide an explanation for why VA is now footing these same costs?

What analysis did VA conduct regarding elevated patient safety event reporting at go-live sites before accelerating the 2031 deployment timeline, and what were the findings?

Given the VA’s plans to accelerate deployment, has VA conducted an assessment of the impacts of deployment pace on cost?

We’ve heard concerns about Pay It Forward resources not being placed in areas with similar workflows, leaving these people unable to help frontline staff. How does VA match Pay It Forward employees to their assignments?

How many employees rely on Information and Communications Technology, or ICT, or other reasonable accommodations to perform their roles and responsibilities at the Department?

Was VA aware when it signed the original contract that Millenium was not Section 508 compliant? If so, why did VA sign it knowing the product was not compliant with federal law, and would limit disabled employees, including veterans, ability to do their jobs?

Has VA’s Section 508 Office performed an assessment of how long it would take to make EHRM 508 compliant? If so, how much would these technical upgrades cost to ensure that this system is compliant with the law?

What is VA’s plan to address Oracle’s lack of 508 compliance?

The Committees on Veterans’ Affairs in the House and Senate have worked closely with VA since the original contract was signed. VA’s decline in transparency, particularly regarding recent contract modifications, is extremely troubling. As such, we demand that VA produce requested documents and written responses to the above questions no later than October 30, 2026.

Should you have any questions, please contact Mr. John Harry, Staff Director for the Subcommittee on Technology Modernization, at John.Harry@mail.house.gov, and Ms. Katie Adams, Counsel, at Katie_Adams@vetaff.senate.gov.

title: Cantwell, Rounds Urge White House to Build Strong, Coordinated Approach to AI Safety & Cyber Defense
text:
Cantwell, Rounds Urge White House to Build Strong, Coordinated Approach to AI Safety & Cyber Defense

POLITICO: “Bipartisan duo maps out AI safety plan as congressional action lags"; Senators call for comprehensive national response built around standards, testing, auditing and defensive AI

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and Mike Rounds (R-SD), Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee Subcommittee on Cybersecurity sent a letter to Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence and Chair of the White House Task Force for Super Intelligence, and Michael Kratsios, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) Director, urging them to take a comprehensive approach to AI safety and the growing cybersecurity threats posed by artificial intelligence.

“AI companies and security researchers are now examining tens of thousands of incidents involving models from OpenAI and Anthropic escaping sandboxes, bypassing safeguards, evading monitoring, and taking other unexpected actions,” the senators wrote.

At the same time, the senators noted, “AI systems are becoming dramatically more capable at discovering software vulnerabilities, writing and executing code, using digital tools, and operating autonomously.”

“We therefore urge the federal government to bring its full capacities to bear on this challenge, building a coordinated national response around standards, testing, auditing, and defensive AI,” they wrote.

READ MORE:

Politico: Bipartisan duo maps out AI safety plan as congressional action lags

Cantwell Outlines Comprehensive Governance Framework for Safe and Secure Frontier AI

The senators outlined three key priorities for a successful AI safety and defense regime:

Strengthening federal AI safety and security standards

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), including its Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), must accelerate the development of standards and risk-management frameworks for advanced AI safety and security. To accomplish this, the Administration needs to ensure that CAISSI has both the budget and the technical expertise to keep pace with the rapid development of AI frontier models.

Expanding independent testing capabilities

Ensure that CAISSI, the Department of Energy (DOE) and the National Laboratories, and other appropriate federal facilities have the capacity to independently test advanced AI models for serious national security risks. Federal government testing should be complemented by qualified third-party testing in order to create a testing ecosystem that can keep pace with AI’s rapid advancement. Auditing provides an additional layer of verification and enhances confidence in the safety and security of the overall AI security ecosystem.

Moving aggressively on defensive AI

The federal government should work with industry, universities, state and local government, and critical infrastructure operators to develop, validate, and deploy defensive AI tools. By establishing standards and supporting the development and deployment of defensive AI tools, we can better detect AI-enabled threats, strengthen and patch vulnerable systems, and help defenders respond more quickly and keep Americans safe from AI-enabled cyber-attacks.

“The United States has an opportunity to lead both sides of this challenge: building the standards, testing, and auditing infrastructure needed for increasingly powerful AI, while harnessing those same capabilities to make American networks harder to attack,” concluded the senators. “The Task Force for Super Intelligence and OSTP are uniquely positioned to bring these efforts together. As Congress continues to develop legislative solutions, we urge you to make them a central part of the Administration’s AI and cybersecurity strategy now.”

The text of today’s letter can be found below and HERE.

Dear Director Clayton and Director Kratsios:

We write to urge a coordinated federal response to the growing cybersecurity threats posed by artificial intelligence.

Recent AI security incidents should serve as a warning. Advanced AI agents have escaped testing environments, bypassed safeguards, and gained unauthorized access to real-world systems owned by government agencies and private organizations. AI companies and security researchers are now examining tens of thousands of incidents involving models from OpenAI and Anthropic escaping sandboxes, bypassing safeguards, evading monitoring, and taking other unexpected actions.

These incidents come as AI systems are becoming dramatically more capable at discovering software vulnerabilities, writing and executing code, using digital tools, and operating autonomously.”

We therefore urge the federal government to bring its full capacities to bear on this challenge, building a coordinated national response around standards, testing, auditing, and defensive AI.

First, strengthen federal AI safety and security standards. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), including its Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), should accelerate the development of technically grounded and measurable standards and risk-management frameworks for advanced AI safety and security. These standards should address the risks posed by advanced AI capabilities, including the potential misuse by malicious actors to conduct sophisticated cyberattacks, automate attacks at scale, and deploy autonomous agents that threaten external systems and critical infrastructure.

The standards should also address the security of the environments in which advanced AI systems are developed, trained, tested, and used internally, including protections against agents escaping testing environments, gaining unauthorized access to external systems, or taking actions beyond their intended permissions. NIST should also work with industry to establish best practices with regard to fundamental aspects of AI development, including standards related to secure testing environments and third-party data sharing and testing. Standards and risk-management frameworks should evolve as capabilities evolve and draw on expertise from across government, industry, academia, and the technical community.

The Administration should also make sure CAISSI has additional resources and the technical expertise necessary to keep pace with rapidly advancing systems, including personnel with deep backgrounds in AI, cybersecurity, model evaluation, and national security. You should look to the private sector to contribute resources and expertise to support CAISSI’s efforts in this critical time.

Second, expand independent testing capabilities. The federal government should build the capacity to independently test advanced AI models for serious national-security risks, including sophisticated cyber capabilities, biological and chemical threats, risks to critical infrastructure, the ability to evade safeguards, and increasingly autonomous behavior. CAISSI, the Department of Energy (DOE) National Laboratories, and other appropriate federal facilities can provide secure environments for these evaluations. The federal government capacity should be complemented by universities, independent research organizations, and qualified third-party evaluators including private sector entities, creating a broader testing ecosystem capable of keeping pace with increasingly powerful models.

A mature standards and testing environment can provide the foundation for a broader independent auditing ecosystem. Clear benchmarks and established testing methods will give auditors a common basis for assessing whether testing was conducted rigorously, results were accurately reported, vulnerabilities were addressed, and safeguards are working as intended. As standards and testing mature, independent auditing can provide an additional layer of verification and confidence in the overall system.

Third, move aggressively on defensive AI. The same advances that are making AI-enabled cyberattacks more capable can also strengthen America’s cyber defenses. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s (DARPA) AI Cyber Challenge has demonstrated the potential for AI to help identify and patch software vulnerabilities. The federal government should build on that progress by working with industry, universities, state and local government, and critical-infrastructure operators to develop and validate defensive AI tools, including open-source tools where possible. These tools can help detect AI-enabled threats, strengthen and patch vulnerable systems, and help defenders respond more quickly.

NIST, DARPA, DOE and the National Laboratories, the National Science Foundation (NSF), National Security Agency (NSA), and other appropriate agencies can help establish standards for these defensive tools, provide secure testing and validation environments, and expand access to the computing resources needed to develop and use them. Proven defensive AI capabilities should ultimately be available to critical-infrastructure operators, manufacturers, small businesses, state and local governments, and others that increasingly face AI-enabled cyber threats. The federal government should work with leading AI companies to make these capabilities available at scale, not just to a small number of agencies, companies, or governments that already have substantial cybersecurity resources. The goal should be to extend advanced defensive capabilities to these organizations that otherwise lack the expertise, computing resources, or access to protect themselves.

The recent incidents make clear that the security infrastructure surrounding advanced AI must advance as quickly as the technology itself. The United States has an opportunity to lead both sides of this challenge: building the standards, testing, and auditing infrastructure needed for increasingly powerful AI, while harnessing those same capabilities to make American networks harder to attack.

The Task Force for Super Intelligence and OSTP are uniquely positioned to bring these efforts together. As Congress continues to develop legislative solutions, we urge you to make them a central part of the Administration’s AI and cybersecurity strategy now.

We look forward to working with you.

title: PHOTOS: Capito Celebrates CDS Projects in Kanawha County
text:
KANAWHA COUNTY, W.Va. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) made stops in Kanawha County celebrating Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS) projects that she helped secure.

First, Senator Capito traveled to Clendenin, W.Va. to attend the groundbreaking of the Leatherwood Water Extension alongside Kanawha County Commissioners and other local officials. In Fiscal Year 2022 (FY22), she helped secure a $5,230,000 CDS allocation to make vital upgrades to the city’s infrastructure. Through this project, the water extension will expand services to residents, serving over 100 households and adding 23 fire hydrants with 6 miles of pipes.

“It was great to be in Clendenin today to celebrate the groundbreaking of the Leatherwood Water Extension,” Senator Capito said. “I was proud to help secure federal funding for this project to support the ongoing economic development and overall growth that’s happening here. This process has been a true collaboration, and I look forward to seeing the many benefits it will have on our communities.”

To finish the day, Senator Capito traveled to Dunbar, W.Va. to attend the Kanawha Metro 911 Command dedication ceremony for their new mobile command unit. While there, she delivered remarks and received updates on their recent CDS projects. In Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26), she secured a $720,000 award to enhance the mobile command unit and a $520,000 award for a backup fire truck. This funding, which is a part of today’s dedication ceremony, will increase critical response times and help save lives.

“It was an honor to be in Dunbar to take part in this dedication ceremony,” Senator Capito said. “I was proud to help secure two incredible CDS awards for this project to help equip our community partners in Dunbar and Kanawha County with the resources they need to protect and serve. As a leader on the Senate Appropriations Committee, I remain committed to advocating for the needs of our law enforcement and first responders.”

“On behalf of the residents of Kanawha County, the County Commission would like to thank Senator Capito for her support. We are proud to have worked with her to secure federal funding to ensure the residents have access to clean water and to purchase a new mobile command unit and fire truck. These critical resources, which would not be possible without Senator Capito’s championing of federal funding, will allow us to respond throughout the county to anything from a house fire to a large-scale disaster.” Ben Salango, President of the Kanawha County Commission, said.

title: Senator Coons celebrates over $600,000 awarded to Delaware for veteran suicide prevention services
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Chris Coons (D-Del.) announced Delaware’s first-ever grant through the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program, a $626,870 award from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to the Mental Health Association in Delaware to expand suicide prevention and mental health services for veterans.

The SSG Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program provides funding to community organizations working to reduce veteran suicide and expand access to mental health services. The award follows bipartisan efforts by Senators Coons and Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) to expand access to SSG Fox funding. The senators introduced the Every State Counts for Veterans Mental Health Act last year, and successfully secured report language in the FY26 MilCon-VA appropriations bill directing the VA to prioritize applications from states that had not previously received funding.

“For too long, Delaware veterans have been shut out of a program designed to support them, and Delaware has been left behind by Washington in its effort to ensure that every veteran who comes home has help when they need it,” said Senator Coons. “I’m proud that my bipartisan work with Senator Cramer changed that, and I’m grateful to the Mental Health Association in Delaware for putting this funding to work and making sure more veterans can get the care they need.”

“We are incredibly honored to be a recipient of the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant. For 16 years, the Mental Health Association in Delaware has been committed to supporting service members, veterans, and their families through our Annual Military & Veterans Mental Health Summit and throughout our broader work in the community. This grant allows us to take that commitment even further. With this funding, we will expand suicide prevention efforts for veterans and for the individuals and organizations that support them. We will also add three peer mentors/case managers to Veterans Treatment Court, one in each county, creating greater access to connection, support, and resources for veterans when they need them most. This is the first time Delaware has received this funding, and we recognize the tremendous responsibility that comes with it. We are honored to be entrusted with this opportunity and deeply committed to making a meaningful difference in the lives of those who have served our country. Our veterans have given so much to all of us; this grant gives us an opportunity to give back by strengthening the safety net of support around them and their families. We are ready to do this work, and we are grateful for the opportunity to serve those who have served,” said Jennifer Smolowitz Ianni, executive director, Mental Health Association in Delaware.

With a long history of military service and a major military presence anchored by Dover Air Force Base, Delaware is home to tens of thousands of veterans and military families. Despite $174 million authorized for the SSG Fox program since its founding in fiscal year 2021, until this year, neither Delaware or North Dakota had received funding.

title: Senator Coons joins bipartisan call for President Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal and enforce sanctions on Putin’s war against Ukraine
text:
“For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation’s resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Yesterday, U.S. Senators Chris Coons (D-Del.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) wrote President Donald Trump urging him to rescind his recent agreement with President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian-origin diesel fuel into global markets.

“Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators wrote.

The senators urged Trump to instead take swift action to implement sanctions authorized by the recently passed Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which President Trump signed into law in September.

“These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict,” the senators wrote.

The full text of the senators’ letter is available here and below.

Dear Mr. President,

Congress and the American people support ending the Russia-Ukraine war, which has cost hundreds of thousands of lives over the last four and a half years because Russia chose to invade its neighbor. A brokered peace, however, must be on just terms. It must uphold democratic values, the sovereignty and security of Ukraine, and their people’s right to choose their future.

The deal you struck with President Vladamir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans. The Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which lifts sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports, only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians. Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded.

We also recognize the urgent need to lower energy costs for American families and address the disruptions caused by the war with Iran. However, allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea. It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury.

Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which you swiftly signed into law. Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace. These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict. For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation’s resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world.

title: Cortez Masto, Horsford Call for Worker Privacy Protections as Spirit Airlines Plans to Sell Employee Data to Train Google AI
text:
Las Vegas, Nev. – U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) joined Congressman Steven Horsford (D-Nev.-04) in urging Spirit Airlines CEO Dave Davis and Google CEO Sundar Pichai to protect the privacy of thousands of former Spirit employees. The letter responds to the proposed $10 million sale of Spirit’s internal data to Google for the purpose of training artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

“According to publicly available court findings, the proposed sale would involve an extraordinary volume of Spirit’s internal records, including approximately 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages, employee records, timecard records, payroll and tax information, and employment contracts,” the lawmakers wrote. “This information was created and provided in the context of an employment relationship and may contain highly sensitive information about individual workers. Consumers have more privacy protections than workers, yet Spirit has collected far more private information about its employees than about its customers.”

“While we understand that Google has stated that it will not receive personally identifiable information and that the data will undergo third-party scrubbing before its transfer, we are concerned that conventional de-identification safeguards may not be sufficient to protect employee privacy in the context of modern artificial intelligence,” they continued. “Removing names, email addresses, or other direct identifiers does not necessarily make a dataset anonymous. As we have seen time and time again, artificial intelligence systems have been able to identify patterns across large datasets, connect seemingly unrelated pieces of information, and potentially infer or reconstruct information about individuals or identifiable groups.”

“Innovation should not come at the expense of workers’ privacy or the confidentiality of information they were required to provide as a condition of employment,” they concluded. “The unprecedented scale and sophistication of modern artificial intelligence make it particularly important that privacy protections keep pace with the technology. We therefore urge Google and Spirit to address these concerns and establish meaningful, enforceable safeguards before the proposed transaction proceeds.”

The full text of the letter can be found here.

Senator Cortez Masto has stood up for Spirit Airline’s displaced workers and has been a champion for consumer privacy. At the start of Spirit’s bankruptcy proceedings, she demanded that employees receive their earned wages and accrued benefits. The Senator has also worked to ensure AI innovation includes strong guardrails to protect American’s privacy and national security. Last year, her legislation to prohibit American investment in Chinese AI companies was passed into law. When President Xi Jinping visited the United States, Cortez Masto urged President Trump to negotiate a formal agreement with President Xi for the development, testing, and use of AI models. Cortez Masto is also leading legislation to crack down on robocalls and robotexts, which are more common and dangerous with the use of AI.

title: Gallego, Colleagues Introduce Resolution Recognizing Indigenous Peoples’ Day
text:
WASHINGTON – Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and 14 of their colleagues in introducing a resolution to recognize the second Monday in October as Indigenous Peoples’ Day. The resolution also supports the official designation of Indigenous Peoples’ Day as a federal holiday. title: New Grassley-Authored Law Delivers Support for Victims of Identity Theft
text:
BUTLER COUNTY, IOWA – A bipartisan bill authored by U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) to assist Iowans impacted by identity theft was signed into law last week. The Improving Social Security’s Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act, cosponsored by U.S. Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), supports victims by strengthening and streamlining the process for Americans whose Social Security numbers have been stolen. Grassley and Hassan both serve on the U.S. Senate Finance Committee.

“Too many Iowans suffer from identity theft each year, and Social Security numbers are a top target. Unfortunately, when victims of identity theft call up the Social Security Administration, they can be jerked around from one contact to another, having to reexplain the situation each time. By providing victims a single point of contact at the agency, our bill will help ease this frustrating and stressful process and make life easier for Iowans who may find themselves in this unfortunate situation. I’m glad this commonsense resource is now the law of the land,” Grassley said.

“Too often, victims of identity theft are forced to navigate a long, confusing process to get support from the Social Security Administration. This process is frustrating to victims and unnecessarily drains the agency’s resources. My bipartisan bill will help streamline support from SSA so that victims of identity theft can get the help that they need more quickly. I worked with colleagues across the aisle to pass this commonsense legislation, and I am glad to see it signed into law. I will continue pushing to make the government work more efficiently for victims of theft, fraud, and scams,” Hassan said.

Background:

The Grassley-Hassan Improving Social Security’s Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act provides a single, focal point of contact at the Social Security Administration to more efficiently resolve an identity theft victim’s issues.

The legislation is endorsed by numerous groups, including AARP, Social Security Works, the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare (NCPSSM), Justice in Aging and the National Organization of Social Security Claimants' Representatives (NOSSCR).

title: Hassan, Grassley Take Action to Improve Access to Cancer Screenings
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Maggie Hassan, Ranking Member of the Senate Finance Subcommittee on Health Care, and Chuck Grassley (R-IA) introduced the Standardizing Cancer Recommendations for Earlier Evaluation and Navigation of Screenings (SCREENS) Act to make cancer screening recommendations more accessible, transparent, and user friendly for patients and health care providers.

“Cancer screenings can identify cancers during the early stages when they are easiest to treat, but patients often do not know when they are due for potentially life-saving screenings,” said Senator Hassan. “This bipartisan bill will help make sure that patients and doctors are informed about federal cancer screening recommendations so that they can catch cancer earlier and get people the treatment that they need. I’m glad to introduce this bill, and I will continue working across the aisle to strengthen preventative care for Granite Staters.”

“Detecting cancer early can save lives. I know that based on the personal experience of my wife, Barbara, a nearly 40-year breast cancer survivor. Unfortunately, patients and providers are navigating a complex and confusing maze just to keep up with cancer screening recommendations. By making these recommendations more accessible through technology, our SCREENS Act would strengthen cancer care and help save lives. For my home state, this bill would proactively support Iowans by helping providers identify patients who could be overdue for a screening,” said Senator Grassley.

Cancer is the second-leading cause of death in the United States. Cancer screenings can increase the chance of earlier treatment and reduce mortality, but screening recommendations are often complex, fragmented and difficult to interpret and navigate.

The bipartisan SCREENS Act would simplify and improve the process by establishing a national data and technology framework for cancer screening recommendations, to make these recommendations more accessible, interoperable and effective for providers and patients.

In 2022, the Presidential Cancer Panel recommended the federal government develop a digitally accessible version of the cancer screening and risk assessment guidelines. The SCREENS Act would enact this recommendation. Under the legislation, the national data and technology framework would be publicly available in machine-readable format for use by health information technologies, interoperability tools and patient-facing applications. The legislation would also help providers identify which patients are at risk and overdue for screenings.

Click here for a section-by-section of the bill.

Click here to see text of the bill.

The SCREENS Act builds on Senator Hassan’s record of expanding access to preventive care and cancer screenings. She has repeatedly fought to protect Title X funding that helps patients access cancer screenings and other preventive care. In 2022, Senator Hassan helped pass into law the bipartisan SERVICE Act to expand access to mammograms for veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic substances.

title: Heinrich Demands Answers on Trump Administration Draining Strategic Petroleum Reserves to Dangerous Low Levels
text:
Heinrich: “I am deeply concerned by reports that recent drawdowns of the SPR could damage the salt caverns that hold millions of barrels of America’s emergency crude”

WASHINGTON — Last week, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, pressed U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Secretary Chris Wright to disclose information on the operational safety and structural integrity of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), which has been depleted to under 300 million barrels of emergency inventory due to Trump’s war with Iran. Repeated drawdowns can harm salt caverns where millions of barrels of the SPR’s crude are stored, and the SPR’s current historically low levels put U.S. energy and economic security at grave risk. In the midst of further shocks, the U.S. will not have SPR capacity to spare which could cause gasoline and diesel prices to rise even further.

The SPR was created in 1975 to reduce the impact of petroleum supply disruptions on Americans and is designed to hold nearly 714 million barrels, making it a valuable energy security measure and national security asset in times of crisis. The SPR currently holds 283.8 million barrels of emergency inventory — the lowest it’s been since 1982 — following Trump’s authorized release of 172 million barrels at the start of the Iran war.

“In April, I wrote to you to express concern regarding the administration’s ill-advised decision to enter into a war with Iran. I asked you about the Department’s preparedness before the Trump administration launched its war in Iran, including if the Department conducted any analysis related to potential SPR releases. The Department failed to substantively respond to my questions,” Heinrich began.

“I am deeply concerned by reports that recent drawdowns of the SPR could damage the salt caverns that hold millions of barrels of America’s emergency crude,” Heinrich continued.

In his letter, Heinrich specifically demanded information on analyses and reviews conducted regarding the impact and consequences of drawing down the SPR. He also presses DOE to disclose a list of maintenance projects underway, schedule of exchange returns, copy of the contract for the new SPR Operator and all documents from the transition documenting the current state of SPR, all buyers and amounts sold from the SPR in 2026, potential new cavern sites analyzed by DOE for future development, backlog maintenance projects for SPR as currently pending, and the contract and all audits performed by the current DOE Auditor for the SPR and any sale of oil activities.

“As our energy demand increases, we need to ensure the SPR is properly maintained, fully operational, and can be counted on when supply is constrained,” Heinrich concluded.

Read the full text of the letter here and below:

Secretary Wright:

I write to request information regarding the operational safety and structural integrity of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). In April, I wrote to you to express concern regarding the Administration’s ill-advised decision to enter into a war with Iran. I asked you about the Department’s preparedness before the Trump administration launched its war in Iran, including if the Department conducted any analysis related to potential SPR releases. The Department failed to substantively respond to my questions. I am deeply concerned by reports that recent drawdowns of the SPR could damage the salt caverns that hold millions of barrels of America’s emergency crude.

In 1975, Congress created the SPR to reduce the impact of petroleum supply disruptions on Americans. The SPR is not only an energy security measure, but a national security asset in times of crisis. It is designed to hold nearly 714 million barrels. For the first time in over 40 years, however, the SPR has now reportedly dropped to under 300 million barrels of emergency inventory. In March, weeks after the U.S. entered into war with Iran, President Trump authorized the release of 172 million barrels from the SPR. As a result of that drawdown, the SPR currently sits at 283.8 million barrels—the lowest level since 1982. The SPR is expected to dip below 250 million barrels once the drawdown concludes. Some analysts have suggested that depleting the SPR to less than 300 million barrels risks damage to the salt caverns. In a June 2026 report, the Government Accountability Office found that “[r]epeated partial drawdowns followed by refill can leach a single part of a cavern repeatedly, leading to undesirable shapes.” The same report warned that the SPR is at risk of failing to safeguard the U.S. from severe petroleum supply disruptions.

In response to the ongoing war in Iran and the consequences of draining vital energy inventories crucial to U.S. energy and national security, I am introducing legislation that mandates long-term planning for the SPR and limits non-emergency SPR sales to avoid further operational inefficiencies, including straining aging infrastructure during ongoing capital projects.

To better understand DOE’s current management of the SPR, I request that you provide the following information by October 23, 2026:

Since January 20, 2025, all Department analysis and reviews conducted to understand the impact and consequences of drawdowns of the SPR to the operational safety and structural integrity of the SPR.

Since January 20, 2025, all Department analysis and reviews conducted to understand the impact and consequences of drawing down the SPR below 300 million barrels.

Since January 20, 2025, all Department analysis and reviews conducted to understand the operational minimum of the SPR.

A current and complete list of all major maintenance projects underway or scheduled over the next 10 years.

A current and complete list and schedule of exchange returns, including premium barrels, as part of the March 2026 release.

A copy of the new contract with the new SPR Operator and all documents on the handoff to the new contractor documenting the current state of the SPR and any related inspections at this time by either party.

A list of all buyers and amounts sold from the SPR in 2026.

A list of all potential new cavern sites analyzed by the DOE for future development.

A list of the backlog of maintenance projects for the SPR as currently pending.

A copy of the contract and all audits performed by the current DOE Auditor for the SPR and any sale of oil activities.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this request. As our energy demand increases, we need to ensure the SPR is properly maintained, fully operational, and can be counted on when supply is constrained. Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact my staff at (202) 224-4971.

Sincerely,

title: Hoeven Announces Project ATLAS Unmanned Research Initiative
text:
GRAND FORKS, N.D. – Senator John Hoeven today announced Project ATLAS, an unmanned research initiative he worked to fund and establish between the University of North Dakota (UND), NASA, the U.S. Department of War (DoW) and the North Dakota National Guard (NDNG). Project ATLAS is a new DoW initiative to integrate the capabilities of unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and unmanned aerial systems (UAS) and incorporate them into daily training, base support and combat operations. UND will work with NASA to conduct experiments to achieve this goal with support from the North Dakota National Guard (NDNG), which will provide access to its range at Camp Grafton.

As a member of the Senate Defense Appropriations Committee, Hoeven secured nearly $2 million in Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 to launch Project ATLAS. Of this, $1 million will support UND and NASA’s operations, while $750,000 will go to the Guard to support activities at Camp Grafton. Hoeven continues working to secure additional funding for the initiative in FY2027.

Project ATLAS’s first task is to identify a ground vehicle to use in future experiments. Next week, the DoW will host a joint unmanned ground vehicle demonstration event, known as Groundbreaker, at Camp Grafton, where the capabilities of various vehicles will be evaluated for inclusion in the initiative. Once a vehicle is selected, NASA and UND will develop experiments linking the UGV and UAS with a focus on improving local base security and logistics. Over time, Project ATLAS will take on increasingly complex tasks, building toward the capability for a single operator to use UAS and UGV systems simultaneously, with the aircraft and ground vehicles collaborating autonomously to accomplish a wide range of objectives, such as:

Assisting with maintenance operations.

Equipment or supply deliveries.

Responding to security threats.

“Project ATLAS, a new partnership between UND, NASA, the Department of War and the North Dakota National Guard, is the result of all the unmanned capabilities we have developed and serves as a logical next step in the growth of our UAS ecosystem. By combining the capabilities of unmanned aircraft with unmanned ground vehicles, we can meet the logistical and security needs of our military and accelerate our leadership in autonomy, with missions from the ground all the way up into space,” said Hoeven. “Today’s discussion with NASA Administrator Isaacman and General Guetlein fits perfectly with the launch of Project ATLAS. We appreciate their attendance at the UAS Summit, as it provides an opportunity to discover new avenues to leverage our expertise in unmanned technology to meet the defense challenges of tomorrow and keep moving the ball forward on our nation’s drone, counter-drone and space capabilities.”

UAS Summit

Hoeven made the announcement as part of his remarks at the UAS Summit today in Grand Forks, where the senator was joined by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and General Mike Guetlein, Director of Golden Dome for America (GDA). Hoeven invited Isaacman and Guetlein to the state as part of his efforts to strengthen North Dakota’s role as a leader in drone and counter-drone technology and space operations, building on 20 years of efforts to establish the state as a leader in unmanned technology.

The senator emphasized the progress the state has made since kicking off this effort as governor in 2006, when he worked to fund and establish UND’s Center of Excellence for UAS Research, Education and Training. Since that time, Hoeven has worked to bring together federal, state, university, military and commercial partners to advance this emerging sector in North Dakota. Among others, these partners include:

The Northern Plains UAS Test Site, which was created through legislation Hoeven passed in 2012.

The Grand Forks Air Force Base.

GrandSKY, a first of its kind UAS business and technology park adjacent to the Grand Forks Air Force Base.

Hoeven worked to advance an Enhanced Use Lease (EUL) between Grand Forks County and the Air Force to establish GrandSKY.

The University of North Dakota.

The U.S. Department of War.

The Space Development Agency.

The Test Resource Management Center.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

Earlier this year, Hoeven secured access to the FAA’s unfiltered radar data feed for the Northern Plains UAS Test Site, the only non-federal entity to have such access.

NASA.

Hoeven first partnered the state’s UAS ecosystem with NASA in 2016, when he secured North Dakota’s role in the agency’s unmanned traffic management (UTM) research program.

A wide range of businesses, from small startups to international corporations.

title: Husted, Barrasso host permitting reform roundtable in Columbus
text:
“We can’t build Ohio’s energy future if it takes up to a decade just to get a permit.”

COLUMBUS – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today hosted a permitting reform roundtable with Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), bringing together state lawmakers, regulators and Ohio energy, manufacturing and business leaders.

Currently, a federal environmental review can take up to a decade. Projects miss deadlines and waste budgets before construction begins. As energy usage adds demand to Ohio’s grid, the grid must keep up.

“Ohio’s economy is growing, and the grid has to keep up. We can’t build Ohio’s energy future and lower costs for working families if it takes up to a decade just to get a permit. I was glad to bring my friend Sen. Barrasso to Columbus to hear directly from the people who build, power and regulate energy in Ohio. We’re also fighting to make sure data centers pay for their own energy so working families aren’t stuck footing the bill for Big Tech,” said Husted.

“America needs to build better, faster, cheaper, and smarter. Right now, critical energy projects spend years trapped in the regulatory penalty box. Senator Husted’s roundtable today underscored how essential permitting reform is to producing more American energy and lowering prices for American families. Senator Husted has led the way in the Senate with thoughtful legislation that will protect families from increased electricity rates. The Senate has also negotiated bipartisan permitting legislation. We need to pass these reforms this year. American families cannot afford to wait,” said Barrasso.

Husted is a member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and has worked with Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) on fixing our broken permitting system. He also introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would make large new data centers pay for their own energy costs, and worked to include stronger protections in the permitting bill.

Husted is also leading efforts in the Senate on permitting reform including:

The New Source Review Permitting Act, which would clarify federal permitting requirements under the Clean Air Act to help manufacturers and energy producers improve efficiency, upgrade equipment and complete pollution control projects.

The American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act of 2026, which would streamline federal permitting, reduce delays from litigation and overlapping reviews, and accelerate construction of critical energy and mineral infrastructure.

The Water Authority and Timely Environmental Review (WATER Act), which aims to streamline permitting for water projects.

Participants discussed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a U.S. Senate bill that would make the permitting process more efficient, effective and predictable while keeping environmental safeguards intact and protecting. The bill is expected to receive a vote in the U.S. Senate when senators return to the Capitol after the October state work period. They also discussed ways to add grid capacity by upgrading existing power lines.

Federal law requires projects like power plants, pipelines and roads to undergo lengthy reviews before construction starts. Those reviews are often open-ended, and permits can be challenged in court for years. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would:

Set deadlines. Environmental assessments would be due within one year and full environmental impact statements within two years.

Limit lawsuits. Claims under the National Environmental Policy Act would have to be filed within 150 days.

Protect issued permits. Federal agencies couldn’t pull or suspend a valid permit except under specific conditions.

Protect ratepayers, using a similar solution to Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act. Data centers using 20 megawatts or more would have to cover their own energy costs.

Keep Ohio in control. Ohio keeps its authority to site transmission lines and sets rates for data centers.

title: Husted secures Cleveland as home of new U.S. Navy’s Submarine Component Repair Center
text:
“Northeast Ohio has the skilled workforce, infrastructure and strategic location to support this critical mission for our U.S. Navy.”

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) applauded President Donald Trump’s announcement that Cleveland has been selected as the home of the U.S. Navy’s new Submarine Component Repair Center.

The announcement follows Husted’s letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao urging the administration to consider Northeast Ohio for the facility.

title: ASI, Members of Congress Support American Sheep Producers
text:
Sixty-Eight members of congress sign letter in support of ASI, American lamb growers and processors

PUBLISHED ON October 13, 2026

DENVER, Colo. — Sen. Steve Daines (R-MT) and Rep. Celeste Maloy (R-UT) submitted a letter to the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) in support of an affirmative determination in the global safeguard investigation into imports of lamb meat under Sections 201 and 202 of the Trade Act of 1974. On Oct. 6, 2026, 68 bicameral members of congress signed on to the USITC letter in support of the American Sheep Industry Association (ASI) and American lamb growers and processors.

The letter stated, “During this investigation, we urge the Commission to carefully consider the data and testimony before it regarding the significant challenges faced by American sheep producers. And should the Commission make an affirmative determination in accordance with the statute, we urge the Commission to recommend a remedy that provides prompt and meaningful relief to the domestic industry.”

“On behalf of the hardworking farm and ranch families we represent, I want to express our sincere gratitude to these Members of Congress for standing up for American sheep producers,” said Mike Michener, ASI Executive Director. “By urging the U.S. International Trade Commission to closely examine the data and recommend swift, meaningful relief through this Section 201 investigation, these lawmakers are fighting to level the playing field. Their support is vital to preserving domestic supply chains and protecting the future of American lamb.”

This effort follows ASI’s request for a safeguard petition, filed with USTR on October 30, 2025, and the U.S. Trade Representative’s (USTR) request for the USITC to initiate a global safeguard investigation into imports of lamb meat on July 13, 2026. USITC has an injury hearing scheduled for October 16 to hear testimony from American processors, international exporters, and American Sheep Producers. ASI will be in attendance on behalf of its 42 state associations and more than 100,000 U.S. sheep farms and ranches.

America’s sheep farmers and ranchers have faced mounting pressures, including from rapidly increasing imports, which negatively impact our rural communities and domestic food production. ASI, with legal counsel Kelley Drye and Warren LLP and economists at Georgetown Economic Services LLC, collected market data, import trend analysis, and documented financial injury on domestic producers in support of its safeguard request. Import statistics indicate that lamb meat imports have increased in recent years and comprise more than 70% of the lamb available to American consumers resulting in lost sales, revenues, and market share as imported lamb meat significantly undersold the domestic product.

title: Hyde-Smith Highlights Rollout of $423 Million Ag Producers
text:
The Daily Bullet - Tuesday, October 13, 2026

Vol. 39 No. 22

U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) recently highlighted the start of an estimated $423 million in farm safety net improvements being made available to Mississippi agricultural producers as the Farm Service Agency begins implementing aspects of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act enacted last year.

The improved Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) payments for Mississippi are part of the $13.8 billion approved by Congress to update the farm safety net by significantly increasing reference prices and crop insurance enhancements. These improvements more accurately recognize the increased costs and changing economic conditions for farming since passage of the 2018 Farm Bill.

“American farmers and ranchers pour their hearts and souls into producing the food and fiber that we all need. The farm safety net is supposed to help them survive global competition, economic uncertainty, and market volatility, and that’s what we’ve successfully strengthened. As such, producers across Mississippi and this great nation will finally get the first meaningful investment in farm safety net programs that they deserve,” said Hyde-Smith.

The Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which became law in July 2025 without a single Democratic vote in support, enhanced risk management tools for producers of row crops, livestock, specialty crops, honeybees, and aquaculture.

title: ICYMI: Kelly Writes Washington Times Op-Ed on Keeping Humans in Command as AI Transforms Warfare
text:
“A pilot still needs to be able to complete the mission when the automation fails. Tomorrow’s warfighters must be able to recognize when an AI system is giving them bad information and know how to continue the mission without it.”

This week, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly published an op-ed in The Washington Times emphasizing the need to keep human judgment and accountability at the center of the military’s growing use of AI. Drawing on his experience as a Navy combat pilot and astronaut, Kelly highlighted legislation he introduced to ensure servicemembers can recognize when AI systems fail, continue operating without them, and maintain human oversight of critical military decisions.

Kelly introduced the Ultimate Human Responsibility in Defense Systems Actand the Warfighter AI Readiness and Preparedness (WARP) Actin June.

Click here to read the full op-ed. See key excerpts below:

On recognizing AI as a tool and understanding its limitations

Artificial intelligence is already changing warfare. […] But after 25 years in the Navy as a combat and test pilot and 15 years as an astronaut, I know having the most advanced technology doesn’t guarantee success. Technology is a tool. What matters is whether our people know how to use it, understand its limitations and can still accomplish the mission when it fails.

On introducing the Warfighter AI Readiness and Preparedness Act

While we need to have the most capable systems, we can’t lose sight of these two principles: our service members must be able to fight when technology fails, and human judgment and responsibility must be at the center of decisions about the use of force.

So first, we need the Department of Defense to assess how reliance on AI affects readiness, identify the skills most impacted by AI and determine how service members keep the judgment they need when those systems are unavailable or compromised. That’s the idea behind my bipartisan Warfighter AI Readiness and Preparedness (WARP) Act, that I introduced with Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.

On introducing the Ultimate Human Responsibility in Defense Systems Act

Tomorrow’s warfighters must be able to recognize when an AI system is giving them bad information and know how to continue the mission without it.

Because while AI can assist human judgment, it cannot replace human responsibility, including for the use of force.

For that reason, we also need a permanent requirement for human judgment and accountability when autonomous weapons and AI systems are involved in the use of force, which is part of my Ultimate Human Responsibility in Defense Systems Act.

On the opportunity to maintain America’s military superiority

Our goal should be a military in which AI allows a service member to understand the battlefield faster, make better decisions and accomplish missions that would otherwise be impossible while still possessing the training, experience and judgment to recognize when technology is wrong and take control.

The countries that figure out that balance will have a major advantage. That edge is ours for the taking.

title: Luján, Murphy, Democratic Senators Say Broadcasters Owe Americans on Trump’s Taxpayer-Funded Campaign Ads
text:
The Senators call for release of all documentation related to the decision to air the self-promoting, federally-funded ads, as well as reimbursement

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) led Senate Democrats in a letter to American broadcasters demanding the release of all documentation on the decision to air Donald Trump’s self-promoting, federally-funded campaign ads.

The letter asserts, by allowing Trump’s publicly funded campaign ads to air, broadcasters failed to follow the law and have an obligation to reimburse taxpayers. Despite committing to pay for future campaign ads through his super PAC, Trump refused to reimburse the Treasury for the more than 10 million in taxpayer dollars already spent.

The Senators wrote: “Under the law, President Trump’s ads might plausibly fall into two categories: the ads are either produced by a ‘legally qualified candidate’ and therefore broadcasters are limited in their ability to censor the ads’ content, or President Trump’s ads are ‘public service announcements’ (PSAs) which would require broadcasters generally to follow all associated rules around the publication of PSAs. In either scenario, broadcasters appear to have failed in their duty to adhere to the spirit and letter of the law.”

In the letter, the Senators made the political nature of Trump’s ads clear, while pointing out the criminal consequences of using federal funds to air them: “These ads are instead a campaign ad designed to bolster the image of an unpopular president and to boost the electoral chances of the slate of Republican congressional candidates. But liability protection for broadcasters does not extend to non-candidates. Furthermore, broadcasters can still refuse to air campaign ads if they violate federal laws. In this case, there are several federal criminal provisions implicated by these ads. They include, but are not limited to, the Anti-Deficiency Act (ADA), the Hatch Act, and several appropriations provisions involving the use of taxpayer funds for propaganda and notably the purpose statute. Lastly, if they were campaign ads, the ads certainly could not be paid for with taxpayer funds, which should have been obvious to any first-year law student.”

Dismissing Trump’s ludicrous claim that these ads were ‘public service announcements,’ the Senators continued: “To most reasonable people, an ad that solely features the President covering the President’s alleged successes, choreographed to a musical performance and aired immediately before an election is undoubtedly a campaign ad. It’s ridiculous to assert otherwise. Furthermore, if these ads are considered PSAs, as the President asserts, they raise several legal and liability questions for broadcasters.

The Senators concluded: “We ask that you voluntarily release all communications with the President, any federal agency, or White House official about the ads to ensure transparency for the American public and clarify which funds you received, from which federal agency, and release the terms of the contract as soon as possible. Additionally, you should recognize these ads are not PSAs, and reimburse the Treasury.”

In addition to Luján and Murphy, Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) also joined the letter.

The full letter is available here and below:

Broadcasters based in the United States:

We write today about the unprecedented self-promoting, taxpayer-funded ads starring President Donald Trump that ran across broadcast networks and online earlier this month. These bizarre ads prominently featured President Trump in a cinematic style with a soundtrack that begged Americans to love him. On October 5, 2026, after facing intense public backlash, the President announced that going forward he would pay for the ad using his super PAC.1 Given the unusual nature of these ads, we write to ask that you ensure the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) rules are followed. Specifically, we request that you voluntarily make any records related to these ads publicly available for inspection and reimburse the Treasury for the ads funded with taxpayer dollars.

Under the law, President Trump’s ads might plausibly fall into two categories: the ads are either produced by a ‘legally qualified candidate’ and therefore broadcasters are limited in their ability to censor the ads’ content, or President Trump’s ads are “public service announcements” (PSAs) which would require broadcasters generally to follow all associated rules around the publication of PSAs. In either scenario, broadcasters appear to have failed in their duty to adhere to the spirit and letter of the law.

Regarding the first category, Trump is not a candidate. These ads are instead a campaign ad designed to bolster the image of an unpopular president and to boost the electoral chances of the slate of Republican congressional candidates. But liability protection for broadcasters does not extend to non-candidates. Furthermore, broadcasters can still refuse to air campaign ads if they violate federal laws. In this case, there are several federal criminal provisions implicated by these ads. They include, but are not limited to, the Anti-Deficiency Act (ADA), the Hatch Act, and several appropriations provisions involving the use of taxpayer funds for propaganda and notably the purpose statute. Lastly, if they were campaign ads, the ads certainly could not be paid for with taxpayer funds, which should have been obvious to any first-year law student.

Regarding the second category, to most reasonable people, an ad that solely features the President covering the President’s alleged successes, choreographed to a musical performance and aired immediately before an election is undoubtedly a campaign ad. It’s ridiculous to assert otherwise. Furthermore, if these ads are considered PSAs, as the President asserts, they raise several legal and liability questions for broadcasters. A Public Service Announcement (PSA) has been defined by the FCC as “one for which no charge is made and which promotes programs, activities, or services of Federal, State or local governments (e.g., recruiting, sales of U.S. Savings Bonds, etc.) or the programs, activities or services of nonprofit organizations (e.g., UGF, Red Cross Blood Donations, etc.) or any other announcements regarded as serving community interests. PSAs are by definition, “announcements that are made for the good of the people.”

In other words, PSAs are generally required to be ads that inform the public. The ‘love me’ ad does not promote a program or a service of the federal government; it promotes alleged successes of the President and public reporting suggests broadcasters might already have taken millions in federal funds. As such, broadcasters have a duty to ensure that PSAs comply with applicable rules and could have easily refused to air the ads as PSAs.

In sum, we ask that you voluntarily release all communications with the President, any federal agency, or White House official about the ads to ensure transparency for the American public and clarify which funds you received, from which federal agency, and release the terms of the contract as soon as possible. Additionally, you should recognize these ads are not PSAs and reimburse the Treasury.

###

title: Bipartisan Senators Call on Trump to Rescind Russian Diesel Deal and Implement Sanctions Authorized by Congress Last Month on Enablers of Putin’s War Against Ukraine
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Mitch McConnell (R-KY), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-ME), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Alan Armstrong (R-OK), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-DE) and John Cornyn (R-TX) wrote President Donald Trump urging him to rescind his recent agreement with President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian-origin diesel fuel into global markets.

“Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators wrote.

The senators urged Trump to instead take swift action to implement sanctions authorized by the recently passed Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which President Trump signed into law in September.

“These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict,” the senators wrote.

The full text of the senators’ letter is available here and copied below.

Dear Mr. President,

Congress and the American people support ending the Russia-Ukraine war, which has cost hundreds of thousands of lives over the last four and a half years because Russia chose to invade its neighbor. A brokered peace, however, must be on just terms. It must uphold democratic values, the sovereignty and security of Ukraine, and their people’s right to choose their future.

The deal you struck with President Vladamir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans. The Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which lifts sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports, only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians. Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded.

We also recognize the urgent need to lower energy costs for American families and address the disruptions caused by the war with Iran. However, allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans. It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea. It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury.

Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which you swiftly signed into law. Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace. These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China, and thereby enhance your negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict. For decades, America has stood as the bastion of freedom against tyranny, and American presidents have embodied our nation’s resistance to tyrants. Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. Maintain our legacy – and the duty America holds – as leader of the free world.

title: Merkley Leads Oregon Lawmakers to Urge Continued Support for Oregon’s Hazelnut Industry
text:
Salem, OR – Today, Oregon’s U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley led members of Oregon’s congressional delegation in a letter to U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins that calls on the Department to deliver critical federal support to Oregon’s hazelnut industry under the federal Section 32 purchase program.

“The hazelnut industry is a massive and integral part of our state’s agricultural economy; its size and longevity represent generations of farmers and handlers who have dedicated their lives to producing and distributing a product many communities depend on for their livelihoods,” wrote the lawmakers.

The lawmakers’ letter calls on USDA to include Oregon hazelnuts, which account for 99 percent of hazelnuts produced in the United States, in this year’s Section 32 purchases, supporting growers, harvesters, processors, and agricultural economies primarily in Oregon’s Willamette Valley during a period of significant market disruption and economic uncertainty in a global market.

They stressed, “In recent years, disruptions in important export markets caused by these compounding issues have been particularly difficult for certain kernel sizes and grades that are high-quality, marketable food products but have fewer commercial outlets. These imbalances and market losses create uncertainty and pressure for our farmers and producers and threaten the steady distribution needed to prevent compounding product surpluses year-to-year.”

In addition to Merkley, the letter was signed by U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) and U.S. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Janelle Bynum (OR-05), and Val Hoyle (OR-04).
