title: Duckworth, Durbin Join Bicameral Coalition in Pressing Trump Administration on Illegal Reallocation of Funding for Minority Serving Institutions
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL) joined U.S. Senator Mazie Hirono and a bicameral coalition in pressing Secretary of Education Linda McMahon on the Administration’s illegal decision to redirect funding from Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) to other institutions. In a letter to Secretary McMahon, the members emphasized that while increasing funding for those institutions is important, the additional investments cannot come at the expense of MSIs that serve millions of students nationwide. The letter also reiterated the illegal nature of the decision to redirect funding that was statutorily authorized in specific amounts for specific purposes—in clear violation of the law.

“This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so,” the members wrote.

There are currently more than 800 federally recognized MSIs which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs) and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). These MSIs serve more than 5 million students collectively and have been receiving congressionally directed federal support for more than 30 years.

In 2019, Congress passed and President Trump signed into law the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act), permanently authorizing $255 million in mandatory funding for HBCUs, TCCUs and MSIs.

“The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year,” the members wrote.

In addition to Duckworth, Durbin and Hirono, the letter was cosigned in the Senate by U.S. Senators Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Patty Murray (D-WA), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Chris Coons (D-DE), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Jack Reed (D-RI), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Ed Markey (D-MA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Mark Warner (D-VA) Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and Michael Bennet (D-CO).

In addition to U.S. Representatives Meng, Espaillat and Clarke, the letter was also cosigned in the House by U.S. Representatives Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-DC-At Large), Mark Takano (D-CA-39), Danny Davis (D-IL-7), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-8), Judy Chu (D-CA-28), Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (D-IL-4), Dina Titus (D-NV-1), Paul Tonko (D-NY-20), Melanie Stansbury (D-NM-1), Jill Tokuda (D-HI-2), Robin Kelly (D-IL-2), Jimmy Gomez (D-CA-34), Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA-10), Emily Randall (D-WA-6), Jasmine Crockett (D-TX-30), Joaquin Castro (D-TX-20), Ed Case (D-HI-1), J. Luis Correa (D-CA-46), Susan Bonamici (D-OR-1), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX-29), Robert Menendez (D-NJ-8), Ted Lieu (D-CA-36), Mike Thompson (D-CA-4), Derek Tran (D-CA-45), Lateefah Simon (D-CA-12), George Whitesides (D-CA-27), Salud Carbajal (D-CA-24), Greg Stanton (D-AZ-4), Linda Sánchez (D-CA-38), Chellie Pingree (D-ME-1), Darren Soto (D-FL-9), Juan Vargas (D-CA-52), Teresa Leger Fernández (D-NM-3), Adelita Grijalva (D-AZ-7), Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-4), Kevin Mullin (D-CA-15) and Robert Garcia (D-CA-42).

The full text of the letter is available on Senator Duckworth’s website and below:

Dear Secretary McMahon:

Your recent decision to reallocate mandatory funding for Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) in Fiscal Year 2025 and Fiscal Year 2026 is an illegal violation of Congress’ spending authority under the Constitution. No court has found these programs that Congress has funded to be unconstitutional, and the administration’s mere belief that they are does not give it the necessary authority to spend those funds for any other purpose or program.

Many of us previously sent you a letter urging you to allocate Title III and Title V discretionary and mandatory funds as Congress directed to the more than 800 federally-recognized MSIs, which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs) and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). Combined, these institutions enroll more than 5 million students in rural and urban communities in states across the country. The Higher Education Act created the statutory framework for grants to these institutions, and has been in place for more than 30 years.

In December 2019, Congress passed and President Trump signed into law the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act), permanently authorizing $255 million in grant funds for MSIs, Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), and Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs). The funds are allocated across seven grant programs, each with a designated funding amount beginning in Fiscal Year 2020 and continuing thereafter. This authorization was an extension of prior mandatory appropriations that began in Fiscal Year 2008 and then expired.

Reallocation of Funds Designated for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs

On September 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education (ED) announced it would reallocate FY25 and FY26 mandatory funds Congress had specifically allocated for MSIs to HBCUs and TCCUs. In the news release announcing this illegal action, ED announced a “significant, one-time investment of more than $174 million in additional funding to strengthen” HBCUs and “a one-time award of more than $61 million in additional funding” for TCCUs.

While we strongly support additional funding for HBCUs and TCCUs, increasing funding for some institutions should not come at the expense of others. Furthermore, as previously stated, ED has no authority to redirect mandatory funding for MSIs—in this case, for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs and NASNTIs—for other purposes or programs. In fact, the entire basis for invalidating and redistributing these funds seems to be a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion from December 2, 2025, which wrongly determined that both discretionary and mandatory grants for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs and NASNTIs and discretionary grants for PBIs, were unconstitutional—without any judicial decision squarely dictating such a conclusion, and lacking any statutory authority to spend mandatory funds for anything other than their required purposes.

Shortly thereafter, ED stated that it was evaluating the full impact of the OLC opinion on the programs. ED then took several actions which made clear that it would not fund the programs, including by not allowing institutions to reapply for eligibility for the programs, and not including them in the eligibility matrix for Title III and Title V funds.

Reallocation of Funds Designated for PBIs

Even by its own baseless standards, the administration determined in the December 2025 OLC memo that the race-based provisions of this program could be severed and stated that ED could continue to provide these competitive grants for the authorized uses in this program, regardless of whether the grant recipient is a PBI. However, rather than adhering to the statute authorizing this grant program—or even OLC’s own wrongful guidance—ED allocated these funds to grantees under a different program with a separate purpose.

Unnecessarily Accelerating Obligation of FY26 Mandatory Funds

On top of all of this, the Trump administration took the completely unnecessary step of obligating FY26 mandatory funding for these programs a full year before it has historically been done, and a full year before the funds expire. These funds are available for two years—funds becoming available in FY26 are available for obligation through FY27. If ED only continued to award funds on the schedule it has historically, FY26 funds would be awarded this time next year.

The administration has claimed it reallocated these funds so they did not lapse and go to waste. While the Trump administration is perfectly willing to let appropriated funds lapse in other cases, including most recently with international education and migrant and seasonal farmworker education programs, half of the MSI funds it reallocated were not going to lapse this year. Even if one were to take the administration’s misguided legal view of these programs at face value, for half of these funds the choice was not between reallocating funding or having the funds lapse. The administration has said repeatedly it wants to work with Congress on solutions to address the legal status of these programs. While we fundamentally disagree with the administration’s view, the administration could have simply continued to administer these funds on the timeline it always has—which means obligating the FY26 funds next September—and waited to see if Congress enacted a solution or a court ruled on the constitutionality of these programs over the course of the next year. In fact, Congress did enact a temporary and albeit imperfect fix in the FY26 Consolidated Appropriations Act when faced with the fact that the Trump administration would otherwise let discretionary funding for MSIs lapse.

This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so. If President Trump and this administration were serious about investing in all of these institutions—as each of us is—the president would push for more funds for them instead of seeking to slash education programs while supersizing the Pentagon’s budget.

The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year. To be clear, mandatory funding for HBCUs, TCCUs, HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs and PBIs—as provided by the FUTURE Act—cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds.

The Executive Branch’s improper use of mandatory funds plainly violates Article I of the Constitution, which delegates the spending power to Congress. By failing to follow the law and fund programs as Congress directed, and to instead allocate funds for other unauthorized purposes, the Executive Branch has clearly exceeded its Constitutional authority. ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs. Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education. We would welcome the opportunity to work on a bipartisan basis with the administration to increase investments in MSIs, HBCUs and TCCUs.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. We look forward to your response.

Sincerely,

-30-

title: Duckworth Joins Colleagues to Demand Answers on Childhood Vaccines EO, Measles Deaths and Delayed Vaccine Access
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) joined U.S. Senator Michael Bennet (D-CO) and U.S. Representative Kim Schrier, M.D. (D-WA-08) along with 29 colleagues in a letter to Dr. Erica Schwartz, the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), to call out efforts to reject settled vaccine science and demand answers about the CDC’s efforts to implement President Trump’s childhood vaccine Executive Order (EO), underreport measles-associated deaths and delay access to childhood immunizations.

“[...] As the United States is experiencing the largest measles outbreak in 35 years, President Trump issued an Executive Order (EO) aimed at dismantling core immunization guidelines, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) to lay the groundwork for fundamentally restructuring the routine childhood immunization schedule. At the same time, reports indicate the CDC, under your leadership, excluded verified state-reported measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania from the public mortality count. All of this is happening while the CDC delayed access to fall respiratory virus vaccines through the Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. We are deeply concerned by this administration’s persistent efforts to reject settled science. As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health,” began the lawmakers.

The United States is facing a decline in childhood immunization rates. Recently, the CDC reported that 280,000 kindergartners did not complete their measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine series. This comes as the Trump administration has actively worked to lower the number of recommended immunizations, break up safe and effective combination shots and promote legal action against states unaligned with such efforts.

Additionally, the CDC has a long-standing agency precedent and prides itself on “objective data collection and reporting.” At the beginning of September, numerous reports exposed that four measles-associated deaths verified and reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health were excluded from the CDC’s public outbreak tracker for weeks, even as internal CDC systems continued to track these fatalities. This omission breaks with agency standards, and raises serious questions about the CDC’s willingness to resist political pressure over settled science.

“The health of American children and families depends on a CDC Director who is willing to follow the science, even when it may be politically inconvenient. We look forward to your response and to seeing whether the CDC under your leadership honors the commitments you made at your confirmation hearing,” concluded the lawmakers.

In addition to Duckworth and Bennet, this letter was co-signed in the Senate by U.S. Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Angus King (I-ME), Ed Markey (D-MA) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR).

In addition to Schrier, the letter was also signed in the House by U.S. Representatives Nanette Barragán (D-CA-44), Troy Carter (D-LA-02), Yvette Clarke (D-NY-09), Madeleine Dean (D-PA-04), Chris Deluzio (D-PA-17), Maxine Dexter (D-OR-03), Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06), Jonathan Jackson (D-IL-01), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-08), Mike Levin (D-CA-49), Doris Matsui (D-CA-07), Betty McCollum (D-MN-04), Joseph Morelle (D-NY-25), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Brittany Pettersen (D-CO-07), Melanie Stansbury (D-NM-01), Mark Takano (D-CA-39), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI-12), Paul Tonko (D-NY-20) and Lori Trahan (D-MA-03).

The full text of the letter is available on Senator Duckworth's website and below:

Dr. Schwartz:

At your confirmation hearing, you said that your “sacred responsibility” as Director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) would be to provide “clear, honest, and evidence-based” public health guidance and to “never betray the science.” In the short time since your confirmation as CDC Director, the health and safety of our children have been subjected to further chaos and confusion. As the United States is experiencing the largest measles outbreak in 35 years, President Trump issued an Executive Order (EO) aimed at dismantling core immunization guidelines, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) to lay the groundwork for fundamentally restructuring the routine childhood immunization schedule. At the same time, reports indicate the CDC, under your leadership, excluded verified state-reported measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania from the public mortality count. All of this is happening while the CDC delayed access to fall respiratory virus vaccines through the Vaccines for Children (VFC) program. We are deeply concerned by this administration’s persistent efforts to reject settled science. As CDC Director, you bear a responsibility to uphold scientific integrity, and we write seeking answers on how the CDC will respond to the EO and the RFI, and how you will honor the pledge you made to ensure that the CDC leads with evidence-based public health.

The CDC recently reported that the number of children up-to-date on their immunizations has continued to decline, including 280,000 kindergartners who did not complete the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) series. Instead of spending time and dedicating resources to promote the need for childhood immunizations, President Trump called for breaking up combination shots like the MMR vaccine into single-disease shots that are not available in the United States, cutting the number of diseases every child is recommended to be protected against from 18 to 11, and directing the Attorney General to advance legal challenges to state laws. Following this EO, HHS issued an RFI on the childhood immunization schedule, aimed at bypassing the CDC and the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which have developed recommendations for over 60 years. These efforts are only a part of the systematic attacks spearheaded by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. CDC’s scientists, not political appointees, should be at the center of any decision about the childhood immunization schedule.

During this same timeframe, CDC’s public actions under your leadership raise serious concerns regarding your willingness to counter these unscientific measures – including reports that four measles-associated deaths verified and reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health were excluded from the CDC’s public national mortality count for weeks, even as internal CDC systems continue to track these fatalities. This is a clear break from long-standing agency precedent, including last year’s standard reporting of measles deaths in Texas and directly contradicts the commitment to “objective data collection and reporting” that has been CDC’s foundation. If the agency under your leadership is altering verified state data to fit political preferences, the pledge you made at your confirmation hearing has already been broken.

We request responses to the following questions in writing by October 16, 2026.

CDC Role on the Executive Order on Childhood Vaccines

Did anyone from the White House or HHS consult you about the Executive Order either before or after it was issued?

a. If so, who reached out, what was discussed, and when did these communication(s) occur?

b. If not, have you raised, or do you plan to raise, any concerns with President Trump, Secretary Kennedy, or any other administration official(s)?

How is the CDC planning to implement the provisions outlined in the EO? What steps have been taken already and what are planned? Please provide a detailed summary of these plans.

What role, if any, did CDC career scientists have in developing the EO’s recommendations?

The EO directs the Secretary, acting through the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, to present plans to the President within 90 days on single-disease vaccine options, the timing and sequencing of childhood vaccines, and safety monitoring. What role does the CDC have in developing those plans, and which CDC officials are participating?

The EO recommends reducing the number of routine immunizations from 18 to 11. Do you support that specific recommendation? What scientific evidence supports removing the other diseases from the immunizations recommended for all children, and has the CDC estimated the additional illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths that could result?

Do you agree that spacing out immunizations across additional visits lengthens the window of vulnerability for infants and young children? If not, please provide the evidence on which CDC relies.

The EO recommends separating combination shots like MMR into single-disease shots. No single-disease MMR vaccine is currently available in the United States. Other countries that have tried this – like Japan in the 1990s – saw increased outbreaks, ultimately resulting in them reverting to a combination shot. Do you support this specific provision even though it is not currently available in the U.S., would require more shots and doctor visits, and lacks scientific backing? Why is the federal government recommending an option to families that does not exist, causing additional confusion?

What scientific evidence supports separating combination vaccines like MMR into single-disease doses? Please provide CDC analyses of peer-reviewed studies, epidemiological analyses, or international precedent that demonstrates this change would actually improve health outcomes. If no such evidence exists, will you decline to implement this provision?

The public comment period for the HHS RFI closed on September 20, 2026. Did CDC scientists review or contribute to the RFI before it was published? What role will CDC scientists have in reviewing the comments and in any resulting changes to the categories of federal vaccine recommendations?

Data Collection and Reporting

Has the CDC instituted a new policy for reviewing, altering, or withholding state-reported health data before public posting?

If so, what scientific evidence supports this change and what deliberations occurred?

If there is no such policy, on what basis were Pennsylvania’s measles deaths excluded from the public tracker, and who at CDC authorized that exclusion?

As of today, the CDC has only included two of the measles-associated deaths reported by the State of Pennsylvania. What specific technical, scientific, or epidemiological basis justified excluding Pennsylvania’s state-reported measles deaths from the CDC's public tracker while still including them on internal trackers?

Did any White House or HHS officials contact you or your staff regarding the public reporting of Pennsylvania’s measles deaths? Please provide all communication between CDC leadership and any White House or HHS official regarding the reporting of state-verified measles deaths since your confirmation.

Vaccines for Children Program

Why did the CDC delay opening orders for COVID vaccines through the Vaccines for Children Program (VFC)? Please provide the timeline of when decisions were made concerning the VFC program.

What made the CDC decide to open ordering for COVID vaccines through the VFC program on September 24, 2026 and not earlier?

Have you personally been asked by Secretary Kennedy, the White House, or any other HHS or Trump administration official to delay or condition VFC activation for the COVID vaccine? If so, please describe the request and identify who made it. If such a request was made in writing, please provide it.

Who at CDC, HHS, or the White House made the decision to delay VFC activation for the COVID vaccine, and on what basis? Please produce all internal communications, memoranda, and legal or scientific analyses supporting that decision.

What guidance has CDC provided to state health departments, pediatricians, and VFC providers about the status of COVID vaccines under VFC? How soon can VFC vaccines be expected to be in the possession of clinicians and accessible for children?

The health of American children and families depends on a CDC Director who is willing to follow the science, even when it may be politically inconvenient. We look forward to your response and to seeing whether the CDC under your leadership honors the commitments you made at your confirmation hearing.

-30-

title: Duckworth Statement on Attempted Mass Shooting on Hindu Place of Worship in Aurora
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) issued the following statement in reaction to police arresting and charging a man with felony crimes for an alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu place of worship in Aurora, Illinois:

“This horrific attempted attack in Aurora goes against everything America stands for. I’m deeply grateful to both the suspect’s coworkers who alerted law enforcement and to the heroic first responders who acted swiftly to save lives. While the worst was prevented and fortunately no one was hurt, it remains a tragedy in and of itself that such an evil plot against the Hindu community was even conceived. It is a stark reminder that when white supremacy knocks, we all have a responsibility to answer loudly and make it clear there is no home for such hatred here in Illinois. In this deeply disturbing moment, we must come together to help ensure every Illinoisan can practice their faith and live without fear.”

In the wake of this attempted attack against Indian Americans at the Hindu temple in Aurora, today Duckworth spoke with U.S. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-8), first responders and community leaders to hear their concerns and offer support. The incident comes amid persistent anti-Asian hate nationwide, with reported anti-Asian hate crimes remaining nearly three times higher in 2024 than the average annual number reported between 2013 and 2018. Duckworth has long been a leader calling for an end to anti-Asian hate, helping lead the COVID-19 Hate Crimes Act that was signed into law by President Biden to help address the rise in anti-Asian hate crimes, improve hate crime reporting, expand public awareness and support affected communities.

title: Fischer Welcomes U.S. Energy Secretary, EXIM CEO to Elk Creek
text:
ELK CREEK – U.S. Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE) visited the NioCorp Elk Creek Critical Minerals Project alongside U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, U.S. Export-Import Bank (EXIM) Chairman John Jovanovic, Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen, Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NE), and Rep. Adrian Smith (NE-03).

Fischer has long supported the Elk Creek Critical Mineral Project, including helping to secure $10 million in federal funding for U.S. aluminum-scandium master alloy production.

“I've long pushed to bring critical mineral production and processing back to the United States,” Fischer said. “I could not be prouder to see Nebraska leading the way in securing America’s energy dominance. I appreciate the administration’s focus on strengthening our domestic critical mineral supply chain, and I thank Secretary Wright and Chairman Jovanovic for supporting NioCorp’s plant in Elk Creek."

“I was proud to join Nebraska’s Congressional delegation to advance the Elk Creek mining project that will deliver prosperity and more than a thousand jobs to residents, while also securing our nation’s critical minerals supply chains,” Wright said.

“The Elk Creek Minerals Project is exactly the type of opportunity EXIM was always designed to support,” Jovanovic said. “By advancing U.S. control over the critical minerals essential to aircraft, automobiles, advanced manufacturing, and our broad industrial base, this project means more good jobs in Nebraska, more opportunities for American workers and a stronger, more secure industrial future for the United States.”

The Elk Creek Project will mine and process niobium, scandium, titanium, all minerals the U.S. imports today, and will support over 1,000 well-paying jobs in rural Nebraska.

The U.S. is entirely dependent on imports for niobium, scandium, and foreign competitors dominate heavy rare earth processing. Elk Creek holds the highest-grade niobium resource in North America, the second largest indicated rare earth resource in the nation, and one of the largest scandium resources in the world.

title: Fischer Applauds over $43M in Federal Investments for Nebraska Rail
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE) released the following statement on the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) decision to award $43.2 in grants from the Federal Railroad Administration’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) program to projects in Nebraska:

“Nebraska’s rail infrastructure supports our strong state economy and connects our world-class products to the rest of the country,” Fischer said. “These investments will modernize our rail system and provide much-needed safety improvements. As Nebraska’s senator, I’ll always support projects that directly benefit our state.”

Fischer wrote letters of support to U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy and Administrator of the Federal Railroad Administration David Fink for these projects.

These federal investments will be directed to three projects in Nebraska:

The Nebraska, Kansas & Colorado Railway’s (NKCR) Logistics Infrastructure to Fast-Track Exception Leveraging of the Imperial Nebraska Line (LIFELINE) project.

The Nebraska Central Railroad Company’s (NCRC) Research and Development of AI-Predictive Technology for Safer Rail Infrastructure Nationwide project.

The Omaha Public Power District’s (OPPD) Arbor Rail Line Enhancement Project.

LIFELINE Project

NKCR will receive $21,149,520 to rehabilitate the 49-mile Imperial Subdivision between Culbertson and Imperial, Nebraska, address critical track deficiencies, and restore the line to a state of good repair. The project will preserve the long-term viability of the line, with a comprehensive tie replacement program that will replace approximately 1,200 ties per mile.

OmniTRAX CEO Colby Tanner said, “Investments in rail infrastructure are investments in a durable American economy. We are thankful for Senator Fischer’s commitment to keep Nebraska’s infrastructure strong and for the CRISI funds that help us keep Nebraska’s supply chains moving for our nation.”

Research and Development of AI-Predictive Technology for Safer Rail Infrastructure Nationwide Project

NCRC will receive $14,888,433 to integrate multiple types of sensors into a single cloud-based platform to provide real-time monitoring, analytics, and predictive alerts. This will allow railroad personnel to identify developing infrastructure risks before they result in service disruptions, track failures, or derailments.

The Nebraska Central Railroad Company said, “Nebraska Central Railroad Company is thrilled to be a recipient of this CRISI grant and grateful for continued support of Sen. Fischer and the Federal Railroad Administration in securing safe, reliable transportation infrastructure. This investment will enable important research, field testing, and technology development that can help identify emerging track conditions earlier and strengthen rail safety. We look forward to working with our partners to deliver practical tools that can benefit short line railroads and the broader rail industry.”

Arbor Rail Line Enhancement Project

OPPD will receive $7,142,850 for rail infrastructure improvements along a 56.4-mile segment of track between Lincoln and Nebraska City, Nebraska. The project will harden and modernize the infrastructure of the Arbor Rail Line, improving its resilience to service disruptions while enhancing overall safety and reliability.

The Omaha Public Power District said, “We are grateful for the strong support from our federal delegation in securing this grant, which will help us strengthen the reliability and resilience of the Arbor Rail Line. We especially appreciate Senator Fischer’s ongoing leadership and partnership in ensuring Nebraska’s energy infrastructure remains dependable for the communities we serve.”

title: On SiriusXM, Gallego Discusses His Economic Policy Plan to Save America’s Middle Class, Rips President Trump’s Russian Oil Deal
text:
WASHINGTON — This week, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined SiriusXM’s “The Julie Mason Show” to discuss his expansive economic policy plan to rebuild the middle class. During the conversation, Senator Gallego noted specific provisions from the plan that would bring the American Dream back within reach, including raising the federal minimum wage to $20-an-hour and creating a New Deal-style jobs program in the wake of uncertainty brought on by Artificial Intelligence. The senator also addressed President Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, which Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky called “a gift” to Putin.

Listen: The Julie Mason Show

On increasing the minimum wage: “We need to start raising the wage and get it to 20 dollars-an-hour … so, that way, people actually have a decent chance to save some money and … breathe a little easier.

“I hear all the time, and I heard this in Arizona when I was running for Senate 2024: [Americans] feel like they’re just drowning. And they’re treading water as much as they can. But every time the end of the month comes, they pay a bill and they realize that there’s just nothing left. And, so, people are just working to survive instead of working to actually have [a] real life.”

On union density and sectoral bargaining: “[Some people] always talk about these amazing days in America … they’re usually talking somewhere between the late 1950s and late 1970s. One wage could get you enough to buy a house and get a car… that’s also when the United States had the highest union density in its history. And it’s not a coincidence that the buying power of middle-class America has gone down as union density has gone down.

On his proposed FDR-style job program: “[This program is] going to be mostly an answer to what, potentially, is going to come from a lot of job losses from AI.

“The goal is to make sure that people don’t have massive disruption like we saw in 2008, for example. As someone from Arizona that saw what happened with bad economic turns, this actually gives an opportunity for people to make wages.”

On the recent diesel deal with Russia: “It’s a corrupt deal. Number one, it’s not in the best interest of this country for us to actually help Russia. The diesel deal is bad to begin with, just on paper.

“In the end, Russia is a country that does not care, and could care less, about the United States and will gladly turn on us at any point. And, so, the fact that Donald Trump fell for that, and we’re screwing over Ukraine in the process, is why most Americans are just aghast by this deal.”

title: Following Gillibrand Demands, Federal Government Releases Heat Assistance Funding To New York State
text:
Today, following the federal government’s release of funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) issued the following statement:

“I am relieved that the federal government has released heating assistance funding, allowing New York State to make these funds available to help New Yorkers heat their homes,” said Senator Gillibrand. “New Yorkers need relief now more than ever as temperatures drop and fuel prices soar because of President Trump’s war with Iran. I was proud to fight for the swift release of these funds, and I will continue working to make sure that New Yorkers have the assistance they need to stay warm this winter.”

President Trump’s war with Iran has caused the price of oil to skyrocket, with prices currently hovering near $100 per barrel. That has driven the average cost of heating oil in New York up to $6.21 per gallon—a 67 percent increase from this time last year. As temperatures drop below freezing in New York, this cost increase is putting massive strain on New Yorkers’ budgets, making it hard for many to heat their homes.

LIHEAP is a federally funded program that helps low-income households pay utility bills, address energy crises, and lower costs by improving home energy efficiency through weatherization. Last year, over 1.1 million in New York households received LIHEAP assistance to help them stay warm.

Funding for LIHEAP was appropriated by Congress in the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 in September. After the funding was appropriated, Senator Gillibrand demanded that the Trump administration immediately release it to states for distribution to Americans in need.

New York is slated to receive an estimated $356 million in LIHEAP funds.

title: Gillibrand, Schumer, Torres Urge Acceleration Of Federal Lithium-Ion Battery Regulation Amidst E-Bike Fatalities
text:
Import of Faulty Lithium-Ion Battery Powered Micromobility Products Linked to Nationwide Deaths

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), along with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Congressman Ritchie Torres (D-NY), called on Peter Feldman, Acting Chair of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), to complete the rulemaking process to set a mandatory federal standard for lithium-ion batteries in micromobility products such as e-bikes and e-scooters. In their letter, the members underscored the concerning number of lithium-ion battery-related fatalities among micromobility products across the country, particularly in New York City.

They wrote, “To prevent further destruction to our communities and protect lives, we urge the Consumer Product Safety Commission…to immediately work through stakeholder comments and swiftly complete the rulemaking process for the proposed rule, ‘Safety Standard for Lithium-Ion Batteries Used in Micromobility Products and Electrical Systems of Micromobility Products Containing Such Batteries.’”

The members cited the CPSC staff’s pre-existing awareness of the dangers of these batteries, as a 2026 CPSC report acknowledged 367 lithium-ion battery-related fires resulting in 45 fatalities from 2017 through 2024 among all micromobility products. While this has become an issue all across the nation, the numbers are especially concerning in New York City. The members wrote that just this year, the Fire Department of the City of New York reported 362 fires and 5 deaths among users of e‑bikes, e-scooters, and similar single‑person devices.

Local communities have attempted to implement safety measures, from setting standards for retailers to banning the use of micromobility products in certain locations. However, the members emphasized the necessity of action on the federal level. They maintained, “While these rules attempt to achieve safety, the only way to effectively prevent future fires is by setting mandatory federal standards for lithium-ion batteries. […] By finalizing this rule and setting standards for these batteries, the Commission can ensure that cheap and defective batteries do not enter the U.S. market.”

Senator Gillibrand has long championed a push toward the enforcement of e-bike safety standards on the federal level. She is the lead Senate sponsor of the Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, which passed the House of Representatives on April 28, 2025 and awaits passage in the Senate.

title: ICYMI: Gillibrand Op-Ed In The Hill: The System Failed Jane Doe. Congress Can Fix It.
text:
In case you missed it, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand published an opinion piece in The Hill demanding that Congress take action to support victims of sexual assault in the wake of allegations of a horrific gang rape at Cornell University.

Senator Gillibrand argues that Congress—after spending two weeks debating regulations for college sports—must find time to protect students on college campuses. She urges passage of her bipartisan legislation, the Campus Accountability and Safety Act (CASA), and describes how that legislation could have helped Jane Doe and stands to help other survivors in the future if passed.

The full text of the op-ed can be found here or below:

The System Failed Jane Doe. Congress Can Fix It.

By Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)

In recent weeks, the horrific allegations of sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house have sparked public outrage.

But as debates about campus culture and law enforcement lapses permeated the public conscience, Congress made clear that it had a very different priority: debating regulations for college sports. Not a second was spent on campus safety at a time that one in four undergraduate women report being sexually assaulted at school. At Cornell, that figure is more than one in three.

There is no question: the system has failed Jane Doe.

This is not just a problem with one case, one fraternity, or one university. Jane Doe’s story echoes a heartbreaking reality on campuses across the country. Time and time again, victims experience the same story: they report, then watch their perpetrators get by with a slap on the wrist.

In 2016, America watched Stanford swimmer Brock Turner serve just three months in jail for raping an unconscious woman behind a campus dumpster. The survivor’s victim impact statement went viral. Over a million people signed petitions calling for the judge in Turner’s case to be removed. Lawmakers changed the state’s sentencing laws.

This should have been a turning point. It wasn’t.

In 2016, Baylor also came under fire after an investigation found administrators had discouraged students from reporting sexual assault. In 2021, USC announced it would pay millions to women who said the university ignored years of complaints about sexual abuse by its campus gynecologist. In the years since, dozens of institutions have come under federal investigation over alleged mishandling of Title IX sexual violence cases.

A system that fails survivors again and again is fundamentally broken. The price of a college education shouldn’t include a 25+% chance of being sexually assaulted.

Congress must do more to protect students.

We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act (CASA).

CASA is commonsense, bipartisan legislation. It would hold institutions accountable, uphold a fair process for students, and give sexual assault survivors a trauma-informed advocate to help them through the adjudication process.

Cornell offers confidential resources for students, and we don’t know the extent to which Jane Doe knew about or used them. But not all universities offer those resources, and even if they do, many students don’t know they exist.

That’s how CASA could help.

First, it would require a trained, confidential advocate to be available to survivors of sexual assault on every campus.

The trauma of sexual assault can impair memory and make bureaucracy feel impossible. Having an advocate who is trained in trauma-informed care ensures that survivors are not re-traumatized by the very system meant to protect them.

Such an advocate could have been life-changing for someone like Jane Doe.

They could have walked Doe through the complex disciplinary process that comes with reporting an assault. They could have talked her through her options, including the difference between Cornell’s disciplinary process and the criminal process. And when Doe chose to report, they could have acted as her liaison with the university and law enforcement, sparing her the trauma of reliving her experience every time she spoke with a different authority figure.

Crucially, CASA would require campus staff who receive reports of sexual assault and domestic violence – including the Cornell Health medical clinic employee Jane Doe saw – to provide those students with contact information for the on-campus advocate and an explanation of the services they offer.

Second, CASA would require uniform, rigorous training for all campus personnel involved in investigating and adjudicating sexual assault cases.

That training could have helped prevent critical errors in Doe’s case.

For example, Doe’s lawyer alleges that the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) never contacted her after she made her initial statement to Cornell police. A New York Times investigation later showed that a key statement from Doe’s testimony—“I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped”—was left out of the six-page statement that was sent to the DA.

Better-trained investigators are far less likely to make that mistake.

At the same time, a CASA advocate could have helped Doe review her testimony and caught the omission. Then, once the complaint was submitted to the DA, they could have helped follow up on her case and demanded that her complaint be taken seriously.

Advocates and training help survivors navigate the system—but that is only half the battle. CASA also fixes the system itself, making it more transparent and fair for all students.

The legislation would mandate a uniform process for conducting campus disciplinary proceedings surrounding sexual assault.

That means no separate track for athletes or students in fraternities.

CASA also protects students who come forward by encouraging the adoption of a practical amnesty policy in cases like Jane Doe’s where alcohol or drugs are involved. CASA would help shield students who report in good faith from campus disciplinary actions for drinking or illegal substance use.

And finally, CASA would require colleges and universities to disclose key data about the prevalence of sexual assault on their campuses and the outcomes of sexual assault investigations. Institutions that fail to comply would face financial penalties.

Transparency creates accountability. If students and families can see what is happening on campus, and how universities respond, institutions will finally be incentivized to put safety first.

Passing CASA will not end sexual violence on college campuses, nor will it undo the harm already inflicted on countless survivors. Changing the culture that allows campus sexual assault to persist will require sustained commitment at every level—from universities, students, families, law enforcement, and lawmakers. But establishing a fair process, giving survivors an advocate, and mandating real accountability is an essential start.

The system failed Jane Doe. It has failed too many survivors for too long. Congress can change that. We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act.

title: New Study: Families In New York Have Had To Spend $6,000+ More Under Trump
text:
JEC Report: The Average Household In New York Has Had To Pay An Additional $6,000+ For Goods And Services Due To Rising Costs Under President Trump

This week, a new Joint Economic Committee (JEC) – Minority report found that as of September 2026, the average household in New York has had to pay an additional $6,000+ for goods and services due to rising costs under President Trump. When campaigning in 2024, candidate Trump promised, “Starting on day one of my new administration, we will end inflation, and we will make America affordable again.”

In response to the new report and Republicans’ broken promises, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand issued the following statement:

“President Trump and congressional Republicans promised to lower costs and end inflation. Instead, they’ve made life $6,000 more expensive for New Yorkers,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Look at what they have done: they gutted Medicaid and cut Medicare and healthcare subsidies to fund tax breaks for billionaires, launched a war that increased gas prices, and supported tariffs to make groceries and essentials more expensive. I will not stop fighting to lower New Yorkers’ costs and hold this administration accountable for hurting working families and small businesses across our state.”

The new report follows JEC’s September study that found that President Trump’s vanity projects – including construction of the new White House ballroom and the no-bid contract to paint the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, among others – are expected to cost more than $1.8 billion, highlighting the administration’s egregiously misplaced priorities and lack of interest in spending money to lower costs and help the American people.

Additional breakdowns of the JEC report:

Housing Costs

New York families have had to spend an additional $1,310 on housing costs such as rent and mortgage payments since President Trump took office.

Grocery Costs

Americans paid $310 more for groceries in President Trump’s first year than in 2024, and grocery prices are now more than 4 percent higher than when Trump took office.

Beef and coffee prices are hitting Americans especially hard. Since the president took office, the average price of ground beef has risen almost every month to a record high of more than $7 per pound. Coffee prices also spiked and are now more than $9 per pound.

Energy Costs

Gas prices have soared since the start of Trump’s Iran war. In total, people across New York have spent an additional $4 billion on gas since the beginning of the war. That has cost the average family in New York an additional $739 in gas costs.

Families in New York spent $190 more on electricity in 2025 under President Trump than they did in 2024. And, in just the first seven months of 2026, they spent $258 more on electricity than they did in the first seven months of 2024.

Home heating oil prices in New York are at record highs, which means it will now cost a family $1,558 to fill their heating oil tank, $598 more than at this time last year. If prices stay this high, then New York families will have to pay a total of $2,504 to heat their homes this winter, a 32 percent increase compared to last winter.

Health Care Costs

Because of Trump and Republicans’ refusal to extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax cuts that help people afford their health insurance, monthly premiums for ACA plans rose over 50 percent on average in 2026 compared to last year. Meanwhile, deductibles surged to record highs, increasing by more than $1,000 on average.

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index and Average Price Data, Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, Joint Economic Committee – Republicans, Bureau of Economic Analysis, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Walmart.com, AAA.com, Federal Highway Administration, Energy Information Administration, Kaiser Family Foundation. Gas cost calculations are current through October 14, 2026, heating oil as of October 5th.

title: Q&A: Manufacturing Boosts Iowa Economy
text:
Q: How important is manufacturing to Iowa’s economy?

A: Iowa ranks among the top five states in the country for our manufacturing sector’s impact on the state economy. It generates nearly $35 billion annually, accounting for 17% of our state’s gross domestic product and employs roughly 14% of workers in rural and metropolitan areas across 99 counties. In 2025, wages from manufacturing jobs in Iowa exceeded $16 billion. These wages from more than 200,000 jobs support Iowa families whose paychecks circulate in communities across the state to boost local businesses and expand the tax base for schools, infrastructure and services. Last year the Republican-led Congress passed the Working Families Tax Cuts Act that stopped the largest tax increase in U.S. history and primed the pump for economic growth. The tax law increased take-home pay for workers and refueled domestic manufacturing by boosting investment, job creation and economic growth.

Signed into law by President Trump, the tax law delivered much-needed certainty for businesses and manufacturers, including full expensing for newly constructed or improved factory structures. Other key provisions include:

Permanent full expensing for machinery and equipment

Permanent immediate deductibility for domestic research and development expenses

Permanent 20 percent small business deduction

Permanent increased cap on the business interest deduction

Permanent America-first international tax reforms

From the policymaking tables in the U.S. Senate, I’ll continue championing pro-growth tax laws, workforce development, commonsense regulations and infrastructure to help keep Iowa punching above its weight and welcoming business and industry to create good-paying jobs in our state.

Q: How are you working to ready the workforce for manufacturing jobs?

A: During my annual county meetings, I hear directly from workers on the factory floor to learn about the challenges and success stories of local businesses and industry across the state. I often say Iowa manufacturers don’t brag enough about the high-quality products and services delivered with world class worker productivity. Iowa’s advanced manufacturing supports construction, agriculture, aerospace electronics, medical devices, transportation, renewable energy, biofuels, the food supply chain and much more. These businesses put increased demand for a skilled workforce to fill good paying jobs.

The Working Families Tax Cuts Act included my legislation known as the Workforce Pell Grant that expanded eligibility for students enrolled in short-term, job-specific technical training programs available in community colleges across the country, including here in Iowa. My legislation essentially kills two birds with one stone. Eligible students obtain skilled training for high-wage jobs with little-to-no student debt. And local employers benefit from a partnership with local community colleges to access a direct pipeline of homegrown talent.

As a member of the Senate Career and Technical Education Caucus, I welcome the recently awarded $10.8 million Department of Labor grant to Iowa’s community college network to invest in workforce training programs that connect student graduates with local employers. Hawkeye Community College will manage implementation of more than 50 Workforce Pell-eligible training programs in advanced manufacturing, construction, skilled trades and healthcare jobs. The federal funding will help Iowa community colleges fill workforce gaps for high-demand skills and allow workers to climb the ladder of prosperity. I also welcome the largest steel plant investment in U.S. history. This is a major win for Iowa workers and our state economy. The decision to build in Iowa is testament to our workforce, natural resources and competitive environment for economic development. This is a transformational opportunity for economic prosperity in America’s heartland that also would strengthen national security and address offshore supply chain disruptions with American-made steel.

October is National Manufacturing Month

title: Hawley Secures USDA Commitment on Continued Farm Service Agency Services in Missouri
text:
WASHINGTON –U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) received confirmation from United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Under Secretary Richard Fordyce that Farm Service Agency (FSA) offices in Missouri will not experience any closures or reductions in service. This announcement comes after Senator Hawley called on USDA in August to preserve the continued operation of FSA offices across Missouri following proposed service reductions in Ralls County.

“Agriculture is the backbone of Missouri, and our farmers depend on reliable access to the resources they need to keep their operations running,” said Senator Hawley. “I welcome USDA’s commitment that Farm Service Agency offices across Missouri will remain open and continue serving farmers, especially as they access critical conservation and disaster assistance.”

Under Secretary Richard Fordyce wrote, “The Department remains committed to ensuring producers have reliable access to the programs and services they depend on to continue feeding, fueling, and clothing our nation and the world. The Department’s Service Centers are central to this mission…As it stands, there are no Missouri field offices which are being transitioned to a part-time or appointment-only status. This includes the Ralls County office, which I am pleased to share, will remain fully operational. Similarly, no field offices in Missouri are being proposed for closure.”

title: Heinrich Meets with Farmers to Hear How Trump’s War with Iran & Illegal Tariffs are Making Food More Expensive, Tours Albuquerque Public Schools’ Scratch Kitchen, Meets with a 102-Year-Old WWII & Korean War Veteran, Tours Albuquerque Semiconductor Company
text:
Photos

CORRALES & ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), a member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture, Rural Development, and Food and Drug Administration, met with New Mexico farmers and ranchers to hear how President Trump’s war with Iran and illegal tariffs are driving up fuel, fertilizer, and farm equipment costs, hurting local producers and making food more expensive for families.

Heinrich met with Pam Roy, Executive Director, Farm to Table NM; Helga Garza, Executive Director, Agri-Cultura Network; Alan Brauer, Senior Director, Indigenous Farm Hub; Johannes Lencer, COO and Interim CEO Frontier Food Hub; Anthony Wagner, Owner, Wagner Farms; Manny Encinas, Owner, Trilogy Beef and Buffalo Creek Ranch; Gilbert Luis, Owner, Acoma Number 8 Ranch; and Zach Ben, Owner, Bidii Baby Foods.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Meets with Farmers to Discuss How Trump’s War with Iran and Illegal Tariffs Are Driving Up the Cost of Groceries, October 13, 2026.

“Here in New Mexico, diesel is averaging more than $6 a gallon, and that means higher costs for farmers and ranchers who grow our food and for families already struggling to afford groceries. Trump’s tariffs are driving up costs, and his war in Iran is putting even more pressure on fuel prices,” said Heinrich. “We need to build a more resilient food system that can help farmers manage these rising costs and withstand extreme weather so they can keep producing the food our families depend on.”

“In 2025, we were paying about $1,000 a month on gas for our cargo truck distributed statewide. Right now, that has doubled. So, every month we're spending anywhere from $2,000 to $2,500 a month on gas....And we purchased a speed steer tractor, and it took months and months and months to get it because of all the tariffs,” said Helga Garza, Executive Director, Agri-Cultura Network.

“It’s too expensive for us, specifically, I mean, diesel prices...My dad checks cows every day, and so he travels about 250 miles a day. And so his diesel expenditures per month have increased by almost $2,000 a month. For us to even service our farmers market, particularly Corrales, we go to restaurants in Santa Fe and Albuquerque. It costs us about $1,000 more a month just to run our trucks. And that's not even getting into the New Mexico growing season. We'll be shipping wheat to Farmington, Gallup, and Las Cruces, where that's likely going to double as the market slows down. So, this definitely impacted us,” said Manny Encinas, Owner, Trilogy Beef and Buffalo Creek Ranch.

“I haven't really been able to buy new equipment. It’s more expensive to buy our equipment. So, I really haven't purchased any equipment this year,” said Anthony Wagner, Owner, Wagner Farms. “We’re trying to just use what we do have: The tractors and equipment and all that...Fertilizer, of course, is more expensive now too. We have to get fertilizer. We use a lot of fertilizer on our farms.”

During their conversation with Heinrich, the small farmers, ranchers, and local distributors also underscored how their operations have been impacted by climate change, including significant flooding and drought.

“It's been challenging these last two years with our orchard. I pretty much have lost my orchard these two years with the drought. I had 750 trees that were 50-year-old trees. And we've been producing all the old-time apples. And with the drought the last years, I lost a lot of my trees,” said Wagner. “We're trying to convert to drip on some of our stuff now because we can't really depend on the river now it seems like...so we're having to try to adapt.”

For more background on Heinrich’s actions to deliver for New Mexico small farmers, ranchers, and local distributors, click here.

For more background on Heinrich’s actions to hold President Trump accountable for his illegal, costly, and reckless war with Iran, click here.

For more background on Heinrich’s work to combat President Trump’s tariffs and lower the cost of groceries and everyday essentials, click here.

Heinrich also toured Albuquerque Public Schools’ scratch kitchen and spoke to students and staff at Tres Volcanes Community Collaborative about his Healthy Meals Help Kids Learn Act, legislation that will make it easier for students to access quality, nutritious school meals.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Tours Albuquerque Public Schools’ Scratch Kitchen and Speaks to Students and Staff at Tres Volcanes Community Collaborative, October 13, 2026.

“New Mexico has shown that when we make healthy school meals available to every student, we give kids a better chance to focus in the classroom, learn, and succeed. But rising costs for food, equipment, and labor are making it harder for schools to put nutritious meals on the table,” said Heinrich. “My Healthy Meals Help Kids Learn Act will give schools like Tres Volcanes in Albuquerque the support they need to keep serving healthy meals, buy more food from local farmers, and make sure every kid has the food they need to learn and thrive.”

School meals help shape lifelong healthy eating habits, and research shows that students who participate in school meal programs have better overall diet quality than nonparticipants. But as the cost of food and equipment continues to rise, school districts are struggling to keep up. Heinrich’s Healthy Meals Help Kids Learn Act will give school districts the certainty they need to strengthen their meal programs, provide nutritious meals to students, and plan for the future. For more information on the bill, click here.

Additionally, Heinrich met with Mr. Raymond Bonda, a 102-year-old veteran of World War II and the Korean War, and presented him with a U.S. flag flown over the U.S. Capitol in his honor, along with a challenge coin.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) meets with Mr. Raymond Bonda, a 102-year-old veteran of World War II and the Korean War, October 13, 2026.

“Raymond Bonda has spent his life in service to others, from serving our country in World War II and the Korean War to dedicating his career to Tribal communities through the Bureau of Indian Affairs and Indian Health Service,” said Heinrich. “He came to New Mexico more than 59 years ago and made it home. His service, creativity, and commitment to our communities embody the very best of New Mexico, and it was an honor to meet him and recognize his remarkable life.”

Mr. Raymond Bonda trained as an aviation metalsmith and welder and served aboard the seaplane tender USS Gardiners Bay (AVP-39) in the Western Pacific. After World War II, he attended New York University on the G.I. Bill, where he earned both a bachelor's and a master's degree in social work. When the Korean War began in 1950, Mr. Bonda was recalled to active duty and assigned to the aircraft carrier USS Princeton (CV-37). He was discharged in 1953.

Mr. Bonda stopped in Albuquerque on his way to San Diego, never expecting that a brief stop would lead him to make New Mexico his home for more than 59 years. He retired in 1984 after a long career with the U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs and the Indian Health Service (IHS). Mr. Bonda went on to complete a bachelor’s degree in Studio Arts at the University of New Mexico. As an artist, he was an active member of the New Mexico Art League, the New Mexico Veterans Art Association, and the Western Federation of Watercolor Societies.

Lastly, Heinrich toured the manufacturing facility of 3D Glass Solutions, an Albuquerque homegrown semiconductor company helping New Mexico lead in space and advanced manufacturing dominance.

Heinrich has advocated to add manufacturing capability for advanced microelectronics packaging and substrates as an eligible use of the Defense Industrial Base Fund, which funds semiconductor work like what is happening at 3D Glass Solutions.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) tours 3D Glass Solutions’ manufacturing facility in Albuquerque, October 13, 2026.

“3D Glass Solutions is a great example of the homegrown innovation happening right here in New Mexico. By investing in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, we are creating more good-paying jobs, strengthening our domestic supply chains, and ensuring America remains a leader in advanced manufacturing and space exploration technologies,” said Heinrich.

title: Hoeven: Efforts Begin on Phase 2 of Crack the Code 2.0, Moving From Individual Wells to Field-Scale Testing
text:
BISMARCK, N.D. – Senator John Hoeven today held a press conference with Governor Kelly Armstrong, Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit, North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, North Dakota Petroleum Council (NDPC) President Ron Ness and Chord Energy President and CEO Danny Brown to provide an update on phase one of Crack the Code 2.0 and discuss efforts to begin the second phase of the initiative, including advancing the field-scale testing of enhanced oil recovery (EOR). Hoeven outlined:

Progress on the first phase of Crack the Code 2.0, which is utilizing $157 million in funding to support six large-scale pilot projects in the Bakken.

Three of the six pilot projects are underway, with one project having received its injection permit and the other two awaiting approval from the North Dakota Industrial Commission.

The funding for phase one consists of $36 million in federal funding that Hoeven worked with Under Secretary Haustveit to secure, combined with $45 million from the state of North Dakota and $76 million from industry.

Efforts to scale up the initiative in phase two, moving from individual wells to using EOR in a whole oil field, which will include up to 200 field test wells.

Hoeven stressed that they will prioritize a field that is close to:

An existing CO2 source, like the Dakota Gasification Company (DGC).

Existing pipelines and other infrastructure.

The senator highlighted that the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance had more than $289 billion in loan authority available at the end of 2025.

Hoeven is working with Haustveit to make this loan guarantee authority available to support the estimated $400 million cost for establishing the field test wells under phase two.

Hoeven, the state of North Dakota and the NDPC are currently looking for additional industry partners to participate in phase two. The senator stressed that private partners will benefit from added revenue streams resulting from:

The additional oil produced by the field test wells.

The 45Q tax credit, which Hoeven worked to increase in the One Big Beautiful Bill (OB3) specifically for EOR operations.

The field test wells come in addition to two other revenue streams that Hoeven is working to incorporate into the second phase of Crack the Code 2.0, including:

Developing lignite coal as a source of rare earth elements (REEs) and other critical minerals.

Expanding fertilizer production at the DGC’s Great Plains Synfuels Plant.

“Phase one of Crack the Code 2.0 is well underway, with a total of six large-scale pilot projects moving forward. But we’re not going to stop there. We are bringing together the partnerships we need for phase two, with the goals of increasing oil production by moving from individuals wells to using EOR in a whole oil field, providing additional revenue streams for our coal producers, developing domestic sources of rare earth elements and increasing fertilizer production. That’s a win-win-win-win,” said Hoeven. “We appreciate Under Secretary Haustveit for again visiting North Dakota with us to help move this initiative forward. The DOE has more than enough loan guarantee authority available to support phase two, and we’re working to ensure that credit and other funding is available so industry partners can move to field-scale testing of EOR. Between the additional oil produced and the improvements we made to the 45Q tax credit, this is a real opportunity for private industry to leverage new revenue streams while helping to prove the viability of EOR, which can both double oil recovery in the Bakken and double the life of our coal-fired power plants.”

Critical Minerals

By creating a domestic source for REEs, this effort will help improve U.S. economic and national security by reducing reliance on foreign nations like China for sourcing these important materials, which are used in a wide variety of high-tech applications.Hoeven highlighted a project he has worked to advance, along with Senator Kevin Cramer and Representative Julie Fedorchak, at the University of North Dakota (UND) to advance the recovery of rare earth elements and other critical materials from coal and coal-based feedstocks.

UND was selected as one of five projects nationwide under the $75 million initiative, following an effort Hoeven led with the North Dakota congressional delegation calling on the Department of Energy (DOE) to support UND’s proposal. The pilot project will be located in Underwood, North Dakota, and UND is currently in negotiations with DOE to finalize its award.

Fertilizer Production

DGC uses coal to produce fertilizers such as ammonium sulfate, anhydrous ammonia and urea. Increasing production would create additional revenue for coal producers while benefiting farmers, who would have access to an affordable, local source of fertilizer. Expanding DGC’s operations would also provide additional CO2 for EOR, supporting increased oil production in the Bakken. For more than 25 years, DGC has captured CO2 for EOR in Weyburn Field in Canada, showing this is a proven model and demonstrating the benefits it can bring to the Bakken under Crack the Code 2.0.

title: Husted, Bessent host education and adoption tax credit roundtable in Columbus
text:
“Every child deserves the opportunity to succeed, and their education should not be limited by their ZIP code.”

COLUMBUS – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today hosted a roundtable with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at Crown Preparatory Academy to discuss the Education Freedom Tax Credit and the expanded adoption tax credit, bringing together Ohio educators, school leaders, adoption advocates, state officials and families.

Under the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, Ohioans who donate to a state-approved scholarship organizations can now claim a federal tax credit. That money goes to scholarships that help students pay for tuition, tutoring, books, computers, transportation and special education services. The law also made the adoption tax credit larger and more helpful to families who need it most.

Husted, who began life in a foster home, joined families at the roundtable to talk about what these changes mean for kids in foster care and the families who open their homes to them. Participants also heard from school leaders and families about how school choice has changed their lives.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to succeed, and their education should not be limited by their ZIP code. Parents know what their kids need better than anyone in Washington, and these tax credits give more families the freedom to choose the right school and the support to open their homes to a child who needs one. I started my life in foster care, so I understand how much it matters when a family steps up. I was honored to have Secretary Bessent in Columbus to hear directly from the Ohioans who are using these tools every day,” Husted said.

“Here in Ohio, Senator Husted championed a scholarship that has helped over 100,000 families find the right education for their children. Now, through the Working Families Tax Cuts, President Trump is scaling that success across the country,” Bessent said.

Husted was an original cosponsor of the Educational Choice for Children Act, which was the basis for the Education Freedom Tax Credit in the Working Families Tax Cuts Act.

Background:

The Education Freedom Tax Credit gives taxpayers a federal credit for donations to approved scholarship granting organizations, which then award scholarships to students. States must opt in, and Gov. title: Husted secures millions in funding for Toledo rail infrastructure project
text:
“Ohioans can count on me to continue fighting to bring infrastructure investments like this home to Ohio to support jobs, grow our economy and keep our communities safe.”

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today announced that he secured $43,550,000 in funding to rehabilitate and modernize the Toledo Swing Bridge over the Maumee River, improving rail safety, reliability and freight transportation in northwest Ohio.

“Ohio’s rail infrastructure plays a critical role in moving goods, supporting businesses and keeping our economy strong. This investment will make the Toledo Swing Bridge safer and more reliable, allowing goods to move more efficiently and strengthening Toledo’s position as a major transportation hub. Ohioans can count on me to continue fighting to bring infrastructure investments like this home to Ohio to support jobs, grow our economy and keep our communities safe,” said Husted.

The funding was awarded through the Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) program following Husted’s advocacy for the project in a letter to Federal Railroad Administration Administrator David Fink.

The project will address a structural bottleneck along an active freight corridor by modernizing the bridge and increasing its load-carrying capacity. These improvements will allow modern railcars to move more efficiently, strengthen freight transportation and support Ohio’s domestic energy supply chain.

The CRISI program supports projects that improve railroad safety, efficiency and reliability, reduce congestion along passenger and freight rail corridors and strengthen connections between transportation systems.

The grant allocation builds on Husted’s work as a member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works and the Senate Appropriations Committee. In these roles, Husted has been a strong advocate for strengthening Ohio’s infrastructure and ensuring that appropriated funds are obligated to projects that will serve Ohioans.

In September 2026, Husted secured funding for the Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority.

In August 2026, Husted secured funding for the City of Toledo and City of Fairfield infrastructure projects.

title: Special Amtrak stop announced for 2026 Peter Anderson Arts & Crafts Festival in Ocean Springs
text:
VIDEO: Amtrak will provide a temporary stop for the 48th annual Peter Anderson Arts & Crafts Festival

By WLOX Staff

OCEAN SPRINGS, Miss. (WLOX) — Amtrak will provide a temporary stop for the 48th annual Peter Anderson Arts & Crafts Festival, the Ocean Springs Chamber of Commerce-Main Street-Tourism Bureau announced Friday afternoon.

The stop will give visitors another way to travel to Ocean Springs and enjoy the beloved festival, scheduled for Nov. 7-8, 2026.

Drawing approximately 100,000 people to downtown Ocean Springs, the annual festival features more than 400 artists, crafters and food vendors, along with downtown shops and restaurants.

The chamber said making the temporary stop possible took diligent work with Amtrak representatives, the City of Ocean Springs, state and federal elected officials, and other partners.

“Thank you to Amtrak and everyone who worked together to make this temporary stop possible,” said Cynthia Sutton, CEO of the Ocean Springs Chamber of Commerce-Main Street-Tourism Bureau. “We’re excited to offer festivalgoers another convenient way to get to the Peter Anderson Festival this year. It’s a wonderful opportunity to help more visitors take part in the festival and enjoy all that Ocean Springs has to offer.”

“There’s no better way to arrive in Ocean Springs than by train during festival season,” said Ocean Springs Mayor Bobby Cox. “We’re grateful that Amtrak sees our city as an important stop and gateway to one of the Southeast’s premier outdoor festivals. From the moment visitors step off the train, they’ll find a community ready to welcome them with open arms and Southern hospitality. We’re rolling out the red carpet and can’t wait to greet everyone who is all aboard for Ocean Springs.”

Amtrak Festival Schedule

From Mobile to Ocean Springs

• 6:25 a.m. departure from Mobile, arriving in Ocean Springs at 7:28 a.m.

• 4:25 p.m. departure from Mobile, arriving in Ocean Springs at 5:28 p.m.

From New Orleans to Ocean Springs

• 7:35 a.m. departure from New Orleans, arriving in Ocean Springs at 9:54 a.m.

title: Kaine's Bipartisan Bill To Help Workers Share In Company Profits Becomes Law
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Tim Kaine’s (D-VA) bipartisan Retire through Ownership Act has become law. The bipartisan legislation, which he introduced with Senator Roger Marshall (R-KS), will facilitate the establishment and operation of employee stock ownership plans (ESOPs). ESOPs allow workers to directly share in the profits they help their company earn, leading to higher wages and more wealth-building.

“Employee stock ownership plans are good for workers and businesses because they provide opportunities for employees to benefit in a company’s financial success and gives them more ownership in their workplace,” said Kaine, a member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. “I’m glad that this bipartisan legislation to provide clearer guidance to businesses that establish and operate ESOPs was signed into law.”

“The Retire Through Ownership Act is about protecting the retirement security of millions of Americans,”said James Bonham, President and CEO of The ESOP Association. “Senators Kaine and Marshall brought strong bipartisan leadership to a challenge that has hindered employee ownership for decades. Their efforts will give employee owners greater confidence in how their shares are valued and business owners a clearer path toward ESOP transitions. We applaud Senator Kaine for helping deliver this commonsense solution.”

The Retire through Ownership Act amends the Employee Retirement Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) to clarify that companies operating in good faith can use long-standing Internal Revenue Service (IRS) guidance on valuing shares to determine “adequate consideration” in an ESOP transaction, thus eliminating a source of uncertainty for companies establishing or operating ESOPs.
