title: Padilla, Durbin, Whitehouse Demand DOJ Commit to Not Seize Ballots, Voting Equipment During Midterm Elections
text:
Following new DOJ demand to block certain ballots in California, Senators urge DOJ to follow the law and reaffirm its longstanding election non-interference policy ahead of 2026 midterm elections, warning that “DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration with jurisdiction over federal elections, Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the Senate Subcommittee on Federal Courts, Oversight, Agency Action and Federal Rights, demanded that Attorney General Todd Blanche confirm that the Department of Justice (DOJ) will not seize ballots, voting machines, or other election materials in connection with the 2026 midterm elections. Padilla recently secured a commitment under oath from Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel that the FBI would not interfere in this year’s midterms, specifically that it would not seize ballots or voting equipment before an election is certified. The letter was sent the same day that the DOJ sued California to block the state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots less than three weeks before the midterm elections.

In the letter to Blanche, the Senators pressed him to reaffirm DOJ’s longstanding policy of election non-interference and commit that it will not pursue any effort to seize ballots or other election materials until all elections have concluded and election results have been certified, given DOJ leadership’s lack of response to earlier inquiries and troubling actions and statements by DOJ when it comes to elections. The letter follows the unprecedented demand by DOJ to the California Secretary of State and Los Angeles County to withhold and segregate ballots from individuals on a list on a USB thumb drive provided by DOJ less than three weeks before Election Day.

“Mail and absentee ballots have already been sent out to millions of voters, and early voting has begun in several states,” wrote the Senators. “However, the Department has failed to affirm its election non-interference policy against a backdrop of the recent weakening of DOJ policies, upheaval in the agency’s workforce, DOJ’s seizure of 2020 election materials in Georgia and Arizona, personal calls by President Trump directly to DOJ attorneys to influence election-related investigations in California and elsewhere, as well as unprecedented partisan political activity by DOJ leadership. A clear and immediate response from the Department is necessary.”

The Senators highlighted several reasons to be concerned about the Trump Administration’s election interference efforts, including DOJ’s quiet removal of the most recent version of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual from its website without explanation. They further outlined DOJ’s lack of explanation when pressed for answers and reiterated the unlawfulness of any DOJ effort to interfere in the 2026 midterm elections.

“Removing ballots from the officials legally charged with maintaining their custody could prevent election officials from satisfying statutory deadlines, interfere with recount or contest procedures, and even prevent lawful votes from being counted or an election from being certified,” continued the Senators. “Any DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable.”

The Senators reiterated the importance of the DOJ reaffirming its election non-interference policy with less than 20 days until Election Day.

“The 2026 midterm elections have begun. We urge you to immediately reaffirm that the Department will forgo any actions that would interfere with the lawful administration of the 2026 elections, including the seizure of ballots, election materials, or election equipment prior to the certification of the 2026 midterm elections,” the Senators concluded.

As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee and California’s former Secretary of State and chief election officer, Padilla has fought relentlessly to protect our elections and strengthen voting rights.

Last month, Padilla introduced the Freedom from Intimidation in Elections Act, legislation to protect voters and election workers from intimidation and threats of violence at polling places.

Padilla also led the congressional response to the bombshell whistleblower report that DHS agents violated state laws as part of the “Unlawful Voter Initiative” and called for an immediate investigation into the agency’s misconduct. He also urged California’s Attorney General to investigate the effects these actions could have on Californians.

Also last month, Padilla convened some of the country’s top labor leaders to discuss how to strengthen our democracy and mobilize against election interference.

In August, he led 27 of his Senate colleagues in demanding the Trump Administration stop its illegal voter roll purges before Election Day.

Padilla also joined Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in launching the first-ever Senate Election Observer Program to protect the 2026 midterms and maintain election integrity nationwide and serves as part of the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force. This week, Padilla announced that more than 100 Senate Democratic staff have been recruited and trained as official congressional election observers to be deployed to polling sites across nine states.

In June, Padilla joined his colleagues in introducing the Protect Our Polls Act to protect the integrity of American elections from federal interference by armed military or federal law enforcement.

Full letter is available here or below:

Dear Attorney General Blanche:

As Election Day draws nearer, we urge the Department of Justice (DOJ or Department) to reaffirm its longstanding election non-interference policy and rule out any attempt to seize ballots or any other election materials or equipment before voting, counting, and/or certification are complete. This confirmation is necessary because Department leaders have been sending conflicting public signals.

Make no doubt, the 2026 midterm elections are well underway. Mail and absentee ballots have already been sent out to millions of voters, and early voting has begun in several states. However, the Department has failed to affirm its election non-interference policy against a backdrop of the recent weakening of DOJ policies. A clear and immediate response from the Department is necessary.

Recent Statements Regarding the Department’s Election Non-Interference Policy

In response to a question during a September 15 public hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel did confirm under oath that the FBI would comply with the Department’s Justice Manual and not seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material prior to certification of an election, matching the commitment by General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff that the U.S. Armed Forces would not interfere with the upcoming election. However, the FBI Director reports to the Attorney General, so his commitment is contingent on your own.

On September 1, Senator Slotkin wrote to you and Director Patel seeking answers to a number of questions, including whether DOJ or the FBI would send armed federal agents to the polls or unlawfully seize election materials of any kind during an active election. To date, neither you nor Director Patel have responded to those letters. Meanwhile, General Caine did respond to a similar letter and reaffirmed the “non-partisan” U.S. Armed Forces’ “steadfast commitment to constitutional principles” and confirmed that the military had “no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections” and “[n]o plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”

On June 8, 2026, Senators Padilla, Durbin, Whitehouse, and 21 Senators wrote to you regarding the Department’s unexplained removal from its website of the most recent version of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual (Election Crimes Manual) that has been in place for decades to prevent the Department from interfering or appearing to interfere in elections. The Department’s August 13 response states that the manual “needs revising and updating” but provided no further explanation, and an updated version has yet to be made available to the public.

DOJ Election Interference is Illegal

The law is clear: neither the Department nor any other federal agency has the authority to disrupt the administration of an election, including by seizing ballots or other election materials in a manner that prevents state and local officials from carrying out their lawful duties.

The U.S. Constitution gives primary authority over elections to the states and Congress, not the Executive Branch, and federal law reinforces these constitutional provisions. The Civil Rights Act of 1960 requires election officers to “retain and preserve” covered election records for 22 months following a federal election. If a federal agency seeks access to election materials, the law requires an appropriate written demand, after which covered records are to be made available for federal “inspection, reproduction, and copying” at the principal office of their custodian. Even this authority is limited, as shown by DOJ’s failure to compel Republican and Democratic-led states alike to hand over unredacted voter data for the Trump Administration to create a national voter file and pressure states to purge voters under the guise of list maintenance.

Federal law enforcement must also respect detailed state laws governing custody of ballots and voting equipment. Maintaining an unbroken chain of custody ensures that the ballots ultimately counted are the ballots American voters actually cast. Removing ballots from the officials legally charged with maintaining their custody could prevent election officials from satisfying statutory deadlines, interfere with recount or contest procedures, and even prevent lawful votes from being counted or an election from being certified. Any DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable.

The Justice Manual and the Election Crimes Manual

The same commitment made by General Caine and Director Patel should represent the position of the Trump Administration. The Department’s Justice Manual unequivocally recognizes the constitutional requirement that “the States—not the federal government—are responsible for administering elections.” While DOJ’s “non-interference policy” was incorporated into the Justice Manual in 2022, it has been in effect through the DOJ Election Crimes Branch for decades. This enduring bipartisan policy reflects the fundamental principle that DOJ and other law enforcement personnel should not interfere with the will of the American people. The Justice Manual’s “non-interference policy” states that DOJ “should generally avoid interfering or appearing to interfere with election administration, tabulation, validation, or certification.” It further provides that DOJ “should not engage in overt criminal investigative measures in matters involving alleged ballot fraud until the election in question has been concluded, its results certified, and all recounts and election contests concluded.” However, the removal of the Election Crimes Manual from the DOJ website remains of special concern because it contains even more explicit instructions against actions that “may deprive state election and judicial authorities of critical materials needed to resolve election disputes, conduct recounts, and certify ultimate winners.” In addition to avoiding seizures, the Election Crimes Manual further confirms the DOJ policy not to conduct overt investigations until after the outcome of the election has been certified.

Adding to the concern, pending revisions to the Justice Manual are creating new uncertainty. The requirement that prosecutors and agents consult with the Public Integrity Section before opening an election-crime matter or undertaking any potentially overt investigative steps—including issuing grand jury subpoenas and executing search warrants—has been “suspended while revisions are ongoing.” Given that it is too late for revisions ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, DOJ should restore this part of its election policy immediately. Failure to maintain a strong, explicit election non-interference policy exposes DOJ prosecutors to political pressure to interfere in elections at the request of the President or other Administration leaders, political parties, candidates, and other influences.

The Department Must Reaffirm Its Election Non-Interference Policy

The 2026 midterm elections have begun. We urge you to immediately reaffirm that the Department will forgo any actions that would interfere with the lawful administration of the 2026 elections, including the seizure of ballots, election materials, or election equipment prior to the certification of the 2026 midterm elections.

In addition to this immediate public commitment, we request that you provide written responses to the following questions by October 29, 2026:

1) Will you commit that DOJ, the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service, and other Department components will not attempt to seize or otherwise remove ballots, voting equipment, or other election materials from the lawful custody of state or local election officials while those materials are necessary for voting, counting, canvassing, recounting, auditing, election contests, or certification?

a) Will you commit not to approve or otherwise facilitate any attempts by any other federal law enforcement agency, including components of the Department of Homeland Security, to take similar actions?

2) Does DOJ continue to adhere to the guidance contained in the eighth edition of the Election Crimes Manual that election-related documents generally should not be removed from local election administrators before certification and expiration of the applicable election-contest period, and that election officials should not be deprived of documents necessary to tally or recount ballots or certify election results?

a) What provisions of the Election Crimes Manual require “revising and updating” as stated in the Department’s previous response letter? Does the Election Crimes Manual remain the policy of the Department, and, if not, has the Department rescinded, superseded, amended, or otherwise withdrawn the eighth edition?

b) If revisions are underway, provide the current draft, identify the officials responsible for those revisions, and state when the revised guidance will be made public.

3) Does DOJ continue to adhere fully to Justice Manual §§ 9-85.300 and 9-85.500, including the prohibition that “[f]ederal prosecutors and agents may never select the timing of any action, including investigative steps, criminal charges, or statements, for the purpose of affecting any election, or for the purpose of giving an advantage or disadvantage to any candidate or political party”?

4) Given that the Justice Manual currently states that the election-crimes consultation requirement in § 9-85.210 is suspended while revisions are underway, what review and approval procedures currently govern applications for search warrants, subpoenas, or other overt investigative measures involving ballots, voting equipment, election officials, or other election materials during an active election?

a) When will the revisions of the manual be complete and available to the public?

5) Has the Department, the FBI, any United States Attorney’s Office, or any other Department component developed, discussed, requested, sought judicial authorization for, or approved any plan to seize ballots, voting machines, tabulation equipment, or other election materials relating to the 2026 federal elections before completion of the applicable counting, recounting, canvassing, contest, and certification processes?

a) If so, provide all applicable policies, legal analyses, directives, memoranda, and approval procedures concerning such actions.

Thank you for your prompt response.

###

title: Padilla, Hirono, Senate Colleagues Press Trump Administration on Illegal Reallocation of Funding for Minority Serving Institutions
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), along with U.S. Representatives Grace Meng (D-N.Y.-06), Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.-13), and Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.-09), pressed U.S. Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon on the Administration’s illegal decision to redirect funding from Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) to other institutions.

In their letter to Secretary McMahon, the lawmakers emphasized that, while increasing funding for those institutions is important, the additional investments cannot come at the expense of MSIs that serve millions of students nationwide. The lawmakers also reiterated the illegal nature of the decision to redirect funding that was statutorily authorized in specific amounts for specific purposes.

“This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so,” wrote the lawmakers.

There are currently more than 800 federally recognized MSIs which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs), and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). These MSIs serve more than five million students collectively and have been receiving Congressionally directed federal support for more than 30 years.

In December 2019, the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act) was signed into law, permanently authorizing $255 million in mandatory funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs), and MSIs.

“The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year,” continued the lawmakers.

The lawmakers outlined how the mandatory funding from the FUTURE Act leaves no room for the Trump Administration to redirect funding from MSIs to any other programs or purpose.

“To be clear, mandatory funding for [these institutions]—as provided by the FUTURE Act—cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds,” wrote the lawmakers.

The lawmakers reiterated the importance of supporting all institutions supporting minority students—including HBCUs and TCCUs.

“ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs,” the lawmakers concluded. “Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education.”

In addition to Padilla, Hirono, Sanders, Murray, Baldwin, Durbin, and Luján, the letter was cosigned by Senators Chris Coons (D-Del.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mark Warner (D-Va.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), and Michael Bennet (D-Colo.).

In addition to Representatives Meng, Espaillat, and Clarke, the letter was also cosigned by Representatives Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.-AL), Mark Takano (D-Calif.-39), Danny Davis (D-Ill.-07), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.-08), Judy Chu (D-Calif.-28), Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (D-Ill.-07), Dina Titus (D-Nev.-01), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.-20), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.-01), Jill Tokuda (D-Hawaii-02), Robin Kelly (D-Ill.-02), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.-34), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.-10), Emily Randall (D-Wash.-06), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas-30), Joaquin Castro (D-Texas-30), Ed Case (D-Hawaii-01), J. Correa (D-Calif.-46), Susan Bonamici (D-Ore.-01), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas-29), Robert Menendez (D-N.J.-08), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.-36), Mike Thompson (D-Calif.-04), Derek Tran (D-Calif.-45), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.-12), George Whitesides (D-Calif.-27), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.-24), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.-04), Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.-38), Chellie Pingree (D-Maine-01), Darren Soto (D-Fla.-09), Juan Vargas (D-Calif.-52), Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.-03), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.-07), Jennifer McClellan (D-Va.-04), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.-15), and Robert Garcia (D-Calif.-42).

As chair of the Senate HSI Caucus, Padilla has led the fight opposing the Trump Administration’s attacks on MSIs. In February, Padilla demanded the Department of Education immediately reverse its decision to deem MSIs unconstitutional and cut off federal funding. Last year, Padilla also led multiple letters opposing the Department of Education’s decision to rescind $350 million in funding from MSIs, including a letter with members from the California delegation about the impact directly on California.

Full text of the letter is available here and below:

Dear Secretary McMahon:

Your recent decision to reallocate mandatory funding for Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) in Fiscal Year 2025 and Fiscal Year 2026 is an illegal violation of Congress’ spending authority under the Constitution. No court has found these programs that Congress has funded to be unconstitutional, and the administration’s mere belief that they are does not give it the necessary authority to spend those funds for any other purpose or program.

Many of us previously sent you a letter urging you to allocate Title III and Title V discretionary and mandatory funds as Congress directed to the more than 800 federally-recognized MSIs, which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs), and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). Combined, these institutions enroll more than 5 million students in rural and urban communities in states across the country. The Higher Education Act created the statutory framework for grants to these institutions, and has been in place for more than 30 years.

In December 2019, Congress passed and President Trump signed into law the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act), permanently authorizing $255 million in grant funds for MSIs, Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), and Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs). The funds are allocated across seven grant programs, each with a designated funding amount beginning in Fiscal Year 2020 and continuing thereafter. This authorization was an extension of prior mandatory appropriations that began in Fiscal Year 2008 and then expired.

Reallocation of Funds Designated for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs

On September 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education (ED) announced it would reallocate FY25 and FY26 mandatory funds Congress had specifically allocated for MSIs to HBCUs and TCCUs. In the news release announcing this illegal action, ED announced a “significant, one-time investment of more than $174 million in additional funding to strengthen” HBCUs, and “a one-time award of more than $61 million in additional funding” for TCCUs.

While we strongly support additional funding for HBCUs and TCCUs, increasing funding for some institutions should not come at the expense of others. Furthermore, as previously stated, ED has no authority to redirect mandatory funding for MSIs—in this case, for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs—for other purposes or programs. In fact, the entire basis for invalidating and redistributing these funds seems to be a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion from December 2, 2025, which wrongly determined that both discretionary and mandatory grants for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs, and discretionary grants for PBIs, were unconstitutional—without any judicial decision squarely dictating such a conclusion, and lacking any statutory authority to spend mandatory funds for anything other than their required purposes.

Shortly thereafter, ED stated that it was evaluating the full impact of the OLC opinion on the programs. ED then took several actions which made clear that it would not fund the programs, including by not allowing institutions to reapply for eligibility for the programs, and not including them in the eligibility matrix for Title III and Title V funds.

Reallocation of Funds Designated for PBIs

Even by its own baseless standards, the administration determined in the December 2025 OLC memo that the race-based provisions of this program could be severed and stated that ED could continue to provide these competitive grants for the authorized uses in this program, regardless of whether the grant recipient is a PBI. However, rather than adhering to the statute authorizing this grant program—or even OLC’s own wrongful guidance—ED allocated these funds to grantees under a different program with a separate purpose.

Unnecessarily Accelerating Obligation of FY26 Mandatory Funds

On top of all of this, the Trump administration took the completely unnecessary step of obligating FY26 mandatory funding for these programs a full year before it has historically been done, and a full year before the funds expire. These funds are available for two years—funds becoming available in FY26 are available for obligation through FY27. If ED only continued to award funds on the schedule it has historically, FY26 funds would be awarded this time next year.

The administration has claimed it reallocated these funds so they did not lapse and go to waste. While the Trump administration is perfectly willing to let appropriated funds lapse in other cases, including most recently with international education and migrant and seasonal farmworker education programs, half of the MSI funds it reallocated were not going to lapse this year. Even if one were to take the administration’s misguided legal view of these programs at face value, for half of these funds the choice was not between reallocating funding or having the funds lapse. The administration has said repeatedly it wants to work with Congress on solutions to address the legal status of these programs. While we fundamentally disagree with the administration’s view, the administration could have simply continued to administer these funds on the timeline it always has—which means obligating the FY26 funds next September—and waited to see if Congress enacted a solution or a court ruled on the constitutionality of these programs over the course of the next year. In fact, Congress did enact a temporary and albeit imperfect fix in the FY26 Consolidated Appropriations Act when faced with the fact that the Trump administration would otherwise let discretionary funding for MSIs lapse.

This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so. If President Trump and this administration were serious about investing in all of these institutions—as each of us is—the president would push for more funds for them instead of seeking to slash education programs while supersizing the Pentagon’s budget.

The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year. To be clear, mandatory funding for HBCUs, TCCUs, HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs—as provided by the FUTURE Act—cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds.

The Executive Branch’s improper use of mandatory funds plainly violates Article I of the Constitution, which delegates the spending power to Congress. By failing to follow the law and fund programs as Congress directed, and to instead allocate funds for other unauthorized purposes, the Executive Branch has clearly exceeded its Constitutional authority. ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs. Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education. We would welcome the opportunity to work on a bipartisan basis with the administration to increase investments in MSIs, HBCUs, and TCCUs.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. We look forward to your response.

Sincerely,

###

title: Senators Peters, Slotkin Announce More Than $880,000 in Federal Support for Mid-Michigan Fire Departments
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Senators Gary Peters (MI) and Elissa Slotkin (MI) announced that local fire departments across Mid-Michigan will receive $884,836 in federal funding. The funding comes from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Assistance to Firefighters Grants (AFG) and Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response (SAFER) grant programs. In 2024, Peters led the charge to extend these federal grant programs that help local fire departments address staffing needs, purchase equipment, develop fire training and education programs, and improve emergency medical services.

“Every single day, firefighters and first responders in Michigan and across the nation put their lives on the line to protect their communities. It’s vital that each department has the resources they need to do their job safely,” said Senator Peters. “I was proud to work in a bipartisan way to extend essential grant programs that support this work, and I'm pleased to announce this federal funding for departments across Mid-Michigan to ensure they have the proper equipment and staffing levels necessary to keep our communities safe.”

“As elected officials, it is our responsibility to ensure that Michigan’s firefighters and front-line responders are protected. I join my colleague, Senator Gary Peters, in welcoming the more than $880,000 in federal support for mid-Michigan firefighters,” said Senator Slotkin. “We’ve worked in a bipartisan way to secure this essential grant funding. And now, these dollars will be used to address staffing needs, enhance safety training, and provide much-needed equipment for the brave folks who put their lives on the line every day to keep Michiganders safe.”

Below are descriptions of each project:

Northeast Ingham Emergency Service: The Northeast Ingham Emergency Service will receive $592,571 to purchase 60 Scott SCBA air packs for use in firefighting and hazardous material incidents.

City of Charlotte: The City of Charlotte has been awarded $223,216 to purchase new fire hose, nozzles, fittings, and other related water-supply equipment.

City of St. Johns: The City of St. Johns will receive $52,380 from the AFG program to provide EMT Training and compensation for department members.

Meridian Township Fire Department: The Meridian Township Fire Department will receive $16,669 to acquire structural Firefighting Personal Protective gear for new employees. This gear is essential during high risk IDLH Atmospheres such as entering a building on fire that is full of smoke and heat to extinguish a fire.

“The City of Charlotte is extremely grateful for Senator Peters’ support in helping make this grant possible,” said Tyger Fullerton, Fire Chief of the City of Charlotte Fire Department. “This funding is a significant investment in the safety and capabilities of our firefighters, allowing Charlotte, Benton Township, and Vermontville Township to replace and upgrade critical fire hose, nozzles, and water-supply equipment that our firefighters depend on when it is needed most.”

“We are very appreciative for the work that Senator Peters and Senator Slotkin did to ensure that the Assistance to Firefighters Grant program was continued and their advocating for our department to be able to be a recipient,” said Kevin Douglas, Fire Chief of the St. John’s Fire Department. “This training will help to improve the level of service we are able to provide.”

“This funding will allow us to purchase personal protective gear that is essential when entering a burning house to extinguish a fire," said Meridian Township Fire Chief Michael Hamel. “We’re thankful for Senator Peters’ support for this grant funding, which will help keep our firefighters safe performing fire rescues in high-risk situations.”

Peters’ Fire Grants and Safety Act reauthorized the SAFER and AFG programs, as well as the United States Fire Administration (USFA), until 2028. It reauthorized $95 million for USFA, a nearly $20 million increase from current authorized levels, and extended the authorization for the SAFER and AFG programs. Fire departments use these federal programs to recruit and retain additional personnel, as well as buy up-to-date vehicles and equipment such as breathing air compressors, hoses, nozzles, and more. Fire stations also use the programs to fund safety training and technical rescue training, as well as health screenings for firefighters. Peters is co-chair, and Slotkin is a member of the Congressional Fire Services Caucus, which works to advance initiatives which support first responders.

More information about these grants can be found here.

title: Reed Helps Lead Bipartisan Push for DOD IG Investigation into Ukraine’s Starlink Restrictions
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Without warning, someone gave the order this past week to suddenly restrict Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, which undermined Ukraine’s ability to counter Russian-launched explosive drones and endangered U.S. military and diplomatic personnel in the region. According to Elon Musk, Starshield is owned and controlled by the U.S. government and operational limits rest with the military and president.

Now, U.S. Senator Jack Reed (D-RI) and a bipartisan group of U.S. Senators are demanding the U.S. Department of Defense’s (DOD) Inspector General (IG) open an investigation into the matter.

Reed, the Ranking Member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, joined Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Susan Collins (R-ME), John Cornyn (R-TX), Chris Coons (D-DE), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) in sending a letter to the Department of Defense’s Inspector General, Platte Moring III, calling for an investigation into the disruption of the U.S.-maintained Starshield systems for Ukrainian partners.

In the letter, the Senators highlight how the disruptions to these critical systems put U.S. diplomatic, military and security personnel in danger and diminished Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. They urge the Inspector General to immediately launch an investigation and determine whether any U.S. officials approved of or had advance knowledge of the disruptions in service. The Senators also request that the Inspector General investigate whether U.S. personnel were unable to reach shelter during Russian attacks that occurred during these disruptions and if immediate corrective measures are being implemented to ensure the safety of American personnel.

“We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities. We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances,” wrote the nine Senators.

“To use Starshield and Starlink as intended, Ukraine needs access to unlimited speeds, which was its service arrangement prior to this reported restriction. We understand that at least some relevant services are provided through contractual arrangements administered by the U.S. Space Force. Any restrictions on these capabilities, particularly without advance notification, raise serious questions about the Department of Defense’s contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services,” continued the Senators.

“The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas. Disruptions to critical intelligence-sharing, threat-warning, or communications capabilities in an active war zone can have life-threatening consequences. The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability,” concluded the Senators.

Full text of the letter follows:

Dear Mr. Moring:

We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical U.S.-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks. We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities. We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances.

According to reports, speed restrictions imposed on SpaceX’s Starlink terminals between October 12 and 14, 2026, disrupted critical communications capabilities supporting Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles and fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft. Ukrainian military testing on October 14 reportedly identified restrictions at speeds exceeding approximately 63 miles per hour, while SpaceX reportedly acknowledged a service restriction at 100 miles per hour. These restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure.

Separately, we are deeply concerned by reports of disruptions or “glitches” affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine. We understand that American personnel experienced serious difficulties reaching safety during Russian air raids. The precise cause of these incidents, including whether they resulted from technical failures, interruptions in intelligence sharing, changes in U.S. government policy, or other factors, remains unclear. Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation.

Starlink and Starshield capabilities are important components of Ukraine’s military communications infrastructure, supporting command and control, unmanned systems, and operational coordination. To use Starshield and Starlink as intended, Ukraine needs access to unlimited speeds, which was its service arrangement prior to this reported restriction. We understand that at least some relevant services are provided through contractual arrangements administered by the U.S. Space Force. Any restrictions on these capabilities, particularly without advance notification, raise serious questions about the Department of Defense’s contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services.

We therefore request that your office immediately investigate:

Whether disruptions to intelligence sharing, threat warnings, or other U.S.-supported capabilities contributed to incidents in which American diplomatic, military, or security personnel were unable to reach shelter during Russian attacks;

Whether any Department of Defense or other U.S. government officials directed, authorized, approved, or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine;

Whether the reported intelligence-sharing disruptions and Starlink restrictions were connected, and whether either resulted from deliberate policy decisions, technical failures, contractor actions, or other causes;

Whether affected U.S. personnel, the U.S. Embassy in Kyiv, and Ukrainian authorities received adequate advance notification of any changes that could compromise their safety or defensive operations;

Whether SpaceX independently imposed restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services, whether those restrictions complied with applicable U.S. government contracts, and what steps the Department of Defense took in response; and

What immediate corrective measures are being implemented to ensure that American personnel receive reliable threat warnings and that essential communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities are maintained.

We also request that you ensure relevant agencies and parties preserve relevant communications, contractual records, technical directives, and correspondence concerning these incidents, including communications between the Department of Defense, SpaceX, and other relevant agencies.

The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas. Disruptions to critical intelligence-sharing, threat-warning, or communications capabilities in an active war zone can have life-threatening consequences. The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability.

We urge your office to initiate an immediate investigation and provide written confirmation of its status, together with an initial briefing, no later than November 1, 2026.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this urgent matter.

Sincerely,

title: Reed, Whitehouse Press Trump DOJ for Allowing Sale of Handguns to Teenagers
text:
WASHINGTON, DC -- U.S. Senators Jack Reed (D-RI) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) today joined Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT), and several colleagues in sending a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers on the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) decision to break with decades of precedent and unilaterally refuse to enforce a prohibition against the sale of handguns to people under the age of 21.

Congress banned firearm dealers from selling handguns and handgun ammunition to people under the age of 21 in the Gun Control Act of 1968. But the Trump Justice Department concluded that the federal government may not impose criminal penalties on federally licensed dealers for selling handguns to 18 to 21 year olds.

In their letter, the twenty U.S. Senators highlighted the enormous risks to public safety of placing handguns in the hands of teenagers: “The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.”

The Senators laid out the decades-long, bipartisan consensus on banning gun dealers from selling firearms to teenagers: “Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that ‘it shall be unlawful’ for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.”

The Senators argued Blanche’s decision is another authoritarian power grab over the judicial branch and Congress: “The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has ‘deeply divided members of the federal bench.’ Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.”

The Senators concluded by requesting Blanche provide the following information on the authority and research supporting his decision:

1. A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

2. All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

3. Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

4. A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

In addition to Reed, Whitehouse, and Murphy, the letter is signed by U.S. Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Chris Coons (D-DE), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ed Markey (D-MA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Peter Welch (D-VT).

Full text of the letter follows:

Dear Attorney General Blanche:

We write regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (the Department) decision to cease enforcement of longstanding federal restrictions on the sale of handguns to individuals under the age of 21 by federally licensed firearms dealers (FFLs). This significant change in federal enforcement policy raises serious questions about the Department’s legal justification, and we request information regarding the analysis underlying its decision.

On September 18, 2026, the Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published a legal opinion concluding that 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1)—the federal prohibition on FFLs selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds—violate the Second Amendment, and that federal prosecutors may no longer prosecute FFLs that sell handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds who are not otherwise prohibited from gun possession.[1] Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that “it shall be unlawful” for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21.[2] Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.

The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has “deeply divided members of the federal bench.” Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.

The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.

The Department’s decision to unilaterally cease enforcement of this provision of law raises serious questions and concerns. Thus, we request the Department provide:

1. A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

2. All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

3. Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

4. A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

Please provide the requested information and documents by November 16, 2026.

Sincerely,

title: Ricketts, Secretary Wright Tour Elk Creek Critical Minerals Project, Discuss Energy Independence at Roundtable
text:
OMAHA, NE – U.S. Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NE) toured NioCorp’s Elk Creek Critical Minerals project on Wednesday. U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) Chairman John Jovanovic, Governor Jim Pillen, U.S. Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE), and U.S. Representative Adrian Smith (R-NE-03) also attended the event.

The Elk Creek Critical Minerals project will return critical mineral mining and processing back to the United States. Critical minerals and rare earth elements necessary for armored vehicles, fighter jets, and naval ships will be made in Nebraska. This strengthens Nebraska’s role in defense and national security.

“Nebraskans play a critical role in strengthening our national security. Advanced minerals needed for key sectors like defense and energy will be made in Elk Creek. The partnership between this community, NioCorp, and EXIM is a model for how we can continue to bolster domestic supply chains,” said Ricketts.

Following the tour, Ricketts joined a roundtable hosted by the Nebraska Farm Bureau. The discussion focused on state ag updates and the important role Nebraska plays in biofuel production and American energy independence. This includes passing year-round E15.

Secretary Wright, Senator Fischer (R-NE), Representative Smith, and U.S. Representative Don Bacon (NE-02) also participated.

“Nebraska is an agriculture state and a biofuels state. We have the crops and the opportunity to help lead the nation in biofuel production. Biofuels provide much needed relief at the pump for consumers. They are also a key component in protecting our national security and American energy independence. Thank you to Secretary Wright and all who participated in this discussion on how Nebraska is leading the way on the world stage,” said Ricketts.

Senator Pete Ricketts supports efforts to pass a permanent solution for the year-round sale of E15. President Donald Trump also supports year-round E15 and has urged Congress to act.

title: Rosen, Lankford Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Expand Child Care Options on Military Bases
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – This week, U.S. Senators Jacky Rosen (D-NV) and James Lankford (R-OK) introduced a bipartisan bill to expand access to child care on military bases for servicemembers and their families. The Best Practices for Military Child Care Homes Act would direct the Department of Defense (DoD) to develop a best practices guide for military families hoping to establish a home-based certified child care center. Military families continue to experience child care shortages across installations. Family Child Care (FCC) homes are an important tool for expanding available child care capacity at installations and increasing opportunities for military spouse employment, but prospective providers often face unnecessary barriers when attempting to start an FCC home program. This bill would streamline the process and improve access to information, making it easier to establish and operate on-base child care centers to meet the growing demand for reliable, flexible child care.

“Our servicemembers and their families sacrifice so much to protect our freedoms. That’s why it’s so important that we make sure they have access to the community and support they need while living on base,” said Senator Rosen. “This bipartisan bill will help us close the gaps in child care services that we are seeing across the country for servicemembers and their families, while opening the door for new providers to bring much-needed services for our military families.”

“Military families shouldn’t have to navigate unnecessary hurdles to find reliable child care. Our servicemembers need to know their children are cared for so they can focus on their mission, and military spouses should have opportunities to support other families while building their own careers,” said Senator Lankford. “This bipartisan bill will help make it easier to establish child care homes on base, expand options for military families, and strengthen military readiness.”

As a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senator Rosen continues to be an advocate for Nevada’s servicemembers and their families. Recently, she introduced the bipartisan Sergeant Dave Crete FORGOTTEN Veterans Act, which would require the Department of Defense to join the Department of Energy in identifying all servicemembers and veterans who worked at locations where radiation and toxic exposure occurred and provide them with the same presumption of exposure, allowing such veterans to better access the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) healthcare and benefits they have earned. Senator Rosen helped advance this year’s bipartisan national defense bill out of committee, which includes 50 provisions she championed, including support for care centers, military construction projects, and support facilities at Nevada’s military installations. In July, she co-led the Honor Gold Star Families Act to increase the gratuity payments for families of fallen service members.
