title: Hawai‘i Congressional Delegation Presses Trump Administration on Honolulu Immigration Court's Shift to In-Person Hearings
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Brian Schatz (D-Hawai‘i) and Mazie K. Hirono (D-Hawai‘i) and U.S. Representatives Ed Case (D-Hawai‘i) and Jill Tokuda (D-Hawai‘i) wrote to U.S. Department of Justice Executive Office for Immigration Review Acting Director Sirce Owen regarding the Honolulu Immigration Court’s recent and dramatic shift away from video appearances and toward in-person hearings for immigrants fighting deportation. The delegation highlighted how the shift is adding costs and burdens for immigrants throughout the state and requested answers on what steps the Trump administration will take to ensure that residents of the neighbor islands who cannot afford inter-island travel are not ordered removed.

“Honolulu is the only immigration court in Hawai‘i, serving respondents who reside on Maui, Kaua‘i, Hawai‘i Island, Moloka‘i and Lana?i. Accessing the court in Honolulu requires these residents to travel by air. For years, to overcome that obstacle, the court has conducted proceedings by video conference,” the delegation wrote. “That established practice has now been abruptly reversed. According to a recent analysis of EOIR’s own case data, 87 percent of neighbor island respondents with proceedings during July and August 2026 were required to travel to O‘ahu for at least one in-person hearing. During the same period in 2025, just under one-third were required to travel to O‘ahu.”

The delegation continued, “The effect on neighbor island families is stark. A single hearing can now entail inter-island airfare, an overnight hotel room on O‘ahu, lost work hours, and unexpected childcare costs—expenses that low-income respondents cannot afford. And when respondents cannot make these appearances, the consequence can be an in absentia order of removal, regardless of the merits of their pending applications for asylum or petitions to adjust their status. Hawai‘i practitioners report that an increasing share of their clients—people who have lived in Hawaii for years, worked, paid taxes and raised families—are forced to waive viable claims rather than facing these costs.”

The full text of the letter is below and available here.

Dear Acting Director Owen:

We write to express our concern regarding the Honolulu Immigration Court’s dramatic shift away from video appearances by respondents and toward in-person hearings. That shift has its most striking impact on Hawai‘i’s neighbor island residents, who now face the choice between flying to O‘ahu at their own expense or risking an in absentia order of removal.

Honolulu is the only immigration court in Hawai‘i, serving respondents who reside on Maui, Kaua‘i, Hawai‘i Island, Moloka‘i and Lana?i. Accessing the court in Honolulu requires these residents to travel by air. For years, to overcome that obstacle, the court has conducted proceedings by video conference. This practice is permitted under the Immigration and Nationality Act and consistent with the longstanding practice of the Executive Office for Immigration Review (“EOIR”). In November 2020, EOIR itself recognized the benefits of video teleconferencing for its immigration courts and respondents. In 2022, EOIR Director’s Memorandum 22-07 directed immigration judges to accommodate a party’s request for a remote appearance where appropriate and practicable.

That established practice has now been abruptly reversed. According to a recent analysis of EOIR’s own case data, 87 percent of neighbor island respondents with proceedings during July and August 2026 were required to travel to O‘ahu for at least one in-person hearing. During the same period in 2025, just under one-third were required to travel to O‘ahu. For respondents with out-of-state addresses, the percentage requiring an in-person appearance jumped to 82 percent, from 14 percent. In August 2026, 176 of the court’s 249 hearings were in-person, compared to just 38 of 120 hearings in August 2025. Approximately 90 percent of hearings scheduled for October 2026 are marked as in-person, compared to 22 percent in October 2025. Practitioners report that respondents are now being ordered to appear in-person even when their counsel is authorized to appear by video.

The effect on neighbor island families is stark. A single hearing can now entail inter-island airfare, an overnight hotel room on O‘ahu, lost work hours, and unexpected childcare costs—expenses that low-income respondents cannot afford. And when respondents cannot make these appearances, the consequence can be an in absentia order of removal, regardless of the merits of their pending applications for asylum or petitions to adjust their status. Hawai‘i practitioners report that an increasing share of their clients—people who have lived in Hawai‘i for years, worked, paid taxes and raised families—are forced to waive viable claims rather than facing these costs.

We understand that in March 2025, EOIR rescinded Director’s Memorandum 22-07. EOIR now asserts that the Director lacks authority to direct immigration judges how they should rule on motions for video hearings. If it is accurate that the decisional independence of immigration judges bars the Director from instructing them to grant such motions, it equally bars EOIR leadership from encouraging their denial.

We request written answers to the following from you by November 5, 2026 to help us understand what has changed and why:

All written guidance, training materials, communications, or informal direction given to immigration judges assigned to the Honolulu Immigration Court since March 14, 2025, regarding video or telephonic appearances by respondents, counsel or witnesses, motions to change venue, or the scheduling of in-person hearings, together with a description of any performance measures or expectations that could affect a judge’s decision to require an in-person appearance.

Has EOIR or the Office of the Chief Immigration Judge implemented any policy, formal or informal, to discourage or limit video appearances at the Honolulu Immigration Court or nationwide? If not, please explain what accounts for the changes described above.

For the Honolulu Immigration Court, for the period June 1 through September 30, 2026, and for the same period in 2025: (a) the number of hearings that were held in-person and by video; (b) the number of motions made by a respondent, counsel, or witness to appear by video, and the number that were granted and denied; (c) the number of motions to change venue that were filed and the number that were granted and denied; and (d) the number of in absentia removal orders that were entered. For both the 2025 and 2026 period, please further break out each of those figures by the county in which the respondent resides (Honolulu, Maui, Kaua‘i or Hawai‘i), by whether the respondent resides out of state, and by whether the respondent is detained or not detained.

The steps EOIR will take to ensure that residents of the neighbor islands who cannot afford inter-island travel are not ordered removed, including whether EOIR will (a) implement a presumption, consistent with the approach of former Director’s Memorandum 22-07, that respondents and counsel who can only reach the court by air may appear by video unless there is a specific finding that an in-person hearing is necessary; (b) set up video hearings or hearing days at least once per month on Maui, Kaua‘i and Hawai‘i Island; and (c) require that a motion for a video appearance filed by a respondent who resides outside Oahu be ruled on with written reasons before the respondent is required to travel.

Hawai‘i’s unique geography does not eliminate the due process rights of our nation’s immigrants. We look forward to your response and thank you for your consideration of this matter.

Sincerely,

###

title: NEWS: Schiff Joins Raskin, Blumenthal in Pressing Kirkland & Ellis for Details of $125 Million Trump “Deal”
text:
Lawmakers Reject Kirkland’s Excuses for Stonewalling Investigation and Demand Immediate Compliance

Washington, D.C. —Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.-08), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations to press Chairman of the law firm Kirkland & Ellis Jon Ballis on refusing to cooperate with the Committees’ investigation into Kirkland’s decision to provide President Trump with $125 million in free legal services that align with his political agenda – rejecting the firm’s previous bogus legal justifications for doing so.

“To date, Kirkland has not cooperated with our legitimate oversight requests. Your firm has failed to produce a single responsive document and has refused to meet with Congressional staff. Instead, Kirkland has devoted its time to compiling a laundry list of legally specious claims of privilege. Notwithstanding Kirkland’s lack of cooperation, we will use every tool at our disposal to pursue this investigation—in this Congress and the next,” wrote the lawmakers.

Kirkland has failed to produce any written agreement memorializing its $125 million deal with the Trump Administration beyond President Trump’s Truth Social posts. Absent a written agreement, Trump continues to be the sole arbiter of Kirkland’s legal obligations under the deal. As the lawmakers point out, Kirkland’s professional judgment is necessarily compromised when it is under constant threat of being deemed in violation of its personal agreement with the famously vindictive President.

To resist congressional oversight, Kirkland provided vague, contradictory and legally unsound privilege claims that are not supported by legal precedent. The lawmakers reject each of these sham claims in detail.

Requests for client identities, hours worked and the value of services do not implicate attorney-client privilege.

Kirkland’s attempt to extend executive privilege to dealings with Trump’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, is unsupported by legal precedent.

Kirkland’s claim of a settlement privilege is similarly flawed as they faced no executive order when it entered negotiations, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) acknowledged in federal court that it engaged in informal information gathering, not an investigation.

The lawmakers are renewing their demands for records and answers concerning Kirkland’s negotiations with the Administration, communications with the President’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, free legal work for federal agencies, potential conflicts with existing clients and efforts to poach attorneys and clients from Paul Weiss while it faced Trump’s retaliatory executive order. They also seek an itemized response to outstanding questions, a detailed log supporting any privilege claims and written confirmation that Kirkland is preserving relevant records, including encrypted or disappearing-message communications.

The inquiry continues an investigation Raskin and Blumenthal launched in April 2025 into Trump’s coercion of major law firms and the deals firms struck to avoid retaliation. Joined by Schiff, they subsequently scrutinized firms’ free legal work for the Commerce Department, sought records of Epshteyn’s role in Kirkland’s deal and pressed Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP over potential conflicts involving its work for Intel and the Commerce Department.

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

Dear Mr. Ballis:

We write for the sixth time regarding Kirkland & Ellis LLP’s (Kirkland) decision to preemptively surrender to President Donald Trump and enter into a legally dubious settlement agreement with the Trump Administration. We have repeatedly requested information and documents about Kirkland’s conduct, including with respect to: (1) Kirkland’s attempts to poach attorneys from a rival law firm that was being extorted by the Trump Administration; (2) Kirkland’s contacts with President Trump’s personal legal fixer, Boris Epshteyn; (3) Kirkland’s commitment to perform $125 million in pro bono legal services that align with President Trump’s political agenda; and, Kirkland’s seemingly unlawful provision of legal services to the U.S. Department of Commerce.

To date, Kirkland has not cooperated with our legitimate oversight requests. Your firm has failed to produce a single responsive document and has refused to meet with congressional staff. Instead, Kirkland has devoted its time to compiling a laundry list of legally specious claims of privilege. Notwithstanding Kirkland’s lack of cooperation, we will use every tool at our disposal to pursue this investigation—in this Congress and the next.

To comprehensively rein in presidential abuses of power through legislative actions, Congress and the American people must learn the full circumstances and nature of Kirkland’s indefensible submission to an out-of-control executive. Why did Kirkland enter into this agreement? What was promised and by whom? And how did the President’s coercion work in practice? Against that backdrop, we address your counsel’s latest response to our congressional staff, dated May 28, 2026, which raises a multitude of vague, contradictory, and legally unsound objections.

I. Attorney-Client Privilege

In the May 28 response, Kirkland objects to responding to our requests for records concerning your pro bono engagements and the provision of other free legal services, contending that it would “reveal client confidences, privileged communications, and attorney work product.” Relying on a Third Circuit decision, United States v. Liebman, you argue the privilege extends to our requests because the documents “would convey the substance of attorney-client communications.” As an initial matter, in the context of a congressional investigation, Congress is not obligated to recognize common law privileges, has never formally done so, and no court has ever held to the contrary. But Kirkland’s position is also plainly inaccurate. Although Kirkland fails to specify which of our requests implicate the attorney-client privilege, even a cursory examination of our requests makes it readily apparent that no such privilege is implicated.

By way of example, we previously requested a list of pro bono matters that Kirkland has undertaken for the U.S. government, non-governmental clients who have been offered pro bono services pursuant to Kirkland’s agreement with President Trump, and a dollar value of the pro bono services rendered. We similarly requested a list of the federal agencies that Kirkland has performed work for, the number of hours spent working for those agencies, and the billable value of those hours.

These requests simply do not implicate any applicable privilege. As Kirkland should know—because it is in the very case that you cited—“It is well established that ‘absent unusual circumstances the identity of the client does not come within the attorney-client privilege.’” As the Liebman case and others demonstrate, the attorney-client privilege does not apply to legal requests—including our requests—that “merely request[] the names of clients who paid fees.” Nor does the attorney-client privilege prohibit disclosures quantifying the “amount of a fee,” or “general information about the nature of the services performed.”

Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters

no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following:

April 18, 2025, letter: A detailed description of all requests for pro bono services you have received from the White House or any executive branch agency since entering into an agreement with the White House, including the nature of such request, the identity of the individual requesting the services, and the services your firm has agreed to provide.

September 24, 2025, letter: A list of the number of hours that Kirkland has contributed to the Commerce Department or the U.S. Government to date.

March 2, 2026, letter: A list of all federal agencies that Kirkland has performed work for, the number of hours spent working for those agencies, and the billable value of those hours.

II. Executive Privilege

In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you contend that Kirkland cannot respond to our requests because they “seek documents related to negotiations conducted on behalf of the President,” arguing, “executive privilege requires an opportunity for the President to assess whether to assert privilege over any of the materials sought and to intervene as necessary.” Once again, that is

incorrect. In support of this radical expansion of the executive privilege, Kirkland relies entirely

on a statement issued by a minority of D.C. Circuit judges in denying a motion for rehearing en

banc. As you well know, that statement has no precedential value and provides no legal basis

for withholding documents that Congress has identified as critical to its legislative function.

Your response also obscures the more fundamental issue with Kirkland’s assertion—the firm was primarily negotiating with someone outside the Trump Administration. It was dealing with Donald Trump’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, whom Trump Administration officials have identified as leveraging his proximity to the President to orchestrate multiple “pay-to-play” schemes. No court has held that the presidential communications component of executive privilege extends to communications with private advisors. But Kirkland’s assertion goes even beyond that farfetched claim, arguing that because someone might advise the President, all of Kirkland’s communications with that advisor similarly implicate executive privilege. Kirkland’s theory could functionally exempt any communication by drawing a line, however attenuated, to a President’s advisor—irrationally expanding a narrow privilege. Such a transformation is clearly unworkable, unsupported by any legal precedent, and raised either in error or in bad faith.

The same holds for our request for a list of Trump Administration officials that Kirkland communicated with involving these matters. This narrow request did not seek the disclosure of the content of the President’s communications—or for that matter, the disclosure of any government official’s communications—and cannot implicate any executive privilege. To be clear, Kirkland’s communications with government officials would, almost entirely, not be subject to executive privilege. But here, our requests do not even implicate those communications.

Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following:

March 2, 2026, letter: All communications from Kirkland, or its agents, with Boris Epshteyn or his agents or associates, including but not limited to, meetings records, phone calls, emails, text messages, or letters.

March 2, 2026, letter: A list of all individuals or entities who corresponded with Kirkland, or any of its agents, to discuss an agreement with the Trump Administration, including the date(s) of any and all contacts.

III. Settlement Privilege

In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you object to the production of communications among Kirkland, the Trump Administration, and Administration representatives that were “made for the purpose of negotiating a mutually acceptable settlement of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) inquiry and anticipated Executive Order.” Kirkland argues that “[a]ny communications made in furtherance of settlement are privileged.” In support of that argument, Kirkland cites a Sixth Circuit case, Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Chiles Power Supply, Inc., for the broad proposition that “confidential settlement communications are a tradition in this country.” To be clear, this is an overbroad, and likely inaccurate, representation of federal law. As other courts have recognized, the Goodyear Tire decision “has not been widely followed.” Indeed, as determined by a D.C. federal court, advocates for a federal settlement privilege have failed to “demonstrate a broad consensus in support of such a privilege.”

As you undoubtedly know, the Federal Rules of Evidence governing settlement negotiations are rules of admissibility for federal courts, not privileges. Moreover, congressional investigations are simply not bound by the Federal Rules of Evidence that underlie Goodyear and related cases. Even if we recognized the federal settlement privilege—which we emphatically do not—the unpublished decision you cited in further support of your argument strongly weighs against the application of the privilege here. Specifically, in Baker v. Secretary, U.S. Department of Transportation, the Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit concluded that a district court was permitted to consider communications between an individual and a federal agency in the context of an employment dispute, observing the settlement privilege did not apply because “no formal complaint had been filed.” Similarly, Kirkland was not the subject of a formal complaint at the time it entered into “negotiations” with the Trump Administration. Although you have previously referenced resolving an “investigation” by the EEOC, the EEOC admitted in federal court that the letter it sent to Kirkland and others “constituted informal information gathering and were not a component of any investigation.” Nor was Kirkland subject to an executive order at the time it entered into its agreement or contract with the President. Kirkland has made no effort to explain why a “negotiation” privilege should attach to its conversations with the Trump Administration about the resolution of a voluntary request and a nonexistent executive order.

Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following:

April 6, 2025, letter: Did you approach the Trump Administration regarding a preemptive settlement to avoid an executive order against Kirkland, or did they approach you? Please describe in detail the timeline of your engagement with the Trump Administration.

April 18, 2025, letter: All records referring or relating to any executive order threatened by President Trump against Kirkland and efforts by Kirkland to negotiate an agreement with President Trump, including but not limited to:

Any communications regarding any threatened executive order or any proposed agreement;

Any communications with any officials in the Trump Administration from March 1, 2025, to the present regarding any threatened executive order and any proposed agreement; and

Draft records constituting or related to any proposed agreement between President Trump and Kirkland.

Deliberative Process

In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you cursorily argue that Kirkland cannot produce documents related to settlement negotiations because you are not “at liberty to waive any deliberative process privilege that the Administration wishes to assert.” In support of this contention, you summarily cite a district court decision, Matter of Nelson, but neglect to quote from the decision or make even the slightest effort to analogize the facts and reasoning to the present matter.

Since Kirkland has failed to explain the case cited in your own communications, we will do so here. The deliberative process privilege is a “limited privilege in several different ways.” First, the privilege “belongs only to the government.” This means that “private parties”—like Kirkland—“can neither assert nor waive the privilege.” Second, it applies “only to that group of communications within the agency or department.” Your communications plainly did not occur within any agency or department of the United States. Third, the privilege must be “lodged by the head of the department which has control over the matter,” a requirement designed to “insure that the privilege remains a narrow privilege which is not indiscriminately invoked.” Your attempt to assert the government’s deliberative privilege process here as a private party is an “indiscriminate” invocation of the privilege. Fourth, there must be a “specification of precise and certain reasons for the need to preserve the confidentiality of the documents at issue.” You have not provided such reasons explaining why communications effecting a shakedown by the President of the United States warrant protection. In sum, this government privilege is completely irrelevant and unavailable to you.

Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following:

April 6, 2025, letter: All records referring or relating to President Trump’s March 14, 2025, Executive Order “Addressing Risks from Paul Weiss,” including but not limited to:

Any communications regarding the March 14, 2025, Executive Order; and

Any communications with any officials in the Trump Administration from March 14, 2025, to the present concerning law firms other than Kirkland.

April 18, 2025, letter: Please describe in detail the circumstances surrounding your April 11, 2025, agreement with President Trump.

Who facilitated your April 11, 2025, agreement with President Trump?

Did Kirkland representatives meet with President Trump or members of his Administration?

If so, describe in detail who participated in the meeting(s), when and where they took place, and what was discussed.

Did you acknowledge any wrongdoing for representing causes President Trump finds objectionable?

Rules of Professional Conduct

In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you cite the American Bar Association’s (ABA) Model Rules of Professional Conduct to justify withholding communications requested by the Committees, arguing that Kirkland “take[s] seriously our ethical obligations to our clients and [is] committed to representing them with the highest standards of professional responsibility.” It is fair to question whether Kirkland’s leadership consulted the ABA Rules before it agreed to enter into a personal agreement with the President of the United States to perform $125 million worth of legal services. Indeed, a plethora of ABA Rules would have counseled against entering into such an agreement. For instance, the ABA directs attorneys to act with “courage and foresight” to “shape the body of the law to the ever-changing relationships of society.” The ABA further directs lawyers to exercise their professional judgment “free of compromising influences and loyalties,” emphasizing, “neither the lawyer’s personal interests, the interests of other clients, nor the desires of third persons should be permitted to dilute the lawyer’s loyalty to the client.” Most relevant here, lawyers must be alert to and disregard third parties who seek to exert “strong economic, political, or social pressures upon the lawyers.” Kirkland’s abject failure to reject an unprecedented, extortionate attempt by the President to control the legal profession, an attempt that multiple other law firms successfully rejected and resisted, implicates numerous professional responsibilities of lawyers, and none more so than its duty not to subject the judgment of the firm, and the interests of its clients, to the whims of a highly volatile and vindictive President.

Critically, Kirkland has failed to produce any written agreement between the Trump Administration and Kirkland beyond what is contained in the President’s Truth Social posts. That leads us to believe that there is no other written agreement. Assuming that is the case, President Trump appears to be the sole arbiter of what is required by the putative “contract” and what would constitute a violation of the professional rules. Under these circumstances, Kirkland’s professional judgment is necessarily compromised as it must always consider the impetuous desires of President Trump—a third party who wields enormous economic and political pressure over Kirkland—as demonstrated by your decision to succumb to this extortionary agreement in the first place. This is borne out by your representation of the Department of Commerce—a representation that was never announced as being part of the scope of the agreement—as well as press reports that the President has a “broader understanding of the terms” of the contract than what is publicly known, including requiring capitulating firms to represent him in a personal capacity.

Kirkland cites a D.C. Bar opinion to further justify its decision to withhold documents from Congress. Again, Kirkland does not appear to have thoroughly vetted the materials it cited. In that very opinion, the D.C. Bar determined an attorney had not violated his ethical obligations by producing documents containing client confidences and secrets to Congress. To be clear, we have not requested materials containing client confidences or secrets, but even if we had, the D.C. Bar’s opinion confirms that the D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct do not prohibit attorneys from complying with congressional oversight requests.

The D.C. Bar’s reasoning for reaching its conclusion is instructive. Because Kirkland apparently has failed once again to thoroughly explain the opinion it cites, we offer an explanation of the relevant principles here. In determining that an attorney could disclose client confidences in response to a congressional request, the D.C. Bar relied on Supreme Court precedent holding that “a contempt of Congress cannot be cured by the lawyer’s later compliance with the subpoena,” as well as the Supreme Court’s holding that “when a witness refuses to answer a question in a mistaken, good faith belief that it would violate his rights to be compelled to answer, his mistake of law will be no defense at a trial on the criminal contempt charge.” Kirkland should be mindful of these precedents as it carefully considers its obligations in responding to requests from Congress.

Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters

no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following:

April 6, 2025, letter: Did members of your firm have contact with known Paul, Weiss clients about securing new or additional business from those clients from March 14, 2025, to March 20, 2025?

If so, which members of your firm and which known Paul, Weiss clients?

If so, please describe the nature of those conversations, including who initiated them, whether members of your firm made an effort to secure new or additional business in light of the executive order entered against Paul, Weiss, and any subsequent action taken in light of these conversations.

If so, please detail the extent to which you or other Kirkland attorneys sought or received any ethical guidance surrounding seeking new or additional business from clients of a firm facing an unconstitutional executive order, including from any state, federal, or other bar association.

April 18, 2025, letter: What were the specific terms of the deal Kirkland agreed to with President Trump?

Does President Trump’s April 11, 2025, social media statement accurately reflect the terms of your deal?

Please detail all client relationships Kirkland has chosen to end from April 11, 2025, to the present.

September 24, 2025, letter: Explain whether Kirkland notified clients adverse to the Administration of Kirkland’s work for the U.S. Government.

March 2, 2026, letter: All agreements made with the Trump Administration, including but not limited to, settlement records, client retainer letters, conflict disclosures, and any communications informing such agreements.

VI. Conclusion

Thus far, Kirkland has failed to cooperate with our investigation by refusing to provide relevant documents, refusing to meet with congressional investigators, and making baseless claims of privilege that do not withstand scrutiny. As illustrated above, the cases Kirkland cites in its defense provide no basis for withholding documents from legitimate congressional oversight. Nor has Kirkland made any meaningful effort to address the questions we have Posed. Vague assertions of privilege and ethereal references to purported legal constraints are not a substitute for identifying the specific basis on which Kirkland contends that particular documents or categories of information may be withheld. We therefore invite you to immediately revisit Kirkland’s willingness to comply with our inquiries.

Please provide all records identified above by October 29, 2026. For other requests not outlined above, Kirkland should submit an itemized response to each of the questions raised in our letters dated April 6, April 18, and September 24, 2025, as well as March 2, 2026. To the extent that Kirkland objects to responding to any specific question posed, please expressly identify the question, state each concrete ground for the objection, and provide the legal authority supporting your position. Any claim of privilege must be accompanied by a detailed privilege log.

We expect your firm to preserve all documents and communications relating to the matters described in this letter. This preservation obligation includes but is not limited to: emails; text messages; messages sent via applications such as Signal, WhatsApp, X, Truth Social, or other encrypted platforms; handwritten notes; draft documents; calendar entries; and call logs.

Please confirm in writing by October 29, 2026, that you have taken all necessary steps to

comply with this preservation requirement. If you, or agents acting on Kirkland’s behalf, have

used ephemeral messaging applications or similar technology to communicate with Trump

Administration officials, or anyone purporting to act on the Administration’s behalf, including,

but not limited to, Boris Epshteyn, please include that information in your written confirmation.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this profoundly important matter.

title: NEWS: Sens. Schiff, Padilla Deliver Nearly $2.5 Million for Bay Area Public Safety Projects
text:
Walnut Creek, CA — Today, Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both-D-Calif.) are announcing that nearly $2.5 million is heading to public safety projects in San Francisco, Alameda, and Walnut Creek. The federal funding was secured by Senators Schiff and Padilla through the Congressionally Directed Spending process for fiscal year 2026.

As a result of the Senators’ efforts, $1 million has been disbursed to the City of Walnut Creek, $900,000 has been disbursed to the City of Alameda, and $550,000 has been disbursed to the City of San Francisco for projects that will prevent crime and keep communities safe. The funding is part of more than $258,959,654 delivered by Senator Schiff since taking office.

“All Californians deserve to live in communities where their families are safe and their businesses can thrive. They also deserve to have the peace of mind of knowing that when a crime does take place, local law enforcement has the tools to bring the perpetrators to justice,” said Senator Schiff. “I’m proud to have secured nearly $2.5 million in federal funding with the partnership of Senator Padilla and Congressman DeSaulnier, which is now headed to Bay Area communities, to deliver on that promise.”

“Keeping our communities safe means investing in the tools and services that help prevent crime, support victims, and hold perpetrators accountable,” said Senator Padilla. “I’m proud to have secured this federal funding for Alameda and San Francisco, delivering resources that strengthen public safety and help ensure Californians get the support and protection they deserve to feel safe in their own communities.”

Read more about the projects below:

City of Walnut Creek Public Safety Body Worn Camera Equipment Upgrade Project

The Walnut Creek Police Department has received $1,000,000 to implement their Public Safety Body Worn Camera Equipment Upgrade Project. The purpose is to provide equipment upgrades and services for the department’s Body Worn Camera (BWC) program. This project is intended to improve accountability and transparency and strengthen data collection and the preservation of digital evidence.

This funding request was led by Senator Schiff and Congressman Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.-10).

“Body-worn cameras are critical in promoting transparency, ensuring accountability, and developing public trust in police departments,”said Congressman DeSaulnier. “I was proud to bring home $1 million for the City of Walnut Creek to upgrade 120 body-worn cameras for their officers and provide cutting-edge technology for the department that will ultimately make our community safer. I am grateful for the leadership of Senators Schiff and Padilla for supporting public safety reforms statewide.”

City of Alameda Crime Victims Initiative

The City of Alameda City Attorney’s Office has received $900,000 in federal funding, which will sustain and expand victim services in response to rapidly increasing caseloads, particularly involving domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, and other misdemeanor crimes, through an embedded victim advocacy program in the Prosecution and Public Rights Unit. The project will increase access to victim services, offer greater continuity of support throughout criminal proceedings, expand service availability, improve awareness of available resources, and sustain and institutionalize a victim advocacy program that strengthens services for crime victims throughout Alameda.

This funding request was led by Senator Padilla and supported by Senator Schiff.

City and County of San Francisco’s Crime Lab Rapid DNA Unit

The San Francisco Police Department-Crime Lab Rapid DNA Unit has received $550,000 to support efforts to acquire and implement two National DNA Index System (NDIS)-approved Rapid DNA instruments, along with the associated software, consumables, validation materials, and training required to integrate this technology into forensic operations. Rapid DNA technology automates DNA extraction, amplification, separation, and profile generation within a single instrument, reducing analysis time from weeks to less than two hours for qualifying samples. This capability will significantly improve investigative timelines, increase laboratory efficiency, and enhance the delivery of critical forensic information to investigators and criminal justice partners.

This funding request was led by Senator Schiff.

title: WATCH: Sen. Schiff Reacts to DOJ Suing California Over False Election Claims: “We’re Fortunate That They’re So Incompetent”
text:
Schiff told viewers of MS Now’s All in with Chris Hayes that voting early is their best tool in responding to attempts by the Trump administration to sow chaos in the upcoming election

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined MS NOW’s All in with Chris Hayes to discuss the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) lawsuit against California, the administration’s latest attempt at sowing chaos before the November elections.

This week, the Los Angeles County Registrar received a thumb drive from the DOJ, which the department claimed contained a list of “likely non-citizens” that California was expected to purge from its voter rolls. The password to the thumb drive came attached via ‘Post-it’ note, and the drive was not reviewed due to security concerns. The DOJ has now sued California for failure to meet the department’s demands and deadline.

Senator Schiff explained that these tactics date back to the aftermath of the 2020 election, and are engineered to generate doubt in the security of our elections. The Senator encouraged Californians to vote early as a response to these attempts to undermine faith in the upcoming midterms.

View the full interview here.

Key Excerpts:

On why the DOJ has lawlessly targeted California’s elections ahead of the midterms:

[…] They know at the Department of Justice because it’s run by one of the president’s criminal lawyers that the president is losing these Midterms badly. He has not brought the cost of living down. His war is unpopular. His tariff war is unpopular. And so, they are using any stratagem they can to try to suppress the vote, to change the vote. And now you have this desperate action in California, where they want California to take some random thumb drive and run it through their system.

On this administration’s previous attempts at election interference and the validity of current claims:

[…] But where this has been tried in other states like in Nevada, the Justice Department, administration, initially claimed that there were 10,000-20,000 ballots of non-citizens and then revised the estimate down to well, maybe more like 100 or 200. The number turned out to be zero. Zero. But I think bigger picture, Chris, they want to cast these doubts now. They assume they will lose this litigation in the run-up to the election so that after the election, if and when they lose, they can try to contest the results.

[…] The feds have very limited role when it comes to elections. That is the province of the states. They lose time after time after time. The civil rights division, which is now the anti-civil rights division, has brought some of these cases. They’ve lost them all. I think they expect to lose this one, too. But nevertheless, you have the Attorney General of the United States soiling the name of that office, soiling his own reputation to put the department’s imprimatur on this disenfranchisement, voter disenfranchisement effort. It’s just scandalous, but thankfully such an incompetent effort.

On what can be done to secure the 2026 elections:

[…] The President in his last term claimed there were millions of undocumented people voting in California. That was a bigger lie, but it’s still all part of the same big lie. So, they might contest seating someone. They might use it as justification to seize ballot boxes. One concern I have is, they’re dispatching all kinds of poll watchers from the Justice Department, from the Civil Rights Division. There are going to be legitimate poll watchers out there. It wouldn’t be difficult to seed the crowd with outside agitators, create violent incidents to give the administration some pretext to call out the guard or call out ICE or call out whoever. The best response in California is vote early, vote by absentee. We’re all mailed a ballot in California where that’s possible, but other states people should vote early if they can. But also, I think people should look at every effort this administration makes to tell them, we don’t want people voting — we don’t want citizens voting, because we’re afraid of losing. We should look at all those efforts to stop people from voting and make it even more of a mission to vote and make sure your voice is heard.

title: What They’re Saying: Diabetes Advocates and Leaders Highlight Urgent Need for Congress to Pass Shaheen’s Bipartisan INSULIN Act to Lower Health Care Costs for Millions of Americans
text:
(Washington, DC) – As U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-NH) legislation to cap monthly out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 continues to enjoy robust bipartisan support in the House of Representatives and the Senate, a broad coalition of diabetes advocates and leaders is underscoring the urgent need for Congress to pass the INSULIN Act to lower health care costs for Americans. Over 40 million Americans live with diabetes, and Shaheen’s legislation would directly impact lower the cost of life-saving insulin for millions across the country.

What they’re saying:

"People with type 1 diabetes don't get even a moment free from the disruptive and dangerous burdens of the disease. On top of that, they shouldn't have to shoulder the weight of unpredictable or exorbitant costs for insulin, the medicine that keeps them alive. Congress has a rare opportunity to help those in the T1D community struggling with insulin costs. With health care costs rising across the board, affordable insulin is a critical need, and one that Congress must stand up to provide,” said Lynn Starr, Breakthrough T1D’s Chief Global Advocacy Officer. “We are so grateful for the tremendous leadership of Senators Shaheen and Collins and Representatives DeGette, Miller-Meeks, Schrier and Bresnahan on this critical issue.”

“Despite advancements in policy, insulin is still unaffordable for a significant number of Americans who rely on it to live. Furthermore, the high cost of insulin has led to 41 percent of households skipping or rationing doses exposing individuals to dangerous health outcomes. Americans report paying more for insulin in 2026 than they did in 2025 with 40 percent report paying more than $150. The ADA strongly supports the INSULIN Act, which limits monthly cost-sharing to $35, and would make insulin affordable for the 2.2 million Americans enrolled in federally regulated commercial plans outside state jurisdiction,” said Lisa Murdock, Chief Advocacy Officer of the American Diabetes Association (ADA’s recent Access and Affordability Survey).

“As a clinical pharmacist, I see firsthand that people with diabetes still struggle to pay for their insulin at the pharmacy counter. Those with commercial insurance are not protected in the same way that Medicare beneficiaries are. The INSULIN Act would cap out-of-pocket costs for insulin for people with diabetes on commercial insurance, making a direct impact for them and their families,” said Nancy D’Hondt, RPh, CDCES, FADCES, Board Chair of the Diabetes Leadership Council.

"For many people with diabetes, insulin is not optional. Yet too many patients continue to face financial barriers that force difficult choices between paying for insulin and meeting other basic needs. As health care costs continue to rise, policies that improve affordability and access to insulin are vital to protecting patients' health. We urge Congress to pass the INSULIN Act to help ensure patients can afford this critical medication,” said Robert Lash, M.D., Chief Medical Officer of the Endocrine Society.

“The stakes for kidney health here are very high. Diabetes accounts for half of all new cases of kidney failure and an estimated 4 in 10 adults with diabetes have kidney disease,” said Jesse Roach, MD, Senior Vice President of Government Relations of the National Kidney Foundation. “The INSULIN Act is an important step toward making insulin more affordable and strengthening safeguards for people who rely on it. We urge Congress to pass it this year.”

Shaheen’s bipartisan Improving Needed Safeguards for Users of Lifesaving Insulin Now (INSULIN) Act would cap monthly out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 for Americans with insurance, expanding the effective price cap for Americans on Medicare. Shaheen has championed efforts to lower insulin costs throughout her time in office, and the bill is closer than ever before to passing out of the U.S. Senate. In July, the INSULIN Act advanced out of the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee, and in September companion legislation was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives.

Senator Shaheen has worked tirelessly to lower health care costs for Granite Staters and Americans. As co-chair of the U.S. Senate Diabetes Caucus, Senator Shaheen has consistently pressed to hold insulin manufacturers, insurers and pharmacy benefit managers accountable for the skyrocketing cost of life-saving insulin and otherwise support patients and families facing diabetes. Polling released from the American Diabetes Association this summer found that 40% of respondents who rely on insulin report paying more than $150 per month for insulin, and 76% of respondents across political parties support a $35 limit on cost sharing for insulin.

title: Senators Peters, Slotkin Announce More Than $880,000 in Federal Support for Mid-Michigan Fire Departments
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Senators Gary Peters (MI) and Elissa Slotkin (MI) announced that local fire departments across Mid-Michigan will receive $884,836 in federal funding. The funding comes from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Assistance to Firefighters Grants (AFG) and Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response (SAFER) grant programs.

“As elected officials, it is our responsibility to ensure that Michigan’s firefighters and front-line responders are protected. I join my colleague, Senator Gary Peters, in welcoming the more than $880,000 in federal support for mid-Michigan firefighters,” said Senator Slotkin. “We’ve worked in a bipartisan way to secure this essential grant funding. And now, these dollars will be used to address staffing needs, enhance safety training, and provide much-needed equipment for the brave folks who put their lives on the line every day to keep Michiganders safe.”

“Every single day, firefighters and first responders in Michigan and across the nation put their lives on the line to protect their communities. It’s vital that each department has the resources they need to do their job safely,” said Senator Peters. “I was proud to work in a bipartisan way to extend essential grant programs that support this work, and I’m pleased to announce this federal funding for departments across Mid-Michigan to ensure they have the proper equipment and staffing levels necessary to keep our communities safe.”

Below are descriptions of each project:

Northeast Ingham Emergency Service: The Northeast Ingham Emergency Service will receive $592,571 to purchase 60 Scott SCBA air packs for use in firefighting and hazardous material incidents.

City of Charlotte: The City of Charlotte has been awarded $223,216 to purchase new fire hose, nozzles, fittings, and other related water-supply equipment.

City of St. Johns: The City of St. Johns will receive $52,380 from the AFG program to provide EMT Training and compensation for department members.

Meridian Township Fire Department: The Meridian Township Fire Department will receive $16,669 to acquire structural Firefighting Personal Protective gear for new employees. This gear is essential during high risk IDLH Atmospheres such as entering a building on fire that is full of smoke and heat to extinguish a fire.

“The City of Charlotte is extremely grateful for Senator Peters’ support in helping make this grant possible,” said Tyger Fullerton, Fire Chief of the City of Charlotte Fire Department.“This funding is a significant investment in the safety and capabilities of our firefighters, allowing Charlotte, Benton Township, and Vermontville Township to replace and upgrade critical fire hose, nozzles, and water-supply equipment that our firefighters depend on when it is needed most.”

“We are very appreciative for the work that Senator Peters and Senator Slotkin did to ensure that the Assistance to Firefighters Grant program was continued and their advocating for our department to be able to be a recipient,” said Kevin Douglas, Fire Chief of the St. John’s Fire Department. “This training will help to improve the level of service we are able to provide.”

“This funding will allow us to purchase personal protective gear that is essential when entering a burning house to extinguish a fire,” said Meridian Township Fire Chief Michael Hamel. “We’re thankful for Senator Peters’ support for this grant funding, which will help keep our firefighters safe performing fire rescues in high-risk situations.”

Fire departments use these federal programs to recruit and retain additional personnel, as well as buy up-to-date vehicles and equipment such as breathing air compressors, hoses, nozzles, and more. Fire stations also use the programs to fund safety training and technical rescue training, as well as health screenings for firefighters.

More information about these grants can be found here.

title: Tillis, Colleagues Call for Investigation Into Starlink Disruptions in Ukraine
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – This week, Senators Thom Tillis (R-NC) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), co-chairs of the Senate NATO Observer Group (SNOG), led a bipartisan group of seven Senators in a letter to Department of Defense’s Inspector General, Platte B. Moring III, calling for an investigation into the disruption of the U.S.-maintained Starshield systems for Ukrainian partners.

“We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities. We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances,” the Senators wrote.

“To use Starshield and Starlink as intended, Ukraine needs access to unlimited speeds, which was its service arrangement prior to this reported restriction. We understand that at least some relevant services are provided through contractual arrangements administered by the U.S. Space Force. Any restrictions on these capabilities, particularly without advance notification, raise serious questions about the Department of Defense’s contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services,” the Senator continued.

“The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas. Disruptions to critical intelligence-sharing, threat-warning, or communications capabilities in an active war zone can have life-threatening consequences. The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability,” the Senators concluded.

The full list of Senators on the letter include Senators Dick Durbin (D-IL), Susan Collins (R-ME), Jack Reed (D-RI), John Cornyn (R-TX), Chris Coons (D-DE), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), and Richard Blumenthal (D-CT).

The full text of the letter is available HERE.

title: Ahead of the Midterm Elections, Warner, Durbin, Padilla & Peters Request Information From DOJ & FBI Regarding the Trump Administration’s Attempted Attacks on Our Elections
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), Vice Chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Dick Durbin (D-IL), Democratic Whip and Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Alex Padilla (D-CA), Ranking Member of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, and Gary Peters (D-MI), Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel requesting information regarding the alarming series of actions the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the FBI have undertaken to target state and local governments’ election administration efforts—and to understand the extent of the agencies’ coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the White House in these efforts.

The senators wrote, “Under your leadership, DOJ and the FBI have sought to upend our federalist system by seizing ballots and election materials, seeking the personal information of election workers and volunteers, showing up at the homes of election officials for questioning, threatening election officials with prosecution, attempting to compel states to provide the federal government with unredacted voter rolls, and raiding the offices of a voting rights nonprofit—often at the apparent behest of President Trump and White House officials, including Stephen Miller. Director Patel has reportedly urged the FBI to persist in these fishing expeditions by exhorting agents to ‘look harder’ because ‘this is a push from 47,’ and senior DOJ officials have threatened to fire or override prosecutors who choose not to pursue election fraud cases that FBI or DHS agents bring them, in contravention of longstanding DOJ rules for prosecutors.”

The senators continued, “These efforts have occurred as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) has taken unprecedented steps to investigate unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud and as the then-Director of National Intelligence took extraordinary steps to insert herself into an already-troubling FBI raid of a local election facility. Taken together, these actions constitute a disturbing, whole-of-government campaign that has weaponized federal law enforcement to relitigate the 2020 election that President Trump lost, attempting to undermine the constitutional election administration powers of states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections and seeking to sow confusion and fear among voters and state and local election officials.”

In the letter, the senators outline the timeline of the Trump administration’s attempted efforts to undermine our elections. The weaponization of DOJ and the FBI as part of this effort became clear last year, when the head of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division (CRT) began filing lawsuits against multiple states to demand they produce unredacted copies of their voter registration lists. CRT sued Fulton County, Georgia last December, seeking records related to the 2020 election. Following this lawsuit, on January 28, 2026, the FBI executed a search warrant at the Fulton County election office in Union City, Georgia. Additionally, the then-Director of National Intelligence inexplicably attended this raid—and escalated this breach of protocol the following day, when she met with FBI agents who had conducted the raid and called President Trump to address the agents. The letter continues to highlight various counties and states the FBI or DOJ has targeted for election-related investigations. These states include Michigan and Arizona—two states President Trump lost in the 2020 election.

The letter also raises concerns that FBI Director Patel is refusing to rule out sending FBI agents to polling locations on Election Day—an illegal tactic that would inevitably intimidate voters.

The senators continued, “The concern over this Administration engaging in intimidation tactics related to the election is not unwarranted. Just one month before election day, President Trump continues to float the idea that he has legal authority to declare a national emergency or invoke the Insurrection Act around the midterms. Moreover, DOJ has already sought to intimidate election officials across the country.”

CRT’s abandonment of its historic mission to protect the right to vote has also bled into the election monitor program, which the Division has in the past used to deploy federal monitors at polling places and ballot counting locations to respond to “incidents of discrimination or interference with the right to vote.” This year, CRT is planning to deploy more than 1,000 election monitors across the country on Election Day, including individuals who helped challenge President Trump’s 2020 election loss.

Just this week, DOJ attempted to escalate these efforts, laying the groundwork to potentially challenge ballots ahead of Election Day with a letter to California election officials, which demanded that they verify the citizenship of individuals listed in a DOJ-provided thumb drive within 48 hours and threatened legal action if they do not follow the Department’s instructions on handling the ballots of these individuals.

The senators concluded, “Furthermore, it is impossible to ignore the brazen partisan intentions behind these actions—not just due to President Trump’s repeated, baseless accusations that Democrats must cheat to win elections, but in light of the unethical political actions you have each taken in recent weeks, including your appearances at an August campaign rally in New York, and Attorney General Blanche’s appearance at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Texasand a campaign event in North Carolina for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley. It is our constitutional duty to conduct oversight over these unprecedented abuses of power to improperly meddle with state and local election administration in the midterm elections that are already underway. The American people deserve to know why federal resources are being diverted from mission critical work to ensure their safety and instead devoted to this costly and, should it further escalate, potentially criminal crusade.”

The senators also noted that despite this brazen, partisan, and coordinated effort to undermine the constitutional structure of our democracy, the rule of law will prevail—countless patriotic Americans across the country are working tirelessly to combat this chaos and distrust and ensure that every eligible American is able to cast their ballot and that their vote is counted. Americans should have confidence that their voices will be heard in November and that these efforts by the Trump administration to weaponize federal law enforcement to meddle in the midterm elections will ultimately fail.

In the letter, the senators request responses to a number of questions and materials related to the administration’s attempts to undermine our elections no later than October 29, 2026.

The full text of the letter can be found here.

title: New Data: Virginia Families Have Had to Spend $3,900+ More Under President Trump
text:
WASHINGTON— U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) are highlighting a new congressional report finding that Virginia families have paid more than $3,900 extra for goods and services since President Trump took office last year. We’ll keep fighting to reverse these harmful policies, end this unnecessary war, and put more money back in Virginians’ pockets.”

Housing Costs

Read the fact sheet for Virginia here and the fact sheet for each congressional district in the Commonwealth here.

Sens. Warner and Kaine are fighting the economic consequences of President Trump’s policies. title: Warnock Names New Chief of Staff, Deputy Chief of Staff
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) named Dylan Laslovich as his Chief of Staff and promoted Josh Delaney to Deputy Chief of Staff/Legislative Director. Mark Libell departs the Senator’s office after serving nearly six years as Senator Warnock’s Chief of Staff. Laslovich will start at the end of the 119th Congress.

“For over a decade, Dylan Laslovich has served as a top advisor for our country’s most influential leaders, navigating both high-stakes elections and landmark legislative negotiations. I’m thrilled that he will bring his invaluable experience to my Senate office,” said Senator Reverend Warnock. “I’m also pleased to promote my top policy advisor Josh Delaney to an expanded role serving the people of Georgia. I’d like to thank my outgoing Chief of Staff, Mark Libell, for his years of service to Georgia and the country.”

title: Congressman Pat Harrigan Introduces Legislation to Protect Americans From Government License Plate Surveillance
text:
Contact: Lexi Kranich (814) 380-4408

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10) introduced the Automated License Plate Reader Accountability Act of 2026, legislation to limit government surveillance through automated license plate readers. These systems can collect and store detailed records of where Americans drive, allowing government agencies to track their movements without meaningful oversight.

“More than half of Americans surveyed oppose police license plate reader programs in their communities, and I understand why. Think about what someone could learn from tracking where you drive every day, from where you work and worship to where you take your kids,” said Congressman Harrigan. “Law enforcement needs the tools to catch dangerous criminals, but the government should have to show probable cause before searching through the movements of law-abiding Americans. The Fourth Amendment doesn't disappear because technology makes surveillance easier.”

The legislation would require government agencies to obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before searching license plate reader databases, with warrants limited to specific vehicles and time periods to prevent broad surveillance of innocent Americans. It would require most records to be permanently deleted within 24 hours, prohibit tracking individuals based on political or religious messages displayed on their vehicles, and bar the use of these systems to enforce civil immigration laws or minor traffic violations. The bill would also prevent private vendors from selling, sharing or repurposing collected information, while allowing emergency access when there is an imminent threat to life or serious bodily injury, subject to judicial review within 48 hours.

To ensure these protections are enforced, the bill would require agencies to maintain detailed records of database searches, publish annual reports on how the technology is used, and undergo regular oversight. States would have two years to adopt comparable safeguards before facing a 10% reduction in certain federal criminal justice grants.

title: FOLLOWING BIPARTISAN PUSH FROM CONGRESSMAN PAT RYAN AND COLLEAGUES DEMANDING TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SPEED UP LIHEAP DISTRIBUTION, HHS RELEASES $356 MILLION FOR NEW YORK
text:
As temperatures begin to drop and fuel prices remain high due to the Iran War, Congressman Ryan demanded that the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) distribute critical home energy funds without delay

This week, $356 million in LIHEAP funding was released to New York, which is the earliest these awards have been granted

Ryan is calling on House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in supplemental LIHEAP funding for FY27

Ryan co-sponsors the “Heating and Cooling Relief Act,” which would expand eligibility for LIHEAP and lower home energy costs for millions more households nationwide

Heating oil prices in New York state are up almost 70% from this time last year, with prices in the Hudson Valley averaging $6.25/ gallon

WASHINGTON, DC – After Congressman Pat Ryan helped lead a bipartisan push demanding the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to distribute Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) funds to the states as soon as possible, HHS announced this week they have distributed $356,163,671 in LIEHAP funds for New York’s Home Energy Assistance Program. Heating oil prices in New York State are up more than 70% from this time last year, with prices in the Hudson Valley averaging $6.22/ gallon.

“After a summer of skyhigh gas prices and utility bills due to Trump’s war in Iran, home heating oil costs are up almost 70 percent. Now, as temperatures start to drop, Hudson Valley families are about to face more expensive heating bills on top of everything else. Thousands of families in our community rely on the LIHEAP program to keep their homes warm. We put the pressure on the administration early to ensure these funds got out the door without delay, and I’m proud they heeded our calls, distributing more than $356 million in LIHEAP funds to New York,” said Congressman Pat Ryan. “The LIHEAP program is chronically underfunded, which is why I’m calling on the Appropriations Committee to increase funding for the program and pushing for legislation to ensure more Hudson Valley families can qualify for assistance.”

This week, Ryan also joined a bipartisan group of 73 members in calling on the House Appropriations Committee to provide an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental appropriations for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) for Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27).

In the letter, the members wrote, “As the war with Iran remains unresolved, energy prices are expected to keep rising, with heating oil up 60% since February. LIHEAP’s $4 billion in funding for the last fiscal year would fall significantly short in meeting the needs of American families this fiscal year.”

“LIHEAP is a critical lifeline for low- and moderate-income individuals, but even if your household qualifies, LIHEAP does not provide guaranteed security. Five out of six families who qualify for LIHEAP receive no financial assistance due to the program’s woefully underfunded status. When adjusting for inflation, LIHEAP funding is lower now than it was in 1981 when the program was first created. If LIHEAP was funded at the same level as it was 45 years ago, the program would have received nearly $7 billion in FY27,” they continued.

“Emergency LIHEAP assistance is urgently needed as winter weather approaches and colder temperatures have already begun. Families should not have to choose between staying warm and purchasing other essential items like food, medication, or rent. Congress must act and not leave families in the cold,” they concluded.

LIHEAP helps low-income individuals and families pay for heating and cooling and mitigates the impacts of rising energy costs and extreme weather events. Across the nation, LIHEAP helps nearly 6 million households afford their energy bills, including nearly 30,000 in NY-18, but Secretary Kennedy’s decision last year to fire all LIHEAP staff last year has put this assistance at risk. Ryan has previously blasted the Trump Administration for threatening to eliminate federal funding for LIHEAP.

Ryan is also a co-sponsor of the Heating and Cooling Relief Act, legislation to modernize LIHEAP, increase investments, and dramatically expand eligibility so that households earning up to 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Line or 80 percent of State Median Income can qualify to apply for assistance. It would lower home energy costs for millions more households nationwide.

Specifically, the Heating and Cooling Relief Act would:

Substantially increase LIHEAP funding to ensure year-round assistance, including an additional $2 billion for emergency energy assistance and $1 billion in Just Transition Grants to help vulnerable households adapt to a changing climate;

Broaden eligibility so that households earning up to 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Line or 80 percent of State Median Income can qualify, while ensuring lower energy burdens for lower-income households and capping household energy burdens at 3 percent of monthly income;

Protect consumers from utility shutoffs, excessive late fees, and predatory energy practices that disproportionately impact vulnerable communities;

Expand emergency assistance, ensuring extreme heat and cold are recognized as qualifying emergencies and that states can provide vital cooling relief;

Increase funding for weatherization and home electrification, to help low-income households reduce energy costs, improve health and safety, and transition to clean, resilient energy systems;

Streamline enrollment and outreach, improving coordination with other federal programs and increasing access through automatic enrollment and simplified verification; and

Strengthen reporting requirements to better track affordability, equity, and climate resilience outcomes.

title: Senator Blackburn Welcomes AG Blanche to Memphis to Host Roundtable on Success of Memphis Safe Task Force
text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. – U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Attorney General Todd Blanche, and U.S. Marshals Service Director Gady Serralta hosted a roundtable discussion on the remarkable success of the Memphis Safe Task Force following its one-year anniversary.

Since the Task Force was launched, there have been more than 13,500 arrests, including more than 1,500 known gang members. Law enforcement has seized more than 1,300 illegal firearms, located nearly 200 missing children, and executed nearly 7,000 warrants.

Senator Blackburn was joined in this discussion by U.S. Attorney Mike Dunavant, U.S. Marshal Tyreece Miller, Memphis Police Chief C.J. Davis, U.S. Representative David Kustoff, and State Senator Brent Taylor.

EXCERPT OF REMARKS

“Good morning, everyone.”

“Thank you all for being here for this discussion.”

“I want to start by expressing my sincere gratitude to Attorney General Blanche for accepting my invitation to come to Memphis today.”

“He has been a true partner in our efforts to make Memphis safer, and I greatly appreciate his working with me every step of the way.”

“We are here this morning because we recently celebrated the one-year anniversary of the Memphis Safe Task Force.”

“And what a year it has been for this city.”

“Today, we will discuss what has already been accomplished and where we go from here to ensure sustained, long-term public safety in Shelby County.”

“Since the launch of the Memphis Safe Task Force last year, we have witnessed a true success story in this historic, iconic city.”

“Crime has declined across all measured categories when comparing 2026 with the same period in 2025.”

“Overall violent crime has dropped by more than 38%.”

“Homicides are down 37%.”

“Carjackings are down 63%.”

“Sexual assaults are down 30%.”

“Robberies have decreased by 47%.”

“By coordinating resources among more than two dozen local, state, and federal agencies—including the FBI, U.S. Marshals Service, Tennessee Highway Patrol, Tennessee National Guard, and Memphis Police Department—the Task Force has been remarkably successful in getting criminals off the streets.”

“Since the Task Force was launched, there have been more than 13,500 arrests, including more than 1,500 known gang members.”

“Law enforcement has seized more than 1,300 illegal firearms, located nearly 200 missing children, and executed nearly 7,000 warrants.”

“I have said it many times, but Memphis truly has become a model for fighting violent crime in a large city.”

“We also have a stellar law enforcement team in place, working hard every day to make this city safer.”

“Many of its members are here this morning, including U.S. Attorney Mike Dunavant, U.S. Marshal Tyreece Miller, Memphis Police Chief Davis, and representatives from the Tennessee Highway Patrol, FBI, DEA, ATF, TBI, and many other agencies.”

“This Task Force has been a resounding success, and the Memphis community is feeling the difference.”

“Sixty-two percent of Memphians say our efforts have been effective in reducing crime.”

“I have made public safety in Memphis a priority in the U.S. Senate.”

“More than two years ago, before President Trump was even reelected, I introduced a resolution urging him to surge federal law enforcement resources into Memphis to crack down on violent crime.”

“After President Trump nominated Kash Patel to lead the FBI, Patel came to meet with me in my office.”

“During that meeting, he was stunned to learn that Memphis at the time had some of the highest—if not the highest—violent crime rates in our country.”

“Over the following months, I worked with Director Patel as he launched what became known as Operation Viper, a targeted effort last summer that took the most dangerous gang members off our streets.”

“This effort ultimately served as the precursor to what became the Memphis Safe Task Force.”

“I am incredibly grateful for President Trump's commitment to Memphis and for Attorney General Blanche's partnership over the past year in helping make Memphis safe again.”

“The Attorney General has truly been an invaluable partner in our efforts to fight crime.”

“Once again, I could not be more grateful that he has taken the time to come to Memphis today.”

“We will not stop our efforts until Memphis is the safest city in the United States.”

title: Congressman Van Drew Confirms Drunk Illegal Immigrant Caused Crash That Seriously Injured South Jersey Police Officer
text:
Washington, DC - Today, Congressman Van Drew announced that, according to information confirmed with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and local officials, the suspected drunk driver who struck and seriously injured Middle Township Police Officer Austin Kapurelos on Friday night is an illegal immigrant with an active ICE detainer.

"I know Austin and his family personally, and they are good, hardworking South Jersey people. Austin is a fine young man who proudly serves his community and his country, and now he is lying in a hospital bed with serious injuries after being hit by a drunk driver who was in this country illegally," said Congressman Van Drew. "I have had enough of this. Just weeks ago, a baby was killed in a New Jersey parking lot by an unlicensed driver who was in this country illegally. Then a six-year-old girl was kidnapped and sexually assaulted by a man who should have been deported. Now we have a young South Jersey police officer fighting to recover from devastating injuries. When is enough enough?

"Meanwhile, Governor Sherrill has committed more than $20 million in taxpayer money to a legal defense fund to keep illegal immigrants facing deportation in this country, while families like Austin's are left dealing with the consequences of failed immigration policies," Congressman Van Drew continued. "It is completely backwards. I am calling on Cape May County Sheriff Nolan to work with ICE and ensure this individual is turned over to federal authorities, and I have no doubt the Sheriff will because he is a good man who believes in upholding the law. We cannot keep allowing preventable tragedies like this to happen to innocent people in New Jersey."

"If this man hadn't been here illegally, Austin would be sitting on the couch with his wife in their new home right now, not lying in a hospital bed," said Tony Kapurelos, Austin's father. "They just got married. They have their whole lives ahead of them, and instead of enjoying this time together, Austin is recovering from surgery, and we're all praying he'll be okay.
