title: Blumenthal & Tillis Readout of Call with President Zelenskyy & Bipartisan, Bicameral Members of Congress
text:
[WASHINGTON, DC] – U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and Thom Tillis (R-NC) released the following statement today after hosting a bipartisan, bicameral video call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to receive an update on Russia’s war in Ukraine:

“During today’s call, President Zelenskyy repeated what we have heard from him for years: Ukraine wants peace. Funding Russia’s war machine, disabling Ukraine’s satellite communications, and crippling its air defense are all impediments to peace. Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties. We organized today’s call to hear directly from President Zelenskyy about what his military is currently facing on the battlefield.”

“President Zelenskyy confirmed that critical Starlink services remain degraded, including on systems traveling at speeds above 100 miles per hour, impeding Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones. He also reported disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing concerning early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches. As a result of these disruptions, civilians – children – are dying. He also raised serious concerns about delays in critical air defense interceptors and the Administration’s decision to waive powerful sanctions against Russia.”

“President Zelenskyy reiterated his willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if Putin agrees to the same – a fair request.”

“Less than a month ago, Congress voted in overwhelming numbers to support crushing sanctions on the enablers of Russia’s war. Democrats and Republicans in Congress understand what will happen if Putin faces no consequences for his murderous invasion. As we conveyed to President Zelenskyy today, we remain committed to Ukraine and our European allies as they seek to end the slaughter in Russia’s war of aggression.”

-30-

title: Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Shaheen, & Coons Demand Answers from SpaceX After Starlink & Starshield Failure Leaves Ukraine Vulnerable to Russian Attacks
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Chris Coons (D-DE) today demanded answers from SpaceX about recent unexpected, life-threatening restrictions to Starlink and Starshield technologies reported by Ukrainian military officials.

In a letter sent to SpaceX Vice President of Legal Christopher Cardaci, the Senators sought answers about any involvement SpaceX may have had in Ukraine’s restricted access to Starshield as well as the role SpaceX plays in Ukraine’s ongoing access to Starlink technology. The Senators’ letter comes after both Donald Trump and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk denied their involvement in restricting Ukraine’s connectivity to these critical battlefield technologies.

“Ukraine has long relied on Starlink for communications and more recently has received access to Starshield services procured by the U.S. Government to support Ukrainian military operations. Starshield is a military and intelligence product developed by SpaceX and used by the U.S. Government, which leverages Starlink technology and allows for enhanced capabilities like encryption. On Tuesday, October 14, Ukrainian officials reported that their access to Starshield had been restricted for devices moving at speeds greater than 100 mph,” the Senators wrote.

“This restriction was particularly devastating to the Ukrainian military’s drone capabilities during an ongoing Russian bombing campaign in Kyiv. SpaceX’s Chief Executive Officer, Elon Musk, has stated that ‘Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,’ and that ‘[a]ny limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,’” the Senators continued.

“At the same time, SpaceX owns and operates the underlying Starlink network and infrastructure upon which certain Starshield services rely. These circumstances raise important questions about the respective technical, contractual, and operational authorities retained by SpaceX and the U.S. government, as well as the ability SpaceX has to restrict access to either Starshield or Starlink services during military operations or national security emergencies,” the Senators concluded.

The full text of the Senators’ letter is available here and below.

Dear Mr. Cardaci:

On October 14, 2026, without warning and amidst a barrage of attacks from the Russian military, Ukrainian officials reported unexpected restrictions to Starlink and Starshield technologies that the Ukrainian military relies upon for critical capabilities on the battlefield.[1] Recent reporting indicates that the decision to restrict access was made by US government officials and that access to services appear to have partially resumed.[2] However, the hasty and life-threatening limitation of Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield has already had grave consequences for the Ukrainian people.[3] It also put at risk the safety of U.S. personnel in Ukraine as these restrictions limited Ukraine’s counter drone abilities.[4] We write to demand answers about SpaceX’s involvement in the recent restriction of Ukraine’s access to Starshield and the role that SpaceX plays in Ukraine’s ongoing access to Starlink technology.

Ukraine has long relied on Starlink for communications and more recently has received access to Starshield services procured by the U.S. Government to support Ukrainian military operations.[5] Starshield is a military and intelligence product developed by SpaceX and used by the U.S. Government, which leverages Starlink technology and allows for enhanced capabilities like encryption.[6] On Tuesday, October 14, Ukrainian officials reported that their access to Starshield had been restricted for devices moving at speeds greater than 100 mph.[7] This restriction was particularly devastating to the Ukrainian military’s drone capabilities during an ongoing Russian bombing campaign in Kyiv.[8] SpaceX’s Chief Executive Officer, Elon Musk, has stated that “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” and that “[a]ny limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”[9] At the same time, SpaceX owns and operates the underlying Starlink network and infrastructure upon which certain Starshield services rely. These circumstances raise important questions about the respective technical, contractual, and operational authorities retained by SpaceX and the U.S. government, as well as the ability SpaceX has to restrict access to either Starshield or Starlink services during military operations or national security emergencies.[10]

These questions have significant consequences for U.S. national security, U.S. support for Ukraine, and the safety of U.S personnel. Accordingly, we request the following information on or before November 2, 2026. To the extent that any of the information requested implicates classified material, please disaggregate that information and we will make arrangements to view that information in a classified setting.

From October 10 to October 15, 2026, please describe any Starshield or Starlink capabilities or access points that were restricted for Ukrainian assets, including the date the restriction went into place and the duration of that restriction.

For each restriction identified in response to Question 1, please identify all personnel involved in or notified of the decision to restrict Starshield services, including for example, the reported restriction affecting devices traveling faster than 100 mph. In the event that SpaceX was not directly involved in the decision, please detail when and how SpaceX was notified of that decision and how the directive to restrict capabilities was communicated to SpaceX.

Considering your contract obligations with the Federal Republic of Germany, which funds Ukraine’s access to Starlink,[11] when did you notify the German government of the decision to degrade Starlink capabilities?

Under SpaceX’s contract with the federal government related to Starshield,

Who can revoke, limit, or otherwise change the terms of Ukraine’s use of Starshield?

How must changes to Ukraine’s access be documented and noticed?

Does SpaceX have discretion to decline, modify, or delay a government-directed change?

How does SpaceX determine whether and when to restrict access to Starlink technology?

Please list the date, time, and location of any restrictions or modifications that SpaceX has made to Ukraine’s access to Starlink technology.

In addition, please provide the following records on or before November 2, 2026.

All Records[12] documenting, approving, or otherwise referring to the restriction of Ukraine’s access to Starlink or Starshield.

All communications between SpaceX and any U.S. federal government entity related to the restriction of Ukraine’s access to Starshield.

All contracts, including any modifications or addendums, between SpaceX and the federal government for the operation or use of Starshield related to Ukraine or support for countries along NATO’s eastern flank. For each contract, please note whether the award was single source, openly competed, or granted under any other set-aside.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this important matter.

Sincerely,

-30-

title: Booker, Pallone Push to Save the Small Fish That Feeds the Jersey Shore
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ) and U.S. Representative Frank Pallone (D-NJ-06) are pressing East Coast fisheries regulators to leave more Atlantic menhaden in the water, warning that a shrinking supply of the small fish threatens the striped bass, ospreys and New Jersey fishing communities that depend on them. In a letter to the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC), the lawmakers call for far deeper cuts than the 20 percent reduction the Commission adopted for the 2026 fishing season.

Known along the Jersey Shore as bunker, menhaden sit at the base of the coastal food web. They feed striped bass, bluefish, whales and ospreys.

"Bunker may be small, but the whole Jersey Shore runs on them," said Senator Booker. "Our striped bass, our ospreys and the families who fish our waters all depend on this little fish. The science is clear that a 20 percent cut falls short, and every season we wait, the food supply for our coastal wildlife shrinks further. I urge the Commission to make a real cut this November and protect the Shore for generations to come."

A 2025 scientific assessment found that menhaden biomass averaged 37 percent lower than previously estimated. The assessment also found that cuts of 50 percent or more would be needed to support the striped bass population. The Commission still cut the coastwide total allowable catch (TAC) by just 20 percent.

In a letter to Joe Cimino, chair of the ASMFC Atlantic Menhaden Management Board, the lawmakers wrote: "This level of reduction is insufficient to address the ecological consequences of declining menhaden abundance. Reduced menhaden availability has been identified as the primary driver of low reproduction in ospreys throughout the Chesapeake Bay. A significant cut to the menhaden TAC is needed to prevent broad ecosystem impacts."

Booker and Pallone warn that excessive menhaden harvesting reduces the food available to predators throughout the Atlantic ecosystem. That includes overfishing by exploitative reduction industrial operations that process the fish into fish meal and oil. The lawmakers argue that fishing limits must account not only for the health of the menhaden population itself, but also for the striped bass, bluefish and other species that depend on it.

The stakes are already visible in New Jersey's skies. In 2025, researchers documented the state's worst osprey breeding season in more than three decades.

"With next year's total allowable catch limits on the table, it's vital that a major cut is made," said Mark Taylor, President of the Jersey Coast Anglers Association. "We have been here before, and we saw our waters explode with life once the cutback was made back in 2013. Our member clubs all have watched menhaden disappear from New Jersey waters except for a short window in early spring and late fall. They're gone. And when bunker disappear, everything that depends on them—striped bass, whales, tuna, dolphins, osprey, eagles—pays the price."

The Commission is expected to set coastwide catch limits for 2027 through 2029 at its November meeting.

title: PHOTOS: Capito Highlights Eastern Panhandle Community Health, Economic Development, Education Investments During Visit
text:
EASTERN PANHANDLE, W.Va. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), traveled to the Eastern Panhandle where she made stops in Martinsburg, Ranson, and Shepherdstown, W.Va.

First, Senator Capito traveled to Martinsburg, W.Va. to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Shenandoah Community Health (SCH) and tour the facility’s recent expansion. SCH is a leader in clinical excellence in West Virginia, with one of the largest regional footprints. Senator Capito has been a long-time supporter of SCH and has secured numerous funding awards for the organization.

“It was great to be in Martinsburg to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Shenandoah Community Health,” Senator Capito said. “SCH goes above and beyond to provide quality patient-first care to our communities. I am proud to support them in their mission to advance health center quality, improve access to comprehensive care, and deliver efficient patient centered care pathways to West Virginians.”

“Over the years, Senator Capito has been a tremendous friend and supporter of Shenandoah Community Health. Whether advocating for the 340B program, supporting health center funding, or championing the needs of rural West Virginia, she understands how important community health centers are to the people we serve. Her leadership helps ensure that issues such as access to care, telehealth, rural health funding, and the future of 340B remain part of the national conversation. We are sincerely grateful for her continued support of Shenandoah and community health centers across West Virginia,” Todd Lockuff, CEO of Shenandoah Community Health said.

Next, Senator Capito traveled to Ranson, W.Va. to visit Jefferson County Community Ministries (JCCM). While there, she received updates on a $300,000 Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS) award, which she helped secure for the facility in Fiscal Year 2024 (FY24). This funding will support a portion of JCCM’s ‘The Neighbor Project’ to build permanent housing for low-income residents. This shelter will be the first localized emergency housing shelter for families in the Eastern Panhandle region.

Additionally, Senator Capito secured a $1 million CDS award in FY24 for Phase 1 of construction of Jefferson County Community Service’s service center project.

“I am proud of the incredible work being done at Jefferson County Community Ministries, which provides essential housing and social services to the Jefferson County community,” Senator Capito said. “JCCM is making an immense impact on the lives of West Virginians and am honored to have played a role in helping them bring their vision of a better, brighter future for our state to life.”

“Jefferson County Community Ministries is rooted in the philosophy of Neighbors Helping Neighbors,” Brooke Grossman, Executive Director of Jefferson County Community Ministries said. “Upon its completion our year-round shelter will not only increase our capacity to provide overnight emergency shelter but also expand our ability to provide vital day services. We appreciate Senator Capito securing a federal earmark to support his project.”

Last, Senator Capito visited the construction site of the new athletic facility and cafeteria at Shepherd University in Shepherdstown, W.Va. alongside new university president, Cam Wesson.

“It was great to join Shepherd University Cam Wesson today to see firsthand the progress being made on the university’s new athletic facility and dining hall. These investments are about enhancing the student experience, supporting student athletes, and ensuring Shepherd University remains a place where students can succeed. I appreciate President Wesson’s leadership and look forward to seeing the positive impact these facilities will have on the university and the surrounding community,” Senator Capito said.

Earlier in the day, Senator Capito also met Berkeley County EDA Director Jennifer Smith for lunch where they caught up on local projects and needs for surrounding area.

title: Cornyn, Colleagues Call for Investigation into Starshield Disruptions in Ukraine
text:
AUSTIN – U.S. Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) joined a letter led by Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) and Thom Tillis (R-NC), along with Senators Susan Collins (R-ME), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-DE), and Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), to Department of War Inspector General Platte Moring III calling for an investigation into the disruption of the U.S.-maintained Starshield systems for Ukrainian partners:

“We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical U.S.-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks… We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances,” wrote the Senators.

“The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas. Disruptions to critical intelligence-sharing, threat-warning, or communications capabilities in an active war zone can have life-threatening consequences. The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability,” the Senators concluded.

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

October 15, 2026

Honorable Platte B. Moring

Inspector General

Department of Defense

800 Mark Center Drive

Alexandria, VA

Dear Mr. Moring:

We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical U.S.-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks. We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids, amid reported disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities. We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents, including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances.

According to reports, speed restrictions imposed on SpaceX’s Starlink terminals between October 12 and 14, 2026, disrupted critical communications capabilities supporting Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles and fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft. Ukrainian military testing on October 14 reportedly identified restrictions at speeds exceeding approximately 63 miles per hour, while SpaceX reportedly acknowledged a service restriction at 100 miles per hour. These restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure.

Separately, we are deeply concerned by reports of disruptions or “glitches” affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine. We understand that American personnel experienced serious difficulties reaching safety during Russian air raids. The precise cause of these incidents, including whether they resulted from technical failures, interruptions in intelligence sharing, changes in U.S. government policy, or other factors, remains unclear. Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation.

Starlink and Starshield capabilities are important components of Ukraine’s military communications infrastructure, supporting command and control, unmanned systems, and operational coordination. To use Starshield and Starlink as intended, Ukraine needs access to unlimited speeds, which was its service arrangement prior to this reported restriction. We understand that at least some relevant services are provided through contractual arrangements administered by the U.S. Space Force. Any restrictions on these capabilities, particularly without advance notification, raise serious questions about the Department of Defense’s contractual oversight and its responsibility to ensure continuity of essential services.

We therefore request that your office immediately investigate:

Whether disruptions to intelligence sharing, threat warnings, or other U.S.-supported capabilities contributed to incidents in which American diplomatic, military, or security personnel were unable to reach shelter during Russian attacks;

Whether any Department of Defense or other U.S. government officials directed, authorized, approved, or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine;

Whether the reported intelligence-sharing disruptions and Starlink restrictions were connected, and whether either resulted from deliberate policy decisions, technical failures, contractor actions, or other causes;

Whether affected U.S. personnel, the U.S. Embassy in Kyiv, and Ukrainian authorities received adequate advance notification of any changes that could compromise their safety or defensive operations;

Whether SpaceX independently imposed restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services, whether those restrictions complied with applicable U.S. government contracts, and what steps the Department of Defense took in response; and

What immediate corrective measures are being implemented to ensure that American personnel receive reliable threat warnings and that essential communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities are maintained.

We also request that you ensure relevant agencies and parties preserve relevant communications, contractual records, technical directives, and correspondence concerning these incidents, including communications between the Department of Defense, SpaceX, and other relevant agencies.

The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas. Disruptions to critical intelligence-sharing, threat-warning, or communications capabilities in an active war zone can have life-threatening consequences. The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability.

We urge your office to initiate an immediate investigation and provide written confirmation of its status, together with an initial briefing, no later than November 1, 2026.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this urgent matter.

Sincerely,

/s/

title: Cornyn: Texas Receives Additional $78 Million to Improve Rural Health Care
text:
AUSTIN – U.S. Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) released the following statement after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced the allocation of an additional $78 million to 216 rural hospital districts in Texas for chronic disease prevention, workforce recruitment and retention, equipment upgrades, and facility improvements. The funding comes from the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), which Sen. Cornyn championed and helped establish through enactment of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act:

“Investing in rural health care is just one of the key components of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which will improve the lives of countless Texans,” said Sen. Cornyn. “I was proud to support this legislation, now law, to establish the Rural Health Transformation Program, and I am glad to see this additional $78 million in funding to help Texans with chronic conditions access care across the Lone Star State.”

Background:

The funding will support community-based prevention, wellness, and nutrition programs to improve health outcomes and address chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory disease, and obesity. These resources are in addition to the initial allocation announced in September of $51 million to 68 rural hospital districts across Texas. Last year, Sen. Cornyn announced the Trump administration allocated $281,319,361 for Texas from the Rural Health Transformation Program. Prior to that, Sen. Cornyn and Congressman August Pfluger (TX-11) led a letter with members of the Texas congressional delegation to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, urging him to prioritize funding for the State of Texas. Sen. Cornyn also released a statement in support of Texas’ application last November.

title: Cramer, FWS Director Nesvik Visit Farmers in Prairie Pothole Region to Assess Impact of Biden-Era FWS Rule
text:
***Click herefor media resources.***

GUELPH, N.D. – U.S. Senator Kevin Cramer (R-ND) joined U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) Director Brian Nesvik on a tour in the heart of prairie pothole territory in Dickey County. Nesvik and his Principal Deputy Tyler Kellogg went to North Dakota at Cramer’s request to see the devastating effects of a rule imposed by the Biden administration in 2024, one Cramer says “is nothing short of theft of property.” The two walked through fields scarred by saline deposits caused by FWS policies barring water management, as well areas where farmers foster healthy habitat.

The Biden rule was another in a long line of federal betrayals of landowners, many of whom are operating on land encumbered by easements which were not sold or recorded accurately, leading to disputes over easement boundaries. President Biden doubled down on this federal overreach by issuing a rule in 2024, claiming control of massive, arbitrary boundaries around wetlands. The FWS is using this ambiguous Biden rule to assert broader control over private land and agricultural activities, for which it never paid landowners and farmers. In one egregious example observed today, the FWS claimed control of an additional 2,800 ft beyond the easement boundary. The breach of contract exploits farmers, steals their land and turns pristine prairie potholes into salt-encrusted eyesores.

“My hope is today’s visit by a high-ranking decision maker in the Trump administration regarding issues surrounding the illegal taking of farmers’ land helps the President better understand how wrong it is to support the Biden Rule,” said Cramer. “I am grateful to Director Nesvik and Principal Deputy Kellogg for taking the issue seriously enough to work directly with the affected landowners, the real stewards of their property. Too many bureaucrats make rules from behind their desks in a marble building, with no consideration for the real-world effects on wildlife and people.”

Farmers are facing costly disputes, complex regulations, and federal criminal liability over water management, farming practices, improvements, and where the government’s authority begins and ends. The Supreme Court’s landmark Waters of the United States decision made it clear, landowners need certainty, and they should know what land is covered and what activities are permitted when legal jeopardy is on the line. They need to know the value and productive use of their property will not be undermined by arbitrary federal interpretations.

Cramer has pressed agency leaders and nominees for changes to the management of wetland easements, including bringing federal officials to North Dakota to meet directly with landowners. Just three weeks earlier, Cramer hosted Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum in Valley City for a roundtable with area farmers whose land has been seized or degraded by the Fish and Wildlife Service’s aggressive practices.

Former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt visited the state in 2019, then-FWS Director Aurelia Skipwith visited in 2020, and Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Shannon Estenoz visited in 2021, as officials sought to hear about the challenges facing landowners in the prairie pothole region.

Cramer’s efforts resulted in an agreement from the FWS to revisit its mapping process and classification methodology, but when the agency announced it was abandoning those efforts to replace the Biden rule, Cramer refused to go along. He has a hold on all Trump nominees until the issue is settled and landowners can farm without fear. He has rewarded “good behavior toward a solution” and released a small number of nominations in response to good-faith efforts by the Department of the Interior and the White House. Cramer has not said whether today’s visit will be similarly rewarded, but noted his patience is wearing thin.

“We need a solution and we need it fast,” continued Cramer. “The alternative is to go to court, and a number of our farmers and organizations are prepared to do that. They’d rather settle their grievances amicably, but so far, the environmental activists seem unwilling to compromise.”

Today’s tour was hosted by North Dakota farmers Steve Hansen, Scott German and his father Mick, who was present when his dad signed the original easement with the FWS, and Drew and Kyle Courtney.

title: Duckworth, Senate Democrats Call on HHS Secretary to Reverse Plans for Trump Administration Lawyers to Represent Unaccompanied Children in Immigration Court
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – Today, U.S. Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Richard J. Durbin (D-IL), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Edward J. Markey (D-MA) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) urged Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to reverse the decision for HHS attorneys to represent unaccompanied children against the Trump Administration’s own deportation machine and restore independent legal counsel immediately. In the letter to Secretary Kennedy, the Senators underscored how failing to reverse this decision would result in a clear conflict of interest, especially since HHS has a responsibility to care for these kids in custody and already shares personal information with immigration enforcement. The Senators’ letter comes after Duckworth held a press conference in Chicago lambasting the Trump Administration for this latest attempt to violate these children’s due process rights and called for the reversal of these egregious plans.

“HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer,” wrote the Senators. “The immigration judge works for the Trump Administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable.”

As a direct result of the Trump Administration cutting funding to facilitate independent legal aid for unaccompanied migrant children, this year tens of thousands of children faced immigration judges with no legal representation. In their letter, the Senators cited how the bipartisan Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 legally requires HHS to make every effort to secure pro bono counsel that will provide independent representation and protect the kids from mistreatment or exploitation. By appointing HHS attorneys to these cases instead, the Administration intends to place these children in removal proceedings led by judges working for the U.S. Department of Justice with legal representation that is anything but independent.

The Senators continued, “Reunifying children with their families is HHS’s job. Legally representing an unaccompanied child, including against HHS in legal proceedings, is not. It is a job for an experienced, expert and independent attorney trained to represent unaccompanied children who are often experiencing extreme stress and trauma.”

Additionally, the Senators highlighted that HHS’s decision would discourage these kids from reporting abuse, trafficking and dangerous family circumstances to their lawyers for fear of the information reaching immigration enforcement. Notably, HHS’s announcement mentions no procedures for screening conflicts, protecting client confidentiality or insulating attorneys from HHS’s custodial functions.

“HHS cannot serve as both custodian and counsel. You must meet your statutory obligation to these children. Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them. We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court,” the Senators concluded.

The full text of the letter is available on Senator Duckworth’s website and below.

We call on you to rescind your decision to have U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) attorneys represent unaccompanied children in immigration proceedings through the newly created Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division (UACLRD). HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer.

The immigration judge works for the Trump administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable. We demand that you:

Rescind the decision creating the UACLRD and confirm in writing, no later than October 30, 2026, that no HHS attorney will represent an unaccompanied child in immigration proceedings; and

Restore independent counsel for these children by making every effort to utilize pro bono counsel, as section 235(c)(5) of the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 (TVPRA) (8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(5)) requires, and by funding experienced, independent legal service providers, as 45 CFR 410.1309 provides, through competitive, merit-based awards.

On September 29, 2026, HHS published a notice in the Federal Register that places the UACLRD within its Office of the General Counsel (OGC). According to the notice, the division “provides direct legal services to unaccompanied alien children,” including “introductory legal orientation concerning immigration proceedings” and representation in immigration court. The division reports to the General Counsel through a designated Deputy General Counsel and “may coordinate with other OGC components and appropriate Federal entities as necessary” to carry out its work. The notice says the division will not advise the Administration for Children and Families or the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) on matters involving its clients, but it sets out no procedures for screening conflicts, protecting client confidentiality or insulating attorneys from HHS’s custodial functions.

HHS has described the division as “an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families.” Reunifying children with their families is HHS’s job. Legally representing an unaccompanied child, including against HHS in legal proceedings, is not. It is a job for an experienced, expert and independent attorney trained to represent unaccompanied children who are often experiencing extreme stress and trauma.

Congress was clear in the bipartisan TVPRA. HHS must ensure, to the greatest extent practicable, that unaccompanied children who are or have been in Federal custody have counsel “to represent them in legal proceedings or matters and protect them from mistreatment, exploitation, and trafficking,” and it must make every effort to utilize the services of pro bono counsel who agree to represent these children without charge.

HHS’s own regulations require that the legal orientation children in ORR custody receive “be provided by an independent legal service provider,” and they provide for funding legal service providers to represent children directly when pro bono counsel is not practicable. The September 29 notice assigns legal orientation to attorneys in your General Counsel’s office. An HHS employee is not an independent legal service provider. For nearly two decades, under administrations of both parties, HHS met these obligations by funding outside legal service providers with the expertise and independence these cases require. HHS has spent more than a year dismantling that system.

ORR withheld payments to legal service providers in late 2025 after they declined to hand over confidential client information, and in August a Federal court ordered HHS to pay more than $65 million in overdue invoices. HHS let the contract covering more than 20,000 children expire on July 31, 2026. Your Department then turned to a small law firm with little immigration experience, which withdrew, and to Our Rescue, a controversial nonprofit with no apparent experience representing children in immigration court, whose $158 million no-bid sole source contract is stayed.

Today, children are left with an ineffective temporary provider, the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, whose representatives have reportedly sat silent at some children’s hearings and missed others. Many children in custody have reportedly not received the legal orientation HHS’s regulations require, and in August a one-year-old appeared in an Arizona immigration court without a lawyer. Having created this gap, HHS now proposes not to fix it but to fill it with its own employees.

The conflict of interest is clear. UACLRD attorneys would be HHS employees supervised by the HHS General Counsel, who answers to you, the official responsible for every custody, placement and release decision HHS makes. In immigration court, they would face U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) attorneys seeking the child’s removal, before an immigration judge who answers to the Attorney General of the United States.

Professional conduct rules in Illinois and across the country prohibit a lawyer from letting the person who employs or pays the lawyer direct or regulate the lawyer’s professional judgment on a client’s behalf. Federal public defenders, sometimes cited as precedent for government-paid counsel, operate under the Federal judiciary, independent of the Department of Justice that prosecutes their clients.

The UACLRD would sit inside the agency that holds its clients in custody. Consider a child abused while in ORR care. Will a UACLRD attorney zealously gather evidence and litigate against HHS colleagues or HHS grantees? If the child may be eligible for a U visa as the victim of a qualifying crime, will the HHS attorney pursue that relief when it exposes failures in HHS’s own program? Will the attorney challenge Executive Office for Immigration Review decisions in Federal court, or argue for an interpretation of immigration law that contradicts the Attorney General?

The conflict is sharpest for children seeking Special Immigrant Juvenile (SIJ) status, a path to lawful permanent residence for children who cannot reunify with one or both parents because of abuse, neglect, abandonment or a similar basis under State law. A child in ORR care in Illinois, as elsewhere, may petition a State court for the findings SIJ status requires. But Federal law bars a juvenile court from determining the custody status or placement of a child in HHS custody unless you specifically consent to that jurisdiction, and ORR decides where each child is placed, including whether to transfer a child to a State where those findings are harder to obtain. A UACLRD attorney would have to ask the attorney’s own employer for that consent and challenge that employer’s placement and release decisions to keep the child’s case alive and win the child’s release to a safe, vetted sponsor. An independent lawyer faces no such conflict.

Children must also be able to tell their lawyers about abuse, trafficking and family circumstances, with confidence that the information will be properly reported and without fear that the information will reach immigration enforcement. Independent legal advocates can play an important role in referring cases with indication of trafficking directly to the Office of Trafficking in Persons (OTIP). But without independent legal advocates, HHS’s recent policy change requiring care providers to refer cases to ORR instead of directly to OTIP in 24 hours, as mandated by Federal regulation, could endanger children at risk of trafficking even more than it already does.

HHS has shown it cannot be trusted to protect children who report abuse or trafficking. According to internal Federal data reported by Reuters, immigration authorities have arrested more than 12,000 people, including children and their sponsors, after tips from ORR. No child can be expected to confide in a lawyer employed by the agency that supplied those tips. The notice does not bar the UACLRD from sharing client information with the Department of Homeland Security. It permits coordination with “appropriate Federal entities,” limited only by the attorneys’ “professional responsibilities” to their clients.

HHS cannot serve as both custodian and counsel. You must meet your statutory obligation to these children. Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them. We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court.

-30-

title: Fischer, Ricketts Applaud Nomination of Eric Hamilton to U.S. District Court of Nebraska
text:
OMAHA – U.S. Senators Deb Fischer (R-NE) and Pete Ricketts (R-NE) today applauded President Donald J. Trump’s nomination of Eric Hamilton to fill an upcoming vacancy on the U.S. District Court for Nebraska. Fischer and Ricketts recommended Hamilton to President Trump to fill the vacancy.

“Eric Hamilton has built an impressive legal career defined by integrity, sound judgment, and a steadfast commitment to the rule of law,” Fischer said. “He has served Nebraska with distinction, and I am confident he will continue that tradition of service on the federal bench. I was proud to recommend his nomination to President Trump and look forward to supporting him through the Senate confirmation process.”

“As Nebraska’s Solicitor General, Eric Hamilton served our state with integrity,” Ricketts said. “I am proud to support his nomination to serve as District Judge of Nebraska. He has dedicated his career to public service and demonstrated a strong commitment to the rule of law. I am confident he will bring those same principles serving in this next role.”

Hamilton currently serves as Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the Federal Programs Branch of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Civil Division, a position he has held since 2025. He previously served as Solicitor General of Nebraska, as an Assistant Solicitor General of Texas, and as Associate Counsel to President Trump during his first term. Hamilton practiced law in Washington, D.C. and clerked for Judge Thomas M. Hardiman of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. Hamilton graduated from Stanford Law School (2013), where he wrote for the Stanford Law Review, and received his undergraduate degree from the University of Nebraska, Lincoln.

title: Gallego, Bicameral Collation Press Trump Administration on Illegal Reallocation of Funding for Minority Serving Institutions
text:
WASHINGTON — Last week, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined Senator Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI) and a bicameral coalition of Democratic lawmakers in pressing U.S. Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon on the administration’s illegal decision to redirect funding from Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) to other institutions.

In the letter to Secretary McMahon, the lawmakers emphasized that while increasing funding for those institutions is important, the additional investments cannot come at the expense of MSIs that serve millions of students nationwide. The letter also reiterated the illegal nature of the decision to redirect funding that was statutorily authorized in specific amounts for specific purposes — in clear violation of the law.

“This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges — while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so,” the lawmakers wrote.

There are currently more than 800 federally recognized MSIs which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs), and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). These MSIs serve more than 5 million students collectively and have been receiving Congressionally directed federal support for more than 30 years.

In December 2019, Congress passed and President Trump signed into law the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act), permanently authorizing $255 million in mandatory funding for HBCUs, TCCUs, and MSIs.

“The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year,” the lawmakers wrote.

“To be clear, mandatory funding for [these institutions] — as provided by the FUTURE Act — cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds,” the lawmakers continued.

The lawmakers concluded their letter by emphasizing the importance of supporting all MSIs — not just HBCUs and TCCUs.

“ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs. Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education,” the lawmakers concluded.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Demand Trump FCC Withdraw Proposal To Undermine E-Rate Program
text:
Lawmakers Argue That Dismantling E-Rate Will Widen The Digital Divide And Raise Costs For The Communities That Can Least Afford It

U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined a bicameral group of colleagues in urging Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr to withdraw the Commission’s damaging proposal to eliminate or limit the E-Rate program. In June, the Carr FCC voted to open a rulemaking examining E-Rate, which helps schools and libraries across the country afford reliable internet access.

“Every school should have the resources it needs to provide our kids with a high-quality education,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Millions of children who lack reliable internet access are at risk of falling behind without the critical connectivity that the E-Rate program provides. I urge the FCC to immediately withdraw its harmful proposal, and I will continue fighting to protect E-Rate and keep investing in our schools, libraries, and future leaders.”

E-Rate helps over 96% of U.S. public schools access high-speed internet. In 2025, nearly $182 million in E-Rate funding was committed to school districts and libraries across New York State, helping them afford reliable internet.

On Long Island, E-Rate saved Suffolk County public libraries over $300,000 last year, covering roughly 60% of their broadband bills. At the same time, internet demand in Nassau County school districts jumped 31% over the past year, a spike that could put significant strain on district budgets without E-Rate discounts.

In the letter, the lawmakers wrote, “Schools and libraries help develop the next generation of engineers, scientists, and cybersecurity professionals, including in communities that have historically lacked access to those opportunities. Cutting E-Rate would narrow that talent pipeline. Maintaining connectivity in every school and library is therefore an investment in America’s technological leadership, economic competitiveness, and national security.”

“We strongly support measures to protect children online and address concerns around excessive screen time. But cutting E-Rate is not a child-safety measure. E-Rate funds broadband connectivity — not laptops, tablets, applications, or online content — and recipients must already comply with the Children’s Internet Protection Act, including by using filtering and blocking tools, adopting internet-safety policies, and educating students about appropriate online behavior. States and local communities, meanwhile, are developing targeted policies governing when and how students use devices in schools — an appropriate way to address screen-time concerns, rather than cutting broadband support. The Commission should not use child safety as a pretext to dismantle the secure, managed broadband infrastructure that schools and libraries need to educate students and help them navigate the digital world safely,” the lawmakers continued.

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Chris Coons (D-DE), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Dick Durbin (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Angus King (I-ME), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Edward Markey (D-MA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Chris Murphy (D-CT), Patty Murray (D-WA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Gary Peters (D-MI), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Tina Smith (D-MN), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Mark Warner (D-VA), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Ron Wyden (D-OR).

It was also signed by U.S. Representatives Doris Matsui (CA-07), Rob Menendez (NJ-08), Grace Meng (NY-06), and more than 60 other members of the House Democratic Caucus.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to hold the FCC accountable and expand internet access for students across New York. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she urged the FCC to immediately provide more E-Rate funding so students learning remotely could access reliable internet from home. She also demanded answers from the FCC about its decision to block states that had already invested in rural broadband from a new federal funding program for unserved communities. Last year, she led the New York delegation in pushing the Trump administration to protect more than $270 million in federal broadband funding that New York can use to make internet service more affordable.

title: Grassley-Backed Infrastructure Law Bringing $62.7 Million in Improvements to Iowa Railroads
text:
BUTLER COUNTY, IOWA – U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) is welcoming over $62.7 million in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Transportation to improve the safety, efficiency and performance of the Cedar Rapids and Iowa City Railway (CRANDIC) and Iowa Interstate Railroad.

The funding comes from the Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grant program, which was first authorized in 2015 and later expanded by the Grassley-backed Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA).

“I'm glad to see the Department of Transportation investing in Iowa to improve the safety and efficiency of our railroads. The bipartisan infrastructure law I supported continues to deliver for our state and grow our economy by helping move Iowa’s world-class products to market safely and swiftly,” Grassley said.

The funding to the Iowa Interstate Railroad will be used to rehabilitate 18 miles of track, including in Iowa City, Des Moines and Davenport. The funding to the Cedar Rapids and Iowa City Railway will be used to procure three Tier 4 line-haul freight locomotives for use in eastern Iowa. Additional details follow.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION

NOTICE OF AWARD FOR IOWA INTERSTATE RAILROAD

Date: 10/19/2026

Grant: FY25-26 CRISI

Project: Fortify Iowa Interstate Railroad with Steel & Ties

Locality: Des Moines, Iowa City, Davenport (IA); Bureau, La Salle, Henry (IL), IA

Applicant:Iowa Interstate Railroad, LLC

Grant Amount: $48,176,960

DOT Agency Disbursing Funds: Federal Railroad Administration

Description: The proposed project was selected for construction and includes track rehabilitation and bridge replacement in Iowa City, Des Moines and Davenport, Iowa and Bureau, La Salle and Henry, Illinois. The project will rehabilitate approximately 18 miles of track by replacing rail, ties and a bridge. The project aligns with the selection criteria by enhancing safety, improving system and service performance and improving reliability as the project will result in FRA Class 3 track standards and reduce the risk of derailments. Iowa Interstate will contribute a 25% non-federal cost share. This project qualifies for the statutory set aside for projects in rural areas.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION

NOTICE OF AWARD FOR CEDAR RAPIDS AND IOWA CITY RAILWAY

Date: 10/19/2026

Grant: FY25-26 CRISI

Project: Cedar Rapids and Iowa City Railway American Diesel Advancement Project (CADAP)

Locality: Cedar Rapids, Iowa City, IA

Applicant: Cedar Rapids and Iowa City Railway

Grant Amount: $14,549,744

DOT Agency Disbursing Funds: Federal Railroad Administration

Description: The proposed project that was selected for construction includes the procurement of three Tier 4, line-haul locomotives for use in Eastern Iowa. The project aligns with the selection criteria by improving system and service performance as the project will ensure safe and efficient railcar movement and allow for more operational flexibility. The Cedar Rapids and Iowa City Railway will contribute a 35% non-Federal cost share.

title: Senator Hassan Visits Canterbury Shaker Village, Highlights New Hampshire Historic Preservation Efforts
text:
CANTERBURY – U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan visited Canterbury Shaker Village and heard from staff about their work to preserve the historic site and educate visitors about New Hampshire’s history. During the visit, Senator Hassan discussed federal funding that she helped secure to support preservation efforts, as well as her bipartisan legislation to help designate Canterbury Shaker Village as a National Heritage Area.

“Canterbury Shaker Village is an important part of New Hampshire’s history and gives visitors an opportunity to learn about the Shakers and their unique way of life,” said Senator Hassan. “It was great to be back at the Village to hear about the staff’s work to preserve this history for future generations. I will keep advocating to bring federal grant dollars back to New Hampshire to support historic sites like Canterbury Shaker Village.”

Established in 1792, Canterbury Shaker Village is among the oldest and most preserved Shaker communities in the country. Today, the Village gives visitors an opportunity to learn about more than 200 years of Shaker history through its historic buildings, exhibits, and educational programs.

Senator Hassan has supported efforts to help preserve the Village’s historic infirmary, improve the care and management of its collections, and develop new exhibits highlighting the Shakers’ economic history and innovations.

Senator Hassan also introduced bipartisan legislation to authorize a study of the feasibility of designating Canterbury Shaker Village as a National Heritage Area, the first step toward securing the designation and making the Village eligible for additional federal support. The legislation advanced out of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee earlier this year.

title: Heinrich, Cassidy Introduce Legislation to Help Improve Kids’ Literacy
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Dr. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), Chair of the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee, introduced the Literacy Improvement For Transformation (LIFT) Act, legislation to improve child literacy outcomes in New Mexico, Louisiana, and nationwide.

Early reading interventions help students build the skills they need to succeed in school and beyond. According to the Annie E. Casey Foundation, children who aren’t reading proficiently by third grade are four times more likely to leave high school without a diploma than their peers who are proficient readers.

Students in rural communities and students with learning disabilities often face additional barriers to developing strong reading skills. Hiring more reading and literacy specialists can help close the literacy gap by providing targeted support and personalized instruction to students who need it most.

The LIFT Act will ensure every K-12 public school has at least one full-time reading or literacy specialist on staff to help students strengthen their reading skills, overcome challenges, and build a strong foundation for lifelong learning.

“Every child deserves the chance to succeed, and that starts with learning to read and write at grade level or above,” said Heinrich. “My LIFT Act will help schools hire dedicated reading specialists to work directly with students and build a strong foundation for success in school and beyond.”

“Children with dyslexia are bright, but without the right support, they are being left behind,” said Dr. Cassidy. “This legislation helps schools put more trained reading specialists in classrooms so students with dyslexia and other struggling readers receive the instruction they need to succeed.”

Heinrich and Cassidy’s LIFT Act establishes a grant program to help state and local education agencies, nonprofits, and Bureau of Indian Education K-12 schools hire full-time reading specialists to improve literacy and close achievement gaps.

Specifically, the LIFT Act:

Ensures reading specialists spend at least 80% of their time working directly with students and teachers.

Supports ongoing professional development for reading specialists, including evidence-based literacy certifications.

Prioritizes hiring reading specialists to support the lowest-performing students and students with disabilities.

The legislation is endorsed by National Center for Learning Disabilities, Teach Plus, The May Center, and Nancy L. Orta, 2026 New Mexico Teacher of the Year.

“Providing every elementary and secondary school in New Mexico with a literacy specialist would build on the momentum created by our state’s investment in the Science of Reading. A literacy specialist can help teachers identify students who are struggling with reading, model effective language arts instruction, and provide coaching and support to educators as they work to meet the needs of every learner,” said Nancy L. Orta, 2026 New Mexico Teacher of the Year, K-12 Intervention & Data Coach, Content Specialist at Las Cruces Public Schools. “New Mexico’s children and their families are too important for us to stop investing in their futures. We have an opportunity to build on the progress we’ve made and continue giving our students the literacy skills they need to succeed.”

title: Hirono, Murphy, Kelly, Schiff Slam Attorney General Blanche for Illegally Allowing Sale of Guns to Teenagers, Increasing Likelihood of School Shootings
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Senator Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI) joined Senators Chris Murphy (D-CT), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), and Adam Schiff (D-CA) on Friday in a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (DOJ) decision to break with decades of precedent and unilaterally refuse to enforce a prohibition against the sale of handguns to people under the age of 21.

The Senators highlighted the enormous risks to public safety when teens have access to handguns: “The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.”

The Senators laid out the decades-long, bipartisan consensus to ban gun dealers from selling firearms to teenagers: “Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that ‘it shall be unlawful’ for a [federally licensed firearms dealer] to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.”

The Senators argued DOJ’s decision is another attempt to seize power from the judicial branch and Congress: “The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has ‘deeply divided members of the federal bench.’ Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.”

The Senators concluded by requesting Blanche provide the following information on the authority and research supporting his decision:

A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

While the State of Hawaii maintains the lowest rate of gun violence in the country because of its strict gun safety laws, Senator Hirono has long advocated for stronger, common-sense gun safety policies nationwide. In June 2026, Senator Hirono slammed the Supreme Court’s Wolford v. Lopez decision, which changed longstanding Hawaii gun regulation and made it easier for people to bring guns onto private property. In June of 2025, she introduced the Gas-Operated Semi-Automatic Firearms Exclusion (GOSAFE) Act, alongside the Banning Unlawful Machinegun Parts (BUMP) Act, designed to protect communities from gun violence, while safeguarding Americans’ constitutional right to own a firearm for legitimate self-defense, hunting, and sporting purposes. In March of that year, she championed the Extreme Risk Protection Order Expansion Act, designed to prevent individuals in crisis from accessing deadly weapons. In February 2025, Hirono introduced the Keep Americans Safe Act (KASA) to reinstate a nationwide ban on the sale, transfer, possession, import, or manufacture of high-capacity gun magazines that hold more than ten rounds. That month, the Senator also cosponsored legislation to raise the minimum age to purchase assault weapons and high-capacity ammunition magazines from 18 to 21.

In sending this oversight letter to DOJ, Senators Hirono, Murphy, Kelly, and Schiff were joined by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Chris Coons (D-DE), Dick Durbin (D-Il), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ed Markey (D-MA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI).

A full transcript of the letter is available below. A copy of the letter is available here.

Dear Attorney General Blanche:

We write regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (the Department) decision to cease enforcement of longstanding federal restrictions on the sale of handguns to individuals under the age of 21 by federally licensed firearms dealers (FFLs). This significant change in federal enforcement policy raises serious questions about the Department’s legal justification, and we request information regarding the analysis underlying its decision.

On September 18, 2026, the Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published a legal opinion concluding that 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1)—the federal prohibition on FFLs selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds—violate the Second Amendment, and that federal prosecutors may no longer prosecute FFLs that sell handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds who are not otherwise prohibited from gun possession.[1] Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that “it shall be unlawful” for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21.[2] Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.

The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has “deeply divided members of the federal bench.” Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.

The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.

The Department’s decision to unilaterally cease enforcement of this provision of law raises serious questions and concerns. Thus, we request the Department provide:

A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

Please provide the requested information and documents by November 16, 2026.

###

title: King Releases Statement After Meeting with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy

title: Lankford, Rosen Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Expand Child Care Options on Military Bases
text:
OKLAHOMA CITY, OK — US Senators James Lankford (R-OK) and Jacky Rosen (D-NV) recently introduced a bipartisan bill to expand access to child care on military bases for servicemembers and their families. The Best Practices for Military Child Care Homes Actwould direct the Department of War (DoW) to develop a best practices guide for military families hoping to establish a home-based certified child care center. Military families continue to experience child care shortages across installations. Family Child Care (FCC) homes are an important tool for expanding available child care capacity at installations and increasing opportunities for military spouse employment, but prospective providers often face unnecessary barriers when attempting to start an FCC home program. This bill would streamline the process and improve access to information, making it easier to establish and operate on-base child care centers to meet the growing demand for reliable, flexible child care.

“Military families shouldn’t have to navigate unnecessary hurdles to find reliable child care. Our servicemembers need to know their children are cared for so they can focus on their mission, and military spouses should have opportunities to support other families while building their own careers,” said Lankford. “This bipartisan bill will help make it easier to establish child care homes on base, expand options for military families, and strengthen military readiness.”

“Our servicemembers and their families sacrifice so much to protect our freedoms. That’s why it’s so important that we make sure they have access to the community and support they need while living on base,” said Rosen. “This bipartisan bill will help us close the gaps in child care services that we are seeing across the country for servicemembers and their families, while opening the door for new providers to bring much-needed services for our military families.”

Background

Lankford has worked to support military families through the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) throughout his entire time in the Senate. The FY2021 NDAA included provisions he supported to allow military spouses to maintain professional licenses across state lines and strengthen oversight of military housing. In 2023, Lankford’s Military Spouse Employment Act was included in the Senate’s FY2024 NDAA, providing authority to hire military spouses for fully remote federal positions. In 2025, he also secured a $54 million investment in a new Child Development Center at Tinker Air Force Base to expand child care facilities for military families.

title: SENATOR MCCORMICK, ATTORNEY GENERAL BLANCHE HIGHLIGHT PROGRESS IN FIGHT AGAINST FENTANYL
text:
WILKES-BARRE, PA — U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) today hosted U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) Administrator Terry Cole, White House Office of National Drug Control Policy Director Sara Carter, U.S. Congressman Rob Bresnahan (R-PA-08), and other federal, state, and local officials for a roundtable and press conference on efforts to combat fentanyl trafficking and reduce overdose deaths across Pennsylvania.

“Every death lost to fentanyl is one too many, and communities across Northeastern Pennsylvania know the devastating toll this drug has taken,” said Senator McCormick. “When federal, state, and local law enforcement have the resources and support they need, we can take on the trafficking networks poisoning our communities and save lives. I’m grateful to President Trump and Attorney General Blanche for making this fight a priority and working with local leaders to turn the tide on this crisis.”

“We are taking the fight against fentanyl seriously because we have a President who knows there are real people affected by these crimes,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “We cannot rest until the parents, brothers, sisters, and children of the victims of fentanyl poisoning know they will never have a friend or neighbor impacted by the scourge of fentanyl.”

“Fentanyl continues to devastate families and communities across Pennsylvania, and we need to do everything we can to stop these deadly drugs from reaching our streets. That means cracking down on drug traffickers, supporting our law enforcement officers, and making sure people struggling with addiction have access to treatment,” said Rep. Bresnahan. “That’s why I secured more than $1 million for the Monroe County District Attorney’s Opioid Crimes Section to help combat drug-related crime and prevent overdose deaths. I thank Attorney General Blanche for joining us today and his work to address this crisis. We need action, accountability, and results to protect our communities and save lives.”

Senator McCormick has made combating fentanyl a priority. His first piece of legislation introduced in the Senate was the bipartisan Joint Task Force to Counter Illicit Synthetic Narcotics Act of 2025, which would strengthen federal coordination to combat fentanyl trafficking, target cartels and money laundering, and address China’s role in supplying precursor chemicals. Senator McCormick supported the HALT Fentanyl Act, signed into law in July 2025, and introduced the Nitazene Control Act to address the emerging threat of highly potent synthetic opioids.

The gathering highlighted the strong partnerships already in place among federal, state, and local law enforcement to disrupt trafficking routes, including the I-81 corridor, and hold those responsible for bringing deadly drugs into Pennsylvania communities accountable. These coordinated efforts are delivering results and demonstrating what can be accomplished when agencies work together toward a common goal. Pennsylvania has seen a significant decline in fentanyl-related deaths, with reported deaths sharply declining from around 4,000 during the peak of the Biden administration to 1,768, according to 2025 preliminary data. Senator McCormick emphasized the importance of building on this progress through continued investment in treatment, recovery, naloxone access, and community organizations helping individuals overcome addiction.
