title: NEWS: Schiff, Murphy, Kelly, Slam Attorney General Blanche for Illegally Allowing Sale of Guns to Teenagers, Increasing Likelihood of School Shootings
text:
Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on Friday led in a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers on the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) decision to break with decades of precedent and unilaterally refuse to enforce a prohibition against the sale of handguns to people under the age of 21.

Schiff, Murphy, and Kelly also fought back against these ATF rule changes through the rulemaking comment process.

The Senators highlighted the enormous risks to public safety if handguns are placed in teens’ hands: “The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.”

The Senators laid out the decades-long, bipartisan consensus on banning gun dealers from selling firearms to teenagers: “Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that ‘it shall be unlawful’ for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.”

The Senators argued Blanche’s decision is another authoritarian power grab over the judicial branch and Congress:“The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has ‘deeply divided members of the federal bench.’ Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.”

The Senators concluded by requesting Blanche provide the following information on the authority and research supporting his decision:

A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

Schiff, Murphy, and Kelly were joined by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

A full transcript of the letter is available below. A copy of the letter is available here.

Dear Attorney General Blanche:

We write regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (the Department) decision to cease enforcement of longstanding federal restrictions on the sale of handguns to individuals under the age of 21 by federally licensed firearms dealers (FFLs). This significant change in federal enforcement policy raises serious questions about the Department’s legal justification, and we request information regarding the analysis underlying its decision.

On September 18, 2026, the Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published a legal opinion concluding that 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1)—the federal prohibition on FFLs selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds—violate the Second Amendment, and that federal prosecutors may no longer prosecute FFLs that sell handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds who are not otherwise prohibited from gun possession.[1] Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that “it shall be unlawful” for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21.[2] Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.

The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has “deeply divided members of the federal bench.” Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.

The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.

The Department’s decision to unilaterally cease enforcement of this provision of law raises serious questions and concerns. Thus, we request the Department provide:

A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

Please provide the requested information and documents by November 16, 2026.

###

title: Shaheen Receives Award at New Hampshire Hospital Association Annual Meeting, Visits Bartlett Experimental Forest to Hear Updates from USDA
text:
(Bartlett, NH) – Yesterday, U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration and Related Agencies (Ag-FDA) Appropriations Subcommittee, attended and delivered remarks at the New Hampshire Hospital Association’s Annual Meeting before heading to Bartlett Experimental Forest to visit the research facilities and hear updates from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Photos from today’s events can be found HERE.

In Bretton Woods, Shaheen received the James A. Hamilton Founder's Award, the highest recognition given by the New Hampshire Hospital Association, in honor of her decades of service to New Hampshire's health care providers and unwavering commitment to expanding access to health care across the Granite State. At the Association’s Annual Meeting, Shaheen delivered remarks focused on the challenges that New Hampshire's health care system is facing – especially following congressional Republicans’ decision to cut billions in health care spending – and in recognition of the health care providers who work tirelessly on behalf of Granite Staters.

“It was an honor to receive the New Hampshire Hospital Association’s highest award and to attend their annual gathering to recognize the strides we’ve made together to improve New Hampshire’s health care system and expand access to quality care for Granite State families,” said Senator Shaheen. “Congressional Republicans’ slashes to federal health care funding in combination with persistent workforce shortages and the expiration of the Affordable Care Act enhanced premium tax credits, are creating great headwinds for the most rural parts of our state. As we confront these challenges, I know the Association and our health care professionals will work hand in hand with communities to find solutions that deliver quality, affordable care for Granite Staters everywhere.”

Shaheen has a long track record of securing resources to support health care facilities and hospitals across New Hampshire and has been a steadfast supporter of programs that help bolster the health care workforce. Shaheen secured millions of dollars to support key health care priorities in New Hampshire in the Fiscal Year 2026 Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education and Related Agencies appropriations bill, including funding for health care facility improvements and workforce development. Recently, Shaheen toured Cottage Hospital in Woodsville to see renovations to the facility and visited Southern New Hampshire Health to see how critical radiology equipment funded in part by Congressionally Directed Spending she secured is helping the hospital to increase health care accessibility.

Later, in Bartlett, Shaheen toured the research lab and other buildings at Bartlett Experimental Forest, a nationally recognized facility that plays a critical role in advancing forest management and environmental research, alongside USDA officials. Shaheen met with stakeholders to discuss the impacts of the Trump Administration’s planned closure of the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) buildings at Bartlett, which threatens the critical research and ongoing efforts to save Bartlett. The visit follows Shaheen’s efforts to protect the facility from closure and ensure the Forest Service continues more than 90 years of research at the site.

“Since the Trump Administration announced their plans to reorganize the Forest Service, threatening both Bartlett and Hubbard Brook experimental forests, I’ve fought to protect these critical research facilities from closure,” said Senator Shaheen. “Earlier this year, I was proud to secure a commitment from Agriculture Secretary Rollins that Hubbard Brook would remain open, but Bartlett’s future remains in doubt. For decades, Bartlett has produced critical research for our state and the entire region, and I don’t intend to let that cease. While today’s discussions with officials from the USDA was productive, there’s more work to be done to protect Bartlett and restore Forest Service staffing.”

As Ranking Member of Ag-FDA Appropriations Subcommittee, Shaheen has been outspoken against the Trump Administration’s plans to reorganize U.S. Forest Service earlier this year. Following the announcement of this effort, Shaheen has led efforts to protect New Hampshire’s experimental forests. Through conversations with Secretary Rollins and New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte, Shaheen secured confirmation that the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) would not close New Hampshire’s Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest and a commitment from Secretary Rollins to review plans at Bartlett Experimental Forest. In June, Shaheen continued her work to hold the Administration accountable by pressing Secretary Rollins to commit to both restoring staffing levels at Bartlett Experimental Forest and to making sure the facilities at Bartlett remain open.

title: Ahead of Midterm Elections, Warner, Padilla, Himes, and Morelle Urge Leading Tech Companies to Not Detract From Efforts to Ensure Elections are Free, Fair, and Secure
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), Vice Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Alex Padilla (D-CA), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, and Representatives Jim Himes (CT-04), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and Joe Morelle (NY-25), Ranking Member of the House Administration Committee, urged leading technology companies to ensure their platforms and tools help protect the integrity of our elections and support free, fair, and secure midterms.

This letter follows up on Sen. Warner’s letter from March where he pushed tech companies to take action against deepfakes and maliciously manipulated media. Additionally, this letter references the 2024 Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI, where leading technology companies – including some of those receiving this letter – pledged to work together to detect and counter harmful AI content surrounding the 2024 elections.

In a letter to the CEOs of Adobe, Alphabet, Anthropic, Black Forest Labs, Bluesky, Discord, ElevenLabs, LinkedIn, Meta, Microsoft, Midjourney, Mistral, OpenAI, Perplexity, Pinterest, Reddit, Reflection AI, Rumble, Snap, SpaceX, Stability AI, Telegram, Thinking Machines Labs, TikTok U.S., and Truth Social, the legislators wrote, “Your platforms play a significant and important role in sharing, disseminating, and in some cases generating information about those elections. Much of the United States—and the world—searches for and receives information from American search engines, American chatbots, and American social media platforms. These connections create opportunities for Americans to come together and debate important topics and share information. But they also create vectors for foreign adversaries and domestic actors to easily and quickly reach—and manipulate—large audiences.”

The legislators explained that their social media platforms and AI tools can quickly generate, execute and disseminate influence campaigns that used to take hundreds of hours of labor. As Americans increasingly turn to AI tools to inform themselves about political candidates, ballot issues, and the logistics of voting, AI tools could be used to spread inaccurate, outdated, manipulated, or biased information.

The legislators reminded the CEOs that many of their companies have committed to ensuring they were not complicit in harming elections or hampering the ability of Americans to vote. Additionally, while many have also committed to authenticating and labeling digital media and adopted policies to increase the odds that users see the most reliable voting and election information, there have been demonstrated inconsistencies among the companies regarding the effectiveness and applicability of their respective policies.

“Unfortunately, there are concerning signs of backsliding on some of your commitments to protecting elections from misuse of your products. These signs are particularly alarming because they come at a time when the capabilities of malign actors are growing in scale and sophistication and our elections are under attack from multiple directions… Public reporting indicates that Russia continues to undermine confidence in U.S. elections through disinformation campaigns executed directly on many of your platforms; though such efforts clearly violate your terms of service, some of your companies have not quickly or consistently removed such content,” wrote the legislators.

They continued, “Equally alarming is that some of your AI chatbots have an unacceptably high error rate when responding to queries about election and voting processes, subjecting users to confusing or inaccurate answers that could result in voter disenfranchisement. And some of your content removal and fact-checking policies are woefully insufficient or even nonexistent, allowing false, manipulated, and misleading content to continue to circulate on your platforms unchecked. In the past, the Federal Trade Commission has notably pursued enforcement actions against companies that don’t live up to the self-regulatory commitments they make, including in a 2012 case against Google for failing to follow the National Advertising Initiative code of conduct.”

The legislators then recommended a list of concrete actions the companies could take, including removing all demonstrably false information related to election and voting logistics once they find it, using independent fact checkers, regularly updating automated tools to review and remove or reduce the reach of false election-related content, and directing all users to authoritative election-related resources.

In regards to generative AI, the legislators recommended actions such as making sure AI-generated responses to questions about election and voting logistics source their information from state and local election offices and trusted news organizations, incorporating disclaimers and flags in AI-generated responses if election and voting logistics may be outdated, and making sure that all AI-generated images and videos are labeled and can be identified as AI-generated content both by users and by technology-based detection tools.

“Again, we strongly urge you to enhance—not reduce—your election security efforts in the final days before the 2026 midterms and to maintain strong efforts in this area on an ongoing basis ahead of future elections as well,” the legislators concluded.

The full letter is available here and below.

We write to urge you to adopt policies and programs that ensure your platforms contribute to, and do not detract from, the effort to ensure that America’s elections are free, fair, and secure.

As the CEOs of America’s largest technology companies, you are aware of the great responsibility that your companies hold in America’s elections. Your platforms play a significant and important role in sharing, disseminating, and in some cases generating information about those elections. Much of the United States—and the world—searches for and receives information from American search engines, American chatbots, and American social media platforms. These connections create opportunities for Americans to come together and debate important topics and share information. But they also create vectors for foreign adversaries and domestic actors to easily and quickly reach—and manipulate—large audiences.

Moreover, American companies’ AI offerings offer both substantial benefits and substantial risks. Your tools can quickly generate, execute, and disseminate entire influence campaigns. While it previously would take hundreds of manhours to achieve such effects, your tools speed and streamline efforts to create material that are inaccurate or false, but nevertheless convincing. Increasingly, some American voters turn to AI tools to research candidates and ballot issues and seek information about voting logistics, increasing the risk of exposure to inaccuracies, outdated or manipulated information, or biased summaries.

Many of your companies have demonstrated a commitment over the past decade to ensuring that your platforms are not used to harm elections or hamper the ability of Americans to vote. After the 2016 elections, many of your companies turned particular focus to identifying and eliminating coordinated inauthentic behavior on your platforms and establishing searchable archives for election ads. With the rise of powerful generative AI tools, your companies further committed to authenticating and labeling digital media, including by joining the Coalition for Content Provenance & Authenticity (C2PA) and signing the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections. Many of your companies have also adopted policies seeking to increase the odds that your users are exposed to only the most authoritative and reliable voting and election information. We believe maintaining and enhancing these kinds of commitments is more important than ever heading into the final days of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

Unfortunately, there are concerning signs of backsliding on some of your commitments to protecting elections from misuse of your products. These signs are particularly alarming because they come at a time when the capabilities of malign actors are growing in scale and sophistication and our elections are under attack from multiple directions. Despite many of your companies having policies prohibiting deception and requiring the labeling of AI-generated content, there have been demonstrated inconsistencies regarding the effectiveness and applicability of your policies. In many cases, some of your social media platforms and AI tools still allow for the creation and/or dissemination of false, synthetic, misleading, or inauthentic election content in direct violation of your policies. Public reporting indicates that Russia continues to undermine confidence in U.S. elections through disinformation campaigns executed directly on many of your platforms; though such efforts clearly violate your terms of service, some of your companies have not quickly or consistently removed such content.

Equally alarming is that some of your AI chatbots have an unacceptably high error rate when responding to queries about election and voting processes, subjecting users to confusing or inaccurate answers that could result in voter disenfranchisement. And some of your content removal and fact-checking policies are woefully insufficient or even nonexistent, allowing false, manipulated, and misleading content to continue to circulate on your platforms unchecked. In the past, the Federal Trade Commission has notably pursued enforcement actions against companies that don’t live up to the self-regulatory commitments they make, including in a 2012 case against Google for failing to follow the National Advertising Initiative code of conduct.

Information related to election and voting logistics—a category that includes registration deadlines, polling hours and locations, requirements about voter ID, rules for mail or provisional voting and ballots, and voter eligibility—is information that is integral to the functioning of our democracy. When objectively false information about election administration is introduced and disseminated with the intent to deceive or to discourage prospective voters, your companies must have robust and consistently applied rules to differentiate that misinformation from ordinary political speech about elections and to take steps to remove that misinformation.

We continue to strongly encourage you to take the actions and adopt the best practices outlined in Senator Warner’s March 2026 letter on anticipating, identifying, and countering malicious manipulated media. These best practices are important steps to protecting vulnerable communities, public trust, and democratic institutions.

We also encourage you to adopt specific policies and actions regarding election-related content. To the extent that your company offers social media or other content access or distribution platforms, we strongly encourage you to take the following actions to keep your platforms free from coordinated inauthentic behavior and election-related misinformation and disinformation:

Immediately remove all demonstrably false information related to election and voting logistics upon becoming aware of it—including information about where and how to register to vote, and where and how to vote.

Support dedicated reporting tools on your platforms for election officials to report examples of false election information.

Improve the speed by which your tools detect and remove false information related to voting logistics and political and election-related violence.

When such tools are used to detect false, misleading, and inauthentic content, ensure that the tools are kept updated, and that their findings are promptly subject to human review and action to remove violative content.

Utilize independent fact checkers in addition to internal fact-checking teams and regularly updated automated tools to review and remove, or at least reduce the reach, impressions, and discoverability of, false, misleading, or inauthentic election-related content.

Engage independent media and civil society organizations to assist in efforts to verify media, generate authenticated media, and educate the public.

Notify users when they have engaged with election-related content that has subsequently been determined to be false, misleading, or inauthentic.

Affirmatively direct all users to authoritative election-related resources, especially if users were determined to have engaged with false, misleading, or inauthentic election-related content.

Immediately remove all content advocating for violence of any kind upon becoming aware of it, but particularly content advocating political and/or election-related violence.

Publish regular reports detailing efforts to identify and remove false election-related information, election-related misinformation and disinformation, election and political violence, and coordinated inauthentic behavior.

To the extent your company offers generative AI products, we strongly encourage you to take the following actions to keep your AI systems and tools safe as they engage with and generate election-related information:

Ensure that AI-generated responses to questions about election and voting logistics pull only from highly authoritative sources and do not pull from social media platforms or other user-generated content. Authoritative resources should be limited to state and local election offices and top trusted news organizations, as well as civil society organizations aggregating content from these other authoritative and reliable sources.

Provide additional resources to pre-deployment guardrail testing for AI-generated election-related content, as well as ongoing reviewing of model performance.

Strengthen guardrails to prevent AI systems from responding to queries with material that can be used in election disinformation campaigns.

Implement continuous auditing until the November federal elections, and for an appropriate time as ballot counting, litigation, or challenges to the results remain ongoing, for accuracy and objectiveness in AI-generated responses to election-related questions, including mechanisms by which users can report inaccurate answers.

Incorporate disclaimers and flags in AI-generated responses if election and voting logistics may be outdated, and direct users to authoritative resources.

Provide inline citations and links for all election-related information provided in an AI-generated response.

Encourage users to independently verify AI-generated answers to questions about election and voting by reviewing authoritative and reliable resources.

Ensure that all AI-generated images and videos are consistently clearly labeled and can be identified as AI-generated content both by the human eye and by technology-based detection tools.

Ensure that election-related responses provided in languages other than English are accurate and reliable.

Many of you have announced content partnerships with highly reliable sources to ensure that your AI and social media platforms only surface the most accurate and reliable information related to election and voting logistics and election results. We strongly support this practice and encourage you to ensure that your platforms properly identify and curate the authoritative and reliable resources from which they pull from on election-related topics to avoid sharing outdated, inaccurate, unreliable, or otherwise incorrect information on this critical topic area that you cannot afford to get wrong. In addition, we urge you to be mindful of Spanish and other foreign language content, which plays a large and important role in the U.S. electorate but often receives less attention and response than online English-language election misinformation.

We also encourage you to be transparent about the efforts that your companies are making on these fronts. Public reporting indicates that in recent years, several of your companies have conducted layoffs, including of personnel on the trust and safety teams responsible for ensuring your platforms’ integrity when it comes to election topics. Firing such personnel after there has been demonstrated evidence and indicators of orchestrated and coordinate foreign misinformation operations exposes your platform to various integrity threats and is cause for serious concern.

Particularly as the 2026 midterm elections are officially underway, your companies should be increasing the staffing and capabilities of your respective trust and safety teams, especially those teams responsible for avoiding platform exploitation relating to election topics. Refusing to grow and expand your election integrity teams—and even shrinking these teams—does not support your stated commitments to countering harmful election content and suggests to bad actors that your policies are not enforceable.

Finally, third-party researchers play a critical role in studying and producing independent reviews of social media platforms and AI systems and tools, particularly as it pertains to auditing the effectiveness of your trust and safety policies. Your companies should collaborate with third-party researchers by granting them access to your products and data, including data on how users are engaging with your platforms on election-related issues, and allow for the testing of your platforms and AI tools.

Again, we strongly urge you to enhance—not reduce—your election security efforts in the final days before the 2026 midterms and to maintain strong efforts in this area on an ongoing basis ahead of future elections as well. We thank you for your attention to these important measures and we look forward to hearing about your efforts in these areas.

###

title: Warner Urges Military Spouse Commission to Hear Directly From Virginia Military Families
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Sen. Mark R. Warner (D-VA) urged the newly formed Department of Defense Military Spouse Commission to expand its outreach to military families across Virginia, particularly spouses who have recently navigated the challenges of extended deployments and spouses of junior enlisted servicemembers. In a letter to the Commission’s leadership, Sen. Warner emphasized the importance of providing venues and opportunities to hear directly from military spouses with a broad range of experiences to ensure their concerns and recommendations are reflected in the Commission’s work. Sen. Warner called for opportunities for Virginia military spouses to provide input directly to the Commission, including through local engagement in the Commonwealth.

In June, Sen. Warner met with military families in Hampton Roads, including spouses of servicemembers who were deployed or had recently returned from deployment, to hear firsthand about the challenges they face. Families described the strain of extended deployments and the difficulties of finding affordable child care, navigating military benefits, accessing timely health care and mental health support, and working with employers on needed support and flexibility during deployment periods, all while managing the stress of a loved one serving in dangerous conditions. These concerns mirror several of the priorities identified by the Commission during its inaugural meeting last month.

This Friday, Sen. Warner will host a follow-up roundtable with military families in Hampton Roads to continue these conversations, discuss progress on the concerns raised earlier this year, and identify additional steps to better support servicemembers and their loved ones.

In a letter to Commission Chairwoman Jennifer Hegseth and Executive Director Desiree Thompson Sayle, Sen. Warner emphasized the need to ensure military spouses have meaningful opportunities to share their experiences and help shape the Commission’s recommendations.

Sen. Warner wrote, “I share the goal of ensuring that we as a nation are supporting the spouses and families who are standing alongside our men and women in uniform. I would urge the Commission to expand opportunities for military spouses to engage your efforts, and to draw from a broad range of perspectives and experiences. Virginia spouses who I have spoken with would add valuable insights to the Commission’s work, and I would invite you to hear from Virginia spouses – including through direct and local engagement.”

Sen. Warner continued, “As the Commission undertakes its mission, I would invite you to engage directly with military spouses in Virginia to ensure their experiences and recommendations are reflected in your work. Ensuring that the Commission is hearing direct feedback and perspectives from a range of spouses – including of junior enlisted personnel – is critically important. I would also urge you to provide opportunities for individuals to engage the Commission directly, in addition to their current ability to submit comments ahead of the Commission’s meetings. Home to some of the nation’s largest military communities, Virginia has a significant stake in the work that you all will conduct, and Virginia spouses have valuable insights that can drive your actions.”

The letter concludes by requesting additional information about how the Commission plans to gather input from military spouses of different backgrounds, provide opportunities for direct engagement, incorporate feedback into its recommendations, and work with military and veteran advocacy groups.

The full letter is available here and below.

Mrs. Hegseth and Hon. Sayle:

One of the privileges and responsibilities that comes from serving as Senator from Virginia, is the opportunity to represent Virginia’s many servicemembers, military spouses, and their families. I write today regarding your efforts on the newly created Military Spouse Commission, which represents an important venue for considering the perspectives of our military families. This is a worthwhile and meaningful endeavor, and I appreciate your commitment to addressing the challenges that military spouses face.

I share the goal of ensuring that we as a nation are supporting the spouses and families who are standing alongside our men and women in uniform. I would urge the Commission to expand opportunities for military spouses to engage your efforts, and to draw from a broad range of perspectives and experiences. Virginia spouses who I have spoken with would add valuable insights to the Commission’s work, and I would invite you to hear from Virginia spouses – including through direct and local engagement.

Over the Commission’s first two engagements, you identified priorities of particular concern including housing, education, healthcare, spousal employment, and childcare. These are indeed concerns I hear about in my conversations with Virginia’s military spouses, and I am encouraged by your attention to these important issues.

In June, I met with military family members in Hampton Roads and heard about many of these same challenges. Many of the family members had a spouse who was deployed or had just returned from deployment – including as part of the USS Gerald R. Ford carrier strike group, and its 11-month deployment. You and the other military spouses who make up the Commission can uniquely understand how these everyday challenges are compounded during a deployment – particularly some of the extended deployments that we have seen in recent months.

Military service is shouldered by the entire family, with partners and spouses, kids, parents, and other family members working to balance the challenges that exist at home while a loved one is deployed. Everything from finding quality, affordable childcare; navigating the web of military benefits and support programs; securing timely healthcare and mental health support; and working with employers on needed support and flexibility during these periods, all become more challenging while managing the stress of a loved one serving in dangerous conditions.

As the Commission undertakes its mission, I would invite you to engage directly with military spouses in Virginia to ensure their experiences and recommendations are reflected in your work. Ensuring that the Commission is hearing direct feedback and perspectives from a range of spouses – including of junior enlisted personnel – is critically important. I would also urge you to provide opportunities for individuals to engage the Commission directly, in addition to their current ability to submit comments ahead of the Commission’s meetings. Home to some of the nation’s largest military communities, Virginia has a significant stake in the work that you all will conduct, and Virginia spouses have valuable insights that can drive your actions.

To better understand how the Commission intends to operate, and to work together to involve more military spouse voices in this process, I would appreciate the opportunity for engagement with you and your team on the following matters:

How will you ensure that the Commission receives input from military spouses representing a broad range of backgrounds and experiences, including spouses of servicemembers of different ranks, Reserve and National Guard families, military caregivers, dual-military couples, and surviving spouses?

Section 2(c) xxi of the President’s Executive Order establishing the Commission provides the Chair and Executive Director the authority to invite other individuals to participate with the Commission. In addition to submitting comments electronically, will there be avenues and opportunities for military spouses to engage directly, to include inviting spouses to attend Commission meetings, hosting in-person listening sessions and field hearings, and meetings at military installations?

How will feedback from military spouses be used to develop the Commission’s recommendations? Will military spouses be able to weigh in on proposals throughout the process, including reviewing and commenting on proposed recommendations as they are developed?

What steps is the Commission taking to engage with Military Service Organizations (MSOs), Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs), and other advocacy groups?

I am grateful for your commitment to supporting military spouses, which is ultimately essential to ensuring mission readiness in our military. I invite the Commission to engage with Virginia spouses directly, and I look forward to reviewing the Commission’s recommendations.

###

title: New Warnock Report Details How Errors in State Medicaid Systems Threaten Health Care Access and Increase Taxpayer Costs
text:
Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock, Ron Wyden, and Elizabeth Warren detail how delays and errors in state Medicaid eligibility systems lead to loss of health care coverage and higher costs for American taxpayers

The new report examines the role of private contractors, including Deloitte, which manages Georgia’s Medicaid eligibility system, in administering systems plagued by costly errors and implementation delays

New Medicaid work reporting requirements enacted by Congressional Republicans in the One Big Beautiful Bill and taking effect in January 2027 could compound existing system errors and put even more Americans at risk of losing health care coverage

In October 2025, Senators Warnock, Wyden, Sanders, and Warren opened an investigation into five large contractors that build and maintain Medicaid management systems across the country

Senator Reverend Warnock, Wyden, Warren: “Medicaid enrollees will face a two-pronged threat to coverage: the draconian requirements of the OBBBA itself, and the shoddy performance record of the contractors processing new mountains of paperwork”

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Ranking Member of the Finance Subcommittee on Trade, Customs, and Global Competitiveness, Ron Wyden (D-OR), Ranking Member of the Senate Finance Committee, and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) released a new report detailing how delays and errors in state Medicaid eligibility systems lead to the loss of health care coverage and higher costs for American taxpayers. The report follows an October 2025 investigation by Senators Warnock, Wyden, Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and Bernie Sanders (I-VT) into five of the nation’s largest contractors that build and maintain Medicaid management systems across the country.

The report warns that new work reporting requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), taking effect in January 2027, could compound existing errors in these systems and put even more Americans at risk of losing health care coverage.

“The core concern of this investigation is that a small handful of companies—some whose technology has a history of grievous errors—will be in charge of implementing historically harsh Medicaid work reporting requirements that never should have been enacted in the first place,” said Senators Warnock, Wyden, and Warren. “Medicaid enrollees will face a two-pronged threat to coverage: the draconian requirements of the OBBBA itself, and the shoddy performance record of the contractors processing new mountains of paperwork.”

Medicaid is a cornerstone of the U.S. health care system, providing health insurance coverage to more than one in five Americans. The program covers 40% of U.S. births, provides 20% of all hospital funding, and is the single largest payer of long-term services and supports, including nursing home care. For years, thousands of eligible Medicaid beneficiaries have erroneously been denied or stripped of their Medicaid coverage due to errors in contractors’ eligibility systems. Georgia offers a particularly revealing example of the challenges associated with these systems.

In Georgia, Deloitte, one of the private contractors examined in the Senators’ investigation, manages the state’s Medicaid eligibility system and serves as a primary consultant for Governor Brian Kemp’s Georgia Pathways to Coverage program. According to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Georgia spent more than twice as much administering Pathways as it did providing health care benefits to enrollees, spending over $54 million on administration costs compared to roughly $26 million on medical care.

Senator Warnock is a leading proponent of Medicaid expansion and has long championed efforts to increase Georgians’ access to affordable health care. Last year, he released a report titled “Healthy People, Healthy Economy,” which found that investing in Medicaid stimulates economic growth and promotes access to employment. In June, Senator Warnock forced a vote pushing for the release of data surrounding Medicaid coverage loss nationwide. Senator Warnock’s effort to release the data was blocked by Senate Republicans.

A copy of the report can be found HERE.

title: Warnock, Colleagues Question IRS Over Administration’s Threats to Revoke Tax-Exempt Status for Universities with Diversity Programs
text:
U.S. Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock, Ron Wyden, and Bernie Sanders are seeking answers from the Internal Revenue Service about a Trump administration proposal to revoke the tax-exempt status of private universities and K-12 programs with diversity programs

The Treasury Department’s proposed rule would affect secondary schools and universities with policies the Trump administration deems racially discriminatory, including certain admissions and scholarship programs

Throughout President Trump’s second term, his administration has threatened universities’ tax-exempt status over diversity policies and programs it opposes as it pushes to eliminate initiatives directed at Black, Hispanic, and other minority students

Senator Warnock launched an inquiry into reports of the Trump administration’s political targeting of nonprofits and authored bipartisan legislation to protect organizations facing the loss of their tax-exempt status

Senator Reverend Warnock, colleagues: “This rulemaking appears to further President Trump’s repeated attempts to weaponize the IRS against those he dislikes”

Washington, D.C. – Today, Senate Finance Member U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Ranking Member of the Senate Finance Committee Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), and Ranking Member of the Senate HELP Committee Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) are seeking answers from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) about a Trump administration proposal to revoke the tax-exempt status of secondary schools and universities with diversity programs. Throughout President Trump’s second term, his administration has threatened universities’ tax-exempt status over diversity policies and programs it opposes as it pushes to eliminate initiatives directed at Black, Hispanic, and other minority students.

“Prior to the proposed rule’s release, President Trump repeatedly and publicly threated to revoke the tax-exempt status of specific private universities he dislikes” wrote the senators. “This rulemaking appears to further President Trump’s repeated attempts to weaponize the IRS against those he dislikes.”

The Treasury Department’s proposed rule would deny tax-exempt status to any private school, including secondary schools and universities, if it has any policy or program—including admissions and scholarships—that the IRS finds to be racially discriminatory. If finalized, the new rule would go into effect in May 2027.

The proposal comes amid broader efforts by the Trump administration to pressure schools and universities to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion policies across the country. This latest effort demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to put its political interests ahead of the American people and erode opportunities for middle class students across the country. In September, Senators Warnock and Wyden launched an inquiry into reports that the Trump administration is developing plans to weaponize the IRS’s tax enforcement authority to target perceived ideological opponents. Senator Warnock also authored bipartisan legislation with Senator James Lankford (R-OK) to give nonprofit organizations the right to appeal IRS decisions denying or revoking their tax-exempt status.

A copy of the letter can be found HERE and text is below:

“Secretary Bessent and Mr. Bisignano:

We write regarding the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s (Treasury) proposed rule, which threatens to remove federal tax-exempt status from an estimated 18,000 private K-12 schools, professional or trade schools, colleges, and universities based on the Administration’s subjective findings. The proposed rule reinterprets the public policy doctrine and chills lawful actions designed to advance educational opportunity. We urge Treasury to rescind this proposal.

On September 3, 2026, Treasury issued proposed regulations to “end federal tax exempt status for private schools that engage in racial discrimination, delivering on President Trump’s Executive Orders ending discrimination and restoring merit-based opportunity.” This is a clear attempt by the Trump Administration to weaponize the tax code and punish educational institutions for political or subjective reasons using a definition of racial discrimination not endorsed by Congress or the Supreme Court. Under the proposed regulations, private K-12 schools, colleges, and universities will no longer be able to maintain policies or practices to support educational opportunities for historically-underserved students in a manner consistent with the Students for Fair Admission v. Harvard (SFFA) decision—or risk their tax-exempt status. This attack on our education system will severely limit admissions, scholarships and loans, athletics, and academic assistance programs that students of all backgrounds rely on to access a quality education.

In its proposal, Treasury notes that it plans to rely on the 1983 Supreme Court case Bob Jones Univ. v. United States, which upheld the IRS’s revocation of tax-exempt status from a pervasively segregationist institution because its racially discriminatory policies violated “fundamental public policy.” In that case, the Supreme Court noted that “there can be no doubt as to the national policy” prohibiting racial segregation because “the position of all three branches of the Federal Government were unmistakably clear.” As Bob Jones makes clear, the IRS must look at the decisions issued by courts, federal statutes, and Congressional intent, not just the administration’s subjective interpretations, when applying the public policy doctrine.

Private schools can lawfully advance diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility, even under recent Supreme Court precedent. In the SFFA decision, which Treasury references in its proposed rulemaking, the Supreme Court repeatedly affirmed this point. For example, the Supreme Court noted universities can continue to employ “race-neutral” policies, such as “focus[ing] on socioeconomic and geographic diversity.” Further, earlier this year, the Supreme Court reiterated that the government can take action based on race in order to remedy specific instances of past discrimination.

Treasury’s proposed rule, however, indicates that educational institutions are ineligible for tax-exempt status “regardless of the intent behind or the legality [of] racial discrimination (for example, where such discrimination is defended as serving remedial or diversity-related objectives).” The proposed rule prohibits what Treasury deems “discrimination . . . for any purpose,” including to achieve commendable goals.

This prohibition is particularly concerning since the Trump Administration has repeatedly claimed lawful programs designed to advance diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility involve “discrimination.” Indeed, guidance from the Department of Justice has stated that universities may violate the law even if they use “[f]acially neutral criteria” such as “geographic targeting.” The administration has also repeatedly targeted educational institutions that admit Black and Latino students, often based on little evidence.

The proposed rule is subjective in its definition of discrimination, and rather than make educational opportunities more equitable, it will threaten academic opportunity and achievement for decades to come. There is substantial evidence that the policies schools and universities employ to create more inclusive learning environments benefit all students and foster critical thinking, empathy, and student achievement. Notably, the Trump administration’s prior attempts to impose extralegal requirements on recipients have frequently been blocked by the courts.

It is unclear why Treasury believes it has the authority to revoke private schools’ or colleges’ tax-exempt status based on supposed violations of fundamental public policy when those actions are explicitly permitted by federal courts, including the Supreme Court.

If Treasury only intends to apply existing law, it is unclear why the proposed rule is necessary. The IRS has a three-part test to determine whether an organization’s activities are consistent with exemption under section 501(c)(3): (1) whether the purpose of the organization is charitable; (2) whether the activities are not illegal, contrary to a clearly defined and established public policy, or in conflict with express statutory restrictions; and (3) whether the activities are in furtherance of the organization’s exempt purpose and are reasonably related to the accomplishment of that purpose.

IRS also already has established procedures clarifying that Section 501(c)(3) schools cannot racially discriminate. In 1971, the IRS issued Revenue Ruling 71-447, providing that a private school with racially discriminatory policies is not “charitable” within the common law concepts reflected in Section 190 and 501(c)(3). Further, in 1975, the IRS issued Revenue Ruling 75-50, setting guidelines for private schools to prove they operate on a racially nondiscriminatory basis to qualify for tax-exempt status under Section 501(c)(3). Revenue Ruling 75-50 includes exceptions that allow schools to adopt certain policies regarding racial minority groups if the explicit goal was to promote or maintain a racially nondiscriminatory environment. Treasury has never advanced the view that it has the unilateral power to revoke 501(c)(3) status from schools based on its own determination of “public policy” in conflict with views advanced by the Supreme Court and Congress.

Finally, the context around Treasury’s proposed rulemaking raises serious legal concerns regarding the politicization of IRS enforcement. Prior to the proposed rule’s release, President Trump repeatedly and publicly threatened to revoke the tax-exempt status of specific private universities he dislikes. Furthermore, in April 2025, his administration reportedly directed then-IRS Acting Chief Counsel De Mello to revoke Harvard University’s tax-exempt status. In recent years, the politicization of the IRS has raised bipartisan concern. This dramatic expansion of the public policy doctrine risks further undermining the IRS’s mission of nonpartisan tax administration and enforcement and, to the extent it responds to the President’s requests to audit specific institutions, may violate federal law.

In light of these significant concerns, we urge the Treasury to rescind this proposal. Furthermore, we also ask Treasury to respond to the following questions by November 19, 2026:

The IRS listed its authority for creation of the Proposed Rule as 26 U.S.C. § 7805(a). This is the Secretary of the Treasury’s general rulemaking authority. No other authority was cited. Do you believe this authority is sufficient to promulgate a rule to deny tax exemptions to private schools absent specific congressional authorization?

The Supreme Court reiterated again this year that the government can take action based on race in order to remedy specific instances of past discrimination. However, the proposed rule indicates that educational institutions are ineligible for tax-exempt status “regardless of the intent behind or the legality of [racial] discrimination (for example, where such discrimination is defended as serving remedial … objectives).” How can remedial actions violate fundamental public policy if they are explicitly permitted by the Supreme Court?

In upholding the IRS’ decision to revoke Bob Jones University’s tax-exempt status for policies excluding Black students, the Supreme Court noted “there can be no doubt as to the national policy” prohibiting these policies because “the position of all three branches of the Federal Government was unmistakably clear.” Do you agree the IRS must look at the decisions issued by courts, federal statutes, and Congressional intent when determining what activities are “discrimination”? How is the IRS determining Congressional intent in this instance?

What expertise do IRS personnel possess to make determinations of unlawful discrimination?

The preamble to the Proposed Rule states that the IRS “expects” donors may continue making gifts to universities to benefit first-generation college students, as well as low-income and geographically diverse students. Will you advise the IRS that these gifts do not constitute unlawful discrimination? Will you affirm that such gifts will not risk a school’s 501(c)(3) exemption?

How would the IRS ensure that any procedure is grounded in the Internal Revenue Code and applicable civil rights law, applied consistently across institutions, and does not improperly penalize organizations for lawful efforts to advance racial equity or equal educational opportunity?

Currently, numerous scholarship programs exist to provide financial assistance to people of Irish, Greek, or other European descent. Would these scholarships violate the proposed rule?

Why did Treasury schedule a telephonic hearing, rather than an in-person hearing, on a topic of this importance?

Do you commit to being forthright, cooperative, and transparent to this Committee as we exercise oversight over the IRS to ensure there is no political interference in tax administration?

title: Warnock, Ossoff Secure Nearly $12.5 Million to Improve Rail Safety Across Southwest Georgia
text:
Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff successfully secured nearly $12.5 million in federal grant funding from the Department of Transportation to improve railway safety in Southwest Georgia

The funding will help rehabilitate rail lines, improve 40 railroad crossings, install measures to prevent trespassing, and improve safety and reliability

The funding will support improvement projects in Dawson, Cuthbert, Arlington, Bainbridge, Cordele, and Americus

Senator Reverend Warnock: “This latest grant will help reduce congestion, build new tracks, and strengthen existing rail infrastructure, making it safer, easier, and more efficient to move goods across our state”

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) and Jon Ossoff (D-GA) secured $12,495,000 in federal funding to improve rail safety and infrastructure across central and southwestern Georgia. The funding, provided through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (DOT) Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) Program, will help rehabilitate rail lines, improve rail service, and increase reliability as part of the Heart of Georgia & Georgia Southwestern Rail Corridor Improvement Final Phase Project.

“Since coming to the Senate, I have been focused on strengthening rail safety and infrastructure in Georgia. That is why I am proud to champion efforts in the Senate to strengthen the CRISI program to deliver more resources to our state,” said Senator Warnock. “This latest grant will help reduce congestion, build new tracks, and strengthen existing rail infrastructure, making it safer, easier, and more efficient to move goods across our state.”

“After hearing from communities statewide about aging railroad infrastructure conditions, Senator Warnock and I elevated this as one of our highest priorities,” said Senator Ossoff. “We are delivering these resources through the bipartisan infrastructure law to communities across the State of Georgia to plan and begin construction to address this crisis. We’ve listened, we’ve heard, we’ve acted, and help is on the way.”

The Project will rehabilitate and improve five short line subdivisions across central and southwestern Georgia, including rail corridors serving Dawson, Cuthbert, Arlington, Bainbridge, Cordele, and Americus. Improvements will include replacing jointed rail with continuous welded rail, installing new ties, surfacing track, resurfacing 40 railroad crossings, renewing two turnouts, and installing trespasser prevention technology.

Senator Warnock successfully strengthened the CRISI Program to deliver for Georgia during negotiations for the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and wrote a letter of support championing funding for the Heart of Georgia & Georgia Southwestern Rail Corridor Improvement Final Phase Project. In 2024, Senators Warnock and Jon Ossoff (D-GA) secured more than $60 million in CRISI funding to strengthen railroad safety across Georgia, including funding for the Georgia Department of Transportation, Georgia Ports Authority, Patriot Rail Company, and OmniTRAX Holdings.

title: Vermont Delegation Announces More Than $60 Million in New Federal Funding to Complete Vermont’s Western Corridor Rail Line
text:
BURLINGTON, VT – U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and U.S. Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL) today announced the delivery of $60.3 million in new federal funding, administered by the Department of Transportation (DOT) to the Vermont Agency of Transportation (VTrans) to rehabilitate and complete approximately 60 miles of railway on Vermont’s Western Corridor rail line.

“Repairing and upgrading our transportation infrastructure is a win-win for Vermont’s rural communities. This federal funding will help improve safety and reliability on the Vermont Railway, and support the development of rural towns up and down the Western Corridor,” said the Vermont Delegation. “With this $60 million investment from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the Western Corridor will be complete, and western Vermont will finally be connected to the New York Penn Station line.”

“This grant will support Vermont businesses who rely on rail to get their products to market regionally and nationally,” said Vermont Transportation Secretary Joe Flynn. “For bulk commodities, shipping by rail is often the most cost-effective, and upgrades to the Vermont Railway in western Vermont will enable our businesses to efficiently tap into the nation’s major Class I railroads.”

This new funding will help replace rail, realign track, and upgrade ties, ballast, turnouts, and 22 at-grade crossings to enhance safety, improve system and service performance, and increase reliability of rail service in Vermont. The funding is made possible through DOT’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) Program.

title: Welch, Britt Headline Edward M. Kennedy Institute’s Seventh Installment of ‘The Senate Project’ Bipartisan Conversation Series
text:
BOSTON, MASS. — U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.) and U.S. Senator Katie Britt (R-Ala.) appeared in Boston this week to participate in The Edward M. Kennedy Institute’s (EMKI) 2026 installment of The Senate Project series. The Senators had an in-depth discussion on timely topics, including interactions and collaborations with fellow senators during their tenure, and their combined work on bipartisan legislation to protect children, curb the effects of social media on youth mental health, and better predict and prepare for water-related disasters. Senator Welch also discussed the need for institutional reform of the Senate and how President Trump’s corruption will impact the upcoming midterm elections.

The Senate Project series aims to reintroduce the culture of seeking common ground and consensus that has been the essence of the Senate since it was conceived in 1789. Martha MacCallum, anchor of The Story with Martha MacCallum, moderated the discussion.

“Our politics are deeply fractured and broken… What I believe is that we step back and look at the problems we face, and Katie was alluding to this: they’re shared problems. We’re all scared about what social media is doing to our kids. We’re all really wondering what happens to our kids when they get out of college and they can’t afford to get a condo, let alone even think about building a house. We’re all concerned about health care—that is getting well beyond anybody’s ability to pay, including our employer-sponsored healthcare programs,” said Senator Welch.

“If you start out where you’re talking about the problems that you share, then it can lead to a concrete discussion about a shared solution. What’s fractured is a lot of things that are hurting it: gerrymandering, money in politics, social media—a lot of those things. But the whole point of politics is about accepting, acknowledging, and solving shared problems. That requires that you do some listening to one another and you have mutual respect for the motivation that everybody you serve with is there to do the same thing that you’re there to do,” the Senator continued.

Watch a livestream of the event here and view photos from the event below:

Images Courtesy of the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the U.S. Senate

Senator Welch on his path to the Senate and the importance of public service:

“It’s inspiring to be here, because what motivates a lot of people who go into public service, whether they have conservative or liberal politics, is public service. There’s a desire on the part of most of us, whatever it is we do, by the way, not just going into elected office—but to have a feeling at the end of the day you’ve helped somebody out and make a step ahead. And it can be a banker who helps somebody get a loan for their first home, it can be a teacher who cracked the code to help a child learn how to read. That sense of service, I think, is what I find is common ground. Katie and I, our backgrounds are totally different, and our politics are different. But you just heard a recitation that I quite admire about her desire to have an opportunity to serve.”

•••

Senator Welch on the need for bipartisanship and how to fix gridlock in Washington:

“I actually believe that all of us who serve in the Senate have to acknowledge that much of the Senate that Senator [Ted] Kennedy served in, Senator Robert Kennedy served in, Senator John Kennedy served in, is broken. We don’t address the critical issues facing the country. We’ve got a huge debt; it’s not even a topic. Social Security is on the brink of being insolvent; we don’t talk about it. We basically have gotten into a situation where the legislating is done through the reconciliation process. You know, the Senate is supposed to be a place where you come together and you do work out differences and hear from the minority, but the reconciliation process is an indication that we’ve given up on that…

“So, I actually think we have to aspire to continue doing the work together that say, Katie and I are doing. But there’s got to be some acknowledgement that there have got to be some significant changes affecting the Senate. I think radical gerrymandering is affecting Congress, less so obviously in the Senate. The money in politics is brutal, and we’re seeing this election that individuals can really overcome it—it has a real impact on what happens on both the Republican and Democratic side.”

•••

Senator Welch on the need for institutional reform and why the Senate must reassert its constitutional responsibilities:

“There is a need for institutional reform in order for us to be able to get back to the Senators being able to work out the differences on major pieces of legislation…What I’ve seen in the Congress, this is when I served in the House and now in the Senate, is that there is a continuing abdication of responsibility by the U.S. Senate of its constitutional prerogatives. We should not have tariffs without a vote of the Senate for those tariffs—those are taxes, and under our Constitution, it’s the Congress that decides. We should not be going to war without a vote—a vote. And we’ve not had the opportunity for a full vote. We’ve got this war in Iran, and that should never have started. We’ve seen the power of Congress to appropriate money is taken away by the executive if he impounds the money that Katie’s Appropriations Committee appropriates.

“So, my view here is that institutionally, if you’re a U.S. senator, you have to insist that the prerogatives under the Constitution of the U.S. Senate are maintained, and that’s to have that competition, and that check, and that balance. But the executive is assuming more authority…My view is that all of us in the Senate should unite around asserting our authority and accept our responsibility.”

•••

Senator Welch on how President Trump’s corruption will impact the upcoming midterm elections:

“The midterms, we all know historically, is a referendum on the incumbent president. So, President Trump is on the ballot, and the outcome of these elections is going to largely be determined by how people feel about him. And his poll numbers are terrible. I think the concerns about corruption are immense. I think the concerns about the erratic behavior are immense…But if the Democrats do get a majority, we have to have a certain amount of humility here. This isn’t about us winning. It’s about Trump losing favor among the American people. It gives us an opportunity to earn trust, and in order to earn trust, we have to make the institution work better…So, and we won’t be able to solve those things if we just do it alone. There’s got to be some humility on the part of the Democrats if, as I hope, we will be successful.”

•••

Senator Welch on how the Trump Administration has exacerbated economic inequality in America:

“Economic inequality that is now institutionalized in this country has never been worse since the Gilded Age, and the process of politics is about trying to create economic conditions where people who are willing to work hard —and by the way, people like to work. Work makes you feel good —then at the end of the month, they can pay their bills. So, we’ve got to work together to solve real problems, and that means we have to assert our authority.”

###

title: Wyden Calls on HHS Secretary to Reverse Plans for Trump Administration Lawyers to Represent Unaccompanied Children in Immigration Court
text:
Washington, DC – U.S. Senator Ron Wyden said today he has joined with five other senators urging Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. to reverse the decision for HHS attorneys to represent unaccompanied children against the Trump administration’s own deportation machine and to restore independent legal counsel immediately.

The senators underscored in a letter to Kennedy how failing to reverse this decision would result in a clear conflict of interest, especially since HHS has a responsibility to care for these children in custody and already shares personal information with immigration enforcement.

“HHS holds these children in custody, decides where they live and shares information about them and their families with immigration enforcement. HHS cannot also be their lawyer,” the senators wrote. “The immigration judge works for the Trump Administration. So does the prosecutor. Under your plan, so would the child’s lawyer. That is unacceptable.”

As a direct result of the Trump administration cutting funding to facilitate independent legal aid for unaccompanied migrant children, tens of thousands of children this year faced immigration judges with no legal representation. In their letter, the senators cited how the bipartisan Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 legally requires HHS to make every effort to secure pro bono counsel that will provide independent representation and protect the kids from mistreatment or exploitation. By appointing HHS attorneys to these cases instead, the administration intends to place these children in removal proceedings led by judges working for the U.S. Department of Justice with legal representation that is anything but independent.

“Reunifying children with their families is HHS’s job. Legally representing an unaccompanied child, including against HHS in legal proceedings, is not,” the lawmakers wrote. “It is a job for an experienced, expert and independent attorney trained to represent unaccompanied children who are often experiencing extreme stress and trauma.”

Additionally, the senators highlighted that HHS’s decision would discourage these kids from reporting abuse, trafficking and dangerous family circumstances to their lawyers for fear of the information reaching immigration enforcement. Notably, HHS’s announcement mentions no procedures for screening conflicts, protecting client confidentiality, or insulating attorneys from HHS’s custodial functions.

“HHS cannot serve as both custodian and counsel. You must meet your statutory obligation to these children. Unaccompanied children deserve lawyers whose only loyalty is to them. We demand that you rescind this harmful policy before a single HHS attorney stands beside a child in immigration court,” the senators concluded.

In addition to Wyden, other signers of the letter are U.S. Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Richard J. Durbin (D-IL), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Edward J. Markey (D-MA) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA)

title: Rep. Young Kim Convenes Roundtable with Housing Leaders to Tackle Affordability in Southern California
text:
ORANGE COUNTY, CA – Today, Congresswoman Young Kim (CA-40) convened a roundtable of credit unions, realtors, housing nonprofits, and community development partners to discuss how recent federal legislation is impacting housing costs and what Congress can do to make the dream of homeownership attainable again in Southern California.

Participants included SchoolsFirst Federal Credit Union, which hosted the roundtable, as well as the National Apartment Association, AARES, NPHS, Inland Empire Community Foundation, NeighborWorks Orange County, Wescom Credit Union, Arrowhead Credit Union, Eagle Community Credit Union, POLAM Federal Credit Union, Financial Partners Credit Union, California’s Credit Unions, and the California Association of Realtors.

California has some of the highest housing costs in the country, and only 22% of households in the state can afford a median-priced home, half the national rate. To help close that gap, Rep. Kim secured two of her provisions in the historic bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July. Her Community Investment and Prosperity Act unlocks more private capital for affordable housing by raising the cap on what banks can invest in community development. Her VALID Act helps veterans make informed choices by ensuring they see VA home loan options alongside conventional and FHA loans.

“California families should not be priced out of the dream of homeownership,” said Rep. Young Kim. “That is why I have fought to make housing attainable for hardworking Californians, from expanding investment in affordable housing and quadrupling the SALT deduction to modernizing credit scoring and strengthening financial literacy. Thank you to Brent and SchoolsFirst Credit Union for hosting us, and to our credit unions, realtors, and housing nonprofits for sharing what they hear from families every day. I look forward to bringing their insights back to Congress as we continue working to bring down costs and keep the American Dream alive in Southern California.”

As a member of the House Financial Services Committee, Congresswoman Young Kim has been working to lower housing costs and help more Southern California families achieve the dream of homeownership. Her housing affordability efforts also include:

Introducing the Credit Access and Inclusion Act, which would allow on-time rent, utility, and phone payments to be reported to credit bureaus, helping credit-invisible Americans build credit and qualify for better mortgage rates.

Securing an increase in the State and Local tax (SALT) deduction cap from $10,000 to $40,000, putting more money back in their pockets for down payments and mortgage payments.

title: Rep. Aguilar Joins Rep. Takano, Local Veterans to Advocate for Passage of Veterans Disability & Retirement Legislation
text:
The Major Richard Star Act, which would ensure veterans with combat-related disabilities are able to collect their full retirement pay and their disability pay, received the necessary 218 signatures requiring a vote on the House floor

SAN BERNARDINO, CA – Rep. Pete Aguilar (CA-33) held a press conference with Rep. Mark Takano (CA-39) and local veterans to call for a House vote on the Major Richard Star Act. The bill would let combat-injured veterans receive both their retirement and their disability pay in full, even if they left service before 20 years.

Under current law, veterans injured while serving our country who leave the military before 20 years of service lose a dollar of retirement pay for every dollar of disability pay they receive. The Major Richard Star Act, which is co-sponsored by Reps. Aguilar and Takano and has broad bipartisan support in the House of Representatives, would end the offset for combat-injured medical retirees. The bill is supported by Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW), Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), Disabled American Veterans (DAV), and many other veteran service organizations.

Rep. Takano, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, and Rep. Raul Ruiz (CA-25) led a discharge petition to force a vote on the bill. In September, the petition reached the required 218 signatures to force the House Speaker to bring the bill up for a vote. The bill is now awaiting a vote on the House floor.

You can watch the full video of the press conference here and find photos from the event above and here.

“When veterans are forced to retire early due to combat-related injuries, they should not pay a penalty with a reduced retirement check because they received a disability payment. That’s just plain wrong,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (CA-33). “That’s a car payment. That’s rent. That’s groceries for the family. These veterans served our nation, and the law today asks them to pay for their injuries. It’s not fair, and it’s not right. It’s time for the House of Representatives to vote on the Major Richard Star Act.”

“Veterans should not have to wait any longer,” said Rep. Mark Takano (CA-39), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs. “A majority of House members want to bring the Major Richard Star Act to the floor, and once we are back in Washington, it will receive a vote. Getting rid of the wounded veteran tax as soon as possible will show these great Americans that their government continues to honor their service and sacrifice.”
