title: Boozman, Womack Celebrate Federal Investment for Crawford County Water Infrastructure
text:
Rep. Womack, Sen. Boozman and USDA official David Branscum presented a USDA grant check to Mountainburg Mayor Susan Wilson.

WASHINGTON—U.S. Senator John Boozman (R-AR) joined Congressman Steve Womack (AR-03) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Rural Development State Director for Arkansas David Branscum to present a check for $8.9 million to the City of Mountainburg to improve its water infrastructure.

The USDA Rural Development award will enable the city to expand its water infrastructure to better serve members of the community.

“Adequate infrastructure is critical for access to clean, safe water. I applaud Mountainburg’s leaders who worked to secure these funds that will ensure this vital resource is available to their community. It is a great example of why I strongly support projects that enhance rural water infrastructure and remain committed to bolstering programs like this that improve the lives of Arkansans by passing Farm Bill 2.0,” Boozman said.

“We cannot allow our rural communities to be left behind, and the federal government can be a critical partner in helping them keep pace. USDA Rural Development’s investment in the first phase of Mountainburg’s water line expansion project in north-central Crawford County will pay dividends for years to come, ensuring families have access to clean, safe drinking water without having to haul water or rely on wells that fail quantity or quality tests. But there is still work to do, which is why I secured $4.4 million in the appropriations bills signed into law this year. This funding will build on the progress already made and extend access to clean water to more than 300 additional residents. I thank Mountainburg Mayor Susan Wilson for her initiative and hard work in engaging with her federal counterparts to meet the needs of both her city and the broader community,” Womack said.

Boozman serves as Chairman of the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee, which has oversight of USDA. Under his leadership, the committee advanced Farm Bill 2.0 in September to boost financing and enhance support for rural water systems to deliver safe and reliable drinking water for rural residents.

The legislation includes more than 100 bipartisan bills and would improve access to USDA Rural Development programs as well as private capital so more communities can strengthen their infrastructure and the vital services that rural residents rely on. Boozman is currently working with his counterparts in the Senate and House of Representatives to craft a compromise farm bill that can pass both chambers of congress by the end of the year.

title: Fischer in Holt County Independent: Reviving Critical Care for O’Neill
McConnell in The Wall Street Journal: Coddling Putin Won’t Bring Peace to Ukraine
text:
WASHINGTON, DC– U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell (R-KY), Chairman of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, submitted the following op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal regarding Ukraine:

President Trump’s gambit to end Russia’s war in Ukraine by pressuring the victim is certain to fail. His approach to the war reveals he misunderstands facts that American voters understand well.

While Vladimir Putin ignores Mr. Trump’s call for an energy cease-fire and continues to murder Ukrainian civilians, the U.S. president claims that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine.” This is factually wrong, strategically naive and morally bankrupt. His obsequious accommodation of Russia, rewarding the aggressor with sanctions relief, won’t persuade Mr. Putin to stop. History shows that such behavior emboldens Russia’s autocrat, who sees it as weakness.

In June 2021, Mr. Putin watched President Biden pause $100 million in lethal security assistance to Ukraine in pursuit of “deliverables” for a U.S.-Russia summit. We know what happened the following year. Yet Mr. Trump seems determined to repeat the mistakes of a predecessor he scorns.

Threatening to withhold security and intelligence assistance or access to crucial satellite communications systems won’t materially weaken Ukraine’s will to defend itself, but it may allow Mr. Putin to make battlefield headway that had until now been out of reach. This could prolong the war, not shorten it. And when Russia’s limited supply of diesel has changed hands, it will have done little to bring down prices at the pump.

Regardless of the midterm election results, Mr. Putin is America’s enemy. He is aligned with China, Iran and North Korea to divide the U.S. from our allies and undermine our global influence.

Americans, including most Republicans, understand this. They sympathize with Ukraine’s defenders, its abducted children, its shivering elderly and persecuted Christians. They know America’s strategic interests are aligned with Kyiv’s.

If the president means what he says about ending the conflict, he should look to the wisdom of the American people, not naive businessmen who seem to think diplomacy entails fawning over adversaries. Mr. Putin is many things, but he is no humanitarian. A Russian victory would have far worse consequences for our economic and national security and our global influence than temporarily high diesel prices.

Mr. Putin has directed cyberattacks against U.S. government agencies, businesses and infrastructure and helped Iran target U.S. personnel and facilities in the Middle East. He is an ally of Xi Jinping. He will continue to seize opportunities to weaken America—and Europe.

The Continent is our biggest trading partner and an engine of American economic growth. An outcome to this war that makes it easier for Russia to threaten Europe harms our own interests. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s innovation on the battlefield against a more powerful aggressor makes its value as a partner obvious.

The destruction of American aircraft, materiel and facilities, and the killing of U.S. personnel by Iranian drones—the same kind of Iranian drones Russia uses against Ukrainian cities—underscores the urgency of working with Ukraine. Senior Army leaders who traveled to Ukraine, like former Secretary Dan Driscoll, Gen. Chris Donahue and Lt. Gen. Curtis Buzzard, understood this. Not a single senior Pentagon policy official appears to have done the same, and it shows.

The Pentagon officials involved in restricting U.S. assistance to Ukraine should explain how abandoning the “Silicon Valley of warfare” and the world’s experts in battlefield drone innovation will help America achieve drone dominance. Next, they should explain why the president blames Ukraine for the U.S. military’s shortage of Tomahawk cruise missiles, even though we haven’t provided any to Ukraine.

The strategic incoherence extends beyond Ukraine. The Pentagon has undercut allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization that are meeting military spending targets faster than we are. This is evident in the Pentagon policy office’s determination that supporting Baltic allies is wasteful and the Pentagon’s failure to commit appropriated funds to the Baltic Security Initiative. These funds are invested directly in the U.S. defense industrial base. The initiative’s procurement equips friends on NATO’s front line and spurs their own far greater investments in American weapons.

European assistance to Ukraine outpaces our own. The Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List lets allies procure American-made weapons for this purpose. But the Trump administration is using PURL to pressure allies to reimburse the U.S. for security assistance Congress already appropriated. This dilutes our allies’ buying power and undermines American leadership and credibility. It also perversely encourages allies to reduce their use of American military hardware as soon as they can.

Securing a just and stable peace in Ukraine will require the moral clarity to assign blame where it belongs and a willingness to speak the only language Mr. Putin understands: strength.

The good news for Americans is that Senate Republicans oppose retreat and appeasement and favor a strong defense. They support Ukraine. They support NATO. They understand Russia, China, North Korea and Iran are enemies. And they want the president to work with Congress to restore American primacy.

Mr. Trump has high hopes for a lame-duck legislative agenda, including the one-time defense spending I’ve urged the administration instead to build into full-year appropriations. Passing this agenda will require working with Republicans who know the difference between the good guys and the bad guys. Ending the obeisance to Mr. Putin may be table stakes for the end-of-year legislation. The president should plan accordingly.

Mr. McConnell, a Republican, is a U.S. senator from Kentucky.

###

title: ICYMI: Murkowski Addresses Alaska Federation of Natives Convention
text:
Anchorage, Alaska— U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Chairman of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, addressed the Alaska Federation of Natives (AFN) at their annual convention in Anchorage, Alaska. The AFN Convention serves as the principal forum and voice for the Alaska Native community in addressing critical issues of public policy and government. This year’s theme is “Rooted in Land and Tradition, Rising in Our Voices.”

Watch the full remarks here.

Senator Murkowski Speech Transcript – Remarks as Delivered

“Thank you to the Board, to Ben, and to the staff. Thank you for the opportunity to be back at AFN yet again. It’s always, always, always good to be here. I always feel smarter after AFN. Maybe it’s because I’m surrounded by the elders who guide us all. It was so great to sit and listen to the wisdom of Rosita Worl this morning.

“Rosita is the one who taught me, and who continues to remind me, to honor my adopted Tlingit name, Aan shaawátk'i, meaning “Lady of the Land.” And she holds me to that, and that’s a good thing.

“But it is also right to be here this morning to recognize our honored and treasured veterans who have served, and to witness the completion of some of the well-earned benefits that those Alaska Native veterans deserve, with the final satisfaction of allotments. We appreciate Assistant Secretary Kirkland being here with us this morning.

“But we’re looking at the backdrop here in front of us, behind us. Sixty years ago – it was 60 years ago that Alaska Native leaders came together because they knew that they were stronger when they stood together. They came from different regions. They spoke different languages. They faced different challenges. But they were united. They were united around the lands and the traditions that had sustained their people for generations and generations.

“And leaders like Marlene Johnson of Hoonah, who we lost just this past year – we miss them. But there are those who are still with us, still sharing their wisdom: Sam Kito and Emil Notti who we heard from earlier in the week; Willie Hensley; I see Roy Huhndorf back there. They came together. They spoke with one voice, and they changed Alaska.

“Your theme that you see reflected, ‘Rooted in Land and Tradition and Rising in Our Voices,’ really captures both that history and where we are today. Across thousands of miles and distinct cultures, those roots are alive in your languages, ceremonies, and practices—from the ?u.éex’ of Southeast, to Kivgiq and Nalukataq in the Arctic, to yuraq in Western Alaska as you’re carrying your knowledge and your traditions forward, bearing the obligations to care for one another and to leave something better for future generations.

“And we’ve seen that strength. We’ve seen that strength for 60 years now at AFN.

“We lost one of those leaders, my friend Joel Jackson. Joel was a man who was so identified with his community. For more than 35 years, he led the Organized Village of Kake, including eight years as Tribal President, and he fought for his community. He fought for the strongest. He spoke up for the murdered and missing Indigenous peoples. He helped lead the long, long effort for acknowledgment of the Navy’s bombardment of Kake.

“And I was so honored, truly honored, to stand with him on his ancestors’ land to witness that historic apology just a couple of years ago. And that was important because it wasn’t just Kake he helped – he helped deliver that apology to the people of Wrangell and the people of Angoon that was so long outstanding.

“But Joel also stood for our fish as well. He was alarmed by the decline of our salmon. He pushed for action, especially on trolling and wasteful bycatch, and he did so not only with the sense of urgency that the situation demands, but with the thoughtfulness and the respect that all Alaskans deserve.

“There’s a lot of debate about bycatch nowadays. You hear it all, and in fairness, we should welcome that debate. We should also remember, as Joel did, that our people and our communities come first. They must come first.

“And while there’s no easy answer, no one answer on this, we can work together without demonizing others to figure this out and to bring our fish back.

“Sixty years gives us a chance to recognize those who brought us here and to talk honestly about where we go next. And we heard that challenge from Dr. Worl this morning.

“I reflect a lot about those who gave much to me, the elders with their wisdom. And I still count as a friend a beautiful man who is no longer with us, Sidney Huntington, a very strong elder from the Interior.

“Sidney was a trapper. He fished. He built boats, and he helped build Galena’s schools. He had a third-grade education, but he became one of Alaska’s strongest advocates for education. He was an unwavering champion for young people.

“On one of my trips to Galena, we flew into the airport there and got off the plane, and here’s Sidney sitting outside on a little bench. And he was waiting for me. He was waiting because he knew I was going to be doing my little meet-and-greet. He wanted a piece of my time to share with me his views on what was important in education. What was I going to be doing for the children, not only in Galena, but all over Alaska.

“He was always ready to give me advice. He believed young people had a responsibility to listen to elders, and elders had a responsibility to share what they knew and to tell the truth.

“Sidney knew that elders are the ultimate ‘social influencers.’ He was kind of one of the originals, I guess. And, you know, I think about, okay, if I got off that plane and Sidney was still there, sitting on that bench, what kind of wisdom would he want to impart on me? And I kind of think he would say, ‘Lisa, you need to give those kids some Auntie advice.’ My auntie advice is to tell them to get off their phones and get outside.

“But we know that guidance, that knowledge from our elders, saves lives. And their respect for land, for traditions, for one another, can help heal and help communities adapt to dramatic economic, technological, demographic, and environmental change.”

“So we have just recently passed the one-year mark since ex-Typhoon Halong devastated Western Alaska. And I was downstairs last year, again just about this time, and I was talking to some young people from Kipnuk and Kwigillingok at Elders and Youth. At that time, they didn’t know the impact on their communities. They didn’t know if they had communities to return to. They didn’t know if they had a home to go to.

“That’s where we were just last year. And that storm scattered those families from Kipnuk and so many other communities. It scattered families here to Anchorage, out to Bethel, up in the Mat-Su Valley, and beyond.

“Now, when you think about the loss, the loss of the house is certainly one thing, but the loss of your community, the loss of your subsistence foods – this has been so devastating for so many.

“Government can do many things to help, but the truly meaningful connections come through us as people, being there for one another.

“I was looking out the window here earlier, and one of the requests that we heard when I visited with many of the Halong families and some of the board from Kipnuk and Kwigillingok —they were commenting that some of the things they missed most were the things that come with spring, like being able to gather seagull eggs and to eat that food that they so identified with.

“And you look around, and there are seagulls all over the place here. We said there must be a way, there must be a way to help them gather during the spring.

“Long story short, we were able to deliver a couple hundred seagull eggs that were plucked from the tops of these buildings that you see out here. It’s not exactly beautiful nesting grounds, but the fact of the matter is, we were able to get eggs to families so that they could taste that taste of home a little bit.

“And then in May, at the Alaska Native Heritage Center, there were seven high school graduates who had been displaced from Kipnuk and Kwig, and they gathered in reunion. They held a rose ceremony where the graduates thanked those who had carried them through. Tanqik “Dunn” Igkurak from Kwig made sure that each graduate had a cake to take home, just as they would have had were they in the village.

“And so it’s those simple things where, again, you’re making that small connection. Those students graduated far from home, and now their families and their communities are deciding what home will look like in the years ahead.

“Tribal leaders, including Kipnuk Tribal Administrator Rayna Paul, have had to keep their communities together while navigating a disaster system that is ill-suited to rural Alaska. They’re weighing relocation sites, land ownership, subsistence access, infrastructure, and above all, whether the next generation can live somewhere safe, to just know that their families will be safe.

“We face many of the same questions, and that’s why, immediately after the storm, your delegation joined together to press for a federal disaster declaration and needed resources.

“And that’s why this spring, as the chairman of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee, I held field hearings in both Anchorage and Bethel so that you could tell me what was working and, more importantly, what was not working.

“At those hearings, we heard from Lucy Martin of Kwigillingok. She described the terror of her home breaking loose from its foundation and floating in the dark floodwaters.

“And we heard very clearly that the relocation programs are fragmented, that disaster assistance does not fit rural Alaska, and that communities need to be consulted before decisions are made for them. And it’s so important to underscore that.

“But this is truly what rising in our voices means. It means Native communities having the power not only to share what they have experienced, but to shape what happens next.

“And we are seeing progress. That’s what’s happening in Allakaket, where residents are helping to design a water system that fits their community. We’re seeing it in the tribal health system, where Alaska Native students are preparing to become that next generation of providers, and also through culturally grounded work being done by CITC, by Tlingit & Haida, and so many more.

“So last year, the crisis as we gathered was Halong. This year, it’s energy and high prices.

“It is wrong. It is wrong that fuel prices are so high. For six months now, I have voted to respond responsibly to the war in Iran, which drove the prices up, and is the key to bringing them down.

“We know that high fuel prices are a threat to everyone, urban and rural alike, from Wasilla to Wrangell. I get it. It is hard to buy groceries. It is hard to fill up your fuel tanks. It is hard to run snow machines or to engage in subsistence hunting. It’s hard to run a business.

“I fear that many Alaskans will struggle to keep warm this winter as they make a choice between keeping warm and buying food. And this is not right.

“We’ve seen some pretty historic efforts, really heroic efforts. James Stevens – he pushed to get fuel to Akta – what he did to try to make sure that they had fuel delivered before winter.

“But again, what is happening. What is happening in your communities, what is happening to your families – it is not right.

“And I recognize that even when prices eventually go back down – which they will – many, many of you, many of us in Alaska, are still going to be paying far more for our energy than most of the rest of the country. So there is so much that we need to do in this space.

“We can push for greater federal assistance, and you know that I do that, whether it’s LIHEAP or weatherization. We’re going to hear some encouraging news from the Department of Energy with regards to grants.

“But my goal, my goal is to help every one of our communities bring down energy prices and bring them down for good. And the solutions are going to look different from community to community, region to region. And it’s not easy. It’s not. That’s our reality.

“But we must work together to meet this challenge, or our communities will not thrive and will not be healthy.

“This week at Elders and Youth, there was some very important discussion about mental health, about bullying in schools, bullying online, and about suicide, as too many continue to lose hope and to take their own lives as well.

“I was really pleased to see the very powerful resolution that passed earlier this week, and it’s why I’m encouraged by Alakanuk’s plan to address Native wellness and suicide prevention with federal grant support.

“Young people—it’s the young people who will shape the response, with traditional teachings alongside counseling, crisis care, and Calricaraq. I really need to work on my languages, but it is the holistic wellness curriculum. But it’s good. What they’re doing there is solid.

“And then earlier this week, I had an opportunity – and again, I just get goosebumps when I think about these young people. I was joined by two outstanding Alaska Native young leaders, Moses Wiseman and Taylor Higgins, and they were presenting. We were all presenting. We were at the National Congress of American Indians conference. It was down in California. There were thousands of people there, and in front of these tribal leaders and these advocates, these two strong young Alaska Native leaders shared their perspectives on the impact of Typhoon Halong, the importance of language revitalization, the importance of mental health services, housing – all of it.

“I was so proud of them. Those two young people, along with two others – they got a standing ovation from this massive audience for speaking from their hearts as young people and talking about how they can make a difference for others.

“On Saturday, Moses and Taylor will be here at AFN for a panel on the next 60 years. So I’m just so proud of them. They’re making a difference for their communities. They’re helping to shape the future of the next generation.

“And you should all, when you see them, give them an attaboy, an attagirl, because they are making a difference for all of us.

“But it’s listening to our young people. That’s how my team and I, in Washington, D.C., and here in Alaska, worked to build and draft our Native Children’s Commission Implementation Act.

“This is legislation that you heard Ben talking about earlier, AFN’s priority, or one of your significant priorities, focused on the health and well-being of Native children around the country.

“One of the titles in that bill would increase direct Tribal set-asides and expand Tribal self-governance for behavioral health programs. That would allow Tribes like Alukanuk to build a single behavioral-health program instead of piecing together several different federal grants.

“So what we did is we listened. We took years to listen. We were traveling all over the state, traveling all over the country, listening to young people.

“Our bill is guided by the commission’s findings: that culture heals and builds resilience, that community control is the key, and that holistic programming better serves our families.

“And this is important. This is important because we have seen, we have seen what happens when government does the opposite, when it separates children from their families, from their communities, from their languages, and from their culture.

“And for generations, unfortunately, that was the policy here in the United States. Native children were taken from their homes. They were sent to boarding schools designed to strip away their identity and assimilate them into another culture.

“This year, another Alaska Native story came full circle at Carlisle.

“Nyché Andrew was an intern for me on the Senate Indian Affairs Committee last year. She’s now a researcher at the Alaska Native Heritage Center, and she has been helping to find descendants of those students who died at the Carlisle boarding school in Pennsylvania.

“She was going through the archives, and she recognized the tavlugun, which is a traditional chin tattoo. She recognized it in a student photograph and discovered a relative of hers who had died there 125 years ago. And they traced her back to her family. Then she and her mother traveled to Carlisle to guide Tummassak back home to Shishmaref.

“Sometimes things happen in your life, and you’re not really quite sure how or why we were placed in the same spot at the same time.

“I was coming back to Alaska from Washington, D.C., and I was in the Seattle airport waiting to board the airplane. A woman comes up to me, and she says, ‘You don’t know me, but you know my daughter, Nyché. She was an intern for you.’

“And I said, ‘Yes, wonderful.’

“And she shared with me that she and Nyché were bringing Tummassak back home. She reached into her bag, and she said, ‘I want you to have this keepsake.’

“And she gave me a little beaded keepsake around an antler horn, with a forget-me-not in the center of it.

“Included with this was a little note that she had printed up, and it says:

“‘Returning home to Shishmaref after 129 years. Tummassak was just 12 when she was taken from the Teller Alaska reindeer station. She arrived at Carlisle, Pennsylvania, on November 14, 1897, and she was only 15 when she passed away from tuberculosis on April 8, 1900. This precious keepsake, made in honor of Alaska’s state flower, the forget-me-not, on a reindeer antler.’

“We will never forget Tummassak. We will never forget those who were separated from our families. We will always remember, and we will put our work toward those efforts.

“And that’s exactly why I’ve been working for as many years as I have to advance legislation to address the legacy of federal Indian boarding school policies, because healing requires truth.

“I’ll tell you that history also is a reminder of why your voices matter in shaping the decisions that affect your communities and your state.

“More than a century ago, William Paul, a young Tlingit man, was also sent to Carlisle. While he was there, he learned the printing press. He brought that to your home, and he used the printed word, the law, and the Alaska Native Brotherhood to fight for land, for civil rights, and for the vote.

“And in 1924, he became the first Alaska Native elected to the territorial legislature.

“An institution that was intended to weaken Native identity gave William Paul a tool that he carried home, and he turned it toward strengthening Native political representation.

“But having rights on paper is not enough if people cannot exercise them.

“I believe our elections must be secure. Now, I’ve supported requiring identification to vote. I think we get that. But I cannot support the so-called SAVE Act as it’s written because of the barriers that it would create for Alaskans, particularly in our rural communities, where we’re seeing many of our tribes working to provide increasingly secure ID cards, including REAL ID-compliant cards, which is great.

“But even those IDs may not necessarily count as documentary proof of citizenship under the bill.

“For an Alaska Native voter in a community off the road system, getting these documents could mean significant additional cost and travel delays. And we do not need new barriers for lawful voters who are American citizens. We need less confusion. We need fewer obstacles to voting.

“For me, saving America starts with preserving your right to vote.

“I don’t see Michelle sitting down here, but I was listening carefully to all of her efforts, and I want to thank Michelle and Get Out the Native Vote. They’re doing a good, strong job here.

“She has traveled across the state, reminding people of the power that they have when they show up and cast their votes.

“You’ve also got the Youth at the Booth program, getting 16- and 17-year-olds involved at polling places. This is how you build the next generation of engaged citizens and leaders.

“But we also need to make sure that the mechanics of voting work in rural Alaska.

“I was thinking about Ivalu Blanchett. She was trying to get to Nunapitchuk on primary day to go help elders and other voters, but her flight was canceled. When she called home that morning, she found out that the polling place had not even opened, and it wasn’t going to be until about five o’clock before people there could actually vote.

“But I also think about how, earlier this year, 75 absentee in-person ballots from rural Alaska arrived after the certification deadline because of mail delays, even though the voters did everything right. And stuff happens.

“So we have to be attuned to this, because where you live should not determine whether your voice is heard and whether your vote is counted.

“Know that I am pushing to preserve your right to vote. But you – you are the one with the power of the vote. You are the one that needs to get out and exercise that and go vote.

“And you heard it from Michelle: making it easy. Here in Anchorage, you can go across the street at City Hall, Midtown Mall. If you’re in the Valley, you can go to the Menards Sports Center in Wasilla or the Mat-Su Borough building in Palmer.

“There’s information everywhere. It’s all around you, downstairs at my booth. But don’t, don’t fail to have your vote count.

“When I think about rising in our voices, I think about the people I’ve heard across Alaska this year: long-term survivors, the tribal leaders in Bethel and Anchorage, when I met with the folks at TCC at the Nenana Health and Wellness Center – exciting what they’ve got coming there – dancers and language speakers at Celebration in Juneau, leaders working for Native children.

“And at one of those gatherings in D.C. earlier this year, I was very honored to be gifted a name from the Mandan tribe of North Dakota. They gifted me the name Hó I´i?´he which means “strong voice.”

“And I thought about that name when I met with tribal leaders in the Lower 48 this week, and I thought about it in Greenland, where I was just last week, when I met with the Inuit people, who are now facing many of the same transitions that you have in years past.

“And I am immensely proud of the respect from Indigenous peoples around the world. But that is only the case because of what I have received from so many of you during my time here at AFN, in your communities, and with all of you.

“You have helped me grow. You have helped me understand that having a strong voice carries a responsibility. It means making sure that the voices of the people that you represent are heard where the decisions are being made.

“And that is the responsibility that I carry with me as I represent you. That is why I work with you to protect our fish, to lower our energy costs, to be ready for the storms that we know are coming.

“And that’s why I will continue to work with Alyce Spotted Bear, Walter Soboleff, and so many Native leaders before us and today, to make sure that every Alaskan community has a voice in its future, and every child has the opportunity to grow up strong, supported, connected to their culture, and deeply rooted in who they are.

“Gunalchéesh. Thank you for the opportunity to be with you yet again.”

Note: This is a rough transcript of the speech and may contain minor deviations from Senator Murkowski’s exact words.

title: Reps. Kim, Beatty Introduce Resolution to Designate October as National Financial Planning Month
Congressman Aderholt Applauds VA Grant for Alabama Veterans Memorial Cemetery-North
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C – Today, Congressman Robert Aderholt (AL-04) highlighted the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ award of more than $18 million through the Veterans Cemetery Grant Program to support the establishment a new veterans cemetery in North Alabama.

In fiscal year 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs awarded a record $106.5 million in grants to 21 cemeteries across U.S. states, territories, and tribal nations. This represents the highest level of annual funding since the Veterans Cemetery Grant Program was established in 1980.

These grants help ensure that more than 94% of veterans living in the United States have access to a veteran’s cemetery within 75 miles of their homes.

As part of the FY2026 awards, $18,094,445 was granted to establish the Alabama Veterans Memorial Cemetery-North in Huntsville. Additionally, the VA will reimburse up to $875,706 for the fabrication and delivery of pre-placed crypts.

Currently, more than 42,000 veterans in North Alabama live outside the 75-mile service radius of an existing state or national veteran’s cemetery. The new facility will help close this gap and is expected to serve veterans and their families in North Alabama for more than 200 years.

“Veterans have given and sacrificed immensely to protect the fundamental liberties of our great country. Their unwavering service has sustained democracy and defended freedom around the world,” said Congressman Aderholt. “We owe our veterans and their families a great debt of gratitude, and this investment is an important step toward ensuring they receive the recognition, respect, and lasting honor they deserve.”

The Alabama Veterans Memorial Cemetery-North will be the state’s second veteran’s cemetery. The only existing veteran’s cemetery in Alabama is located in Spanish Fort, a six-hour drive from parts of North Alabama.

This investment will help ensure that North Alabama’s veterans and their families have access to a dignified final resting place that reflects our deep gratitude for their service and sacrifice.

title: Amo Celebrates $1.2 Million Federal Investment in Cumberland Stormwater Improvements to Protect Local Businesses and Jobs
text:
Cumberland, RI – TODAY, Congressman Gabe Amo (D-RI-01) joined local leaders today to celebrate the completion of a $1.2 million stormwater infrastructure project along Industrial Road, helping Cumberland address chronic flooding in its largest commercial area and better protect the businesses, workers, and infrastructure that keep its economy moving.

Industrial Road is Cumberland’s largest commercial area and business park, home to more than 30 businesses. During increasingly frequent heavy rainstorms, outdated drainage infrastructure has contributed to flooding that disrupts business operations, delays deliveries, and can prevent employees from getting to work.

The completed project upgrades the area’s stormwater system to capture, manage, and treat runoff before returning it to the state’s drainage system. These improvements help reduce flooding, protect nearby infrastructure, support reliable business operations during severe weather, and safeguard water quality and the surrounding environment.

“Federal resources should make a real difference in people’s lives and in the communities they call home,” said Congressman Gabe Amo. “This $1.2 million investment led by my predecessor, Congressman Cicilline, is helping Cumberland tackle a longstanding problem for local businesses and workers. By improving stormwater infrastructure, we’re helping protect jobs, keep goods moving, and strengthen one of Cumberland’s most important business areas. I’m proud to continue delivering for Rhode Islanders.”

Background

Community project funding was secured by Senators Jack Reed (D-RI), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and former Congressman David Cicilline (D-RI-01) through a FY2023 funding package.

Industrial Road is Cumberland's largest commercial area and business park, home to over thirty businesses. The federal funding was used to implement an efficient stormwater drainage system to prevent flooding during heavy rainfall events.

title: Arrington Fights to End Illegal Immigrant Exploitation of Federal Housing Program
text:
Washington, D.C. – House Budget Chairman Jodey Arrington (TX-19) introduced his LIHTC Security Act, legislation to prevent illegal immigrants from exploiting the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program, which provides nearly $15 billion annually in federal tax incentives to support affordable rental housing. The bill would establish citizenship and immigration-status eligibility requirements for tenants in qualifying low-income housing units and require states to enforce those standards or accept a 5% reduction in their annual housing tax credit allocation.

“Securing the border and stopping illegal immigration are fundamentally about addressing the perverse incentives that encourage people to cut the line and break our laws,” said Chairman Jodey Arrington. “Every year, Washington provides nearly $15 billion through the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) to support the development of affordable rental housing, with no requirement to verify tenants’ citizenship or legal status. That loophole allows illegal immigrants to exploit the program at the expense of low-income American families struggling to find affordable housing. Hardworking American taxpayers shouldn’t be forced to foot the bill for housing people who are in this country illegally. My LIHTC Security Act closes this loophole by establishing commonsense eligibility standards and holding states accountable for ensuring these tax credits benefit American citizens, not illegal immigrants.”

“With the national debt having recently surpassed the $40 trillion mark, Washington must do everything it can to ensure that taxpayer-funded programs benefit only U.S. citizens and legal residents,” said Alexander Ciccone, the Policy and Government Affairs Manager at the National Taxpayers Union. “By setting clear eligibility standards for federally subsidized housing, Representative Arrington’s commonsense legislation is exactly the kind of good-government measure that promotes accountability for taxpayer dollars and helps restore public trust in government.”

“Housing affordability is a top issue for Americans right now, and Congress needs to ensure it is doing its part to protect existing housing options, especially for young families,” said Terry Schilling, the President of the American Principles Project. “This bill ensures that only Americans who need the most help getting on their feet are eligible for American housing assistance. It's a no-brainer, and APP is proud to support it.”

Background:

The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program provides federal tax incentives to state housing authorities to help developers build affordable rental housing, costing taxpayers approximately $15 billion annually.

There is no current federal requirement that tenants living in LIHTC-subsidized housing be U.S. citizens or legal residents, leaving the door open for illegal aliens to take advantage of federal subsidies meant to benefit low-income Americans.

Chairman Arrington’s LIHTC Security Act would establish a requirement for tenants living in qualifying housing projects to be U.S. citizens or legal residents in order for housing developers to receive federal tax credits.

If a state chooses not to comply, it will be penalized with a reduction of its housing tax credit allocation.

title: Balint Urges FTC to Block $29.1 Billion Sysco-Restaurant Depot Merger
text:
BRATTLEBORO, VT – Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL) joined Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) and other colleagues in sending a letter to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) urging rejection of Sysco Corporation’s proposed $29.1 billion acquisition of Jetro Restaurant Depot. Members warned that the merger would reduce competition, drive up costs for independent restaurants, and threaten small businesses that anchor local economies across the nation.

Across the country, independent restaurants are already facing mounting financial pressure, with food costs up 38 percent nationwide since 2019 and nearly half of restaurant operators reporting that their businesses were unprofitable in 2025. Sysco’s acquisition of Restaurant Depot would eliminate a critical source of price competition, leaving independent restaurant owners with fewer options to control costs and putting additional pressure on businesses already struggling to keep prices affordable for their customers.

“Independent restaurants are already struggling because of rising food costs,” said Rep. Becca Balint. “By buying Restaurant Depot, Sysco would eliminate a key source of competition that independent restaurants rely on to get a fair price on food and supplies. That means higher costs for local restaurants and more expensive meals for working families. We need regulators to be serious about pushing back against this wave of corporate consolidation so that people can afford to live their lives and so our small, local businesses can have a fair shot.”

“Independent restaurants are part of the fabric of Western New York. They employ our neighbors, support local suppliers, and give our communities places to come together. These small businesses are already being squeezed by rising food prices and operating costs, and they cannot afford another hit,” said Rep. Kennedy. “This merger would put even more power in the hands of a major distributor while taking away one of the few tools independent restaurants have to keep their costs down. When competition disappears, small businesses pay the price and those costs ultimately reach the families sitting down at the table. The FTC must stand up for independent businesses, protect competition, and reject this deal.”

“Independent restaurants are operating on razor-thin margins, and Restaurant Depot is one of the few tools they have to check broadline prices and keep their costs in line. We are grateful to Congressman Tim Kennedy for his leadership urging the FTC to reject Sysco's proposed acquisition of Restaurant Depot. When competition disappears from the supply chain, the consequences reach well beyond a restaurant’s doors putting farmers, local artisans and the economic stability of communities at risk.” Erika Polmar, Executive Director, Independent Restaurant Coalition

Lawmakers underscored the importance of protecting competition as families and small businesses continue to face affordability challenges. Allowing further consolidation in the foodservice supply chain would leave independent restaurants with fewer choices and less leverage to manage costs, threatening the local businesses and jobs that communities depend on.

Background

Restaurant Depot operates 167 warehouse locations across 35 states, serving more than 725,000 independent restaurants and foodservice operators. Its cash-and-carry model allows restaurant owners to compare prices directly with traditional wholesale distributors like Sysco and negotiate more competitive terms. This proposed acquisition would place both distribution channels under the same corporate ownership, eliminating an important check on pricing in the foodservice supply chain. Independent restaurants employ approximately 11 million workers nationwide and support more than five million additional jobs across supply chains that include farms, fisheries, dairies, equipment suppliers, and specialty food producers. By hiring locally, purchasing from local suppliers, and banking with local financial institutions, these businesses help sustain the communities they serve. The FTC has previously recognized the competitive risks of consolidation in foodservice distribution: in 2015, the Commission opposed Sysco’s proposed acquisition of US Foods, arguing that the merger would substantially reduce competition and likely increase prices for restaurants. After a federal district court granted the FTC’s request for a preliminary injunction, the companies abandoned the deal.

Full text of the letter can be found here.

title: Barr Announces $1M Federal Grant to University of Kentucky to Build Critical Minerals Workforce
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Andy Barr (R-KY-06) announced that the University of Kentucky (UK) has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to receive $1 million through the PROSPECT Planning Prize. The award will help UK train the next generation of mining engineers and critical minerals professionals. Barr voted for the federal funding that is being delivered to UK to boost this program.

"Kentucky helped power this country for generations, and our state has a central role to play in America's energy and mineral independence," said Congressman Barr. "Right now, we depend far too much on China and other foreign adversaries for the critical minerals behind everything from our power grid to our defense systems. Fixing that starts with the workforce. I was proud to vote for the funding behind this program, and I congratulate the University of Kentucky on earning this award. UK's mining engineering program will help ensure the minerals we need are produced, processed, and recycled by American workers on American soil."

“Meeting the energy needs of the future will take new ideas, strong partnerships and a workforce prepared to put those ideas into practice,” said Zach Agioutantis, Ph.D., chair of mining engineering in the Stanley and Karen Pigman College of Engineering. “At UK, we are bringing those pieces together — giving students meaningful opportunities, while advancing solutions that benefit Kentucky and communities across the country.”

About PROSPECT

On October 26, DOE's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) selected 16 universities to share a total of $16 million through the PROSPECT Planning Prize. The prize supports universities in developing the skilled workforce required to produce, process, recover, and recycle critical minerals in the United States. Other selected schools include Colorado School of Mines, Penn State, Virginia Tech, and West Virginia University.

The Planning Prize is part of DOE's broader $100 million Providing Opportunities for Specialized Education in Critical Technologies (PROSPECT) initiative. PROSPECT aims to double the number of graduates with mining, minerals, and related supply chain credentials within two years. Over the long term, it will support new curricula, modern teaching tools, scholarships, financial aid, and other incentives to grow these fields. The initiative also seeks to modernize critical minerals education with emerging technologies like automation, data science, advanced manufacturing, and systems engineering.

The need is urgent. Enrollment in American mining programs has fallen by roughly 45 percent since 2015, and DOE estimates the nation will need approximately 6,000 new mining engineers over the next decade. Critical minerals and rare earth elements are essential to manufacturing energy infrastructure, defense systems, automobiles, and consumer electronics.

UK's Leadership in Mining and Critical Minerals

UK's Department of Mining Engineering is one of the oldest programs of its kind in the country and one of only 14 accredited mining engineering programs in the nation. Students train hands-on at UK's Experimental Mine, a one-of-a-kind facility for research and instruction in blasting and explosives, rock mechanics, ventilation, and mine safety.

UK's Center for Applied Energy Research (CAER) is a national leader in recovering critical minerals and rare earth elements from domestic sources, including Kentucky coal. Researchers have developed processes to extract valuable metals and minerals from coal byproducts in the Western Kentucky coalfields. They have also studied Eastern Kentucky, home to a significant domestic source of rare earth elements.

UK is also a partner in DOE's nearly $25 million "Building the Mine of the Future" initiative, which will create a national proving ground for autonomous and connected mining technologies in underground and surface environments. Earlier this month, Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson visited UK's campus to tour the Experimental Mine, meet with mining engineering students, and see CAER's critical minerals research firsthand.

The PROSPECT Planning Prize is funded by CMEI and managed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies under the American-Made prize program. More information is available here.

title: Baumgartner Honors Service by Hiring Veteran, Gold Star Family Member, or Active-Duty Spouse for Congressional Aide Role
text:
SPOKANE, WA — Congressman Michael Baumgartner (WA-05) is currently seeking qualified candidates for a two-year, full-time paid position through the Green & Gold Congressional Aide Program. This important role will focus on supporting military members and their families by managing veteran-related casework and serving as a vital liaison between constituents and federal, state, and local agencies.

The Green and Gold Congressional Aide Program was established by the House of Representatives to provide employment opportunities for veterans. The position is based in Congressman Baumgartner’s Spokane or Colville district offices. However, applicants residing anywhere within Washington state’s 5th Congressional District are encouraged to apply.

“This program offers a unique opportunity to serve the veterans and military families of Eastern Washington while gaining invaluable experience working with government agencies,” said Congressman Baumgartner. “I encourage all eligible veterans, Gold Star family members, and active-duty spouses to consider applying.”

Eligibility Requirements:

Veterans must meet all the following criteria:

Honorably discharged;

Released from active duty within the last six years;

Pay grades at or below E-5, O-3, or W-2;

Veterans promoted to E-6, O-4, or W-3 within six months of separation are eligible if all other criteria are met;

Veterans receiving 20-year or Temporary Early Retirement Authorization (TERA) retirement are not eligible.

Gold Star Family Members must be a surviving child (including stepchild), spouse, parent, or sibling of:

A service member who died in the line of duty (including reserves and National Guard), unless due to willful misconduct; or

A veteran with an Honorable Discharge who died from a service-connected disability within four years of separation.

Active-Duty Spouses must be the spouse of a full-time active-duty service member. Please note that spouses of Title X mobilized service members are not eligible.

title: Ciscomani Welcomes Secretary Rollins to Tucson, Highlights Agricultural Advancements in Southern Arizona
text:
Tucson, AZ - U.S. Representative Juan Ciscomani welcomed U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brooke Rollins to Tucson, for a visit highlighting the agricultural strength of Arizona’s Sixth Congressional District and the Administration’s work to support Southern Arizona’s farmers and ranchers.

Secretary Rollins and Representative Ciscomani attended a ribbon cutting ceremony at the Southwest Watershed Research Center, a new Agriculture Research Service facility in Tucson. Following the ceremony, Rollins and Ciscomani held a press conference, joined by USDA Under Secretary for Research, Education, and Economics, Dr. Scott Hutchins to discuss the impact this new facility will have on the agricultural community of Southern Arizona, and to highlight the Administration’s work in supporting and strengthening Arizona’s farmers and ranchers.

"I was proud to join Secretary Rollins for the ribbon cutting of this new research facility, which will make a real difference for farmers and ranchers across Southern Arizona," said Rep. Juan Ciscomani. "Secretary Rollins has been a tremendous partner in delivering results for Southern Arizona, and today’s ribbon cutting is another example of what we can accomplish when we work together with local leaders to address the needs of our communities. This new Agricultural Research Service facility will help strengthen our agricultural industry and support the farmers and ranchers who keep our communities and our economy moving forward. By investing in research and innovation, we can help ensure Southern Arizona’s agricultural industry remains strong and competitive for generations to come."

"From water research to cotton to screwworm, Representative Ciscomani has been an outstanding partner as USDA puts farmers and ranchers first," said Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins. "I was honored to join him in Tuscon today as we opened a research facility that will give our farmers the tools they need to conserve water, protect soil, and sustain productive working lands. I saw firsthand the preparations to soon reopen the Port of Nogales to cattle trade as we keep fighting New World Screwworm and protect the Great American herd. I am grateful to work with a member of Congress who shares USDA’s commitment to protecting American agriculture, strengthening our nation’s food supply, and investing in solutions that benefit producers, communities, and future generations."

Ciscomani has been a continued advocate for the local agricultural community throughout his time in office, especially in the effort to prepare against the threat of New World Screwworm.

Earlier this year, Ciscomani championed the University of Arizona’s successful application for a $3.74 million USDA New World Screwworm Grand Challenge Grant, which will be used to expand research, surveillance, education, outreach, and the development of innovative detection technologies to strengthen Southern Arizona’s preparedness and rapid-response capabilities in the fight against New World Screwworm.

Ciscomani also worked with Secretary Rollins, USDA officials, and Arizona producers to secure a $25 million investment for a sterile fly dispersal facility in Cochise County and to reopen the Douglas Port of Entry for livestock trade. These efforts will strengthen the nation’s long-term response to New World Screwworm.

During today’s visit, Rollins and Ciscomani also traveled visited the Nogales/Mariposa Port of Entry for a roundtable with local agricultural leaders, to highlight the above efforts and discuss their continued dedication to the needs of farmers and ranchers in Southern Arizona.

Rep. Ciscomani remains committed to advocating on behalf of the agricultural community in Arizona’s Sixth District and looks forward to continuing partnership with Secretary Rollins, the USDA, and local producers to ensure Arizona’s farmers and ranchers have the federal resources they need to thrive.

###

title: Congressman Ciscomani, HUD Secretary Turner Tour Tucson’s Center of Opportunity to Address Homelessness and Housing
text:
Tucson, AZ - Congressman Juan Ciscomani and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Secretary Scott Turner toured Gospel Rescue Mission in Tucson today to see firsthand how local partnerships are helping individuals experiencing homelessness find stability, opportunity, and a path forward.

"Everyone deserves the opportunity to rebuild their life, find a place to call home, and pursue their own version of the American Dream. Gospel Rescue Mission is making a real difference right here in Southern Arizona by meeting people where they are and helping them build a path toward a brighter future. I’m grateful to Secretary Turner for joining me to highlight the incredible work happening in our community and bring Southern Arizona’s efforts to the national conversation. Together, we can connect local solutions with federal resources to help more Arizonans get back on their feet," said Congressman Ciscomani.

At the heart of Gospel Rescue Mission’s work is the Center of Opportunity, which brings together housing, recovery services, workforce development, healthcare access, and spiritual support under one roof. Through more than 50 community partnerships with nonprofits, churches, healthcare providers, educational institutions, employers, and social-service agencies, the mission helps individuals address the root causes of homelessness and work toward long-term stability.

"It’s great to be back in Arizona with my friend Congressman Juan Ciscomani. Today, we toured the Gospel Rescue Mission, a faith-based organization leading the way and transforming lives from homelessness to wholeness. It’s an honor to highlight their incredible results-driven work and partner with Congressman Ciscomani who is delivering for Arizona families," said Secretary Scott Turner.

During the tour, Secretary Turner highlighted HUD’s mission to help Americans find stability and opportunity, including through the Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) initiative. The program helps young adults transitioning out of foster care access housing assistance and supportive services to prevent homelessness. Turner has supported a $1.8 million investment in the initiative to assist more than 100 young Americans aging out of foster care.

Expanding access to housing also requires increasing the supply of homes and addressing the barriers that drive up costs. Ciscomani has supported the bipartisan FAST Housing Act to accelerate housing construction by reducing regulatory barriers and introduced the bipartisan CONSTRUCTS Act to address workforce shortages in residential construction. Together, these efforts reflect the importance of pairing immediate support for vulnerable populations with long-term solutions that make housing more accessible and affordable.

That same commitment to lasting solutions is reflected in Gospel Rescue Mission’s work. Through its holistic, faith-based approach and more than 50 community partnerships, the organization helps individuals move beyond crisis toward stability, independence, and a fresh start. The visit highlighted how federal initiatives, local organizations, and community partnerships can work together to address homelessness and expand housing opportunities across Southern Arizona.

title: Rep. Cisneros Introduces Bill Requiring Oversight of Military Suicide Prevention Programs
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. — Congressman Gil Cisneros (CA-31) introduced legislation to conduct oversight into the Department of Defense’s (DoD) suicide prevention measures. If enacted, this legislation would require the DoD’s Inspector General to review efforts by the services to prevent incidents of deaths by suicide, suicide attempts, and suicidal ideation among members of the Armed Forces.

“There has not been an investigation into each military branch’s suicide prevention programs since 2021, when there was a string of suicides on the USS George Washington at port in Norfolk,” said Congressman Cisneros. “Unfortunately, that report confirmed the Navy could have done more. Mental health legislation, like the Brandon Act, is not being carried out to its full extent, and servicemembers are suffering because of it. The military branches owe it to servicemembers and their families to do everything they can to prevent suicide.”

Read the full text of the bill here.

Rep. Cisneros is a Navy Veteran and the former Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness. He currently serves on the House Armed Services Committee, Subcommittee on Military Personnel, and Subcommittee on Intelligence and Special Operations. Rep. Cisneros is a member of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and serves on its leadership team as the Freshman Representative.

title: Representatives Cohen, Kamlager-Dove and Scott Introduce the Death in Custody Reporting Reform Act
text:
WASHINGTON – Representatives Steve Cohen (TN-9), Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37) and Bobby Scott (VA-3) have introduced the Death in Custody Reporting Reform Act (DCRRA) to correct deficient and incomplete reporting of deaths on law enforcement custody despite prior efforts to assure accurate reporting in the Death in Custody Reporting acts of 2000 and 2013. The bill eliminates the vagueness of what law enforcement agencies are required to report deaths in custody, including deaths in healthcare settings, temporary detention centers and immigration detention centers, shifts data collection back to a statistical agency, requires the addition of a checkbox to death certificates to indicate a death in custody, and directs the National Institute of Justice to study aggregate deaths in custody and recommend policy improvements.

Congressman Cohen made the following statement:

“The United States houses nearly 25 percent of the world’s prison population yet the U.S. government does not know how many people die in law enforcement custody despite previous efforts to correct this deficiency. Our bill will finally make clear who and how law enforcement agencies report these deaths, including of those in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody. These reforms will help inform policy on how to reduce and hopefully eliminate all deaths in custody. These changes are long overdue and will assure proper accountability.”

Congresswoman Kamlager-Dove made the following statement:

“It is shameful that our systems still fail to provide families with critical information when a loved one dies in custody. This legislation tackles long‑standing gaps in death‑in‑custody reporting by setting clear definitions, expanding which facilities must report deaths, and strengthening accountability for federal and immigration enforcement agencies. We have a responsibility to improve safety within the system and end the uncertainty and inconsistency that has kept families in the dark when a loved one dies in custody.”

Congressman Scott made the following statement:

“Accurate and timely information on deaths of individuals detained or arrested by law enforcement is critical to determining how we can reduce avoidable deaths in our criminal justice system. When I helped enact the Death in Custody Reporting Act, the goal was to collect reliable data to better understand and prevent these deaths, and gathering data was only intended to be the first step. Frustratingly, multiple Administrations have failed to fully implement the law. This legislation strengthens the law with additional reporting requirements to ensure Congress receives an accurate picture of who is dying in custody.”

Endorsing organization statements:

“Behind every death in custody is a person, a family, and a community burdened with unanswered questions. For too long, failures in our reporting systems have allowed deaths to go uncounted and unexplained. This bill would bring the transparency and accountability necessary to understand why and how people are dying while in custody, hold states and local governments accountable, and prevent future tragedies.” -- Aiden Cotter, director of federal advocacy, the Vera Institute of Justice

“If people were inexplicably dying in your community, the obvious first questions would be: Why? How many? How can we protect others? This bill is a critical step to begin answering those questions so that we can reduce needless deaths in custody and support both patients and correctional staff.” -- William Weber, MD, MPH, Medical Director of the Medical Justice Alliance

Specifically, DCRRA will provide:

Definitional additions eliminate ambiguity about what entities need to report, and what details are necessary.

Expanding death reporting to include healthcare settings, temporary law enforcement detention centers, and immigration detention centers.

Ensuring all deaths at immigration facilities, both privately and government-run, are reported.

Shifting data collection responsibility back to the Bureau of Justice Statistics from the Bureau of Justice Assistance

Requiring the Director of the Bureau of Justice Statistics to submit demographic and cause and manner of death data on deaths in custody to Congress annually, as well as to publish this data on a publicly accessible website.

Establishing a 6-member review panel of experts to assess barriers to compliance and accurate reporting.

Directs the National Institute of Justice to study reported death in custody data and recommend policy improvements.

Requires the Director of the National Center for Health Statistics to add a checkbox to the United States standard certificate of death to indicate the death occurred in custody.

Authorizing $6 million to be appropriated every fiscal year until FY 2037 for data collection, report drafting, and database publishing purposes, up from $0.

Altering the Byrne JAG penalty to allow for more targeted compliance prior to penalty enforcement.

Original cosponsors of the measure are Representatives Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12), Danny K. Davis (IL-07), Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), and Summer Lee (PA-12)

title: CORREA CONVENES ORANGE COUNTY HEALTH LEADERS ON H.R. 1'S TOLL, ONE YEAR LATER
text:
SANTA ANA, Calif. – Congressman Lou Correa (CA-46) today hosted a roundtable with local health care leaders to discuss what H.R. 1, the Republican "One Big Beautiful Bill," has meant for Orange County one year after it became law.

"One year ago, I voted no on H.R. 1 because I knew who would get hurt," said Correa. "Today I heard it directly from the people on the front lines. Clinics, hospitals, and county workers are being asked to do more with less, and Orange County families are paying the price."

Over 900,000 Orange County residents rely on Medi-Cal. Because of Republican cuts to Medi-Cal in the Big Ugly Law, approximately 74,000 Orange County residents could lose Medi-Cal coverage.

The County estimates H.R. 1 will cost it about $396 million, including roughly $380 million in indigent care and $16 million in new administrative costs. The need for care doesn't go away when coverage does. The county is still legally required to treat people who can't pay. Providers at the roundtable expect more emergency room visits, more uncompensated care, and more strain on county clinics, behavioral health services, and public health programs.

“H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill, will not make health care less expensive,” Correa said. "It just moves the bill to the county government, the emergency room, and the family. Kids need food, seniors need care, and working families need a doctor they can afford. I will keep fighting to reverse these cuts."

"It has been over a year since the passage of H.R. 1, and our Community Health Centers (CHCs) continue to navigate significant federal and state policy changes while being asked to do far more with far less. As the backbone of our healthcare safety net, CHCs provide high-quality, comprehensive care to our most vulnerable neighbors, regardless of their ability to pay. Federal cuts, California’s response, and changes to Medicaid eligibility have placed immense pressure on CHCs as they work to ensure Orange County’s 340,000 patients can continue to access the care they deserve. Six counties account for 80.4% of California’s high-risk members. Los Angeles County has the largest number of medium- and high-risk members facing significant continuity-of-care risks, including active dialysis, placement in facilities not yet ready to support the transition, and reliance on providers who cannot bill FFS for withdrawal-risk medications. Orange County ranks second in the number of high-risk members, underscoring the urgent need for proactive care coordination and transition planning to prevent disruptions in care," Isabel Becerra, President and Chief Executive Officer of Coalition of Orange County Community Health Centers, said.

title: Rep. Costa, Joined by Rep. Carbajal and Local Leaders, Demands Transparency and Accountability Over ICE Operations
text:
FRESNO, Calif. – Congressman Jim Costa (CA-21) was joined by Congressman Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Fresno County Supervisor Luis Chavez, and Nora Zaragoza-Yáñez of Faith in the Valley in a virtual press conference today to address recent immigration enforcement operations across the San Joaquin Valley and Central Coast and demand greater transparency and accountability from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

During the press conference, Costa highlighted his efforts to lead members of California’s congressional delegation, including U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, in demanding answers from federal immigration authorities about enforcement priorities, detention practices, and the impact of recent operations on California communities.

BACKGROUND

Since January 2025, the Trump Administration has expanded federal immigration enforcement operations across the country, including in California's San Joaquin Valley and Central Coast. Recent enforcement activity beginning October 2026, has raised concerns among local families, community advocates, and elected officials about detention practices, enforcement priorities, and access to information about individuals taken into custody.

In response, Congressman Costa led a group of 12 legislators in a letter raising serious concerns about federal immigration enforcement tactics and emphasized the responsibility of federal agencies to operate with transparency, accountability, and respect for the constitutional rights and safety of California residents.

In their letter, the lawmakers requested detailed responses to the following:

Explain the purpose and duration of ICE operations across California, including increased enforcement activity in the San Joaquin Valley beginning October 5, 2026.

Clarify immigration enforcement priorities by identifying the criteria ICE agents use to question, arrest, and detain individuals, including whether operations are targeted or involve broader enforcement activities.

Provide transparency on arrests and detentions by releasing a county-by-county breakdown on individuals detained since October 5, including those prior criminal convictions, pending criminal charges, or no criminal record.

Ensure proper agent vetting and training by detailing background checks, screening requirements, and training standards, including whether any requirements have been modified, shortened, or waived.

Strengthen personnel accountability and oversight by requesting details on ICE officer deployments, professional conduct standards, agent training on constitutional rights and use of force, and procedures for investigating alleged misconduct, including any administrative review or personnel investigation initiated following the October 9 incident involving an off-duty ICE officer in Fresno.

Protect due process and access to essential services by demanding transparency on detention locations, processing and transfer procedures, access to legal counsel, notification of rights, family communication, and necessary medical care following an arrest.

Strengthen coordination with local authorities by clarifying whether state and local law enforcement agencies and elected official were notified or consulted before ICE operations began and outlining protocols to ensure public safety and address community concerns.

The lawmakers also emphasized that enforcing federal immigration law does not diminish the government's responsibility to protect public safety, uphold due process, and ensure accountability for the actions of federal officers.

The Members of Congress and Senators requested a written response from ICE and DHS no later than October 30, 2026.

The letter was signed by: Congressman Jim Costa (CA-21), Senators Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Representatives Zoe Lofgren (CA-18), Josh Harder (CA-09), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Adam Gray (CA-13), Lou Correa (CA-46), Gil Cisneros (CA-31), Robert Garcia (CA-42), Nanette Barragán (CA-44), and Norma Torres (CA-35).

The full text of the letter can be found HERE.

title: Rep. Crane and Secretary Turner Tour Arizona Homebuilders, Work to Expand Housing Options
text:
Yesterday, Rep. Eli Crane (R-AZ) joined Secretary Scott Turner of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to discuss expanding access to affordable housing across Arizona. Throughout the day, they toured two home manufacturers, Cavco Industries and Champion Homes, to strengthen public-private partnerships and identify ways to lower costs for homebuyers.

Factory-built homes are constructed inside a controlled facility before being transported to their final site. This method allows producers to purchase materials in bulk, standardize their processes, and limit weather delays. As a result, projects are often completed faster and for less than traditional on-site construction. Since taking office, Secretary Turner has worked to make homeownership a reality for more Americans. Collaborating with industry is central to that mission and helps bring more of these homes to market.

In the morning, Rep. Crane and Secretary Turner started at Cavco’s manufacturing plant in Phoenix. The company, founded in the Valley in 1965, has grown into one of the nation’s leading off-site builders. Its catalog includes manufactured and modular homes, as well as park model RVs. Today, Cavco employs hundreds of Arizonans and strives to keep quality housing within reach of working families. During the visit, Cavco’s team guided the group across the production floor and through one of the company’s homes.

Along the way, Rep. Crane and Secretary Turner discussed the importance of modernizing outdated codes and rolling back burdensome regulations that inflate construction costs. They also touched on the Trump administration’s efforts to overhaul the federal approach to homelessness. HUD is now shifting away from Housing First policies to prioritize treatment, recovery, and self-sufficiency. Rep. Crane commended Secretary Turner’s leadership in driving this reform.

Later that afternoon, Rep. Crane and Secretary Turner visited Champion Homes’ plant within Arizona’s Second Congressional District. Headquartered in Michigan, Champion operates 46 production facilities across North America. Over the summer, the company broadened its reach in Arizona by acquiring Homes Direct, one of the largest independent manufactured and modular home dealers in the western U.S.

On site, Champion’s team walked the group along the assembly line before talking through shared priorities. Rep. Crane stressed that reducing red tape is essential to lowering prices and keeping homeownership attainable for local buyers. He praised Champion for producing quality homes and supporting jobs across the region.

“I’m grateful to Secretary Turner for visiting our state and for his tireless commitment to helping more families become homeowners across the country. As HUD Secretary, he has disrupted business as usual and advanced policies that put hardworking citizens first. Engagements like these demonstrate what government and the private sector can accomplish together, and we’re thankful to Cavco Industries and Champion Homes for opening their doors and partnering with us on solutions. I look forward to building on this progress as we fight to cut costs and expand housing options for Arizonans,” said Rep. Crane.

title: Crow Introduces Bipartisan Legislation to Block Purchase of Russian Oil
text:
AURORA — Congressman Jason Crow (D-CO), a former paratrooper and Army Ranger who serves on the House Armed Services Committee and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, introduced bipartisan legislation to uphold longstanding sanctions that block the purchase of Russian diesel in the United States.

President Trump recently lifted sanctions on the delivery of Russian diesel, offering Vladimir Putin a financial lifeline as Russia continues to wage an unprovoked and illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. Crow’s Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act would block the Trump Administration’s deal with Vladimir Putin and force Trump Administration officials to crack down on our adversary Russia. It prevents the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russian energy; nullifies general licenses recently issued by the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and prohibits the Office from granting future licenses; and mandates that the Trump Administration impose sanctions on Russian energy.

Joining Congressman Crow on this bill are Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee Gregory Meeks (D-NY) and 17 bipartisan Members of Congress.

“The President’s failed trade policies and reckless war with Iran have raised prices. As his popularity plummets at home, he’s shamefully abandoning our allies and once again cozying up to dictators. We need to stand with the people of Ukraine as Russia continues its war of aggression, not fund Putin’s war machine that is killing civilians,” said Congressman Crow.

Congressman Crow has been a strong supporter of the Ukrainian people. Upon news of the Starshield disruption, he immediately pressed the Trump Administration for answers on who authorized the changes and what its impacts were and subsequently demanded SpaceX explain its own role in the disruption. He recently introduced a bill to protect Ukrainian nationals already in the U.S. against the threat of deportation by extending their Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

When Putin’s invasion began, Crow immediately called for the U.S. to send military and humanitarian support to Ukraine, for international sanctions against Russia, and for a stronger NATO alliance to meet these new security threats. Weeks later, as Ukrainians fled their homes, Congressman Crow and other members advocated for an expedited immigration status for Ukrainians fleeing to the U.S. Crow has visited Ukraine several times since Russia’s invasion.

The Congressman has been one of the earliest and strongest supporters of military, development, and humanitarian assistance for Ukraine. He voted for, and strongly advocated for, every supplemental package provided to Ukraine.

Full text of the bill is available here.
